{"type": "TEXT_FILE", "path": ".github/workflows/release.yml", "bytes": 13515, "sha256": "0815fd68e4bf61fac5479c237724db073df26f62d998a10ae1c7c8590ce9ad33", "mtime_utc": "2026-05-15T20:00:40.463273+00:00", "encoding": "utf-8", "lang": "yaml", "generated": false, "secret_hits": []}

   1: name: release
   2: 
   3: # Reproducible-build + signed-attestation pipeline for tagged releases.
   4: # Goals:
   5: #   1. Anyone can rebuild from source and get the same binary.
   6: #   2. Each release artifact carries a Sigstore attestation in the
   7: #      public Rekor transparency log so consumers can verify
   8: #      "this artifact was built from this commit by GitHub Actions
   9: #      on this date" without trusting a single private signing key.
  10: #   3. SHA-256 manifest published alongside the artifacts so a
  11: #      stripped-down verify path (curl + sha256sum) works for
  12: #      users who can't or won't install sigstore.
  13: #
  14: # Sovereignty note: Sigstore's Fulcio + Rekor are operated by the
  15: # Linux Foundation OpenSSF and ARE corporate-substrate dependencies.
  16: # The trust model is "transparent append-only log," not "trust the
  17: # operator," so a compromised Fulcio can't quietly forge a sig
  18: # without the forgery showing up in Rekor (which we and our users
  19: # audit). Once the project incorporates as a non-profit foundation
  20: # and stands up its own HSM-backed multi-maintainer threshold key
  21: # (see NOTICE), this workflow will switch to the in-house signing
  22: # pipeline. Until then Sigstore is the pragmatic baseline.
  23: 
  24: on:
  25:   push:
  26:     tags:
  27:       - "v*"
  28:   workflow_dispatch:
  29: 
  30: permissions:
  31:   contents: write    # create release + upload assets
  32:   id-token: write    # OIDC token for Sigstore keyless signing
  33:   attestations: write
  34: 
  35: jobs:
  36:   build:
  37:     name: build reproducible artifacts
  38:     runs-on: ubuntu-latest
  39:     outputs:
  40:       version: ${{ steps.meta.outputs.version }}
  41:       source_date_epoch: ${{ steps.meta.outputs.source_date_epoch }}
  42: 
  43:     steps:
  44:       - uses: actions/checkout@v4
  45:         with:
  46:           # Full history so SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH = commit date is
  47:           # deterministic across re-runs.
  48:           fetch-depth: 0
  49: 
  50:       - name: setup Python
  51:         uses: actions/setup-python@v5
  52:         with:
  53:           python-version: "3.12"
  54: 
  55:       - name: read version + source-date-epoch
  56:         id: meta
  57:         # Use the tag's commit timestamp as SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH so
  58:         # rebuild-from-source by anyone on any machine produces
  59:         # byte-identical sdist + wheel. The Python build backend
  60:         # (setuptools) honors SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH when zipping.
  61:         run: |
  62:           version="${GITHUB_REF#refs/tags/v}"
  63:           if [ "$version" = "$GITHUB_REF" ]; then
  64:             version=$(grep -E '^version' pyproject.toml | head -1 | sed -E 's/.*"([^"]+)".*/\1/')
  65:           fi
  66:           source_date_epoch=$(git log -1 --format=%ct)
  67:           echo "version=$version" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
  68:           echo "source_date_epoch=$source_date_epoch" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
  69:           echo "Building One Link $version (SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH=$source_date_epoch)"
  70: 
  71:       - name: install build tooling
  72:         run: |
  73:           python -m pip install --upgrade pip
  74:           pip install build
  75: 
  76:       - name: build sdist + wheel reproducibly
  77:         env:
  78:           SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH: ${{ steps.meta.outputs.source_date_epoch }}
  79:           PYTHONHASHSEED: 0
  80:         run: |
  81:           # Clean any prior artifacts that would taint the hash
  82:           rm -rf dist/ build/ *.egg-info
  83:           python -m build --sdist --wheel --outdir dist/
  84: 
  85:       - name: compute SHA-256 manifest
  86:         run: |
  87:           cd dist
  88:           # Generate a deterministic manifest of (hash, filename)
  89:           # pairs sorted by filename so two builds produce
  90:           # byte-identical SHA256SUMS files.
  91:           sha256sum * | sort -k 2 > SHA256SUMS
  92:           cat SHA256SUMS
  93: 
  94:       - name: upload build artifacts
  95:         uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
  96:         with:
  97:           name: dist
  98:           path: |
  99:             dist/*.whl
 100:             dist/*.tar.gz
 101:             dist/SHA256SUMS
 102:

 104:   # AEAD, WAL, QUIC, coherence-field). abi3 means one wheel per OS
 105:   # covers Python 3.11+, so this is a 3-job matrix rather than 9.

 108:     needs: build

 110:       fail-fast: false

 149:         with:
 150:           name: ${{ matrix.artifact }}

 154:   # from the website. PyInstaller bundles Python + all deps + the

 157:   binaries:

   1: # File engine v2 — reproducible signed release build.
   2: #
   3: # Per FILE_ENGINE_V2_PLAN.md Phase C item #12:
   4: #
   5: #     "Reproducible builds + multi-party signing: Sigstore-style
   6: #     transparency log; multi-signer release."
   7: #
   8: # This workflow runs on every annotated tag matching `v*`. It:
   9: #
  10: # 1. Builds the native workspace + Python wheel deterministically (pinned
  11: #    toolchain version, locked cargo registry, `SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH` from
  12: #    the tag commit, `-C codegen-units=1` etc).
  13: # 2. Records a BLAKE3 hash of every artifact.
  14: # 3. Signs each artifact with Sigstore (cosign keyless via OIDC) and
  15: #    uploads the bundle to the public transparency log.
  16: # 4. Optionally requires a second signature from a designated co-signer
  17: #    (configured at the org level as a repository secret).
  18: #
  19: # Acceptance gate is structural: a second run on a fresh worker MUST
  20: # produce byte-identical artifacts. The hash-of-hashes is checked in to
  21: # the release notes so external verifiers can confirm without running CI.
  22: 
  23: name: reproducible release
  24: 
  25: on:
  26:   push:
  27:     tags: ["v*"]

  95:                   out[p.name] = blake3.blake3(p.read_bytes()).hexdigest()

 154:           import pathlib, blake3, sys
 155:           def hash_dir(d):
 156:               return {p.name: blake3.blake3(p.read_bytes()).hexdigest()
 157:                       for p in sorted(pathlib.Path(d).rglob("*"))
 158:                       if p.is_file() and p.suffix == ".whl"}
 159:           a = hash_dir("dist1")
 160:           b = hash_dir("dist2")
 161:           if a != b:
 162:               print("REPRODUCIBILITY FAILURE: byte-divergent rebuild")
 163:               print(f"  build 1: {a}")
 164:               print(f"  build 2: {b}")
 165:               sys.exit(1)
 166:           print("Reproducible build verified — byte-identical wheels.")

   1: # Benchmark baselines
   2: 
   3: This directory holds the per-benchmark baselines that the file-engine v2
   4: benchmark gate (`.github/workflows/native_bench_gate.yml` +
   5: `scripts/bench_gate.py`) checks every PR against. A PR fails the gate if
   6: any tracked metric regresses by more than 5% vs. the baseline.
   7: 
   8: ## How baselines are produced
   9: 
  10: After Phase A1 Step Zero lands and the first reference CI run completes:
  11: 
  12: 1. CI runs `python -m one_link.perf_lab_native --json --no-legacy --size-mib 64`
  13: 2. The `bench_gate.py --baseline` argument points here. With no file present,
  14:    the gate exits NEUTRAL and prints the fresh JSON.
  15: 3. The maintainer reviews the fresh JSON, commits it to
  16:    `native_chunk.json` (this directory) as the initial baseline.
  17: 4. From the next PR onward, the gate enforces no >5% regression.
  18: 
  19: ## Updating a baseline
  20: 
  21: Baselines are *only* updated by a maintainer in the same PR that intentionally
  22: changes the kernel (e.g., switching from FastCDC v2020 to a future kernel).
  23: The commit message must include:
  24: 
  25: - The reason for the regression / change.
  26: - The ADR amendment that covers it.
  27: - The expected throughput delta and rationale.
  28: 
  29: The gate has no auto-update path on purpose.
  30: 
  31: ## Hardware drift
  32: 
  33: Baselines are tied to the GitHub-hosted runner class (Ubuntu latest, x86-64).
  34: If the runner class changes substantially (e.g., GitHub upgrades default
  35: runner CPUs), the baselines will need to be re-pinned. This is a manual
  36: maintenance step.
  37: 
  38: ## Files
  39: 
  40: - `native_chunk.json` — pinned native CDC + BLAKE3 + derivation throughputs
  41:   (created on first reference run).

   1: # One Link CHANGELOG
   2: 
   3: Per-release notes for One Link. Each entry summarises the ADRs landed
   4: in that release; full architectural rationale lives in
   5: [`docs/decisions/`](docs/decisions/).
   6: 
   7: The version scheme is semver-aligned but pre-1.0: 0.x.y means alpha,
   8: breaking wire changes allowed between minor versions. Wire-format
   9: compatibility with prior peers is preserved via capability negotiation
  10: where practical (`NATIVE_TRANSFER_V1`, `DOUBLE_RATCHET_V1`).
  11: 
  12: ---
  13: 
  14: ## [0.21.0-alpha] — 2026-05-11 — File engine v2
  15: 
  16: **Headline**: complete implementation of [`FILE_ENGINE_V2_PLAN.md`](docs/FILE_ENGINE_V2_PLAN.md)
  17: Phase A1 + A2 + B + C + D + Coherence ↔ Rust codegen scaffold.
  18: 16 Rust crates in `native/`; production-ready native chunk-store
  19: transport pipeline with full daemon cutover.
  20: 
  21: ### Phase A1: chunk store foundation (ADRs 0001–0008)
  22: 
  23: - `ol_chunk` — content-addressed FastCDC v2020 (8/64/256 KiB) + BLAKE3
  24:   chunk addressing + chunk envelope.
  25: - `ol_chunk_store` — LSM-indexed content-addressed chunk log + bloom-
  26:   filter front + WAL-coupled durability.
  27: - `ol_aead` — per-chunk multi-frame AEAD (AES-256-GCM / ChaCha20-
  28:   Poly1305) backed by `ring` (BoringSSL-derived assembly).
  29: - `ol_wal` — crash-only write-ahead log with CRC32-Castagnoli per-
  30:   record + tail-truncation recovery.
  31: - `one_link_native` — pyo3 binding crate exposing every native crate
  32:   as `one_link_native.<submodule>` (abi3-py311+).
  33: 
  34: ### Phase A2: transport (ADR-0009, ADR-0010)
  35: 
  36: - `ol_quic` — QUIC transport via `quinn` 0.11. Self-signed identity-
  37:   bound TLS via `rustls` + `aws-lc-rs`. Multi-stream, multi-path, 0-
  38:   RTT, connection migration. Replaces WebRTC/DTLS-SRTP for daemon↔
  39:   daemon; WebRTC retained for browser-as-peer.
  40: 
  41: ### Phase B: genius layer (ADRs 0011–0016)
  42: 
  43: - `ol_bloom` — Bloom-filter transfer init. Receiver sends Bloom of
  44:   chunk hashes; sender XORs against manifest; ships only the true delta.
  45: - `ol_fountain` — RaptorQ fountain codes (RFC 6330).
  46: - `ol_fec` — Reed-Solomon FEC over GF(2^8) with SSSE3 PSHUFB SIMD.
  47: - `ol_erasure` — Erasure-coded durability with stripe descriptor
  48:   metadata.
  49: 
  50: ### Phase C: multi-axis baseline (ADRs 0017–0027)
  51: 
  52: - **ADR-0017** PQ-hybrid KEM (ML-KEM-768 + X25519 via BLAKE3 X-Wing
  53:   combiner). `ol_pqkem` crate.
  54: - **ADR-0019** Multi-armed bandit auto-tuning (Beta-Bernoulli Thompson
  55:   sampling). `ol_bandit` crate.
  56: - **ADR-0020** Per-chunk forward-secret ratchet (BLAKE3 keyed-hash
  57:   chain). `ol_ratchet` crate.
  58: - **ADR-0021** Capability layer — macaroon-style HMAC-chained caveats
  59:   over BLAKE3. `ol_capability` crate. **1M-iter attenuation soundness
  60:   gate** (`child.accepts(ctx) ⇒ parent.accepts(ctx)`) passes in
  61:   5.94 s with 0 violations.
  62: - **ADR-0022** CRDT shared folders — vector clock + OR-set + LWW
  63:   register composition. `ol_crdt` crate. **1M-iter lattice-laws gate**
  64:   (commutativity + associativity + idempotency) passes in 7.46 s.
  65: - **ADR-0023** Hardware-bound keys, TOFU-degrading. `ol_hwkey` crate.
  66: - **ADR-0024** Phase C-3 wiring status — shadow / dual-issue posture
  67:   for the 5 daemon migration primitives.
  68: - **ADR-0025** Chunk-store transport pipeline — composed
  69:   `NativeTransferSession` (KEM + ratchet + CDC + AEAD + ChunkStore).
  70:   Bench: native is **1.14–1.44× faster than legacy** at every size
  71:   16 KiB → 64 MiB after the BoringSSL fast-path default.
  72: - **ADR-0026** `NATIVE_TRANSFER_V1` capability + `FILE_NATIVE_CHUNK`
  73:   wire format. Capability-gated; default-on for capable peers
  74:   (rollback via `ONE_LINK_NATIVE_TRANSFER=0`).
  75: - **ADR-0027** Shadow → authoritative cutovers: bandit drives route
  76:   picks in `AdaptiveTransferBrain.decide()`; folder mirror active
  77:   cross-check + divergence counter; macaroon advertised on
  78:   `CAPABILITY_GRANT` wire as `macaroon_b64`.
  79: 
  80: ### Phase D: visionary layer (ADRs 0028, 0033)
  81: 
  82: - **ADR-0028 #1** Tau-field routing — `ol_routing` crate. τ_c-
  83:   weighted Dijkstra + hysteresis-gated next-hop swap. Harvest from
  84:   `OneField/onefield/mesh/routing.cl`. **Acceptance gate**: 100%
  85:   chunk-loss reduction on fragile-graph benchmark (plan: ≥20%).
  86: - **#2** Byzantine-tolerant tau — `ol_routing::byzantine` module.
  87:   BFT thresholds (`floor((N-1)/3)`) + random-geometric graph density
  88:   + `tau_claim_corroborated` (catches malicious peers reporting fake
  89:   high τ_c).
  90: - **#3** Active inference prefetch — `ol_prefetch` crate. Time-
  91:   weighted co-occurrence predictor over (peer, file_id) access
  92:   traces. **Acceptance gate**: cold-start convergence ≤50 iters;
  93:   cohort prior transfer converges in 1 iter.
  94: - **#4** Persistent homology durability — `ol_homology` crate. H0
  95:   components + bridge detection via DFS; composite `fragility_score`
  96:   for replication priority. **Acceptance gate**: partition flag in 1
  97:   round, 0% FP on 100 random 4-regular graphs (plan: ≤5% FP).
  98: - **#5** Grammar compression — `ol_grammar` crate. Re-Pair on byte
  99:   streams.
 100: - **#6** Plausibly deniable storage — `ol_duress` crate. `DuressGate`
 101:   with constant-time real-vs-decoy decision + covert ratchet-header
 102:   signal. **CT timing gate**: 1.014× wall-clock variance (plan:
 103:   <1.20×). The validation pass caught + fixed a real side-channel
 104:   (1.448× → 1.014×).
 105: - **#7** Formal verification — TLA+ specification at
 106:   `docs/formal/Capability.tla` modelling the capability grant + revoke
 107:   + attenuation state machine. Verified safety invariants:
 108:   `NoKeyReuse`, `NoDoubleGrant`, `NoReplay`, `ClockMonotonic`.
 109: - **Coherence ↔ Rust codegen scaffold** — `ol_codegen` crate. Minimal
 110:   CL `struct` grammar parser + Rust struct + canonical-LE encoder
 111:   emitter. **Byte-equivalence CI gate**: 1M random struct shapes
 112:   round-trip in 1.79 s.

   1: # Contributing to One Link
   2: 
   3: Thanks for considering a contribution. This document is short and
   4: covers the things that matter most.
   5: 
   6: ## Before you start
   7: 
   8: - **Read [`NOTICE`](NOTICE)** - the project's "for the people"
   9:   charter and the reasoning behind the AGPLv3 license. By
  10:   contributing, you agree your contribution will be licensed
  11:   under AGPLv3.
  12: - **Read [`docs/SECURITY.md`](docs/SECURITY.md)** - the threat
  13:   model. Anything you ship has to live up to it.
  14: - **Read [`docs/PRINCIPLES.md`](docs/PRINCIPLES.md)** - the
  15:   Reach / Hide / Async / Depth / Defang ship-gate.
  16: 
  17: ## How we review changes
  18: 
  19: Every change passes these gates:
  20: 
  21: 1. **Tests stay green.** `python -m pytest -q` must pass on a
  22:    fresh checkout before review. CI runs the same gate.
  23: 2. **No new dependencies without justification.** Each new
  24:    dependency is supply-chain risk. The bar is "no other path
  25:    exists" or "this is a vetted, audited library with no
  26:    telemetry."
  27: 3. **No telemetry, no analytics, no phone-home of any kind.**
  28:    This is non-negotiable. If your change adds an outbound HTTP
  29:    request to an origin the user did not configure, it gets
  30:    reverted at review.
  31: 4. **Threat-model alignment.** If the change introduces a new
  32:    surface (a new wire kind, a new endpoint, a new file format),
  33:    the PR description must say which threat tiers (T1-T9) the
  34:    surface affects and how it's defended.
  35: 5. **Reproducible.** Build outputs must be deterministic. If
  36:    your change introduces non-determinism (timestamp embedding,
  37:    random padding without a seed, etc.), fix it before merge.
  38: 
  39: ## Security-sensitive changes
  40: 
  41: Anything touching:
  42: 
  43: - `src/one_link/channel.py`
  44: - `src/one_link/double_ratchet.py`
  45: - `src/one_link/groups_crypto.py`
  46: - `src/one_link/identity.py`
  47: - `src/one_link/lockbox.py`
  48: - `src/one_link/pairing.py`
  49: - `src/one_link/rendezvous_proto.py` / `rendezvous_server.py`
  50: 
  51: …is under stricter review. Expect a longer review window and
  52: likely a request for an external cryptographic review before
  53: merge if the change touches a primitive.
  54: 
  55: If you're not sure whether your change qualifies, err on the side
  56: of asking in the PR description.
  57: 
  58: ## Reporting vulnerabilities
  59: 
  60: **Do not file public PRs / issues for security bugs.** See
  61: [`SECURITY.md`](SECURITY.md) for the responsible-disclosure
  62: process.
  63: 
  64: ## Style
  65: 
  66: - Python: PEP 8 with descriptive docstrings on public functions.
  67:   Existing code is the reference.
  68: - JavaScript: same. ES2017+, no transpiler.
  69: - Comments document the **why**, not the **what**. Code reviewers
  70:   read both; future maintainers read the comments.
  71: 
  72: ## License
  73: 
  74: By submitting a contribution, you certify that you have the right
  75: to license your work under AGPL-3.0-or-later, and you agree your
  76: contribution will be released under that license. (This is the
  77: "DCO-style" agreement; we don't require a CLA.)
  78: 
  79: ## Maintainer
  80: 
  81: Until the project incorporates as a non-profit foundation,
  82: contributions go to:
  83: 
  84: - Maintainer: One Link contributors <weareone@oneunity.earth>
  85: - Code: https://github.com/coherence-energy-labs/one-link

<<<CONTENT_BEGIN>>>
   1: # One Link rendezvous — operator quickstart
   2: 
   3: A small server. Doesn't see your messages. Lets paired devices find
   4: each other across the internet.
   5: 
   6: ## 30-second deploy
   7: 
   8: ```bash
   9: cd deploy/rendezvous
  10: docker compose up -d
  11: curl -sS http://localhost:7118/health
  12: # {"ok": true, ...}
  13: ```
  14: 
  15: That gives you a rendezvous on port 7118 of your box. To make it
  16: reachable from the public internet, see the **TLS** section below or
  17: the full [`docs/RENDEZVOUS_DEPLOY.md`](../../docs/RENDEZVOUS_DEPLOY.md).
  18: 
  19: ## Files
  20: 
  21: - `Dockerfile` — two-stage build, minimal runtime, non-root user.
  22: - `entrypoint.sh` — env → flags shim.
  23: - `docker-compose.yml` — production-shape compose with hardening.
  24: - `nginx.conf.example` — drop-in TLS termination via Let's Encrypt.
  25: 
  26: ## Telling your One Link clients to use it
  27: 
  28: In the One Link app: **Settings → Connect across networks** → paste
  29: the URL (with `https://` prefix once TLS is set up). The status dot
  30: turns green and shows the public IP your clients announce to each
  31: other.
  32: 
  33: You can run multiple rendezvous instances and your clients will
  34: register with all of them in parallel for redundancy.
  35: 
  36: ## TLS
  37: 
  38: Always front this with HTTPS. The rendezvous protocol is signed
  39: end-to-end so a compromised TLS hop can't read or forge content, but
  40: TLS prevents passive observers from seeing which pubkeys look up
  41: which.
  42: 
  43: Easiest path:
  44: 
  45: ```bash
  46: sudo cp nginx.conf.example /etc/nginx/sites-available/one-link-rendezvous.conf
  47: # edit server_name to your domain
  48: sudo ln -s ../sites-available/one-link-rendezvous.conf /etc/nginx/sites-enabled/
  49: sudo certbot --nginx -d rendezvous.your-domain.example
  50: sudo systemctl reload nginx
  51: ```
  52: 
  53: Cloudflare alternative: point an A record at your VPS, enable orange-
  54: cloud (proxy on), set SSL/TLS mode to **Full (strict)**.
  55: 
  56: ## Monitoring
  57: 
  58: ```bash
  59: curl -sS http://localhost:7118/metrics
  60: ```
  61: 
  62: Returns plain JSON keys — easy to relabel into Prometheus.
  63: 
  64: ## Resource shape
  65: 
  66: - ~1 KB process memory per active registration.
  67: - Default cap: 200,000 registrations (~200 MB peak).
  68: - CPU: idle. Bandwidth: tens of KB/s.
  69: - A $5/month VPS is overkill for any reasonable user base.
  70: 
  71: ## Reading the logs
  72: 
  73: The default INFO log line shows registers / lookups / rate-limit hits.
  74: At DEBUG you also see eviction counts and per-request signature
  75: verifies. Set `ONE_LINK_RDZ_LOG_LEVEL=DEBUG` in the compose file to
  76: turn those on.
  77: 
  78: ## Restart-safe
  79: 
  80: The rendezvous holds presence in memory only. A restart loses all
  81: current registrations — devices re-register within minutes (every
  82: TTL/2, default 150 s). No persistent data lives in this container,
  83: so the `read_only: true` filesystem in compose is correct.
  84: 
  85: ## Federation
  86: 
  87: There's no protocol-level state sync between rendezvous instances.
  88: Federation is a client-side concept: clients register with multiple
  89: rendezvous in parallel and lookups race them. Run yours, and tell
  90: your friends to add it alongside whatever they're already using.
  91: 
  92: ## Compliance / metadata
  93: 
  94: This rendezvous sees only signed presence beacons:
  95: `(pubkey, source_IP, advertised_endpoints)`. No payloads, no group
  96: membership, no messages. If you operate one publicly, your privacy
  97: posture should reflect that you're holding **online-status metadata
  98: of pubkey-keyed devices** — not contents.
<<<CONTENT_END>>>

   1: # Architecture — v0.15.0 → v1.0.0 implementation specification
   2: 
   3: Status: living document. Implementation-grade depth for the PWA
   4: pivot. Every ship between v0.15.0 and v1.0.0 has a frontier, a
   5: primitive, a wire-format addition, a state migration, a test
   6: contract, and a defang cross-reference.
   7: 
   8: Companion docs:
   9: - [`PRINCIPLES.md`](./PRINCIPLES.md) — the four-principle gate.
  10: - [`SOVEREIGNTY.md`](./SOVEREIGNTY.md) — corporate-substrate defangs.
  11: - [`ROADMAP.md`](./ROADMAP.md) — ship ordering.
  12: - [`PHONE_TIER.md`](./PHONE_TIER.md) — phone surface specification.
  13: 
  14: Last updated: 2026-05-08.
  15: 
  16: ---
  17: 
  18: ## North-star architecture
  19: 
  20: By v1.0.0, One Link runs as a **pure-browser P2P chat + file sync
  21: PWA** on any modern phone or desktop browser, with the existing
  22: Python daemon as an optional same-protocol peer. Both speak the
  23: same wire format; neither knows or cares which side is "native."
  24: 
  25: The architecture has eight layers. Each layer has its own ship in
  26: the v0.15.0+ sequence. Each layer specifies the corporate-floor
  27: defang it ships. Each layer reuses Coherence Language stdlib
  28: primitives where they exist, with explicit cross-references.
  29: 
  30: ```
  31: ┌─ User-visible UX ──────────────────────────────────┐
  32: │  Tier-selector, pair-flow, settings, conversation │
  33: ├─ Intelligence ─────────────────────────────────────┤
  34: │  WebGPU LLM, federated learning, predictive cache  │
  35: ├─ Sync ─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  36: │  CRDT (Yjs/Automerge), HLC, lazy sync, Web Push    │
  37: ├─ Cryptography ─────────────────────────────────────┤
  38: │  Double Ratchet, MLS, sealed sender, cover traffic │
  39: │  Post-quantum hybrid (ML-KEM + X25519)              │
  40: ├─ Identity ─────────────────────────────────────────┤
  41: │  Threshold-of-N, Passkey opt-in, attestation,      │
  42: │  verifiable revocation log, plausibly deniable     │
  43: ├─ Storage ──────────────────────────────────────────┤
  44: │  OPFS for blobs, IDB for indexed records, AES-GCM  │
  45: │  at rest, multi-source entropy                     │
  46: ├─ Transport ────────────────────────────────────────┤
  47: │  WebRTC DataChannel + WebTransport, BLE proximity, │
  48: │  ultrasonic, mDNS-equiv, adaptive bandit, mix-net  │
  49: ├─ Bootstrap ────────────────────────────────────────┤
  50: │  PWA shell, Service Worker, signed updates,        │
  51: │  IPFS / .onion / signed-archive distribution       │
  52: └────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  53: ```
  54: 
  55: ---
  56: 
  57: ## Cross-cutting: Coherence stdlib reuse
  58: 
  59: The Coherence Language stdlib at
  60: `coherence_lang/coherence_lang/bootstrap/stdlib/std/` already
  61: contains production implementations of several primitives we need.
  62: Where reuse is possible, the v0.15.0+ ships **port** rather than
  63: **reinvent**.
  64: 
  65: | Primitive | Coherence module | Reuse mode | One Link target |
  66: |---|---|---|---|
  67: | HKDF | `std/crypto/kdf.cl` | Direct port (call Web Crypto under the hood) | All key derivation; ratchets; entropy mixing |
  68: | Argon2id | `std/crypto/kdf.cl` | Direct port | At-rest passphrase derivation (OPFS encryption key) |
  69: | AES-GCM (with GHASH) | `std/crypto/symmetric.cl` | Reference impl; production uses Web Crypto AES-GCM | At-rest OPFS / IDB; Double Ratchet symmetric phase |
  70: | ChaCha20-Poly1305 | `std/crypto/symmetric.cl` (RFC 8439) | Direct port for browsers without AES-GCM hardware acceleration; otherwise prefer AES-GCM | Transport layer; mix-net hop encryption |
  71: | Hybrid Logical Clock | `std/crdt/causality.cl::HybridLogicalClock` | Direct port | Message ordering across devices, conflict-free without OS clock trust |
  72: | Vector clock / DotContext | `std/crdt/vector_clock.cl` | Direct port | Multi-device causal ordering |
  73: | Interval Tree Clock | `std/crdt/vector_clock.cl::IntervalTreeClock` | Direct port | Threshold-of-N device membership churn |
  74: | Causal delivery / graph | `std/crdt/causality.cl` | Direct port | Message sequencing in groups |
  75: | Merge strategies (LWW, FWW, etc.) | `std/crdt/merge.cl` | Direct port (compose with Yjs) | Conflict resolution policy framework |
  76: | GCounter / PNCounter | `std/crdt/counters/` | Direct port | Read counters, message counters |
  77: | ORSet / AWSet | `std/crdt/sets/` | Direct port | Group membership presence |
  78: | LWWMap / MVMap | `std/crdt/maps/` | Direct port | Settings sync, profile fields |
  79: | RGA / YATA / Logoot | `std/crdt/sequences/` | Direct port (alt to Yjs sequences) | Long-form message ordering, edit-friendly |
  80: | Post-quantum (ML-KEM + X25519) | `std/crypto/quantum_safe.cl` | Direct port if implementations are mature; else use `@noble/post-quantum` | Hybrid key agreement |
  81: | Signature schemes (Ed25519, ECDSA) | `std/crypto/asymmetric.cl` | Direct port (Web Crypto wrapper) | Sealed sender, revocation log signatures |
  82: | Identity provenance | `std/identity/provenance.cl` | Pattern reuse | Device attestation chain |
  83: | Anti-deception / spoofing | `std/identity/anti_deception.cl` | Pattern reuse | Risk model for pair-flow simplification |
  84: | Session types (binary) | `std/session/binary/channel.cl` | Pattern reuse | Wire-format protocol design |
  85: | Multiparty session types | `std/session/multiparty/` | Pattern reuse | MLS group ratchet protocol structure |
  86: 
  87: This table is the canonical reuse manifest. When a v0.15.0+ ship
  88: implements one of these primitives, the spec MUST cite the
  89: Coherence module it ports from + document any deviations.
  90: 
  91: ---
  92: 
  93: ## v0.15.0 — PWA shell + Web Crypto identity foundation
  94: 
  95: **Frontier:** PWA install criteria fully met on iOS Safari + Android
  96: Chrome; Web Crypto identity keypair generation reproducibly executes
  97: in <50ms p95 on a 5-year-old phone.
  98: 
  99: **Primitives:**
 100: - `manifest.json` with PNG icons (192×192, 512×512, maskable variants)
 101: - Service Worker registered (already shipped v0.14.0; refresh)
 102: - Ed25519 keypair generation via `subtle.crypto.generateKey({name: "Ed25519"})`
 103: - Hybrid keypair: also generate X25519 for ECDH
 104: - Future-proofing: ML-KEM-768 keypair (via `@noble/post-quantum`) generated
 105:   alongside, used in hybrid mode from v0.21.0+
 106: 
 107: **Wire-format additions:** none yet (this ship is local).
 108: 
 109: **State migration:** new IDB store `identity.v1` with fields:
 110: `{fingerprint, ed25519_pub, ed25519_priv_wrapped, x25519_pub,
 111: x25519_priv_wrapped, mlkem_pub, mlkem_priv_wrapped, created_ms,
 112: attestation}`. Wrapping uses AES-GCM with a key derived from a
 113: passphrase (Argon2id from `std/crypto/kdf.cl`). On first launch
 114: the user sets the passphrase; subsequent unlocks use it.
 115: 
 116: **Test contract:** `tests/test_pwa_shell_v0150.py`
 117: - manifest.json validates against W3C PWA criteria
 118: - Service Worker registration succeeds on a TestServer
 119: - Ed25519 + X25519 + ML-KEM keypair generation completes
 120: - Identity reproducibly persists/loads across SW restart
 121: 
 122: **Defang shipped:** signed-update verification in SW (defangs CDN
 123: compromise). See `SOVEREIGNTY.md` § "TLS / Certificate Authorities."
 124: 
 125: **Stdlib reuse:** `std/crypto/kdf.cl::Argon2id` (port to JS for the
 126: passphrase-to-wrap-key derivation).
 127: 
 128: **Ship-gate:**
 129: - Reach: anyone with a phone + a URL can install One Link to home
 130:   screen without a desktop.
 131: - Hide: no new jargon; install prompt copy is "Install One Link?".
 132: - Async: identity is local-first; Service Worker survives tab close.
 133: - Depth: <50ms keypair generation as a measured SLA; signed-update
 134:   refusal-on-mismatch as a regression-tested invariant.
 135: - Defang: signed updates pinned in source.
 136: 
 137: ---
 138: 
 139: ## v0.16.0 — OPFS storage layer + at-rest encryption
 140: 
 141: **Frontier:** every byte One Link writes to disk in the browser is
 142: AES-GCM encrypted with a per-device key never visible to the OS or
 143: to JS unless the user has unlocked the app in this session.
 144: 
 145: **Primitives:**
 146: - OPFS API (`navigator.storage.getDirectory()`) for blobs, chunks,
 147:   attachments, anything > 64KB
 148: - IDB for indexed records (messages, peers, settings) — also encrypted
 149: - AES-GCM 256-bit at rest, key derived from the v0.15.0 passphrase
 150:   via Argon2id
 151: - Plausibly deniable storage: outer file/blob carries no header that
 152:   identifies it as One Link data; bytes look random
 153: 
 154: **Wire-format additions:** none.
 155: 
 156: **State migration:** schema v16 (or whatever the next sequential
 157: version is). New OPFS layout:
 158: ```
 159: /blobs/<hash-prefix>/<full-hash>          encrypted chunk content
 160: /messages.idb                              encrypted message index
 161: /peers.idb                                 encrypted peer record
 162: /groups.idb                                encrypted group state
 163: /_meta/version                             unencrypted version pin
 164: ```
 165: The `_meta/version` is the only unencrypted file; everything else
 166: is opaque to a forensic exfiltrator without the unlocked session.
 167: 
 168: **Test contract:** `tests/test_opfs_storage_v0160.py`
 169: - Round-trip a 10MB blob through OPFS encrypted; decrypt; byte-equal
 170: - IDB-stored message round-trip with AES-GCM
 171: - Wrong passphrase → decryption fails; storage looks like noise
 172: - Outer file headers do not identify content type (plausibly deniable)
 173: 
 174: **Defang shipped:** OPFS-stored identity, never OS keychain (defangs
 175: iCloud / Google Password Manager). See `SOVEREIGNTY.md` § "OS keychain."
 176: Plus: multi-source entropy mixing (defangs hardware RNG).
 177: 
 178: **Stdlib reuse:** `std/crypto/symmetric.cl::AES-GCM` reference impl
 179: for verification; production calls Web Crypto `subtle.encrypt`. Plus
 180: `std/crypto/kdf.cl::HKDF` for nonce derivation patterns.
 181: 
 182: ---
 183: 
 184: ## v0.17.0 — Threshold-of-N device bootstrap
 185: 
 186: **Frontier:** adding a new device to your identity requires consent
 187: from at least 2 of your existing N devices via a P2P-only ceremony,
 188: zero corporate substrate involvement. Lose a single device → identity
 189: intact.
 190: 
 191: **Primitives:**
 192: - Shamir Secret Sharing (or BLS threshold signatures) over the
 193:   identity master secret. N=3 minimum (split into 3 shares; any 2
 194:   reconstruct).
 195: - Pairing ceremony: new device generates a Web Crypto keypair locally,
 196:   broadcasts an enrollment request over P2P (LAN, BLE, or rendezvous)
 197:   signed by zero existing shares; existing devices accept-or-reject;
 198:   on 2+ accepts, devices each transmit their share to the new device,
 199:   which combines them locally to derive the master.
 200: - Master secret never leaves any device in clear. Each share is
 201:   encrypted to the new device's public key during transmission.
 202: - Optional Passkey integration (opt-in) for users who want
 203:   iCloud / Google sync as a fallback recovery path; tier-gated.
 204: 
 205: **Wire-format additions:**
 206: - New CAPS field `threshold_v1: true`
 207: - New wire kind `THRESHOLD_ENROLL_REQUEST`,
 208:   `THRESHOLD_ENROLL_GRANT`, `THRESHOLD_ENROLL_SHARE`
 209: - Backward compatible: peers without `threshold_v1` use single-device
 210:   identity (legacy).
 211: 
 212: **State migration:** v17 schema:
 213: - `device_cluster.v1` IDB store
 214: - `{device_id, ed_pub, x25519_pub, mlkem_pub, joined_ms,
 215:    share_index, share_encrypted}`
 216: - `cluster_threshold` setting: N (default 3), M (default 2)
 217: 
 218: **Test contract:** `tests/test_threshold_bootstrap_v0170.py`
 219: - 3 devices generate cluster; 1 device added with 2 grants → identity
 220:   reconstructs
 221: - 1 grant → enrollment refused
 222: - Lost device (revoked) → cluster reseals; lost device's share useless
 223: - Cluster works over LAN-only (air-gap tier)
 224: 
 225: **Defang shipped:** threshold-of-N (defangs OS-keychain dependency
 226: for cross-device identity). Lost-phone resilience is structural,
 227: not corporate-recovery-dependent.
 228: 
 229: **Stdlib reuse:**
 230: - `std/crypto/asymmetric.cl` for signature primitives
 231: - `std/crdt/vector_clock.cl::IntervalTreeClock` for cluster
 232:   membership churn (joining and leaving threshold devices)
 233: - `std/identity/provenance.cl` patterns for device attestation chain
 234: 
 235: ---
 236: 
 237: ## v0.18.0 — WebRTC DataChannel transport (the biggest single ship)
 238: 
 239: **Frontier:** browser-to-browser direct P2P encrypted transport with
 240: NAT traversal, sub-second handshake on LAN, sub-3-second handshake
 241: across networks via STUN.
 242: 
 243: **Primitives:**
 244: - `RTCPeerConnection` with our own ICE candidate handling
 245: - Multi-vendor STUN list (6 orgs, rotated)
 246: - DataChannel(s): 1 control channel (reliable, ordered) + 1 bulk
 247:   channel (unreliable, unordered) for chunk traffic
 248: - Signaling: project-hosted rendezvous OR manual QR-mode (zero servers)
 249: - WebRTC's encryption (DTLS-SRTP) is the outer layer; our Double
 250:   Ratchet (v0.7.2 primitive) is the inner layer. Defense in depth.
 251: 
 252: **Wire-format additions:**
 253: - All existing wire kinds run identically over WebRTC DataChannel as
 254:   they did over WebSocket; no protocol change. The DataChannel is
 255:   framed-message; same JSON encoding (with binary FILE_BIN_CHUNK).
 256: - New ICE-related kinds: `ICE_OFFER`, `ICE_ANSWER`, `ICE_CANDIDATE`
 257:   (relay over signaling).
 258: 
 259: **State migration:** none persisted; live state only.
 260: 
 261: **Test contract:** `tests/test_webrtc_transport_v0180.py`
 262: - LAN-only handshake completes in <1s p95
 263: - Cross-network with STUN handshake completes in <3s p95
 264: - Manual-QR signaling completes (no rendezvous touched)
 265: - Same-LAN mode skips STUN entirely (verify no STUN packets sent)
 266: 
 267: **Defang shipped:** multi-vendor STUN (defangs single-STUN
 268: observation); manual-QR mode (total elision). See `SOVEREIGNTY.md`.
 269: 
 270: **Stdlib reuse:** session-type patterns from
 271: `std/session/binary/channel.cl` inform the DataChannel framing
 272: abstraction (typed messages, in-order delivery contracts).
 273: 
 274: ---
 275: 
 276: ## v0.19.0 — WebTransport bulk path + adaptive transport selector
 277: 
 278: **Frontier:** large file transfers use HTTP/3 + QUIC's built-in
 279: connection migration so a Wi-Fi → cellular → Wi-Fi handoff doesn't
 280: drop the transfer. Adaptive selector picks the fastest live path
 281: per peer per chunk.
 282: 
 283: **Primitives:**
 284: - `WebTransport` API for HTTP/3 streams (iOS Safari 17.4+, Android
 285:   Chrome 97+)
 286: - Adaptive bandit (multi-armed bandit; ε-greedy with decay) over
 287:   available paths per peer: BLE, LAN, WebRTC, WebTransport, relay
 288: - Path quality: EWMA over recent throughput + recent failure rate
 289: - Optional Web Push for "wake on incoming" (off by default)
 290: 
 291: **Wire-format additions:** `transport_caps` field in CAPS frame
 292: advertising which paths the peer supports. Backward compatible.
 293: 
 294: **State migration:** new IDB store `path_stats.v1`:
 295: `{peer_fp, path_kind, ewma_throughput_bps, ewma_failure_rate,
 296:  last_used_ms, samples}`.
 297: 
 298: **Test contract:** `tests/test_webtransport_v0190.py`
 299: - WebTransport handshake completes for browsers that support it
 300: - Adaptive selector chooses fastest path on a synthetic 3-path
 301:   test (LAN fast, WiFi slow, relay slowest)
 302: - Path stats persist across restart
 303: - Handoff: simulate Wi-Fi → cellular interface change; transfer
 304:   resumes without restart
 305: 
 306: **Defang shipped:** Web Push optional (off by default). Encrypted
 307: payloads + per-device rotating pseudonym.
 308: 
 309: **Stdlib reuse:**
 310: - Adaptive bandit reuses patterns from `std/concurrent/async/scheduler.cl`
 311:   task-priority semantics (architectural inspiration)
 312:

 315: ## v0.20.0 — BLE proximity + ultrasonic pairing
 316: 
 317: **Frontier:** "hold two phones close, both see each other and
 318: offer to pair" — AirDrop-style on Android via Web Bluetooth; on iOS
 319: fallback to QR + ultrasonic chirp pairing in <2s.
 320: 
 321: **Primitives:**
 322: - Web Bluetooth API on Android Chrome (iOS blocks it; we detect)
 323: - Ultrasonic data-over-audio: 18-22kHz inaudible carrier; transmits a
 324:   16-byte pairing token. Implementation via `OfflineAudioContext`
 325:   + DSP. ~50bps reliable.
 326: - QR code: generated client-side via canvas, scanned via
 327:   `BarcodeDetector` API where available, else manual photo + decode
 328: - Pairing token is a one-time random 256-bit blob; expires in 60s
 329: - Token bootstraps a WebRTC offer/answer exchange
 330: 
 331: **Wire-format additions:** none new; reuses ICE_OFFER/ANSWER from
 332: v0.18.0.
 333: 
 334: **State migration:** none.
 335: 
 336: **Test contract:** `tests/test_proximity_pairing_v0200.py`
 337: - Mock Web Bluetooth → pairing succeeds
 338: - Ultrasonic encode/decode round-trip on synthetic audio
 339: - QR encode/decode round-trip
 340: - Token expires after 60s
 341: 
 342: **Defang shipped:** total elision of network for pairing — proximity
 343: modes use no internet at all. Air-gap tier ready.
 344: 
 345: **Stdlib reuse:** `std/identity/anti_deception.cl` informs the
 346: risk-model that decides whether SAS is required (BLE proximity =
 347: low-risk, skip SAS by default; cold internet contact = high-risk,
 348: demand SAS).

 351: 
 352: ## v0.21.0 — MLS group ratchet (RFC 9420)
 353: 
 354: **Frontier:** properly forward-secret group chat at scale.
 355: Replaces the v0.6.x sender-key scheme with deniable, post-compromise
 356: secure, scalable group encryption.
 357: 
 358: **Primitives:**
 359: - MLS protocol (RFC 9420) — TreeKEM, key rotation on every member
 360:   add/remove, application messages encrypted with epoch keys
 361: - Post-quantum hybrid: ML-KEM-768 + X25519 in the HPKE layer
 362: - Reuse identity keys from v0.15.0+ (Ed25519 + X25519 + ML-KEM)
 363: 
 364: **Wire-format additions:**
 365: - New CAPS field `mls_v1: true`
 366: - New wire kinds: `MLS_WELCOME`, `MLS_COMMIT`, `MLS_PROPOSAL`,
 367:   `MLS_APPLICATION`
 368: - Backward compatible: peers without `mls_v1` fall back to v0.6.x
 369:   sender-key for groups they share with such peers; new groups
 370:   formed entirely among `mls_v1` peers use MLS.
 371: 
 372: **State migration:** v21 schema:
 373: - `mls_groups.v1`: TreeKEM state, current epoch, member roster
 374: - `mls_keys.v1`: pending key packages
 375: 
 376: **Test contract:** `tests/test_mls_group_v0210.py`
 377: - 3-member group; commit; epoch advances; old keys can't decrypt
 378:   new messages
 379: - Member removal: removed member can't decrypt subsequent epoch
 380: - Member rejoin: new key packages, new tree position
 381: - Cross-version compat: an MLS group with all-MLS members works
 382:   alongside legacy groups in the same UI
 383: 
 384: **Defang shipped:** post-quantum hybrid in the HPKE layer (defangs
 385: harvest-now-decrypt-later future quantum threats).
 386: 
 387: **Stdlib reuse:**
 388: - `std/crypto/kdf.cl::HKDF` for tree-key derivation
 389: - `std/crypto/asymmetric.cl` for signatures
 390: - `std/crypto/quantum_safe.cl` for ML-KEM if mature; else `@noble/post-quantum`
 391: - `std/session/multiparty/` patterns for multiparty protocol structure
 392: 
 393: ---
 394: 
 395: ## v0.22.0 — Sealed sender + cover traffic
 396: 
 397: **Frontier:** even an adversary with full traffic visibility cannot
 398: build a contact graph. Recipients can decrypt who a message is from;
 399: nobody else can. Plus per-link cover traffic + mix-net hop routing
 400: makes traffic timing/shape uninformative.
 401: 
 402: **Primitives:**
 403: - Sealed sender (Signal-style): outer envelope identifies only the
 404:   recipient; sender identity is in the encrypted-to-recipient inner
 405:   envelope. The rendezvous and any observer see "someone sent peer
 406:   X a message."
 407: - Per-message random sender pseudonym for outer envelope so even
 408:   the rendezvous can't link two messages as same-sender.
 409: - Cover traffic: each peer emits dummy padded frames at a fixed
 410:   Poisson rate (e.g., λ = 1/30s) when active. Real messages slot
 411:   into the same shape.
 412: - Mix-net cover routing (optional, hardened-tier default-on):
 413:   messages route through 2-3 hops of volunteer peers; each hop
 414:   sees only previous + next; payload onion-encrypted at each hop.
 415: 
 416: **Wire-format additions:**
 417: - All messages now wrapped in sealed-sender envelope
 418: - New wire kinds: `MIX_HOP` (relay frame for mix-net), `COVER_DUMMY`
 419:   (indistinguishable from real)
 420: - Backward compatible: peers without `sealed_sender_v1` cap fall
 421:   back to plaintext-sender envelopes for messages between them.
 422: 
 423: **State migration:** v22 schema:
 424: - `mix_volunteers.v1`: peers willing to relay (consent-gated)
 425: 
 426: **Test contract:** `tests/test_sealed_sender_v0220.py`
 427: - A passive observer between rendezvous and recipient cannot
 428:   determine the sender from the wire
 429: - Cover traffic emits at Poisson rate when idle; real msgs slot in
 430: - Mix-net 2-hop routing: hop A knows source + B, hop B knows A + dest;
 431:   source identity not visible to hop B
 432: - All messages padded to fixed sizes (256B, 1KB, 4KB, 16KB buckets)
 433: 
 434: **Defang shipped:** sealed sender + cover traffic + mix-net (defangs
 435: rendezvous metadata; defangs traffic-shape analysis).
 436: 
 437: **Stdlib reuse:**
 438: - `std/identity/anti_deception.cl` informs sender-pseudonym rotation
 439: - `std/crdt/causality.cl::CausalDelivery` for in-order delivery
 440:   through mix-net hops with reordering tolerance
 441: 
 442: ---
 443: 
 444: ## v0.23.0 — CRDT layer (Yjs/Automerge integration)
 445: 
 446: **Frontier:** every mergeable piece of state (messages, drafts,
 447: group membership, settings, profile) is a CRDT. No "last write wins"
 448: surprises across devices. Lazy sync via the Markov chain: pre-decode
 449: the right history before the user taps.
 450: 
 451: **Primitives:**
 452: - Yjs (chosen over Automerge for smaller wire size + more battle-tested
 453:   in browsers) as the CRDT engine
 454: - Layer our wire-protocol message format atop Yjs document updates
 455: - HybridLogicalClock (port from `coherence_lang/std/crdt/causality.cl`)
 456:   for cross-device causal ordering. Wall time is a hint; HLC is
 457:   authoritative.
 458: - Markov-chain prefetch (already shipped v0.14.0) extends to
 459:   pre-fetch *the right CRDT subdoc* for the predicted next conversation
 460: 
 461: **Wire-format additions:**
 462: - New CAPS field `crdt_v1: true`
 463: - Yjs document updates carried in `CRDT_UPDATE` wire frames
 464: - Backward compatible: legacy peers receive flattened
 465:   individual messages.
 466: 
 467: **State migration:** v23 schema:
 468: - `crdt_docs.v1`: per-conversation Yjs document state
 469: - HLC fields added to existing `messages.v1` rows
 470: 
 471: **Test contract:** `tests/test_crdt_v0230.py`
 472: - 3-device merge: each device offline-edits a different message; all
 473:   merge converges to the same state without "winner" picking
 474: - Group settings (color, archive, mute) merge across devices
 475: - HLC ordering survives a 6-month-skewed device clock
 476: - Prefetch hits the right Yjs subdoc on conversation switch
 477: 
 478: **Defang shipped:** HLC for ordering (defangs OS-clock dependency).
 479: 
 480: **Stdlib reuse:**
 481: - `std/crdt/causality.cl::HybridLogicalClock` — direct port
 482: - `std/crdt/merge.cl::MergeStrategy` traits — compose with Yjs
 483: - `std/crdt/maps/LWWMap`, `std/crdt/maps/MVMap` — port for Yjs maps
 484: - `std/crdt/sequences/RGA` — fallback alternative to Yjs sequences
 485:   if we ever want to swap engines
 486: - `std/crdt/sets/ORSet`, `std/crdt/sets/AWSet` — group membership
 487: 
 488: ---
 489: 
 490: ## v0.24.0 — On-device LLM (WebGPU + tiny model)
 491: 
 492: **Frontier:** smart features that other chat apps ship to the cloud
 493: run entirely on-device. Semantic search, smart-reply suggestions,
 494: thread summarization, harassment heuristics. Nothing leaves the device.
 495: 
 496: **Primitives:**
 497: - WebGPU (Chrome 113+, Safari 18+, Firefox 121+ behind flag)
 498: - Quantized small model: 1-3B parameters (e.g., Phi-3-mini-int4 or
 499:   similar; ~1-2GB on disk; ~700MB RAM)
 500: - Inference engine: `transformers.js` or `webllm` (open-source, no
 501:   vendor)
 502: - Runs in a Web Worker so it doesn't block the UI thread
 503: - Battery + thermal monitoring: yields when device temp > 40°C or
 504:   battery < 20%; falls back to keyword-only path
 505: 
 506: **Wire-format additions:** none (this is local).
 507: 
 508: **State migration:** OPFS layout extension:
 509: - `/_models/<model-id>/` — model files, encrypted at rest
 510: 
 511: **Test contract:** `tests/test_on_device_llm_v0240.py`
 512: - Model loads in <30s on a mid-tier 2022 device (initial download)
 513: - Semantic search returns relevant results for a 100-msg test corpus
 514: - Smart-reply suggestions are generated in <5s for an open conversation
 515: - Battery threshold: simulate <20% battery → LLM yields, falls back
 516: - WebGPU absence → smart features absent, no degraded experience
 517: 
 518: **Defang shipped:** total elision of cloud LLM dependency.
 519: 
 520: **Stdlib reuse:** none directly (Coherence stdlib doesn't have ML).
 521: 
 522: ---
 523: 
 524: ## v0.25.0 — Federated learning across user's devices
 525: 
 526: **Frontier:** the on-device LLM is fine-tuned on the user's actual
 527: usage, but the training stays local. Updates propagate from your
 528: phone to your laptop over the existing P2P link. Nobody's data
 529: center sees a token.
 530: 
 531: **Primitives:**
 532: - Federated Averaging (FedAvg) over the user's device cluster
 533: - LoRA-style adapter weights (small; ~10MB per device per epoch)
 534: - Updates wrapped in CRDT updates (using v0.23.0 layer)
 535: - Threshold-quorum signed: model update is accepted across cluster
 536:   only if signed by 2-of-N devices
 537: 
 538: **Wire-format additions:**
 539: - New wire kind: `MODEL_UPDATE` (encrypted to cluster, signed by 2-of-N)
 540: 
 541: **State migration:**
 542: - `model_state.v1` IDB store: per-device LoRA weights + version
 543: 
 544: **Test contract:** `tests/test_federated_learning_v0250.py`
 545: - 3-device cluster: each device trains 1 epoch; weights average;
 546:   resulting model performs >= individual device performance on
 547:   held-out test set
 548: - Single-device cluster: federated path silently disabled
 549: - Compromised device: rejected updates (without 2-of-N signing)
 550: 
 551: **Defang shipped:** federated learning entirely on-device (defangs
 552: cloud-training corporate dependency).
 553: 
 554: **Stdlib reuse:**
 555: - `std/crypto/asymmetric.cl` for threshold signing
 556: - `std/crdt/merge.cl::WeightedMerge` patterns for averaging logic
 557:   (port the merge-strategy framework, not the specific weighted impl)
 558:

 561: ## v1.0.0 — One Link Web (the phone-only milestone)
 562: 
 563: **Frontier:** all 11 prior ships compose into a single coherent PWA
 564: that a phone-only user can install, use, and rely on with zero
 565: computer involvement and minimum corporate substrate exposure.
 566: 
 567: **Primitives:** none new; this ship is integration + paranoia-tier
 568: selector + final polish + signed release.
 569: 
 570: **Wire-format additions:** none.
 571: 
 572: **State migration:** none.
 573: 
 574: **Test contract:** `tests/test_one_link_web_v1.py` — end-to-end
 575: journey:
 576: - Fresh phone, never installed: visit URL, install, set up identity,
 577:   pair with a friend's phone via QR, send messages, receive messages,
 578:   send a file, receive a file. All without a single tap on
 579:   "Settings → Advanced."
 580: - All three paranoia tiers selectable; all three behave per the
 581:   matrix in `SOVEREIGNTY.md`.
 582: - Reproducible build: clone source, build, hash matches signed release.
 583: 
 584: **Defang shipped:** v1.0.0 is the **complete defang ladder fully
 585: deployed**:
 586: - IPFS distribution + `.onion` mirror + signed `.html` archive
 587: - OPFS-stored identity, no OS keychain by default
 588: - Multi-vendor STUN + same-LAN mode + manual-QR mode
 589: - Sealed sender + cover traffic + mix-net (hardened tier on)
 590: - HLC for ordering
 591: - Multi-source entropy
 592: - Reproducible builds + SLSA-3 attestation
 593: - Three paranoia tiers selectable in setup
 594: 
 595: This is the "no computer required, free of corporations by default,
 596: just works" ship. The promise is met.

 620: 
 621: ## Beyond v1.0.0 — long-term frontier items
 622: 
 623: These don't have a fixed slot but are tracked here so they're not
 624: lost:
 625: 
 626: - **Decentralized rendezvous via DHT + gossip.** Replaces project-hosted
 627:   rendezvous entirely. Connection requests route via consistent-hashing
 628:   over the active peer set.
 629: - **Verifiable revocation log per identity.** Append-only signed log
 630:   of device revocations; gossiped across the user's contacts; checked
 631:   on every key change.
 632: - **Hardware attestation chain.** WebAuthn attestation extension
 633:   proves the keypair was generated in a Secure Enclave / StrongBox.
 634: - **Anonymous group membership via blind signatures.** Members prove
 635:   membership without revealing which member.
 636: - **Private set intersection for contact discovery.** "Which of my
 637:   address book is on One Link?" answered cryptographically with no
 638:   central server, no diff exposure.
 639: - **Encrypted searchable indexes (SSE).** Full-text search over
 640:   encrypted history without leaking queries.
 641: - **Duress codes + decoy identity.** Optional second passphrase
 642:   unlocks a parallel decoy identity. Plausible deniability under
 643:   compulsion.
 644: - **Constant-time everything.** Cryptographic ops in constant time
 645:   + memory. No timing/cache side-channels.
 646: - **Self-healing peer recovery.** Resync local state from another
 647:   of your devices OR from a friend's copy of the public-side
 648:   conversation, with cryptographic injection-detection.
 649: 
 650: Each of these can land as a v1.x or v2.x ship; they're noted for
 651: continuity.

 680: 
 681: Every ship in this document is gated by `PRINCIPLES.md` checklist.

 683: each ship:

 690:   or moving.

 694:   in `SOVEREIGNTY.md`.

  11: ## ol_bloom (ADR-0011)
  12: 
  13: | Bench | N=1024 | N=16384 | N=262144 |
  14: |---|---|---|---|
  15: | `bloom_insert` | **66.5 Melem/s** | 66.4 Melem/s | 65.0 Melem/s |
  16: | `bloom_contains` | **38.5 Melem/s** | 38.4 Melem/s | 35.8 Melem/s |
  17: | `bloom_contains_many` (batch) | ~68 Melem/s | ~69 Melem/s | ~67 Melem/s |
  18: | `bloom_codec/encode` | 28.5 GiB/s | 94.2 GiB/s | 65.0 GiB/s |
  19: | `bloom_codec/decode` | 34.4 GiB/s | 80.8 GiB/s | 62.3 GiB/s |
  20: | `bloom_extend_par` (rayon) | — | 87 Melem/s | 63-96 Melem/s (>1M ids) |
  21: 
  22: **Optimizations landed this phase (cumulative speedup from original Phase B drop):**
  23: 1. Cached-keyed `OnceLock` BLAKE3 → 3.4-4.4× speedup.
  24: 2. **BLAKE3 → xxh3-128** swap (Bloom only needs uniform distribution, not collision resistance) → another **2.6-3.4×** on top.
  25: 
  26: **Net: 8-15× speedup vs original Phase B Bloom (4.7 → 38-66 M elem/s).**
  27: 
  28: Phase B target (ADR-0011): "Bloom-init reduces bytes-on-wire by ≥90% on workload where receiver has ≥80% of chunks." Verified by `cargo test -p ol_transfer --test engine_e2e bloom_handshake_returns_missing_chunks`.
  29: 
  30: ## ol_fountain (ADR-0015)
  31: 
  32: | Bench | K=8 | K=64 | K=256 |
  33: |---|---|---|---|
  34: | `fountain_encode_symbol` | **4.27 GiB/s** | 3.01 GiB/s | 2.28 GiB/s |
  35: | `fountain_decode_chunk` | 2.05 GiB/s | **1.69 GiB/s** | **0.83 GiB/s** |
  36: | `fountain_packet/encode` | 15.5 GiB/s | — | — |
  37: | `fountain_packet/decode` | 26.8 GiB/s | — | — |
  38: 
  39: **Optimizations landed this phase:**
  40: 1. **Degree-1 queue** in decoder propagation replaces O(pending) linear scan.
  41: 2. **SIMD u64-wide XOR** via `ptr::read_unaligned` (compiler vectorizes to AVX2 `vpxor` / NEON `eor`).
  42: 3. **Move-not-clone** of resolved payload Vec into `self.sources` slot.
  43: 4. **Skip zero-fill in encoder**: first-neighbor source copies directly into output buffer instead of `vec![0; N]` + XOR-against-zero.
  44: 
  45: **Net: K=256 decode +40% (595 → 834 MiB/s), K=64 decode +19%, encode +4-13% across K.**
  46: 
  47: **ADR-0015 acceptance gate** (decode ≥99% at 5% loss across 1000 random seeds for K ∈ {8, 64, 256}): VERIFIED via `cargo test -p ol_fountain --test acceptance`. Tests passed for all three K values in release mode.
  48: 
  49: K=64 (the common 64 KiB chunk) decodes at 1.42 GiB/s — well above typical QUIC bandwidth, so the encoder isn't the bottleneck on the network path.
  50: 
  51: ## ol_chunk format-aware (ADR-0014)
  52: 
  53: | Bench | Throughput |
  54: |---|---|
  55: | `zip_lfh_walk/10x16KiB` | **142 GiB/s** |
  56: | `zip_lfh_walk/80x16KiB` | 111 GiB/s |
  57: | `zip_lfh_walk/10x1024KiB` | 45.8 GiB/s |
  58: | `format_aware_scan/zip_100entries_512K` (50 MiB) | **1.78 GiB/s** |
  59: | `format_aware_scan/pure_cdc_baseline` (50 MiB) | 1.95 GiB/s |
  60: 
  61: **Optimization landed this phase:** SIMD `memchr` replaces byte-at-a-time scan for ZIP local-file-header search.
  62: 
  63: **Format-aware overhead:** 1.95 GiB/s pure CDC → 1.78 GiB/s format-aware = **8.7% overhead** for 100% dedup recovery on the "edit one file in a ZIP" workload. Verified by `single_byte_edit_only_changes_one_chunk_family` test.
  64: 
  65: ## ol_chunk (ADR-0001) — pinned in Phase A1
  66: 
  67: CDC + BLAKE3 baselines remain pinned at the Phase A1 numbers:
  68: 
  69: - `cdc_scan_random_1gib`: ≥1.2 GiB/s/core scalar, ≥3 GiB/s/core SIMD
  70: - `blake3_address/raw/64`: ≥3 GiB/s/core
  71: - `derive_aead_key`: <300 ns
  72: 
  73: ### Phase B-2 parallel CDC scan baseline (rayon BLAKE3 hashing)
  74: 
  75: `scan_to_vec_parallel` keeps boundary discovery sequential but shards BLAKE3 hashing of each discovered chunk across cores. The CDC kernel itself stays sequential because the rolling hash carries state across bytes.
  76: 
  77: | Buffer | Sequential | Parallel | Speedup |
  78: |---|---|---|---|
  79: | 16 MiB | 2.21 GiB/s | **2.92 GiB/s** | **1.32×** |
  80: | 64 MiB | 2.16 GiB/s | 2.82 GiB/s | 1.31× |
  81: | 256 MiB | 2.08 GiB/s | **3.08 GiB/s** | **1.48×** |
  82: 
  83: Sequential FastCDC discovery is now the throughput floor (~2 GiB/s). Pushing past it requires shard-with-stitch-zone parallelism (research-grade; Phase C+).
  84: 
  85: ## ol_aead convergent (ADR-0012)
  86: 
  87: Identical performance to standard AES-256-GCM path (4-5 GiB/s/core on AES-NI hardware) — the only added cost is the `BLAKE3.derive_key(plaintext)` call to compute the convergent key, which is dominated by the BLAKE3 throughput (~3 GiB/s/core for the plaintext-length hash). For typical 64 KiB chunks: ~20µs overhead per chunk (one-time per chunk).
  88: 
  89: ## ol_aead parallel multi-chunk (Phase B-2)
  90: 
  91: Multi-chunk encrypt/decrypt parallelized across cores via rayon. Each chunk's AEAD is independent (different chunk_id → different nonce + AAD), so the work shards cleanly.
  92: 
  93: | Bench (64 KiB chunks) | Sequential | Parallel | Speedup |
  94: |---|---|---|---|
  95: | 32 chunks | 943 µs (2.07 GiB/s) | **469 µs (4.17 GiB/s)** | **2.0×** |
  96: | 128 chunks | 3.84 ms (2.03 GiB/s) | **1.10 ms (7.13 GiB/s)** | **3.5×** |
  97: 
  98: Speedup scales with batch size (rayon dispatch cost amortizes over more chunks). For typical ingest workloads (≥ 100 chunks per file), `encrypt_chunks_par` is the right path.
  99: 
 100: ## ol_transfer (ADR-0013)
 101: 
 102: End-to-end fetch latency on loopback QUIC with identity-bound TLS (measured via `cargo bench -p ol_transfer --bench transfer_bench`):
 103: 
 104: | Operation | Loopback latency | Note |
 105: |---|---|---|
 106: | `fetch_chunk_local` | **1.27 µs** | Already in store; Bloom + memtable + read |
 107: | `fetch_chunk_warm_1KiB` | 599 µs | Single fetch (one fsync). Wire round-trip + append + fsync |
 108: | `fetch_many_batched_x32` | **2.94 ms / 32 = 92 µs/chunk** | **Group commit: 1 fsync for batch** |
 109: | `concurrent_fetch_x200` (test) | **4.68 ms / 200 = 23 µs/chunk** | Group commit + per-peer concurrency |
 110: | `sequential_fetch_chunk_x32` | 21.55 ms / 32 = 673 µs/chunk | 32 separate fsyncs (control) |
 111: | `bloom_handshake_warm_1k` | 99 µs | 1000-chunk manifest scope |
 112: | `full_scan_10k_server` | **4.96 ms** | Server walks 10K-chunk memtable |
 113: | `scoped_200_want_10k_server` | **98 µs** | **50× faster** — server walks just want_list |
 114: | `warm_chunk_response_16KiB` | 705 µs | Single ChunkResponse |
 115: | `fountain_16KiB` | 15.7 ms | K=16 LT-fountain delivery (loopback overhead; wins on lossy/multi-receiver) |
 116: 
 117: **Optimizations landed in Phase B-2:**
 118: 1. `Arc<RwLock<ChunkStore>>` replacing `Arc<Mutex<...>>` so concurrent reads parallelize.
 119: 2. **Group commit**: `fetch_many` uses `write_local_no_flush` for each task + one `commit()` at the end. **7.3× speedup on multi-chunk fetch** (92 µs/chunk vs 673 µs/chunk).
 120: 3. Per-chunk `fsync` cost is now amortized across the whole batch; warm-path fetches are QUIC-RTT-bound (~100 µs) rather than disk-bound.
 121: 
 122: **New API:**
 123: - `TransferEngine::commit()` — explicit batched-commit barrier.
 124: - `TransferEngine::fetch_chunk_fountain(peer, chunk_id)` — ADR-0015 LT-fountain delivery; uses new `FountainRequest`/`FountainBurst`/`FountainAck` wire kinds.
 125: - `TransferEngine::bloom_handshake_scoped(peer, already_have, want_list)` — client-supplied want_list avoids the server-side full memtable scan (ADR-0011 v2).

  27: ## ol_fec (ADR-0016)
  28: 
  29: Reed-Solomon over GF(2^8) with a **Cauchy systematic matrix** + **SSSE3 PSHUFB SIMD path** (Plank-Greenan-Miller 2013). No external RS-codec dependency.
  30: 
  31: | Bench | Encode throughput (SIMD) | Decode throughput |
  32: |---|---|---|
  33: | RS(4,2) at 16 KiB shards | **17.18 GiB/s** | ~17 GiB/s |
  34: | RS(10,4) at 64 KiB shards | **8.98 GiB/s** | ~9 GiB/s |
  35: | RS(16,8) at 64 KiB shards | **4.48 GiB/s** | ~4 GiB/s |
  36: 
  37: **Acceptance gate (Phase C plan line 287):**
  38: > Reed-Solomon (10,4) survives any 4-shard erasure with 100% recovery across ≥10,000 seeds.
  39: 
  40: **PASSED:** 10,000 random RS(10,4) decodes + all 1001 enumerated `C(14, 4)` erasure patterns recover 100% byte-exact. See `ol_fec/tests/acceptance.rs`.
  41: 
  42: **Performance vs target:** ADR-0016 targets ≥500 MiB/s/core scalar. Achieved 1.13 GiB/s at RS(10,4), 64 KiB shards — **2.2× the target**. The "Klauspost trick" (per-coefficient 256-entry multiplication tables) is the win. SIMD upgrade (AVX2 PSHUFB / NEON TBL) is a clear Phase D opportunity to push to 5+ GiB/s.
  43: 
  44: ## ol_pqkem (ADR-0017)
  45: 
  46: Hybrid KEM = ML-KEM-768 + X25519 with a BLAKE3 combiner.
  47: 
  48: | Operation | Time |
  49: |---|---|
  50: | `keypair` | ~50 µs (ML-KEM dominated) |
  51: | `encapsulate` | ~80 µs |
  52: | `decapsulate` | ~70 µs |
  53: | End-to-end round trip | **~200 µs** |
  54: 
  55: 10,000 random round trips complete in **1.84 s** in release mode = average 184 µs/handshake.
  56: 
  57: **Acceptance gate (Phase C plan line 290):**
  58: > ML-KEM-768 + X25519 hybrid completes handshake at PQ-conservative parameters.
  59: 
  60: **PASSED:**
  61: - 10,000 random `(keypair, encap, decap)` round trips: byte-equivalent shared secrets across all seeds.
  62: - Wire-format determinism: `to_bytes` / `from_bytes` round trip preserves the derived secret.
  63: - Distinct sessions produce distinct shared secrets (encap is randomized).

  74: ## Constant-time audit (Phase C plan item #9)
  75: 
  76: Fixed `One_link/src/one_link/double_ratchet._is_small_order_x25519`:
  77: 
  78: - **Before:** `frozenset[bytes]` lookup — Python's `dict.__contains__` short-circuits on byte-mismatch in CPython, leaking which entry matched (or whether any matched) via timing.
  79: - **After:** linear scan over a tuple, comparing every entry with `hmac.compare_digest` (CT byte-wise) and OR'ing results into an int accumulator. No short-circuit branch.
  80:

  82: |---|---|
  83: | All 13 block-list entries correctly detected | ✅ |
  84: | 1000 random keys correctly pass | ✅ |
  85: | Wrong-length inputs rejected up front | ✅ |
  86: | Does NOT short-circuit on first-entry match (semantic) | ✅ |
  87: | Timing variance bounded (loose 2× spread at Python level) | ✅ |
  88: 
  89: 47 existing ratchet tests pass unchanged + 5 new constant-time audit tests pass. The 1% timing variance target in the plan is a Rust/Criterion-level acceptance for crypto primitives elsewhere; the Python ratchet is bounded to "no order-of-magnitude leak" (the underlying `compare_digest` is C-level CT).

 122: ## ol_ratchet (ADR-0020)
 123: 
 124: Symmetric BLAKE3 chain ratchet with per-step domain-separation tags (0x4D for message keys, 0x43 for chain keys). Bootstraps from `ol_pqkem` shared secret.
 125: 
 126: - `Chain::next_message_key` — per-chunk forward-secret AEAD key.
 127: - `Chain::peek_message_key(step)` — derive a future step's key without mutating state (skipped-key reconstruction).
 128: - `Chain::fast_forward(step)` — skip ahead without emitting keys.
 129: - `SkippedKeyStore` — bounded LRU (default cap 1024) for out-of-order delivery (fountain ADR-0015).
 130:

 132: - 13 chain + skipped-key unit tests.

   1: # Coherence Mesh Plan — sovereign-network track
   2: 
   3: > Status: planning-of-record. Living document.
   4: > Last updated: 2026-05-12.
   5: 
   6: ## What this is
   7: 
   8: The architectural track that turns One Link from "best-in-class file
   9: + chat engine" into "a global communications layer that no company,
  10: government, ISP, or attacker can lock out, surveil, censor, or
  11: destroy — and that any person can use without understanding any of
  12: that."
  13: 
  14: This plan lives alongside [FILE_ENGINE_V2_PLAN.md](./FILE_ENGINE_V2_PLAN.md)
  15: (the engine substrate, all phases now structurally complete) and
  16: [ARCHITECTURE.md](./ARCHITECTURE.md) (the PWA pivot). The Coherence
  17: Mesh is the **network + identity + trust layer above the engine**:
  18: how devices find each other, how identities federate, how messages
  19: route privately, and how the user's own devices act as both ONE
  20: contact (to friends) and SEPARATE addressable peers (to themselves).
  21: 
  22: ## The single load-bearing insight
  23: 
  24: > **Three trust tiers, three default privacy modes.** Self-traffic
  25: > is direct + fast because there's no metadata to hide. Friend-traffic
  26: > is 1-hop-onion + sealed-sender because the network observer must
  27: > not learn the social graph. Paranoid mode is 3-hop-onion + cover
  28: > traffic for users in hostile environments. The user never picks
  29: > which tier — pair-by-QR puts your devices in self-mesh, the
  30: > friend's contact lands in pinned, and paranoid is an explicit opt-in.
  31: 
  32: This is the only architectural decision that makes "insanely
  33: secure" and "insanely fast" compatible.
  34: 
  35: ## The 10-layer stack
  36: 
  37: | # | Layer | Status | What it delivers |
  38: |---|---|---|---|
  39: | 1 | **Post-quantum identity** | ✓ SHIPPED 2026-05-13 (`ol_pqsig` Ed25519 + ML-DSA-65 hybrid; PQ KEM already in `ol_pqkem` + Sphinx) | Ed25519 + Dilithium hybrid master key; ML-KEM-768 + X25519 hybrid per-device KEM; hardware-bound (Secure Enclave / StrongBox / TPM) where available; TOFU-degrading where not. Survives quantum. |
  40: | 2 | **Pair-by-QR + channel-reciprocity 2FA** | ✓ SHIPPED 2026-05-12 (Phase F2) | `ol_pair_qr` crate: Ed25519-signed Invite + transcript-bound PairResponse + PairConfirm + 5-word SAS over 30 bits + X25519 chain-key derivation. Optional Factor-2 mix-in via `ol_proximity_pair`. Refuses cross-invite replay + key-substitution + transcript-swap. Daemon-side via `pair_qr_native.{Inviter,Scanner}`. |
  41: | 3 | **Sovereign discovery** | ✓ SHIPPED 2026-05-13 | `ol_discovery` Kademlia DHT + `DhtNode` production orchestrator + Row 3 maintenance loops (`refresh_stale_buckets`, `republish_records`, `tick_maintenance`) + Python `run_maintenance_loop` asyncio helper. |
  42: | 4 | **Coherence-field routing** | ✓ SHIPPED 2026-05-11 (Phase E) | τ_c PDE-routed mesh transport. Routes through high-coherence peers; auto-avoids fragility before partition.   48: | 10 | **Confidential-compute daemon** | ❌ NEW BUILD | Where hardware supports (Intel SGX, AMD SEV-SNP, Apple Secure Memory, ARM TrustZone), daemon runs in an enclave so even local malware can't extract keys. Beyond Signal. Beyond what any consumer messenger ships. |
  49: 
  50: ## Personal Device Mesh — the multi-device-per-identity capability
  51: 
  52: > Your phone, laptop, tablet, desktop are ONE identity to your friends
  53: > and SEPARATE addressable peers to you. Both at the same time.
  54: 
  55: ### Identity hierarchy
  56: 
  57: ```
  58: Master identity (Ed25519 + Dilithium hybrid, hardware-bound when possible)
  59: ├─ Phone subkey   (derived; per-device; revocable)
  60: ├─ Laptop subkey  (derived; per-device; revocable)
  61: ├─ Tablet subkey  (derived; per-device; revocable)
  62: └─ Desktop subkey (derived; per-device; revocable)
  63: ```
  64: 
  65: The **master pubkey is what friends pin.** Per-device subkeys are
  66: derived from the master via deterministic key derivation (HKDF + a
  67: device-class context tag). When a friend sends to "you," the mesh
  68: delivers to whichever device's subkey is currently reachable. From
  69: the friend's point of view, you're ONE contact.
  70: 
  71: ### Internal addressing (what YOU see)
  72: 
  73: In your own UI, your devices appear as a small addressable group:
  74: 
  75: ```
  76: You (Alex)
  77: ├─ My phone        (online, last-seen 0s ago)
  78: ├─ My laptop       (offline, last-seen 4h ago)
  79: ├─ My tablet       (online, last-seen 2m ago)
  80: └─ My desktop      (online, last-seen 12s ago)
  81: ```
  82: 
  83: You can target a specific device explicitly when you want
  84: ("Send this 20GB screen recording to MY LAPTOP specifically because
  85: it has the disk space") or leave it as "any" and the mesh routes
  86: to whichever wakes first.
  87: 
  88: ### Self-mesh routing
  89: 
  90: Traffic between YOUR OWN devices is **self-traffic** — different
  91: routing semantics from friend-traffic:
  92: 
  93: | | Self-traffic | Friend-traffic |
  94: |---|---|---|
  95: | Encryption | E2E AEAD (always) | E2E AEAD (always) |
  96: | Onion routing | **Skipped** (no metadata to hide — it's you talking to you) | 1-hop default, 3-hop paranoid |
  97: | Cover traffic | **Skipped** | On between pinned contacts |
  98: | NAT traversal | UDP hole punching via STUN-by-paired-peer | Same |
  99: | Path selection | Direct or circuit-relay via paired peer if NATs hostile | Coherence-field routing via paired peers |
 100: | Latency budget | Network speed only (~10-50ms) | +30-80ms onion (1-hop) or +100-200ms (3-hop) |
 101: 
 102: The user said it best: **"can we also somehow be separate, like if
 103: you want to grab a file from your computer to send but on your phone
 104: in another state?"** That's self-traffic. No onion, no cover, no
 105: latency penalty. Just a direct encrypted transfer between two of
 106: your devices, NAT-traversed, at full network speed.
 107: 
 108: ### Two flavors of cross-device file access
 109: 
 110: **Pull-and-forward (phone pays bandwidth twice):**
 111: ```
 112: Phone in TX                  Laptop in CA               Friend
 113:    │                              │                       │
 114:    ├── "list files" ─────────────>│                       │
 115:    │<──── file manifest ──────────│                       │
 116:    ├── "pull file X" ────────────>│                       │
 117:    │<──── file bytes ─────────────│                       │
 118:    ├──────── "send file X to friend" ──────────────────── │
 119:    │                              │                       │
 120: ```
 121: 
 122: User can preview / scrub on phone first; phone bears the bandwidth.
 123: Right answer for small files or "I want to look at it before
 124: sending."
 125: 
 126: **Remote-instruct (phone pays kilobytes; laptop pays bandwidth):**
 127: ```
 128: Phone in TX                  Laptop in CA               Friend
 129:    │                              │                       │
 130:    ├── "send blob X to friend ────│                       │
 131:    │    Y, signed by me, scope =  │                       │
 132:    │    single-file" ─────────────│                       │
 133:    │   (~200 bytes)               │──── file bytes ──────>│
 134:    │                              │                       │
 135:    │<───── "sent, ack" ───────────│                       │
 136: ```
 137: 
 138: Capability-token command goes phone → laptop (signed by phone's
 139: subkey, which laptop verifies against master pubkey). Laptop
 140: forwards the file directly to friend. Phone pays ~kilobytes;
 141: laptop bears the bandwidth. **Right answer for huge files** (4K
 142: video, full project folders, dataset uploads). Total time =
 143: laptop-to-friend transfer time, period.
 144: 
 145: ### Sleep/wake handoff
 146: 
 147: When the phone backgrounds and the screen goes off, its mesh
 148: presence drops to "asleep." Friends sending to "Alex" land on
 149: whichever-device-is-awake. When the phone wakes, it pulls the
 150: delta from the device that received during sleep.
 151: 
 152: This is implemented via a **device-presence CRDT** that all your
 153: devices share. Each device announces presence + last-seen + battery
 154: state. The receiving-device for any inbound message is chosen by
 155: the sender's mesh routing using:
 156: - presence score (awake / asleep / dormant)
 157: - battery score (>20% preferred over <20%)
 158: - network quality (Wi-Fi > cellular > LE)
 159: - recency (most-recently-active device gets priority)
 160: 
 161: ### Revocation
 162: 
 163: Lose a device → revoke its subkey from any other paired device.
 164: The revocation propagates through the mesh; within the mesh's
 165: sync interval (~minutes) every paired contact and every other
 166: device of yours knows the lost subkey is dead. Inbound messages
 167: to it are rejected; the device, if it ever comes back online, can
 168: no longer participate.
 169: 
 170: ## How it stays insanely fast under all the security
 171: 
 172: Five mechanisms hide the security overhead from perceived latency:
 173: 
 174: 1. **Tiered routing.** Self-mesh skips onion + cover entirely.
 175:    Pinned-contact friend-chat uses 1-hop, not 3-hop. 3-hop is
 176:    explicit paranoid-mode opt-in for activists/journalists. Most
 177:    users never pay the heavy overhead.
 178: 
 179: 2. **Pre-established circuits.** Active inference + bandit (Phase D,
 180:    shipped) learns who you message often. Pre-warms onion circuits
 181:    to those friends in idle time so first-hop is hot when you send.
 182: 
 183: 3. **Coherence-field path selection.** The τ_c routing (Phase E,
 184:    shipped) picks high-coherence (= low loss + low latency) paths.
 185:    Onion through high-τ_c peers is barely slower than direct
 186:    because the chosen paths are the fastest available.
 187: 
 188: 4. **Multi-path racing.** Critical messages send over 2-3 paths
 189:    simultaneously; whichever arrives first wins. Trades bandwidth
 190:    for tail-latency. Opt-in per message ("send fast" mode).
 191: 
 192: 5. **0-RTT resume.** QUIC 0-RTT (Phase A2 gate, scaffold shipped)
 193:    means returning circuits resume instantly with no handshake.
 194:    Sub-50ms warm-cache latency.
 195: 
 196: ### End-state perceived latency
 197: 
 198: - **Self-mesh (phone↔laptop):** network speed only (~30-60ms
 199:   cross-country). Indistinguishable from a raw QUIC connection.
 200: - **Friend chat (pinned-contact default):** +30-80ms via 1-hop
 201:   onion. Imperceptible vs Signal/iMessage.
 202: - **Paranoid mode (3-hop + cover):** +100-200ms. Noticeable but
 203:   acceptable; only when the user explicitly chose it.
 204: 
 205: ## Phase F sequence
 206: 
 207: Each ship below has a falsifiable acceptance gate. No phase ships
 208: without passing its gate.
 209: 
 210: ### Phase F1 — Harvest the easy wins (parallel)
 211: 
 212: Three OneField Mesh primitives port straight over:
 213: 
 214: | Item | Source | Action |
 215: |---|---|---|
 216: | `ol_threshold_recovery` | `OneField/onefield/privacy/sharding.cl` (Tier 15 production) | Port Shamir(k,n) over GF(2^8) to Rust crate; wire to identity master-key seed; UI for "Add this friend as a recovery contact" |
 217: | `ol_discovery` scaffold | `OneField/onefield/bridge/discovery.cl` | Port TTL + announce cadence logic; add Kademlia DHT layer with signed-peer-announcement entries on top |
 218: | `ol_proximity_pair` | `OneField/onefield/mesh/bootstrap.cl` | Port channel-reciprocity 128-probe protocol; wire as optional Factor-2 alongside QR-scan Factor-1 |
 219: 
 220: **Phase F1 acceptance gate:**
 221: - Lose 2 of 5 trusted devices, recover identity from remaining 3 (Shamir round-trip test ≥ 1000 random seeds)
 222: - Two daemons find each other via DHT without any rendezvous server (LAN + cross-NAT both)
 223: - Captured-QR + remote-actor attack fails the channel-reciprocity gate
 224: 
 225: ### Phase F2 — Pair-by-QR (foundation under everything else)
 226: 
 227: Replace the `--lan` token URL with a proper Ed25519 + Dilithium pair
 228: handshake initiated by QR scan. Eliminates the entire class of
 229: remote-pair vulnerabilities.
 230: 
 231: **Phase F2 acceptance gate:**
 232: - Scan QR with phone → phone becomes paired peer of laptop
 233: - Laptop UI port is NEVER bound to LAN during the entire flow
 234: - Adversary on same WiFi cannot replay or MITM the pair handshake
 235: - Adversary with the captured QR but no proximity fails channel-reciprocity Factor 2
 236: 
 237: ### Phase F3 — Onion circuits
 238: 
 239: 1-hop default for pinned-contact friend-traffic; 3-hop for paranoid
 240: mode. Path selection via Phase E coherence-field routing.
 241: 
 242: **Phase F3 acceptance gate:**
 243: - 1-hop circuit added latency < 80ms over LAN; < 200ms over cross-country WAN
 244: - 3-hop circuit added latency < 250ms cross-country
 245: - Each hop only knows previous + next (cryptographic verification:
 246:   no hop can decrypt destination metadata)
 247: - Path selection prefers high-τ_c relays (measurable via Phase E metrics)
 248: 
 249: ### Phase F4 — Sealed sender + cover traffic
 250: 
 251: Hide sender identity from observers (sealed sender like Signal's,
 252: extended to the mesh). Add Loopix-style constant-rate cover traffic
 253: between pinned contacts.
 254: 
 255: **Phase F4 acceptance gate:**
 256: - Observer sniffing WiFi cannot determine who-talks-to-whom from
 257:   timing analysis over 24h capture
 258: - Cover-traffic byte budget < 50KB/hour per pinned contact
 259: 
 260: ### Phase F5 — Personal Device Mesh
 261: 
 262: The multi-device-per-identity capability. Master identity + per-device
 263: subkeys + device-presence CRDT + remote-instruct command channel.
 264:

 294: - `/api/self-mesh/allowed-roots` plus the Activity-panel "Trust folder"

 378:

 384:   One Link bytes from random HTTPS sample across ≥ 10,000 connections

 399: 
 400: Where hardware supports, run the daemon (or at minimum the

 403: **Phase F8 acceptance gate (per platform):**
 404: - macOS: keys held in Secure Enclave; sealed cipher operations
 405: - Windows: TPM-bound; remote attestation chain validates
