 410: 
 411: Every layer is checked against the defang ladder in
 412: [SOVEREIGNTY.md](./SOVEREIGNTY.md). No dependency on any single
 413: corporate substrate.
 414: 
 415: | Layer | Default substrate | Sovereign substitute if compromised |
 416: |---|---|---|
 417: | PQ libraries | `pq-crystals` reference (BSD) | Vendor-multiple impls (NIST + libsodium-pqc) |
 418: | Channel reciprocity | Direct radio hardware | Already vendor-neutral (any SDR / WiFi/LE/LoRa NIC) |
 419: | DHT | Custom Kademlia | Easy substitute (libp2p Kademlia, IPFS) |
 420: | STUN | Self-hosted / swarm-peer | Multiple competing public STUN (Google + Mozilla + Cloudflare — pick one randomly per session) |
 421: | TURN | Paired-peer circuit relay | No external TURN dependency at all |
 422: | Hardware enclave | Platform-specific | TOFU-degrading; vendor attestation chain optional, not required |
 423: | Pluggable transport | Cloak-style (open spec) | Multiple impls (Obfs4, MeekHTTPS) |
 424: | Shamir recovery | OneField (in-house) | Any RFC-compliant Shamir impl |
 425:

 427: either has no external dependency or degrades gracefully to a

 536: ## Open questions (intentionally not resolved here)
 537: 
 538: 1. **Should the per-device subkey be derived deterministically from
 539:    master (HKDF-with-device-tag) OR generated independently and
 540:    bound by master signature?** Tradeoff: deterministic = simpler
 541:    recovery, harder revocation (revoked key derivable). Independent
 542:    = easier revocation, recovery needs master-key access. Lean:
 543:    independent + master signature.
 544: 2. **What's the device-presence CRDT exact shape?** OR-Set
 545:    (presence is add-wins) vs LWW-Register (last-write-wins). Lean:
 546:    OR-Set for presence, LWW for last-seen timestamp.
 547: 3. **Confidential compute: how much of the daemon goes in the
 548:    enclave?** Just the key handling (smallest TCB, easiest port)?
 549:    Or the full crypto pipeline (more secure, larger TCB)? Lean:
 550:    start with keys-only; expand.
 551: 4. **Channel-reciprocity 2FA: is it mandatory or optional?**
 552:    Mandatory = harder for some users (need RF-capable devices);
 553:    optional = weaker. Lean: optional Factor 2 on hardware that
 554:    supports it; mandatory only in Hardened tier.
 555: 
 556: These get resolved at ADR time as each phase starts.

   1: # Coherence Transfer Brain
   2: 
   3: Status: in_progress for v0.11.0.
   4: 
   5: One Link should not blindly use the most advanced transfer protocol every time.
   6: The correct behavior is context-aware:
   7: 
   8: - if the peer is old, use the fastest shared protocol;
   9: - if the receiver has no prior chunks, avoid slow CDC planning unless it buys
  10:   resilience;
  11: - if the receiver has almost the whole object already, pay the CDC cost when
  12:   the wire savings beat the manifest CPU cost;
  13: - if multiple trusted devices have pieces, split missing chunks across them;
  14: - if a route degrades, automatically refresh route/session and simplify the
  15:   protocol until health recovers.
  16: 
  17: ## Coherence Sources Mined
  18: 
  19: From `$HOME\Projects\Coherence\coherence_lang\coherence_lang`:
  20: 
  21: - `npe/strategy/adaptive_cost.py`
  22:   - calibration tiers: cold, warming, warm, hot, verified;
  23:   - confidence from observed runtime behavior;
  24:   - hardware/route-aware cost predictions;
  25:   - multi-objective optimization.
  26: - `npe/coherence/regulator.py`
  27:   - autonomic health loop;
  28:   - healthy, observing, constrained, repair states;
  29:   - graduated response instead of scary user errors.
  30: - `loovm/dataflow_scheduler.py`
  31:   - prove independence, then parallelize;
  32:   - conservative fallback when independence is unknown.
  33: - `npe/strategy/quantum_solver.py`
  34:   - Pareto frontier selection;
  35:   - route/backend switching for hot regions.
  36: 
  37: ## What Landed
  38: 
  39: `one_link.transfer_brain` adds a deterministic planning core:
  40: 
  41: - route observations with EMA latency/bandwidth/energy;
  42: - reliability and calibration confidence;
  43: - Pareto-frontier transfer candidate selection;
  44: - health regulator states;
  45: - strategy estimates for:
  46:   - `hash_stream`
  47:   - `fixed_manifest`
  48:   - `cdc_manifest`
  49:   - `swarm_cdc`
  50: 
  51: This does not require a server or cloud. It is local learning on the user's own
  52: device.
  53: 
  54: The live daemon now also uses the same conclusion operationally: peers that
  55: support CDC no longer force large first-time sends through Python CDC. For
  56: files above `128 MiB`, One Link automatically uses the fast stream lane unless
  57: the transfer is already resuming an existing CDC send. That directly fixes the
  58: "video never arrived because planning was too slow" class of failure while
  59: keeping CDC for the cases where it is currently worth it.
  60: 
  61: v0.11.3 adds the next speed layer: the fast stream lane is pipelined. Instead
  62: of sending one chunk and waiting for one ACK, it keeps a bounded window of
  63: encrypted chunks in flight. Chunk size scales with file size up to `4 MiB`, and
  64: the in-flight window is capped at `24 MiB` / `16` chunks so One Link can push
  65: hard on Wi-Fi/Ethernet without unbounded RAM growth.
  66: 
  67: v0.11.6 adds the first binary stream lane. Peers that advertise
  68: `file_binary_frame` still use the same authenticated encrypted channel, but
  69: file chunks are carried as `OLB1 + compact-json-header + raw-bytes` instead of
  70: JSON with base64 content. Older peers automatically keep using the JSON stream
  71: fallback. This removes the base64 expansion tax for upgraded peers without
  72: splitting security into a second transport.
  73: 
  74: ## Current Important Result
  75: 
  76: The current Python CDC implementation is about `8 MiB/s` on the local Windows
  77: dev machine. The new fast identity lanes measured:
  78: 
  79: - hash-only manifest: about `1.6 GiB/s`;
  80: - fixed-size manifest: about `1.2 GiB/s`;
  81: - CDC manifest: about `8 MiB/s`.
  82: 
  83: That means One Link must be selective:
  84: 
  85: - old/non-CDC peer -> hash-only stream;
  86: - new video with no prior knowledge -> hash-only or fixed manifest;
  87: - related file/version/video with high prior knowledge -> CDC or swarm CDC
  88:   once CDC indexing is fast enough to beat plain streaming;
  89: - degraded route -> simpler protocol + automatic route/session repair.
  90: 
  91: ## Next Build Steps
  92: 
  93: 1. Feed real transfer observations into `AdaptiveTransferBrain` from the daemon.
  94: 2. Persist per-peer route stats in SQLite.
  95: 3. Add prior-hit-rate estimates from chunk cache before choosing CDC.
  96: 4. Add fixed-manifest wire negotiation for aligned media blocks.
  97: 5. Add swarm CDC fetch execution, not just planning.
  98: 6. Add perf gates so a change cannot silently make transfer planning slower.
  99: 7. Measure binary-frame LAN throughput on two upgraded devices and use the
 100:    result to tune the adaptive stream window.
 101: 
 102: ## Critical Finding
 103: 
 104: The transfer brain does not blindly choose CDC. With today's Python CDC speed,
 105: a huge file on a fast LAN can still be faster as `hash_stream` even when the
 106: receiver has most of the bytes already. That is not a failure of the planner;
 107: it is evidence that the next breakthrough is a native CDC engine. Once CDC
 108: rises from ~`8 MiB/s` to native-class throughput, the same planner flips
 109: high-prior large files to CDC/swarm and sends only the missing pieces.
 110: 
 111: The goal is not to look advanced. The goal is to make the advanced path
 112: disappear behind "send anything and it arrives."

   1: # ADR-0001: Content-Defined Chunking Kernel — FastCDC with Gear Hash + AVX-512 SIMD
   2: 
   3: **Status:** ACCEPTED (Phase A1 acceptance number — do not revisit without ADR amendment)
   4: **Phase:** A1 (item #2: native CDC kernel choice)
   5: **Supersedes:** existing `src/one_link/cdc.py` (Python rolling-hash CDC at ~8 MiB/s)
   6: 
   7: ---
   8: 
   9: ## Context
  10: 
  11: CDC is on the per-byte hot path. Every byte ingested by One Link gets fed through the rolling hash; chunk boundaries determined by the kernel control dedup quality, transfer initiation cost (Bloom filter sizing), and storage amplification. The kernel choice locks in:
  12: 
  13: 1. **Throughput floor.** A 1 GiB/s ingest gate (Phase A1 acceptance) requires the rolling hash to run faster than the rest of the pipeline. FastCDC reference C runs ~1.5 GiB/s/core; SIMD-accelerated FastCDC (AVX-512) runs 5+ GiB/s/core; Gear-only (no boundary normalization) goes higher. Anything slower than 1.5 GiB/s/core ends up the bottleneck once AEAD (~5 GiB/s/core via AES-NI) and BLAKE3 (~3 GiB/s/core) are running.
  14: 
  15: 2. **Chunk size distribution.** Determines bloom filter sizing for transfer initiation (ADR-0008), erasure-stripe sizing (ADR-0004), AEAD frame size (ADR-0002). All three depend on the chunk size statistics the kernel produces. Picking a kernel without committing to a distribution = downstream blast radius.
  16: 
  17: 3. **Cross-platform determinism.** Same input must produce same chunk boundaries on x86-64, ARM64 (Apple Silicon), and (eventually) RISC-V. SIMD acceleration must not produce different boundaries than the reference.
  18: 
  19: ## Decision
  20: 
  21: **Use FastCDC with Gear hash + AVX-512 / NEON SIMD acceleration. Reference scalar implementation as fallback for non-SIMD platforms.**
  22: 
  23: Parameters:
  24: 
  25: | Parameter | Value | Rationale |
  26: |---|---|---|
  27: | Min chunk size | **8 KiB** | Below this, dedup metadata overhead (32-byte BLAKE3 hash + 16-byte ratchet-key-id + bloom-filter slot) dominates. |
  28: | Average chunk size | **64 KiB** | Standard FastCDC parameter; matches Tarsnap, Restic, Borg, OneField production. Hits Bloom-filter sweet spot at ~8 bits/chunk for receivers with ~1 GiB corpus. |
  29: | Max chunk size | **256 KiB** | Above this, FUSE read amplification gets bad (a 64 KiB userspace read decrypts a full chunk). Joint with AEAD frame size (ADR-0002). |
  30: | Boundary mask | **0x0000_0070_0703_0190** (FastCDC small-mask), **0x0000_0058_0303_0590** (FastCDC large-mask) | Standard FastCDC published parameters; produces the documented chunk size distribution centered on 64 KiB. |
  31: | Hash kernel | **Gear-256** (256-entry random table, 64-bit rolling state) | Bytes per cycle ~1.5 scalar; ~4-6 with AVX-512 VPMULLQ + VPSLLQ. NEON: ~3-4. |
  32: 
  33: **Rejected alternatives:**
  34: 
  35: - **Rabin fingerprinting** (Borg, original LBFS): 0.5-1 GiB/s/core scalar, hard to SIMD because of polynomial-arithmetic dependencies. Too slow for the engine budget.
  36: - **Buzhash** (rsync, BorgBackup older): similar perf to Rabin, same SIMD problem.
  37: - **AE (asymmetric extremum)**: better dedup ratio than Gear in some workloads but ~30% slower; not enough to justify against Gear+SIMD.
  38: - **CDC-Less / fixed-size chunking**: kills dedup on insertions; only useful for already-aligned content (database pages). Reject as a primary kernel; expose as an optional manifest-format mode for use cases where alignment is guaranteed.
  39: 
  40: ## Consequences
  41: 
  42: **Positive:**
  43: - Throughput floor of 5+ GiB/s/core on AVX-512 hardware ≈ 8x the engine's 1 GiB/s gate. Plenty of headroom for the rest of the pipeline.
  44: - Cross-platform determinism via same Gear-256 table on every arch. SIMD changes microarchitecture, not the byte-output.
  45: - Chunk size distribution well-characterized; downstream sizing decisions (Bloom filter, AEAD frame, stripe) can be set with confidence.
  46: - OneField Mesh `transport/cdc_dedup.cl` already uses this family (FNV-1a-based, similar shape). Algorithmic understanding shared across projects.
  47: 
  48: **Negative:**
  49: - AVX-512 isn't universal. Pre-Zen-4 AMD lacks it; Intel post-2018 has it on most server SKUs but Alder Lake P-cores have it disabled in BIOS by default. NEON is universal on ARM64. Mitigation: scalar reference path is never slower than 1.2 GiB/s/core (FastCDC paper benchmark), still meets engine budget on a single core for orchestration, and SIMD is a dispatched runtime selection, not a hard requirement.
  50: - 256-byte hash table consumes 2 KiB of cache per-thread. Acceptable; L1 is 32-48 KiB.
  51: 
  52: ## Verification
  53: 
  54: Acceptance criteria for the CDC implementation:
  55: 
  56: 1. **Throughput gate**: 1 GiB unique-data ingest in <500ms on a single core (≥2 GiB/s/core measured). Stretch: ≥5 GiB/s/core with AVX-512.
  57: 2. **Determinism gate**: byte-for-byte identical chunk boundaries on x86-64, ARM64 (Apple Silicon), and Windows (MSVC + GCC + Clang builds). Test corpus = 100 MiB random-bytes pinned by SEED=42 + 100 MiB real-world file mix.
  58: 3. **Distribution gate**: on a 1 GiB Linux kernel source tree, chunk size mean ∈ [60 KiB, 68 KiB], P5 ≥ 12 KiB, P95 ≤ 192 KiB.
  59: 4. **Algebraic correctness gate**: scanned boundaries tile the input exactly (no gaps, no overlap, first.start = 0, last.end = buf.len). Each boundary's raw_address equals BLAKE3-256 of `buf[start..end]`. Verified by property tests.
  60: 5. **Reference-fixture pin**: a fixed pseudo-random 1 MiB input produces a pinned set of boundary offsets. Any change to that pinned set is a wire-format break and requires an ADR amendment plus a migration plan.
  61: 
  62: ## Wire-compat note (vs existing Python `src/one_link/cdc.py`)
  63: 
  64: The existing v0.20.x Python kernel is a custom Gear-CDC variant (16 KiB min, 64 KiB avg, 256 KiB max, single boundary mask). FastCDC v2020 is a different algorithm (8 KiB min per this ADR, two-mask normalized chunking) and produces different boundaries on the same input. **This is a deliberate kernel upgrade.**
  65: 
  66: Migration path:
  67: 
  68: - Phase A1 ships FastCDC v2020 as the *new* kernel. Chunks ingested under A1 onwards use it.
  69: - Existing chunks from v0.20.x stay readable — they were stored under the old kernel but are content-addressed by their BLAKE3 hashes; the chunk store doesn't care which kernel produced the boundaries.
  70: - Folder sync between a v0.21.0+ peer and a v0.20.x peer for *new* content gets a graceful protocol downgrade if both peers haven't upgraded; engineering: foldersync.py negotiates kernel version during pairing, falls back to legacy Gear-CDC when talking to v0.20.x. Wire-compat preserved across the transition.
  71: - Internal storage: the chunk_log records (per ADR-0003) carry no kernel-identifier flag because chunks are content-addressed; the kernel that produced a chunk is irrelevant once the chunk exists.
  72: 
  73: ## References
  74: 
  75: - FastCDC paper: Xia et al., USENIX ATC 2016.
  76: - FastCDC C reference: https://github.com/nlfiedler/fastcdc-rs (port basis)
  77: - Gear hash: Xia et al., ATC 2014.
  78: - OneField Mesh design: `OneField Mesh/onefield/transport/cdc_dedup.cl` (~195 lines, 13 tests).
  79: - Existing One Link Python impl: `src/one_link/cdc.py` (regression baseline).

   1: # ADR-0002: AEAD Primitive and Frame Size
   2: 
   3: **Status:** ACCEPTED (Phase A1 acceptance number — do not revisit without ADR amendment)
   4: **Phase:** A1 (item #6: AEAD frame size decision; item #7: per-chunk AEAD)
   5: **Depends on:** ADR-0001 (CDC chunk size distribution)
   6: 
   7: ---
   8: 
   9: ## Context
  10: 
  11: Per the FILE_ENGINE_V2_PLAN.md stress-test critique #3: AEAD frame size governs FUSE read amplification. Chunks decrypt as a unit; if a userspace `read(offset, 64 KiB)` translates to "decrypt the full 256 KiB chunk that contains this offset," the engine wastes 75% of its AEAD budget on bytes nobody asked for. This MUST be decided in A1 — not discovered when FUSE ships in B.
  12: 
  13: Additionally, the AEAD primitive choice locks in:
  14: 
  15: 1. **Throughput.** Phase A1 acceptance gate: ≥4 GiB/s/core (AES-NI) or ≥3 GiB/s/core (ChaCha20).
  16: 2. **Forward secrecy interaction.** Per-chunk forward-secret ratchet (Phase C) means each chunk's key is independently derived. The AEAD must accept fresh keys per chunk without per-chunk key-schedule cost dominating.
  17: 3. **Side-channel posture.** Constant-time per-block. AES-NI is hardware constant-time on every modern x86. ChaCha20 is constant-time by construction in software.
  18: 4. **Browser compatibility.** WebRTC DataChannel browsers in v0.20.x already do AES-128-GCM via DTLS-SRTP. Our AEAD is at a different layer (per-chunk) but shares the JS-side primitives if browser-as-peer ever needs to verify chunks.
  19: 
  20: ## Decision
  21: 
  22: **Primary AEAD: AES-256-GCM via AES-NI / VAES intrinsics. Fallback: ChaCha20-Poly1305 on hardware lacking AES-NI.**
  23: 
  24: **Frame size = chunk size, but each chunk is internally divided into 16 KiB AEAD frames with independent nonces.**
  25: 
  26: Critical clarifying detail: a "chunk" (the CDC output, 8-256 KiB per ADR-0001) is the dedup unit. A "frame" (16 KiB internal subdivision) is the AEAD unit. One chunk = one or more sequential frames. This split is what makes FUSE random-access reads cheap.
  27: 
  28: Parameters:
  29: 
  30: | Parameter | Value | Rationale |
  31: |---|---|---|
  32: | Primary cipher | **AES-256-GCM** | AES-NI / VAES = ~5 GiB/s/core x86; HW-accelerated constant-time; PQ-relevant key length (256 bit ≈ 128-bit PQ security per Grover halving). |
  33: | Fallback cipher | **ChaCha20-Poly1305** | ARM64 NEON path; ~3 GiB/s/core; constant-time by construction. |
  34: | AEAD frame size | **16 KiB plaintext payload** | At a 64 KiB chunk-size mean, a chunk holds 4 frames. FUSE 64-KiB random read decrypts 1 frame (16 KiB), worst-case 2 frames if cross-frame. 4× amplification reduction vs whole-chunk-frames. |
  35: | Nonce structure | **96-bit: chunk_id_lo64 \|\| frame_index_u32** | chunk_id_lo64 = lower 64 bits of BLAKE3(chunk_plaintext); guaranteed unique per chunk under content-addressing. frame_index distinguishes frames within a chunk. Reuse-impossible by construction. |
  36: | AAD | **chunk_id_full256 (32 bytes BLAKE3)** | Binds frame-level encryption to the chunk identity; tamper of chunk_id invalidates auth tag. |
  37: | Tag size | **128 bit (full GCM tag, 16 bytes Poly1305)** | Truncation savings (~3% per 16 KiB frame) not worth the security loss. |
  38: | Per-chunk overhead | **frames × 16 bytes (auth tags)** | A 64 KiB chunk → 4 frames × 16 = 64 bytes overhead = 0.097%. Negligible. |
  39: | Key derivation | **chunk_key = HKDF-Expand-Label(ratchet_chain_key, "ol-chunk", chunk_id_full256, 32)** | Per-chunk key independent from session ratchet state; future per-chunk forward-secret ratchet (Phase C) re-derives chain_key per chunk too, completing the ratchet. |
  40: 
  41: **Rejected alternatives:**
  42: 
  43: - **Whole-chunk-as-one-frame (no internal frames)**: simpler, but FUSE read amplification is unbounded. Reject.
  44: - **AES-128-GCM**: 128-bit security ≈ 64-bit PQ. Reject for PQ-conservative posture.
  45: - **AES-256-OCB**: better software perf than GCM, but AES-NI gives GCM hardware advantage that OCB can't match. Reject.
  46: - **AES-256-GCM-SIV**: nonce-misuse-resistant, but our nonce structure is reuse-impossible by construction (content-addressed chunk_id). The SIV cost (extra cipher pass for synthetic IV) buys us nothing. Reject.
  47: - **XChaCha20-Poly1305**: 192-bit nonce. Buys nothing beyond ChaCha20-Poly1305 here because our nonce structure is constructed, not random. Reject.
  48: 
  49: ## Consequences
  50: 
  51: **Positive:**
  52: - FUSE read amplification capped at 16 KiB per random read (worst case 32 KiB if cross-frame). Bounded.
  53: - AES-NI throughput far exceeds the 1 GiB/s engine gate. Headroom for parallelism.
  54: - Per-chunk forward-secret ratchet (Phase C) integrates cleanly: ratchet step happens at chunk boundary, frame keys derived from per-chunk key. Fits Signal-class double-ratchet without overhead per frame.
  55: - Nonce reuse impossible. 64-bit chunk_id collision probability < 2^-64; in practice the BLAKE3 256-bit address is the canonical identifier and 64-bit prefix collision is birthday-bound to ~2^32 chunks (4 billion); engine will refuse to write a chunk whose 64-bit prefix collides with an existing one.
  56: 
  57: **Negative:**
  58: - 16 KiB frame size is below typical CPU L1 working sets but above L1 line size. Two-pass: encrypt then auth, or interleaved; with AES-NI VAES, single pass dominates either way.
  59: - ChaCha20-Poly1305 fallback isn't constant-time-equivalent to AES-NI in throughput. ARM64 systems pay ~40% perf on this layer. Acceptable; ARM64 is not the line-rate target machine for v1.
  60: 
  61: ## Verification
  62: 
  63: 1. **Throughput gate (A1, software AES)**: encrypt + auth 256 KiB chunks, single core: ≥ 2 GiB/s sustained for both AES-GCM (software) and ChaCha20-Poly1305. This is the honest baseline measured with the RustCrypto crates' default backend.
  64: 1a. **Throughput gate (Phase B optimization, AES-NI)**: target ≥ 4 GiB/s/core for AES-256-GCM via AES-NI hardware acceleration. Attempted in A1 via `RUSTFLAGS="-C target-feature=+aes,+pclmulqdq"` but blocked on this dev box by Windows Smart App Control / WDAC; production wheels will enable AES-NI at the build matrix level (cibuildwheel + per-platform target-feature) and the 4 GiB/s gate becomes load-bearing then. Tracked as a Phase B deliverable, not a Phase A1 release blocker.
  65: 2. **FUSE read amplification gate**: random 64 KiB read on a 100 GiB virtual file induces ≤32 KiB AEAD work. Measured via instrumented decrypt counter.
  66: 3. **Nonce reuse impossible-test**: write 100M chunks; assert no 64-bit chunk_id collision; if collision detected, engine MUST refuse the write.
  67: 4. **Per-chunk-key independence**: revealing one chunk's key reveals nothing about adjacent chunks (property test against derivation function).
  68: 
  69: ## References
  70: 
  71: - AES-NI / VAES throughput: Intel Optimization Reference Manual; tested via OpenSSL `evp_aes_256_gcm`.
  72: - BLAKE3 hash: https://github.com/BLAKE3-team/BLAKE3 (Rust crate is reference impl).
  73: - HKDF-Expand-Label: TLS 1.3 RFC 8446 §7.1, adapted with our label scheme.
  74: - Signal double ratchet: signal.org spec; our per-chunk variant generalizes the per-message ratchet to per-content-addressed-chunk.

   1: # ADR-0003: Chunk Store On-Disk Format
   2: 
   3: **Status:** ACCEPTED (Phase A1 acceptance number — do not revisit without ADR amendment)
   4: **Phase:** A1 (items #4 crash-only WAL, #5 LSM index, #8 manifest WAL)
   5: **Depends on:** ADR-0001 (chunk sizes), ADR-0002 (frame structure)
   6: 
   7: ---
   8: 
   9: ## Context
  10: 
  11: The chunk store is the engine's durability surface. Per the plan stress-test #1 and #3, the on-disk format must support:
  12: 
  13: 1. **Crash-only recovery.** `kill -9` at any byte must leave the store consistent. Replay reconstructs intent from the WAL.
  14: 2. **Both raw-BLAKE3 AND convergent-BLAKE3 chunk addressing from day one.** Phase B can flip the Bloom-init default to convergent encryption without breaking existing manifests.
  15: 3. **Stripe layout from day one.** Reed-Solomon erasure coding ships in Phase C; the on-disk format must already be able to record stripe membership without a format break.
  16: 4. **Per-chunk ratchet-key-id field from day one.** Phase C per-chunk ratchet integrates without format break.
  17: 5. **Bloom filter front for the LSM index.** Sub-microsecond chunk-presence checks.
  18: 6. **Mmap-friendly reads.** Hot path reads chunks via mmap; pre-allocated, page-aligned writes via `fallocate` / `SetEndOfFile`.
  19: 
  20: This format is the load-bearing constraint for the entire engine. Get it wrong and every later layer pays the cost of working around it.
  21: 
  22: ## Decision
  23: 
  24: **Three on-disk components, all crash-only:**
  25: 
  26: ```
  27: <data_dir>/store/
  28: ├── chunk_log/               # Append-only chunk content WAL (the durability log)
  29: │   ├── 000001.clog          # 256 MiB per file; rotates by size
  30: │   ├── 000002.clog
  31: │   └── ...
  32: ├── manifest_log/            # Append-only manifest WAL (tied to chunk_log via WAL Coupling)
  33: │   ├── 000001.mlog
  34: │   └── ...
  35: └── index/                   # LSM index over chunk_log + manifest_log
  36:     ├── memtable.wal         # In-memory table backing log
  37:     ├── L0/000001.sst        # Sorted string tables, level 0 (newest, possibly overlapping)
  38:     ├── L1/...               # Compacted, non-overlapping
  39:     └── bloom/               # Bloom filter front (one per SST)
  40: ```
  41: 
  42: ### chunk_log record format (on-disk, little-endian):
  43: 
  44: ```
  45: +--------+------------------------------------------------------------------+
  46: | Offset | Field                                                            |
  47: +--------+------------------------------------------------------------------+
  48: | 0      | record_kind: u8                                                  |
  49: |        |   0x01 = ChunkBlob                                                |
  50: |        |   0x02 = StripeParity                                             |
  51: |        |   0xFE = TombstoneRef (chunk reclaimed; address still valid)     |
  52: |        |   0xFF = Sentinel (rotation marker)                               |
  53: | 1      | flags: u8                                                        |
  54: |        |   bit 0: address_kind (0=raw-BLAKE3, 1=convergent-BLAKE3)         |
  55: |        |   bit 1: aead_kind (0=AES-256-GCM, 1=ChaCha20-Poly1305)           |
  56: |        |   bit 2: compressed (0=raw, 1=zstd-encoded plaintext before AEAD) |
  57: |        |   bit 3: format_aware (0=CDC, 1=format-aware boundary)            |
  58: |        |   bit 4-7: reserved (must be zero)                                |
  59: | 2      | reserved: u16 (must be zero)                                     |
  60: | 4      | length_plaintext: u32 (8 KiB - 256 KiB per ADR-0001)             |
  61: | 8      | length_ciphertext: u32 (length_plaintext + frame_count*16)       |
  62: | 12     | chunk_id_full: [u8; 32] (BLAKE3-256 of plaintext OR convergent)  |
  63: | 44     | ratchet_key_id: [u8; 16] (HKDF derivation seed; ADR-0006)        |
  64: | 60     | stripe_descriptor: StripeDescriptor (24 bytes; ADR-0004)          |
  65: | 84     | aead_frames: [AeadFrame; frame_count] (16 KiB plaintext + 16 byte tag each)
  66: | ...    | (frame_count = ceil(length_plaintext / 16384))                    |
  67: +--------+------------------------------------------------------------------+
  68: | End    | record_crc32c: u32 (CRC32-Castagnoli of header + frames)         |
  69: +--------+------------------------------------------------------------------+
  70: ```
  71: 
  72: Header is fixed 84 bytes. Body is `length_ciphertext` bytes. Trailer is 4 bytes CRC.
  73: 
  74: ### manifest_log record format:
  75: 
  76: ```
  77: +--------+------------------------------------------------------------------+
  78: | 0      | record_kind: u8                                                  |
  79: |        |   0x10 = ManifestVersion (a CRDT op on a folder)                  |
  80: |        |   0x11 = CapabilityGrant                                          |
  81: |        |   0x12 = CapabilityRevoke                                         |
  82: |        |   0x13 = MerkleRevocationLogEntry                                 |
  83: |        |   0x14 = ShareLink                                                |
  84: |        |   0xFF = Sentinel                                                 |
  85: | 1      | flags: u8 (reserved=0)                                           |
  86: | 2      | length: u16 (record body length, max 64 KiB)                     |
  87: | 4      | hlc_timestamp: u64 (hybrid logical clock)                        |
  88: | 12     | actor_id: [u8; 32] (peer fingerprint; CRDT actor identifier)     |
  89: | 44     | chunk_log_anchor: u64 (chunk_log offset this record commits *with*; ADR-0005 WAL coupling) |
  90: | 52     | body: [u8; length] (canonically-encoded record per std.codec.canon)
  91: | ...    |                                                                  |
  92: +--------+------------------------------------------------------------------+
  93: | End    | record_crc32c: u32                                               |
  94: +--------+------------------------------------------------------------------+
  95: ```
  96: 
  97: ### Index SST format:
  98: 
  99: Standard sorted-string-table layout, key = chunk_id_full (32 bytes), value = (clog_file_id, clog_offset, length_ciphertext, ratchet_key_id, stripe_descriptor). Each SST has a sidecar Bloom filter (10 bits/key, ~1% false positive rate, ~1.25 MB per million chunks).
 100: 
 101: ### Atomicity contract:
 102: 
 103: Every write follows this sequence:
 104: 1. Append AEAD-encrypted chunk frames + header + CRC to `chunk_log/NNNNNN.clog` via `write()` then `fdatasync()`.
 105: 2. Append manifest record (with `chunk_log_anchor = clog_offset_just_written`) to `manifest_log/NNNNNN.mlog` then `fdatasync()`.
 106: 3. Update in-memory index (memtable). Memtable is durable via the chunk_log+manifest_log; no separate memtable WAL needed (eliminates one durability path = simpler crash recovery).
 107: 4. When memtable ≥ 64 MiB, flush to L0 SST. Flush is a non-durability operation (chunk_log + manifest_log are still authoritative); SST is rebuildable from them.
 108: 
 109: ### Recovery contract (crash-only):
 110: 
 111: 1. On boot, scan all `chunk_log/*.clog` files. For each record, verify CRC; reject torn/corrupt records (last record of last file is the only legitimate truncation point). Build chunk_id → location map in memory.
 112: 2. Scan all `manifest_log/*.mlog` files. For each record, verify CRC; verify `chunk_log_anchor` references a valid chunk_log offset (otherwise the manifest commit happened *after* a chunk write that was lost; reject the manifest record).
 113: 3. Rebuild memtable from manifest_log records newer than the most recent flushed SST.
 114: 4. Rebuild SSTs that are missing or whose CRC sidecar fails.
 115: 
 116: No "graceful shutdown" path. No "did the file get fully synced" ambiguity. The CRC is the truth.
 117: 
 118: ## Consequences
 119: 
 120: **Positive:**
 121: - Both-address support (bit 0 of flags) means convergent encryption ships in B without format break.
 122: - Stripe descriptor reserved from day one (24 bytes always); EC encode/decode in C plugs in without rewriting the chunk_log format.
 123: - Ratchet-key-id reserved from day one; per-chunk forward-secret ratchet in C plugs in.
 124: - Crash-only by design: no graceful shutdown to break, no "shutdown_clean.txt" sentinel to forge.
 125: - Mmap-friendly: chunk frames are aligned to 16 KiB plaintext boundaries within a chunk; the 84-byte header is small enough to fit in a single page even for max-size chunks.
 126: - Manifest WAL coupling via `chunk_log_anchor` resolves stress-test #1: a manifest commit that references a chunk write that didn't make it to disk is detectable and rejected on recovery.
 127: - LSM index is rebuildable from the logs; bloom filter sidecar is rebuildable from the SST. Loss of either is recoverable.
 128: - Compatible with reproducible builds: all on-disk integers are little-endian by spec; CRC32-Castagnoli is deterministic.
 129: 
 130: **Negative:**
 131: - 84-byte chunk header is overhead at 0.13% for 64 KiB chunks. Acceptable.
 132: - Two-WAL design (chunk_log + manifest_log) doubles the syncs per logical write. Mitigated by group commit (ADR-0007): N concurrent writes batch into one fdatasync per WAL.
 133: - `chunk_log_anchor` couples manifest commits to specific chunk_log offsets. If we ever introduce log compaction that rewrites chunk_log offsets, the anchor must be re-mapped. Mitigation: log compaction operates only on full files and rewrites anchors atomically.
 134: 
 135: ## Verification
 136: 
 137: 1. **Crash injection gate**: kill -9 the writer at every byte offset of a 1 GiB workload (>10,000 random offsets). Recovery must produce a chunk store consistent with "every chunk whose record CRC validates is durable; every chunk whose record CRC fails or is torn is reject-on-load."
 138: 2. **Both-address gate**: write 1 M chunks half raw-BLAKE3, half convergent. Read back: both addressable, neither corrupts the other.
 139: 3. **Stripe descriptor compatibility**: in A1, stripe descriptor is always zero (no EC yet). In C, when EC encoder fills the field, A1-vintage chunks (zero descriptor) coexist with C-vintage chunks (filled descriptor) without index migration.
 140: 4. **Mmap read amplification**: a 64 KiB read at random offset within a 64 KiB chunk decrypts ≤32 KiB (one or two AEAD frames). Measured via instrumented decrypt counter.
 141: 5. **Recovery convergence**: write 10K chunks with WAL coupling; kill -9 between chunk_log and manifest_log appends; recovery rejects the orphaned chunk write OR forward-applies the matching manifest, but never produces a divergent state.
 142: 
 143: ## References
 144: 
 145: - LSM tree (LevelDB / RocksDB design): O'Neil et al., "The Log-Structured Merge-Tree," 1996.
 146: - Crash-only software: Candea + Fox, HotOS 2003.
 147: - WAL group commit: PostgreSQL `wal_writer` design.
 148: - CRC32-Castagnoli: hardware-accelerated on x86 (CRC32 instruction) and ARM64 (CRC32 extension).
 149: - BLAKE3: Reference https://github.com/BLAKE3-team/BLAKE3.
 150: - Sorted string tables: Bigtable paper, Chang et al., OSDI 2006.

   1: # ADR-0004: Erasure Coding Stripe Layout
   2: 
   3: **Status:** ACCEPTED (Phase A1 acceptance number — encoded in chunk_log header even before encoder ships in C)
   4: **Phase:** A1 (item #9: stripe layout decision); used by Phase C item #2 (erasure-coded durability)
   5: **Depends on:** ADR-0001 (chunk size), ADR-0003 (chunk_log header)
   6: 
   7: ---
   8: 
   9: ## Context
  10: 
  11: Per the FILE_ENGINE_V2_PLAN.md stress-test #1: erasure coding stripes need stripe metadata in the chunk-store layout. If A1 ships without stripe-descriptor support, retrofitting EC in C means a second blob namespace and dual writes — significant complexity. Decision: stripe layout is decided in A1; encoder/decoder ship in C.
  12: 
  13: Additionally, per stress-test #3: dedup is on data shards only; parity shards are per-storer (because parity over a stripe of chunks mixes ciphertexts; two peers with different stripe boundaries get different parity shards even if data shards are byte-identical).
  14: 
  15: This ADR locks in:
  16: 
  17: 1. **Stripe descriptor format** in the chunk_log header (ADR-0003 reserved bytes 60-83).
  18: 2. **Reed-Solomon parameters** (k data, m parity).
  19: 3. **Stripe boundary policy** (how chunks are grouped into stripes).
  20: 4. **Parity ownership rules** (who computes, who stores, who reads).
  21: 
  22: ## Decision
  23: 
  24: **Reed-Solomon (10, 4) over GF(2^8). Stripe boundaries follow CDC chunk boundaries deterministically. Data shards dedup; parity shards are per-storer-cohort.**
  25: 
  26: ### Stripe descriptor (24 bytes in chunk_log header):
  27: 
  28: ```
  29: struct StripeDescriptor {
  30:     stripe_id_lo64:        u64,    // BLAKE3-prefix(64) of canonical-encoded stripe membership list
  31:     stripe_role:           u8,     // 0=Data, 1=Parity, 2=NotStriped (chunk standalone)
  32:     stripe_index:          u8,     // 0..k-1 for Data; 0..m-1 for Parity (within this stripe)
  33:     stripe_k:              u8,     // Number of data shards (10 in initial parameter set)
  34:     stripe_m:              u8,     // Number of parity shards (4)
  35:     cohort_id_lo64:        u64,    // BLAKE3-prefix(64) of the storer cohort identity (for parity ownership)
  36:     reserved:              [u8; 4],// Must be zero
  37: }
  38: ```
  39: 
  40: Rationale per field:
  41: 
  42: - `stripe_id_lo64`: identifies which stripe this chunk belongs to. The full identity is the canonical-encoded sorted list of (stripe_k member chunk_ids); the 64-bit prefix is enough for stripe lookup with extremely low collision probability (birthday-bounded ~2^32 stripes).
  43: - `stripe_role`: distinguishes data vs parity. NotStriped = chunk is not part of any stripe (standalone or pre-EC chunks from A1 vintage).
  44: - `stripe_k` / `stripe_m`: encoded per-chunk so future parameter changes (e.g., RS(20, 6) for higher durability) don't break existing stripes. Engine reads the per-chunk values; doesn't assume globals.
  45: - `cohort_id_lo64`: identifies which group of storers this parity shard belongs to. **This is the field that breaks parity dedup** intentionally — two cohorts produce different parity for the same data because their cohort_id mixes into the parity derivation.
  46: 
  47: ### Reed-Solomon parameters: RS(10, 4) over GF(2^8)
  48: 
  49: - **k = 10 data shards.** Each shard is a CDC chunk (8-256 KiB per ADR-0001). Stripe size variance: 80 KiB worst-case minimum stripe (10× 8 KiB) to 2.56 MiB worst-case maximum (10× 256 KiB).
  50: - **m = 4 parity shards.** Survives any 4 simultaneous shard losses. Storage overhead: 40% (4 parity / 10 data). Acceptable for "lose any 2 of 5 devices" policy with ≥1.5× redundancy distributed across user's own devices + trusted peers.
  51: - **Galois field GF(2^8).** Standard RS field; matches OneField Mesh `transport/udp_fec.cl`. SIMD-accelerated on x86 (PCLMUL) and ARM64 (PMULL). Reference throughput: ~3 GiB/s/core encode, ~2 GiB/s/core decode (Backblaze reedsolomon and Klauspost reedsolomon-go benchmarks).
  52: 
  53: ### Stripe boundary policy: deterministic by content-hash
  54: 
  55: To ensure two peers who receive the same content compute the same stripe boundaries (so data shards dedup), stripe membership is determined by a deterministic content-hash function:
  56: 
  57: ```
  58: fn stripe_assignment(chunk_id: BlakeHash256, k: u8) -> (stripe_seed: u64, position: u8) {
  59:     let h = BLAKE3(b"ol-stripe-v1" || chunk_id || k.to_le_bytes()).first_64_bits();
  60:     let stripe_seed = h & !((1 << 6) - 1);  // Clear low 6 bits; positions occupy them
  61:     let position = (h & 0x3F) % k;          // Position within the stripe
  62:     (stripe_seed, position)
  63: }
  64: ```
  65: 
  66: Two peers each receiving 1000 chunks compute the same `stripe_seed` for chunks with identical chunk_ids. Stripes form when 10 chunks happen to share a `stripe_seed`. Because stripe_seed has 58 bits of entropy (64 - 6 reserved), seed collisions form natural stripe groupings without coordination.
  67: 
  68: **Why not contiguous-content stripes?** (Stripe_n = chunks 10n..10n+9 in arrival order.) Two peers receiving the same content in different order would compute different stripes, and no data shard would dedup. Hash-based assignment is order-independent.
  69: 
  70: **Why content-hash + reserve low bits for position?** Forces 1-of-k uniform distribution within a stripe. Without reservation, a hot chunk_id might end up at position 0 in 100 different stripes, defeating the spread.
  71: 
  72: ### Parity ownership rules
  73: 
  74: - Data shards live in the chunk store of every peer that has the underlying chunk content (normal dedup applies).
  75: - Parity shards are computed and stored by **storers** in a cohort. A "cohort" is a set of peers committed to maintaining redundancy for a folder. Each cohort has a `cohort_id` (32-byte BLAKE3 of canonical-encoded cohort membership).
  76: - A storer in cohort_id=X computes parity for stripes its cohort is responsible for; the parity shard is stored with `cohort_id_lo64 = first_64_bits(X)`. Other cohorts compute different parity (because cohort_id mixes into the parity derivation), so two cohorts holding the same 10 data shards each compute their own 4 parity shards. Parity does not dedup cross-cohort.
  77: - Reconstruction proceeds as standard RS: any 10 of 14 shards reconstructs the data.
  78: 
  79: ### Pre-Phase-C compatibility
  80: 
  81: In Phase A1, before EC encoder ships, every chunk_log record has `stripe_role = NotStriped (2)`, `stripe_id_lo64 = 0`, `cohort_id_lo64 = 0`. Phase C ships the encoder + decoder; new chunks written under EC-enabled cohorts get filled stripe descriptors. Old A1-vintage chunks remain `NotStriped` and are simply not part of any stripe (durability for them is from device-level replication, not RS).
  82: 
  83: ## Consequences
  84: 
  85: **Positive:**
  86: - Stripe descriptor reserved in A1 means C plugs in without a chunk_log format break.
  87: - Hash-based stripe assignment means data shards dedup across peers (good for sovereignty: parity is per-cohort, but data is universally dedupable).
  88: - RS(10, 4) at GF(2^8) is well-understood, SIMD-accelerated, and matches OneField's UDP FEC family. Cross-project consistency.
  89: - Engineer can change parameters per-stripe (k, m encoded per-chunk) so future RS(20, 6) deployments don't break existing stripes.
  90: - Parity ownership cleanly decouples cohorts. Two friend groups maintaining redundancy for overlapping content do not interfere.
  91: 
  92: **Negative:**
  93: - 24 bytes of header overhead per chunk for stripe descriptor, even when not striped (NotStriped uses 0 in those bytes; not free of bytes, but free of computational cost).
  94: - Hash-based stripe boundary means stripe membership is a function of which chunks happen to share a stripe_seed prefix. A folder might end up with most chunks in stripes spread across thousands of partial-stripe groupings. Mitigation: parity is computed only when a stripe is "full enough" (≥ k=10 members in same stripe_seed); incomplete stripes are not parity-protected, fall back to device-level replication. The engine surfaces stripe-completeness as a durability metric.
  95: - Reed-Solomon over GF(2^8) caps stripe size at 256 shards (255 actually, for non-trivial parity). Our k=10 + m=4 is well under this. If we ever want RS(64, 32), still fits.
  96: 
  97: ## Verification
  98: 
  99: 1. **Determinism gate**: two independent peers, given the same set of 1000 chunk_ids, compute identical stripe_seed for every chunk.
 100: 2. **Position uniformity**: position distribution across 1M chunks is within 5% of uniform across all k positions.
 101: 3. **RS encode/decode gate (Phase C, but layout-tested in A1)**: stripe descriptor field round-trips through chunk_log write/read; pre-EC, value is always (NotStriped, 0, 0, 0, 0). Phase C populates with valid encode parameters.
 102: 4. **Cohort isolation**: two cohorts holding identical data compute different parity (cohort_id_lo64 mixes into the RS derivation; verified by property test).
 103: 5. **Pre-EC compatibility**: A1-vintage chunks (all NotStriped) read correctly after Phase C lands; C-vintage chunks coexist without index migration.
 104: 
 105: ## References
 106: 
 107: - Reed-Solomon erasure coding: Plank, "Erasure Codes for Storage Applications," 2005.
 108: - Backblaze open-source reedsolomon: Java reference impl.
 109: - klauspost/reedsolomon: Go reference impl with SIMD.
 110: - OneField Mesh `transport/udp_fec.cl`: K+P Reed-Solomon over GF(2) for the UDP FEC layer (~189 lines, 13 tests).
 111: - BLAKE3 keyed-hash for stripe_seed derivation: BLAKE3 spec, "derive_key" mode.

   1: # ADR-0005: Manifest WAL Coupled to Chunk WAL
   2: 
   3: **Status:** ACCEPTED (Phase A1 acceptance number — must ship in A1, not C)
   4: **Phase:** A1 (item #4 crash-only WAL, item #8 manifest WAL)
   5: **Depends on:** ADR-0003 (chunk_log + manifest_log on-disk format)
   6: 
   7: ---
   8: 
   9: ## Context
  10: 
  11: Per the FILE_ENGINE_V2_PLAN.md stress-test critique #1: "Manifest WAL not coupled to chunk WAL → FUSE data loss on crash." Mitigation: manifest WAL is an A1 deliverable, NOT implicit in C.
  12: 
  13: The FUSE consistency hazard is concrete: the kernel returns `write()` success to userspace before the engine's WAL has fsync'd. If the daemon crashes between (a) appending the chunk to chunk_log and (b) appending the matching manifest entry to manifest_log, the engine boots with a chunk that has no manifest reference (orphan), or worse — boots with a manifest reference to a chunk that was lost in a torn write.
  14: 
  15: Without WAL coupling, the engine ships a FUSE that loses data on crash and may not detect it for hours or days.
  16: 
  17: This ADR specifies how the two logs are coupled atomically.
  18: 
  19: ## Decision
  20: 
  21: **Two-phase commit with chunk_log_anchor cross-reference, both fdatasync'd before the operation completes. Recovery rejects orphans on either side.**
  22: 
  23: ### Write protocol (per logical write of a new chunk):
  24: 
  25: ```
  26: phase 1: append chunk to chunk_log
  27:   1.1 serialize ChunkRecord {header + frames + crc} into a buffer
  28:   1.2 atomic append to chunk_log/NNNNNN.clog at offset O via write()
  29:   1.3 fdatasync(chunk_log_fd)
  30:   1.4 record (clog_file_id=NNNNNN, clog_offset=O, length_ciphertext=L) for phase 2
  31: 
  32: phase 2: append manifest entry to manifest_log (with the chunk_log_anchor referencing phase 1's location)
  33:   2.1 serialize ManifestRecord {hlc + actor + chunk_log_anchor=(NNNNNN, O) + body + crc}
  34:   2.2 atomic append to manifest_log/NNNNNN.mlog
  35:   2.3 fdatasync(manifest_log_fd)
  36: 
  37: phase 3 (memtable update; not durability-critical, rebuildable from logs):
  38:   3.1 insert into memtable: chunk_id -> (NNNNNN, O, L, ratchet_key_id, stripe_descriptor)
  39:   3.2 increment write counter for memtable flush threshold check
  40: ```
  41: 
  42: ### Crash points and outcomes:
  43: 
  44: | Crash before | Recovery sees | Action |
  45: |---|---|---|
  46: | 1.3 fdatasync chunk_log | Chunk record may be torn; CRC will fail | Reject torn record; treat as if write never happened. Manifest entry never appended. Consistent. |
  47: | 1.3 done, before 2.2 | Chunk record valid in chunk_log; no matching manifest record | Orphan chunk: visible in chunk_log scan but no manifest references it. Recovery: leave chunk in place; mark as "unreferenced" in memtable. GC reclaims later. |
  48: | 2.3 fdatasync manifest_log | Manifest record may be torn; CRC will fail | Reject torn record; matching chunk in chunk_log is now an orphan (same as above). Consistent. |
  49: | After 2.3 | Both records valid; recovery succeeds normally | Memtable rebuilt from logs. |
  50: 
  51: **Key invariant**: a manifest record's `chunk_log_anchor` references a specific (clog_file_id, clog_offset) that was already fsync'd before the manifest record itself was appended. Recovery validates the anchor: if the chunk_log doesn't have a valid CRC'd record at that offset, the manifest record is rejected. This means no manifest record ever survives that points to a chunk that was lost.
  52: 
  53: ### Group commit (performance):
  54: 
  55: A naive impl does 2 fdatasyncs per logical write. At ~1 ms per fsync on NVMe, this caps writes at 500/s/thread. Group commit batches:
  56: 
  57: ```
  58: fn write_batch(ops: Vec<ChunkWrite>) -> Result<()> {
  59:     // Phase 1 batch: append all chunk records, single fdatasync
  60:     for op in &ops {
  61:         serialize(&op.chunk_record).append_to(chunk_log)?;
  62:     }
  63:     fdatasync(chunk_log_fd)?;
  64: 
  65:     // Phase 2 batch: append all manifest records, single fdatasync
  66:     for op in &ops {
  67:         serialize(&op.manifest_record).append_to(manifest_log)?;
  68:     }
  69:     fdatasync(manifest_log_fd)?;
  70: 
  71:     // Phase 3 batch: memtable updates
  72:     for op in &ops {
  73:         memtable.insert(op.chunk_id, op.location);
  74:     }
  75: 
  76:     Ok(())
  77: }
  78: ```
  79: 
  80: A batch of 100 writes is 2 fdatasyncs total instead of 200. Throughput goes from 500/s/thread to 50,000+/s/thread (limited by NVMe IOPS, not fsync count).
  81: 
  82: Concurrent writers: a coordinator thread accumulates pending writes for ≤1 ms or until N writes accumulate, whichever first. Writers block on a Future that resolves when their batch's phase 2 fdatasync returns. This bounds latency at 1 ms while amortizing fdatasync cost.
  83: 
  84: ### Fsync semantics on each platform:
  85: 
  86: - **Linux**: `fdatasync(2)` = data + size metadata, no atime/mtime. Sufficient.
  87: - **macOS**: `F_FULLFSYNC` via `fcntl()` is the only way to get genuine durability past disk write cache. Plain `fsync(2)` lies. Use `F_FULLFSYNC` on the chunk_log and manifest_log fds.
  88: - **Windows**: `FlushFileBuffers()` is sufficient when the file is opened with `FILE_FLAG_WRITE_THROUGH` AND the underlying disk has its write cache disabled OR honors FUA. We open both logs with `FILE_FLAG_WRITE_THROUGH | FILE_FLAG_NO_BUFFERING` for chunk_log (8 KiB-aligned writes only) and `FILE_FLAG_WRITE_THROUGH` for manifest_log.
  89: 
  90: ### What's NOT durability-critical (and thus doesn't need fsync):
  91: 
  92: - Memtable updates: rebuildable from chunk_log + manifest_log.
  93: - SST flushes: rebuildable from memtable + logs.
  94: - Bloom filter sidecars: rebuildable from SSTs.
  95: - LSM compactions: rebuildable from L0 SSTs.
  96: 
  97: This minimizes the durability syscall count to exactly 2 per batch.
  98: 
  99: ## Consequences
 100: 
 101: **Positive:**
 102: - FUSE consistency hazard closed in A1, not deferred.
 103: - Crash recovery is monotonic: any state recovery sees is consistent with some prefix of operations actually committed.
 104: - Group commit amortizes fdatasync cost; throughput target (≥10K logical writes/s/thread on NVMe) is reachable.
 105: - Two separate log files mean parallel writers can append concurrently to chunk_log without blocking on manifest_log writers (and vice versa) — only the fdatasync is serialized.
 106: - Recovery is simple: linear scan + CRC validation + anchor cross-reference. No complex log-structured-merge replay logic.
 107: 
 108: **Negative:**
 109: - Two fdatasync per batch instead of one. Acceptable; group commit makes this near-free.
 110: - Orphan chunks accumulate (chunks whose manifest commit failed). GC must scan for them periodically. Mitigation: chunk_log records carry a reference-count flag updated by manifest_log scans on boot; orphans (refcount=0) are reclaimed by background GC.
 111: - Anchor-based recovery means we cannot reorder log files post-write (would invalidate anchors). Mitigation: chunk_log files are append-only and immutable until reclaimed by full-file GC; never edited.
 112: 
 113: ## Verification
 114: 
 115: 1. **Crash injection gate (the canonical Phase A1 acceptance test)**: kill -9 the writer at every byte offset of a 100K-write workload (random crash points). Recovery convergence: manifest references valid chunks; chunks without manifest are flagged as orphans (not durable for the user, but the engine state is consistent).
 116: 2. **Group commit throughput gate**: 100K logical writes (chunks of 64 KiB) sustained at ≥10K writes/s/thread on local NVMe.
 117: 3. **Fsync guarantee gate**: power-fail injection (fault-injection layer simulating cache loss). Recovery state matches "operations whose batch fsync returned" — never anything more.
 118: 4. **macOS F_FULLFSYNC verification**: on macOS, plain fsync is not sufficient; tested via fault-injection that simulates dirty disk-cache loss.
 119: 5. **Anchor cross-validation**: synthetic test with a manifest_log record whose chunk_log_anchor points to a torn/missing chunk_log offset. Recovery MUST reject the manifest record.
 120: 
 121: ## References
 122: 
 123: - Crash-only software: Candea + Fox, HotOS 2003.
 124: - WAL group commit: PostgreSQL `wal_writer.c`.
 125: - macOS F_FULLFSYNC: Apple `fsync(2)` man page; CockroachDB and SQLite use this for durability.
 126: - Linux fdatasync: `man 2 fdatasync`; faster than `fsync` for our case (no metadata changes).
 127: - "Files Are Hard": Pillai et al., OSDI 2014 — taxonomy of crash-consistency bugs we are designing to avoid.

   1: # ADR-0006: BLAKE3 Domain-Separated Derivation Scheme
   2: 
   3: **Status:** ACCEPTED (Phase A1 acceptance number)
   4: **Phase:** A1 (used by ADR-0001, 0002, 0003, 0004; touches every cryptographic layer)
   5: **Depends on:** nothing (this is a foundational ADR)
   6: 
   7: ---
   8: 
   9: ## Context
  10: 
  11: BLAKE3 underpins the engine: chunk addresses (raw + convergent), AEAD per-chunk key derivation, stripe seed assignment, capability hash, manifest content-addressing, ratchet key derivation. Every use of BLAKE3 in the engine MUST be domain-separated: a hash output from one purpose must NOT collide with or be predictable from a hash output for another purpose, even with the same input.
  12: 
  13: Without domain separation:
  14: - An attacker who learns one chunk's address can predict the convergent address of the same content (acceptable; addresses are not secrets) BUT could also predict the stripe_seed and the chunk's AEAD-key derivation seed if they share a derivation path. That's a problem.
  15: - An adversary who can choose plaintext and observe its chunk address could potentially derive the AEAD-key for that chunk.
  16: 
  17: This ADR specifies the **single canonical scheme** for every BLAKE3 use in the engine.
  18: 
  19: ## Decision
  20: 
  21: **Use BLAKE3's keyed-hash and derive_key modes with explicit, versioned domain separators. Every domain has a unique purpose-string, version-pinned, registered in this ADR.**
  22: 
  23: ### Three BLAKE3 modes used:
  24: 
  25: 1. **`hash(input)`** — unkeyed plain hash. Used ONLY for content-addressing (raw chunk addresses, manifest content-hashes) where output is publicly derivable from input.
  26: 2. **`keyed_hash(key, input)`** — keyed MAC mode. Used for derivations where the key is a secret (ratchet chain key, session key).
  27: 3. **`derive_key(context, key_material)`** — context-string-bound key derivation. Used for purpose-domain-separated subkeys from a master input.
  28: 
  29: ### Registered domain contexts (all start with `ol-` prefix and a version):
  30: 
  31: ```
  32: "ol-chunk-addr-raw-v1"            -> raw-BLAKE3 chunk address (BLAKE3 hash, NOT derive_key)
  33: "ol-chunk-addr-convergent-v1"     -> convergent-encryption chunk address (used as KEY input to AEAD)
  34: "ol-chunk-aead-key-v1"            -> AEAD key per chunk (derive_key context)
  35: "ol-chunk-frame-nonce-v1"         -> per-frame nonce derivation within a chunk (NOT actually used in production: nonce is constructed from chunk_id_lo64 || frame_index per ADR-0002; this context exists as a sanity check that nobody confuses derived-key with constructed-nonce)
  36: "ol-chunk-ratchet-id-v1"          -> 16-byte ratchet_key_id stored in chunk_log header
  37: "ol-stripe-seed-v1"               -> stripe assignment seed (ADR-0004)
  38: "ol-stripe-cohort-mix-v1"         -> cohort_id mixing for parity derivation
  39: "ol-manifest-id-v1"               -> manifest content-address (canonical-encoded manifest body)
  40: "ol-capability-id-v1"             -> capability fingerprint (canonical-encoded cap body)
  41: "ol-revocation-leaf-v1"           -> Merkle revocation log leaf hash
  42: "ol-revocation-internal-v1"       -> Merkle revocation log internal-node hash
  43: "ol-folder-crdt-actor-v1"         -> CRDT actor_id derivation (peer fingerprint -> actor_id)
  44: "ol-share-link-id-v1"             -> share-link fingerprint (canonical-encoded share body)
  45: "ol-bloom-init-key-v1"            -> Bloom filter hash-function seed (Phase B; reserved here)
  46: "ol-fountain-symbol-id-v1"        -> RaptorQ encoded-symbol identifier (Phase B; reserved)
  47: "ol-network-coding-id-v1"         -> XOR network-coding combined-symbol identifier (Phase B; reserved)
  48: "ol-pq-hybrid-derive-v1"          -> ML-KEM + X25519 hybrid combiner KDF (Phase C; reserved)
  49: ```
  50: 
  51: Reserved contexts for future phases are listed here so phases B/C/D do not accidentally collide with each other; ADR amendment required to add new contexts.
  52: 
  53: ### Use-site rules:
  54: 
  55: **Rule 1: Raw chunk address (ADR-0003 chunk_id_full when flags.address_kind = raw):**
  56: ```
  57: chunk_id_full = BLAKE3.hash(plaintext_chunk_bytes)
  58: ```
  59: No domain separator; this is the canonical content-address. Compatibility with external content-addressed-storage tooling depends on plain BLAKE3.
  60: 
  61: **Rule 2: Convergent chunk address (chunk_id_full when flags.address_kind = convergent):**
  62: ```
  63: chunk_id_full = BLAKE3.derive_key(
  64:     context = "ol-chunk-addr-convergent-v1",
  65:     key_material = plaintext_chunk_bytes,
  66:     output_length = 32,
  67: )
  68: ```
  69: Domain-separated from raw address so a single chunk has different addresses under each scheme; engine never confuses them.
  70: 
  71: **Rule 3: AEAD per-chunk key:**
  72: ```
  73: aead_key = BLAKE3.derive_key(
  74:     context = "ol-chunk-aead-key-v1",
  75:     key_material = ratchet_chain_key || chunk_id_full,
  76:     output_length = 32,  // AES-256
  77: )
  78: ```
  79: For convergent encryption, `ratchet_chain_key` is replaced by the chunk's content (derived deterministically) — guaranteeing identical plaintext → identical AEAD key → identical ciphertext from any sender.
  80: 
  81: **Rule 4: Ratchet key id (16 bytes stored in chunk_log header):**
  82: ```
  83: ratchet_key_id = BLAKE3.derive_key(
  84:     context = "ol-chunk-ratchet-id-v1",
  85:     key_material = ratchet_chain_key || chunk_id_full,
  86:     output_length = 16,
  87: )
  88: ```
  89: Used at recovery to look up which ratchet generation a chunk's AEAD key came from.
  90: 
  91: **Rule 5: Stripe seed (ADR-0004):**
  92: ```
  93: let h = BLAKE3.derive_key(
  94:     context = "ol-stripe-seed-v1",
  95:     key_material = chunk_id_full || stripe_k.to_le_bytes(),
  96:     output_length = 8,
  97: );
  98: let stripe_seed = u64::from_le_bytes(h) & !((1 << 6) - 1);  // Reserve low 6 bits for position
  99: let position = (u64::from_le_bytes(h) & 0x3F) % stripe_k;
 100: ```
 101: 
 102: **Rule 6: Cohort-mixed parity derivation:**
 103: Reed-Solomon parity computation incorporates `cohort_id` such that:
 104: ```
 105: parity_seed = BLAKE3.derive_key(
 106:     context = "ol-stripe-cohort-mix-v1",
 107:     key_material = stripe_id || cohort_id,
 108:     output_length = 32,
 109: )
 110: // parity_seed XOR-mixed into RS encode coefficients
 111: ```
 112: Result: two cohorts holding the same stripe data compute different parity. (Implementation detail in C-phase RS encoder; spec'd here.)
 113: 
 114: **Rule 7: Capability fingerprint:**
 115: ```
 116: cap_id = BLAKE3.derive_key(
 117:     context = "ol-capability-id-v1",
 118:     key_material = canonical_encode(cap_body),
 119:     output_length = 32,
 120: )
 121: ```
 122: Domain separates from manifest IDs; engine never confuses the two.
 123: 
 124: **Rule 8: Manifest content-address:**
 125: ```
 126: manifest_id = BLAKE3.derive_key(
 127:     context = "ol-manifest-id-v1",
 128:     key_material = canonical_encode(manifest_body),
 129:     output_length = 32,
 130: )
 131: ```
 132: 
 133: **Rule 9: Merkle revocation log:**
 134: ```
 135: leaf_hash = BLAKE3.derive_key(
 136:     context = "ol-revocation-leaf-v1",
 137:     key_material = canonical_encode(revocation_event),
 138:     output_length = 32,
 139: )
 140: internal_hash = BLAKE3.derive_key(
 141:     context = "ol-revocation-internal-v1",
 142:     key_material = left_child_hash || right_child_hash,
 143:     output_length = 32,
 144: )
 145: ```
 146: Domain-separated leaf vs internal so an attacker cannot present an internal-node hash as a leaf or vice versa (the second-preimage attack on naive Merkle trees).
 147: 
 148: ### Forbidden uses:
 149: 
 150: - **No string-concatenation pseudo-domain-separators.** `BLAKE3.hash("aead-key-" || chunk_id)` is forbidden. Use `derive_key`.
 151: - **No reuse of derived keys across purposes.** A key derived with `"ol-chunk-aead-key-v1"` MUST NOT be used as a ratchet input. Each derived key has exactly one purpose.
 152: - **No domain-separator-version reuse.** When the protocol semantics of a domain change, the version increments (`v1` → `v2`). Both versions remain valid (engine handles legacy chunks); an ADR amendment registers the new context.
 153: 
 154: ### Property tests:
 155: 
 156: - For every two distinct contexts c1 != c2 and every input x, `derive_key(c1, x) != derive_key(c2, x)` (probabilistically; collision is ~2^-256).
 157: - For every context c and inputs x1 != x2, `derive_key(c, x1) != derive_key(c, x2)`.
 158: - For raw vs convergent addressing: same plaintext produces different chunk_ids under the two modes.
 159: 
 160: ## Consequences
 161: 
 162: **Positive:**
 163: - All cryptographic boundaries domain-separated. An adversary who learns one derived key learns nothing about other derived keys, even with the same input.
 164: - Single canonical registry of contexts in this ADR; no ambiguity about what a given hash output means.
 165: - Versioned: protocol evolution doesn't break old chunks (engine recognizes both versions; can migrate gradually).
 166: - Aligns with NIST SP 800-185 KMAC pattern and BLAKE3 spec recommendations for derive_key.
 167: 
 168: **Negative:**
 169: - 16-byte context strings cost memory + a small fixed CPU overhead per BLAKE3 call. Negligible.
 170: - Adding a new domain requires ADR amendment, not just a code change. This is a feature: prevents accidental domain duplication across phases.
 171: 
 172: ## Verification
 173: 
 174: 1. **Domain-separation property test**: for each pair (c1, c2) in the registered context list, and 1M random inputs, verify `derive_key(c1, x) != derive_key(c2, x)`.
 175: 2. **Cross-version isolation**: when v2 of any domain ships, engine handles v1-vintage chunks via fallback path; v1 and v2 hashes never collide.
 176: 3. **No raw-keyed-hash ambiguity test**: assert that nothing in the codebase calls `BLAKE3.hash` with a runtime-string concatenation as input. Static lint check: any BLAKE3 use must be either (a) plain hash with literal input, (b) keyed_hash with explicit key parameter, (c) derive_key with one of the registered contexts.
 177: 
 178: ## References
 179: 
 180: - BLAKE3 spec: https://github.com/BLAKE3-team/BLAKE3-specs
 181: - BLAKE3 derive_key: spec §6.4
 182: - NIST SP 800-185 KMAC: parallel domain separation pattern
 183: - "Cryptographic Right Answers" Aumasson et al.: domain separation discussion
 184: - HKDF (RFC 5869): historical analog; we use BLAKE3.derive_key for stronger composability

   1: # ADR-0007: Crash-Only WAL Format and Replay Invariants
   2: 
   3: **Status:** ACCEPTED (Phase A1 acceptance number)
   4: **Phase:** A1 (item #4: crash-only WAL)
   5: **Depends on:** ADR-0003 (chunk_log + manifest_log on-disk format), ADR-0005 (WAL coupling protocol), ADR-0006 (BLAKE3 derive scheme)
   6: 
   7: ---
   8: 
   9: ## Context
  10: 
  11: Per the FILE_ENGINE_V2_PLAN.md, Phase A1 acceptance gate: "kill -9 survival across ≥10,000 randomized injection points; zero chunk loss; zero manifest divergence after recovery."
  12: 
  13: A WAL that's almost-crash-only ships subtle bugs for years. This ADR specifies the exact replay invariants and the exact failure modes the WAL handles.
  14: 
  15: The WAL must:
  16: 
  17: 1. Never lose a write whose batch's fdatasync returned success.
  18: 2. Never resurrect a write that was rolled back / never committed.
  19: 3. Detect and reject torn writes (kernel buffer page-size bounds; physical sector tearing).
  20: 4. Detect and reject corrupted records (bit-flips on disk, RAM corruption during write).
  21: 5. Allow safe rotation of log files (close old, open new) without losing in-flight writes.
  22: 6. Allow safe truncation of the tail of the most-recent log file when CRC fails on the last record.
  23: 7. Replay deterministically: two independent recovery runs of the same crashed state produce byte-identical recovered states.
  24: 
  25: ## Decision
  26: 
  27: **WAL format: append-only, length-prefixed records with CRC32-Castagnoli trailer. Replay scans linearly, validates CRCs, stops at first invalid record per file. File rotation creates a new file once size threshold is hit; old files are immutable until reclaimed by full-file GC.**
  28: 
  29: ### Per-file structure:
  30: 
  31: ```
  32: +---------+--------------------------------------------------------+
  33: | Offset  | Field                                                  |
  34: +---------+--------------------------------------------------------+
  35: | 0       | magic: [u8; 8] = b"OL-CLOG1" or b"OL-MLOG1"           |
  36: | 8       | format_version: u32 = 1                                |
  37: | 12      | log_kind: u32 (1 = chunk_log, 2 = manifest_log)        |
  38: | 16      | created_unix_micros: u64 (informational only; not load-bearing for recovery) |
  39: | 24      | reserved: [u8; 40] (zero-filled, must verify zero)     |
  40: | 64      | first_record: ...                                      |
  41: | ...     | (records)                                              |
  42: | EOF     | (last record may be torn; see truncation rules)        |
  43: +---------+--------------------------------------------------------+
  44: ```
  45: 
  46: The 64-byte file header is fsync'd at file creation, before the first record is written.
  47: 
  48: ### Per-record structure:
  49: 
  50: ```
  51: +---------+--------------------------------------------------------+
  52: | 0       | record_kind + flags (per-log-kind, see ADR-0003)       |
  53: | ...     | record header fields (per ADR-0003)                    |
  54: | ...     | record body                                            |
  55: | End     | record_crc32c: u32 (CRC of header + body)              |
  56: +---------+--------------------------------------------------------+
  57: ```
  58: 
  59: CRC is the **last 4 bytes** of every record. To compute, the writer:
  60: 
  61: 1. Builds the in-memory record buffer with CRC bytes set to zero placeholder.
  62: 2. Computes CRC32C over header + body.
  63: 3. Writes CRC bytes into the placeholder.
  64: 4. Issues a single `pwrite()` of the complete record at the next append offset.
  65: 5. Increments append offset by record length.
  66: 
  67: **Why not "write header, write body, write trailer separately"?** Because partial writes can interleave with concurrent writers and the kernel may flush a partial record to disk after a power-fail. A single `pwrite()` of the complete buffer is atomic at the syscall level (Linux: `pwrite` is atomic up to PIPE_BUF, but for files it's atomic relative to other syscalls in the same fd; we serialize writes through a single writer thread per log file, eliminating intra-file concurrency).
  68: 
  69: **Why not store CRC in a header field at the start?** Streaming writers cannot CRC before they know the length; CRC at the end means we know everything before computing it. Also matches LevelDB / RocksDB / BadgerDB convention.
  70: 
  71: ### Page-aligned writes (Windows, optionally Linux O_DIRECT):
  72: 
  73: On Windows with `FILE_FLAG_NO_BUFFERING`, writes must be sector-aligned (typically 512 bytes or 4 KiB). Records are not naturally sector-sized. Solution: writer pads each record's tail to the next 512-byte boundary with zero bytes (between the CRC32C trailer and the next record start). Padding bytes are not part of any record and not CRC'd; recovery skips zero-byte runs between records.
  74: 
  75: On Linux without O_DIRECT, no padding needed; the kernel page cache handles unaligned writes.
  76: 
  77: ### Replay algorithm:
  78: 
  79: ```rust
  80: fn replay_log(log_path: &Path) -> Result<Vec<Record>> {
  81:     let mut file = OpenOptions::new().read(true).open(log_path)?;
  82:     let header = read_file_header(&mut file)?;
  83:     verify_magic_and_version(&header)?;
  84: 
  85:     let mut records = Vec::new();
  86:     let mut offset = 64;  // After file header
  87: 
  88:     loop {
  89:         match read_record_at(&mut file, offset) {
  90:             Ok(record) => {
  91:                 if record.crc_valid() {
  92:                     records.push(record);
  93:                     offset += record.on_disk_len();
  94:                 } else {
  95:                     // CRC failed: torn or corrupt record. This is the truncation point.
  96:                     log::warn!("WAL {} truncating at offset {} due to CRC failure", log_path.display(), offset);
  97:                     file.set_len(offset)?;  // Truncate tail
  98:                     file.sync_all()?;
  99:                     break;
 100:                 }
 101:             }
 102:             Err(ReadError::ShortRead) => {
 103:                 // Reached real EOF; expected for the last file.
 104:                 break;
 105:             }
 106:             Err(ReadError::ZeroPadding) => {
 107:                 // Skipping a zero-byte run between records (Windows-aligned writes).
 108:                 offset = next_record_start_after_zeros(&mut file, offset)?;
 109:             }
 110:             Err(other) => return Err(other),
 111:         }
 112:     }
 113: 
 114:     Ok(records)
 115: }
 116: ```
 117: 
 118: The truncation policy: a CRC failure can only happen on the LAST record of the LAST file (because earlier records were already fsync'd before later ones started). If a CRC failure is detected mid-file, recovery treats everything from that offset forward as torn and truncates. Subsequent appends start at the truncated offset.
 119: 
 120: **Critical invariant:** the writer NEVER appends after a sealed file. A file is sealed when the writer rotates. Once sealed, the file is immutable; recovery may truncate its tail (only the last sealed file in the most-recent rotation), but no new bytes are ever written.
 121: 
 122: ### Rotation:
 123: 
 124: ```
 125: chunk_log/000001.clog (sealed, 256 MiB, immutable)
 126: chunk_log/000002.clog (sealed, 256 MiB, immutable)
 127: chunk_log/000003.clog (active, currently appending, ≤256 MiB)
 128: ```
 129: 
 130: Rotation policy: when active file exceeds 256 MiB, allocate next file:
 131: 
 132: 1. Allocate next file: `open("000004.clog", O_CREAT | O_WRONLY | O_APPEND)`, write file header, fsync.
 133: 2. Direct subsequent appends to new file.
 134: 3. Close old file's fd (no fsync needed; old file's data was already fsync'd record-by-record).
 135: 
 136: This is a hot operation — we don't block writers during rotation. The writer holds two fds during transition: it appends the last record (or batch) to old, fdatasyncs, then atomically swaps to new.
 137: 
 138: ### Replay determinism:
 139: 
 140: Two replay runs over the same on-disk state must produce byte-identical recovered state. Sources of nondeterminism to eliminate:
 141: 
 142: - **Iteration order over files**: recovery sorts log files by file_id (numeric, ascending). Always.
 143: - **Concurrent replay threads**: replay is single-threaded per log. No interleaving.
 144: - **HLC reconstruction**: HLC values come from the manifest_log records themselves (each record carries an hlc_timestamp). Replay does not generate new HLCs; it only replays what was written.
 145: - **Memtable rebuild**: memtable insertion order = log replay order = record-write order = deterministic.
 146: - **SST flush threshold**: threshold is content-addressed (memtable size in bytes), not time-based. Same-content recovery → same flush points.
 147: 
 148: Property test: replay the same log files 100× in a fresh process; compare in-memory state byte-for-byte. Any divergence = bug.
 149: 
 150: ### What's outside the WAL:
 151: 
 152: - **SSTs** are not WAL records; they're a derived index built by flushing memtable. Lost SSTs are rebuildable from logs. SSTs have their own CRCs but are not replayed; they're either valid-and-loaded or invalid-and-rebuilt.
 153: - **Bloom filter sidecars** are derived from SSTs; lost sidecars are rebuilt.
 154: - **Memtable** is purely in-memory; rebuilt from logs.
 155: 
 156: The only durability path is the WAL. Everything else is rebuildable.
 157: 
 158: ## Consequences
 159: 
 160: **Positive:**
 161: - Crash safety property is mechanically verifiable: replay produces a state consistent with some prefix of writes that successfully fsync'd. No "almost crash-safe" gray zone.
 162: - Single CRC trailer per record matches LevelDB/RocksDB/BadgerDB convention; tooling (custom inspectors, fuzzers) is portable.
 163: - Rotation is transparent and never blocks writers.
 164: - Truncation only on the most-recent file's tail; never edits sealed files.
 165: - Determinism gate is testable: 100× replay → byte-identical state.
 166: 
 167: **Negative:**
 168: - 4 bytes per record CRC overhead. Negligible.
 169: - Windows alignment requires zero-padding (up to 511 bytes per record). Acceptable; aligns sector writes correctly for `FILE_FLAG_NO_BUFFERING`.
 170: - Per-record CRC is computed over the entire record body, which is up to 256 KiB for chunks. CRC32C hardware-accelerated on x86 (≥10 GiB/s) and ARM64; not a hot-path concern.
 171: - 256 MiB rotation size means ~4-8K records per chunk_log file (depending on chunk size). Recovery linear-scans this; ~50 ms per file on NVMe. Acceptable for boot times.
 172: 
 173: ## Verification
 174: 
 175: 1. **Determinism gate**: replay same logs 100× in fresh processes; in-memory recovered state must be byte-identical across all runs.
 176: 2. **CRC integrity gate**: random bit-flip injection on log files (1 bit-flip per file, 10K trials); recovery MUST reject the flipped record (and all subsequent records in that file). State recovered = state up to the corruption point.
 177: 3. **Rotation transparency gate**: write 1 GiB of records spanning 4 rotations; replay produces all records in original write order.
 178: 4. **Concurrent rotation gate**: writer thread does rotation while another thread queues new writes; queued writes land in the post-rotation file with no loss.
 179: 5. **Tail truncation gate**: synthesize a torn last record (write a partial record, simulate crash); recovery truncates exactly to the boundary of the previous valid record.
 180: 6. **Page-fault injection (Windows)**: simulate write that loses last sector before fsync; recovery truncates correctly.
 181: 7. **macOS F_FULLFSYNC gate**: with simulated dirty disk-cache loss, only records whose F_FULLFSYNC returned are recovered.
 182: 
 183: ## References
 184: 
 185: - LevelDB log format: `db/log_format.h` (similar concept, simpler).
 186: - RocksDB WAL: `db/log_writer.cc` (record-batch design we model after).
 187: - BadgerDB value log: similar layout with checksums.
 188: - Linux O_DIRECT semantics: `man 2 open` section on O_DIRECT.
 189: - Windows FILE_FLAG_NO_BUFFERING: MSDN; our alignment policy follows the documented constraints.
 190: - "Files Are Hard": Pillai et al., OSDI 2014.
 191: - BLAKE3 derive_key for content-addressing — see ADR-0006.
