   1: # Performance Lab
   2: 
   3: Status: in_progress for v0.11.0.
   4: 
   5: Correctness tests prove One Link should work. The performance lab proves whether
   6: it is getting faster, tighter, and more efficient.
   7: 
   8: ## Run
   9: 
  10: ```powershell
  11: python scripts\perf_lab.py --scale quick
  12: python scripts\perf_lab.py --scale standard
  13: python scripts\perf_lab.py --scale standard --compare benchmarks\results\older.json
  14: ```
  15: 
  16: Reports are written to `benchmarks/results/*.json` and ignored by git.
  17: Use `--compare` to print speed ratios against an older report. That gives us a
  18: simple before/after view after each optimization pass.
  19: 
  20: ## What It Measures
  21: 
  22: - **Hash-only manifest throughput**: how fast One Link can identify a file
  23:   without building a chunk manifest.
  24: - **Fixed-manifest throughput**: how fast One Link can build aligned block
  25:   manifests for large media.
  26: - **CDC indexing throughput**: how fast One Link can split and hash a file for
  27:   prior-knowledge dedup.
  28: - **Prior-knowledge savings**: how many bytes can be skipped when the receiver
  29:   already has a related object.
  30: - **Swarm scheduler throughput**: how quickly One Link can assign chunks across
  31:   trusted devices.
  32: - **Never-lose torture sim**: whether retry, corruption, and offline behavior
  33:   still delivers.
  34: - **SQLite transfer ledger pressure**: how many transfer updates per second the
  35:   durable ledger can absorb.
  36: - **Compression throughput**: zlib level-1 speed and ratio for easy data.
  37: - **Adaptive transfer brain**: whether local cost planning chooses fast lanes
  38:   when prior knowledge is low and CDC/swarm when prior knowledge is high.
  39: - **Stream pipeline profile**: the adaptive chunk/window plan for keeping
  40:   baseline sends saturated without unbounded memory.
  41: 
  42: ## How To Read The Report
  43: 
  44: Useful first-pass signals:
  45: 
  46: - `hash_only_manifest.metrics.mib_per_s`: higher is better.
  47: - `fixed_indexing.metrics.mib_per_s`: higher is better.
  48: - `cdc_indexing.metrics.mib_per_s`: higher is better, but CDC should only be
  49:   selected when its skipped bytes justify its CPU cost.
  50: - `prior_knowledge_dedup.metrics.bandwidth_reduction`: closer to `1.0` is
  51:   better when files are related.
  52: - `swarm_scheduler.metrics.chunks_per_s`: higher means the planner can scale
  53:   to very large transfers and many helpers.
  54: - `never_lose_torture_sim.metrics.delivered`: must be `true`.
  55: - `sqlite_transfer_ledger.metrics.writes_per_s`: higher means smoother live UI
  56:   updates under many transfers.
  57: - `zlib_level1_compression.metrics.mib_per_s`: higher means compression is less
  58:   likely to become the bottleneck.
  59: - `adaptive_transfer_brain.metrics.low_prior_mode`: should prefer a fast lane.
  60: - `adaptive_transfer_brain.metrics.high_prior_python_mode`: shows the honest
  61:   decision with today's Python CDC speed.
  62: - `adaptive_transfer_brain.metrics.high_prior_accelerated_mode`: shows the
  63:   target decision once native/GPU CDC lands.
  64: - `stream_pipeline_profiles.metrics.huge_window_bytes`: maximum baseline stream
  65:   bytes in flight for huge sends.
  66: 
  67: ## What Is Not Yet Measured
  68: 
  69: This lab is local and deterministic. It does not yet replace:
  70: 
  71: - two-machine LAN throughput;
  72: - relay/rendezvous internet throughput;
  73: - Windows/macOS/Linux power usage;
  74: - browser frame-time profiling;
  75: - real multi-GB disk send/receive benchmarks;
  76: - CI regression thresholds.
  77: 
  78: Those are the next performance gates.
  79: 
  80: ## Current Local Snapshot
  81: 
  82: On the current Windows dev machine, `quick` scale after the v0.11.0 fast-lane
  83: work produced:
  84: 
  85: - Hash-only manifest: about `1.6 GiB/s`.
  86: - Fixed manifest: about `1.2 GiB/s`.
  87: - CDC indexing: about `8 MiB/s`.
  88: - Adaptive transfer brain: thousands of local decisions per second; with
  89:   current Python CDC it still often chooses hash-stream for huge fast-LAN
  90:   transfers, while accelerated CDC flips high-prior cases to CDC/swarm.
  91: - Stream pipeline: huge sends use up to `4 MiB` chunks with a bounded
  92:   `24 MiB` in-flight window.
  93: 
  94: On the same machine before this work, `standard` scale produced:
  95: 
  96: - Prior-knowledge related-file savings: about `99%` bytes skipped.
  97: - Swarm scheduling: about `388k chunks/s`.
  98: - SQLite transfer ledger: about `17k writes/s`.
  99: - Compression: several GiB/s on easy data.
 100: 
 101: Interpretation: the scheduler and ledger are not the bottleneck right now. The
 102: largest obvious optimization target was blindly paying CDC indexing cost. v0.11
 103: adds the fast lanes and transfer brain needed to stop doing that for peers or
 104: files that cannot benefit from CDC.

   1: # Phase A2 QUIC Cutover — Deferred with Plan
   2: 
   3: > **Status: deliberately deferred.** The `ol_quic` crate ships; the
   4: > daemon does NOT yet route daemon↔daemon traffic through it.
   5: > This document explains why the cutover hasn't happened and what
   6: > the cutover work actually looks like, so the next person to pick
   7: > it up has a clean target.
   8: 
   9: ## Why deferred
  10: 
  11: The daemon's WebRTC/DTLS-SRTP transport works. Replacing it is
  12: a multi-day project where breakage is silent + catastrophic:
  13: 
  14: 1. **Pairing handshake** runs on the same socket as in-flight
  15:    transfers. A broken QUIC handshake doesn't just lose a packet;
  16:    it loses the peer.
  17: 2. **Browser-as-peer** must stay on WebRTC (browsers don't speak
  18:    QUIC datagrams to arbitrary peers without WebTransport, which
  19:    has its own deployment story).
  20: 3. **Connection migration** (cellular ↔ WiFi) is a Phase A2 gate.
  21:    QUIC supports it natively; WebRTC doesn't. But verifying it
  22:    requires real cellular handoff — hardware not on the dev box.
  23: 
  24: Doing a half-cutover that "mostly works" would break shipped flows
  25: (iOS pair, browser-as-peer fallback, etc.) in ways the test suite
  26: doesn't catch.
  27: 
  28: ## What's done
  29: 
  30: - `native/ol_quic/` crate exists with `quinn`-based transport.
  31: - pyo3 binding (`one_link_native.quic`) exposes encode/decode +
  32:   bulk-frame helpers.
  33: - 6 native crate tests + perf benches passing.
  34: - Loopback throughput scaffold (`scripts/quic_measurement_scaffold.py`)
  35:   reports 29.8 GiB/s encode.
  36: 
  37: ## What the cutover requires
  38: 
  39: In dependency order:
  40: 
  41: ### Step 1: Dual-stack transport selector
  42: 
  43: Daemon already has `peer_rtc.py` (WebRTC). Add `peer_quic.py` (QUIC)
  44: that exposes the same `OutboundSession` / `InboundSession` interface.
  45: The daemon's `send_text` / `send_file` paths call through the
  46: interface; they don't care which transport is underneath.
  47: 
  48: ```python
  49: class PeerTransport(Protocol):
  50:     async def open_outbound(self, peer: Peer) -> OutboundSession: ...
  51:     async def accept_inbound(self, ...) -> InboundSession: ...
  52: ```
  53: 
  54: Both `WebRTCTransport` and `QUICTransport` implement this.
  55: 
  56: ### Step 2: Capability-gated negotiation
  57: 
  58: Add a `QUIC_TRANSPORT_V1` capability. During pairing handshake,
  59: each peer advertises which transports they support. If both
  60: advertise QUIC, use QUIC; otherwise fall back to WebRTC.
  61: 
  62: This means a v0.21+ daemon talking to a v0.20.x daemon stays on
  63: WebRTC — no flag day, no breakage.
  64: 
  65: ### Step 3: Per-peer transport state
  66: 
  67: The daemon keeps per-peer connection state. When peer P is QUIC,
  68: that state lives in a `QUICSession`; when P is WebRTC, in an
  69: `RtcSession`. The lookup table is keyed by peer fingerprint.
  70: 
  71: ### Step 4: Migration path for in-flight transfers
  72: 
  73: If a transfer is in flight via WebRTC and the daemon restarts with
  74: QUIC available, the transfer should resume on QUIC. Resume requires:
  75: - Same chunk-id / manifest-id (already content-addressed; works).
  76: - Same channel keys (DH-derived; transport-agnostic; works).
  77: - Connection migration on the wire (QUIC's built-in `CONN_ID`
  78:   migration — needs daemon to track + re-negotiate).
  79: 
  80: ### Step 5: 0-RTT resume cache
  81: 
  82: Cache QUIC session tickets per peer. On reconnect, use the ticket
  83: for a 0-RTT handshake (plan gate: <50ms warm cache).
  84: 
  85: ### Step 6: Cellular ↔ WiFi migration verification
  86: 
  87: Real device, dual NIC, force handoff mid-transfer. Verify the
  88: daemon's QUIC connection migrates without app-visible drop.
  89: 
  90: ### Step 7: TCP fallback measurement
  91: 
  92: Real LAN, measure QUIC stream throughput vs `iperf3` TCP baseline.
  93: Plan gate: within 10% of TCP.
  94: 
  95: ## Acceptance gates per plan
  96: 
  97: | Gate | Plan target | What it takes |
  98: |---|---|---|
  99: | Stream throughput | within 10% of TCP on tuned LAN | Step 7 |
 100: | 0-RTT resume | <50ms warm | Step 5 + real LAN |
 101: | Migration | zero app-visible drop on cellular↔WiFi | Step 6 + real device |
 102: | Daemon cutover | daemon↔daemon over QUIC | Steps 1–4 |
 103: 
 104: ## Estimated effort
 105: 
 106: Steps 1–3 (dual-stack + negotiation + per-peer state):
 107: **3-5 days** of careful work + thorough integration tests.
 108: 
 109: Steps 4–5 (resume + 0-RTT): **2 days**.
 110: 
 111: Steps 6–7 (real-hardware verification): hardware-blocked. Cannot
 112: estimate without access.
 113: 
 114: ## What we did instead
 115: 
 116: Built the rest of Phase A1+B+C+D+E so the entire stack is ready
 117: to ride QUIC the moment the cutover happens. The daemon's
 118: performance, durability, and Phase E machinery are all locked in
 119: on the WebRTC transport. Switching transports doesn't require
 120: re-architecting anything above the transport layer.
 121: 
 122: ## When to do this
 123: 
 124: When at least three conditions hold:
 125: 1. v0.21.x has soaked in production for ≥ 1 release cycle without
 126:    regressions.
 127: 2. Hardware for the migration gates (real LAN + real cellular)
 128:    is available.
 129: 3. The full transport interface refactor (Step 1) can be done
 130:    in a focused multi-day window without other architectural
 131:    work in flight.
 132: 
 133: Until then, **the engine is production-ready on WebRTC.** The
 134: Phase A2 cutover is an upgrade, not a blocker.
<<<CONTENT_END>>>

   1: # Phase E Operator Runbook
   2: 
   3: > Quick reference for diagnosing the coherence-field substrate in
   4: > production. Read this BEFORE the field is acting up.
   5: 
   6: ## What Phase E actually does (in 30 seconds)
   7: 
   8: The daemon owns a background-ticking `FieldSnapshotManager` that:
   9: 1. Mirrors the current peer-graph (peers + edge weights).
  10: 2. Every 5 seconds, solves the Helmholtz equation
  11:    `(Γ·I + D·L)·δτ_c = S` to recover a per-peer "coherence" scalar.
  12: 3. Caches the result.
  13: 
  14: Downstream consumers (relay scoring via BE-RAR, ratchet cadence, bandit
  15: priors, prefetch ranking) read the cache. Without the field, the daemon
  16: falls back to Phase D heuristics. Nothing in Phase E is on the critical
  17: send path.
  18: 
  19: ## "Is it working?"
  20: 
  21: Hit `/api/metrics` on the daemon (UI port, auth-token gated):
  22: 
  23: ```bash
  24: curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" http://127.0.0.1:$UI_PORT/api/metrics
  25: ```
  26: 
  27: Healthy output snippet:
  28: 
  29: ```json
  30: {
  31:   "native": {
  32:     "coherence_field": {
  33:       "available": true,
  34:       "calibration": {"d": 100.0, "gamma": 0.01, "screening_length": 100.0, ...},
  35:       "snapshot_metrics": {
  36:         "field_solve_count": 47,
  37:         "field_solve_failures": 0,
  38:         "field_snapshot_age_ms": 2103.5,
  39:         "field_snapshot_peer_count": 12,
  40:         "field_snapshot_iterations": 18,
  41:         "field_snapshot_residual": 7.3e-7
  42:       }
  43:     }
  44:   },
  45:   "per_peer_field_advisories": {
  46:     "abc12345": {"cadence_bytes": 250000, "field_score": 0.42}
  47:   }
  48: }
  49: ```
  50: 
  51: Green flags:
  52: - `coherence_field.available: true`
  53: - `field_solve_count` increasing over time
  54: - `field_solve_failures` stays at 0
  55: - `field_snapshot_age_ms < 6000` (one update_interval + a tick budget)
  56: - `field_snapshot_residual < 1e-5`
  57: - `field_snapshot_iterations <= 50`
  58: 
  59: Red flags (and what they mean):
  60: 
  61: | Symptom | Likely cause | Fix |
  62: |---|---|---|
  63: | `available: false` | `ol_coherence_field` not built | `cd native && maturin develop --release` |
  64: | `field_solve_count: 0` after several minutes | No peers yet, or `field_topology_edge_count` is zero | Verify peers actually paired; field skips solve below `min_peers=3` |
  65: | `field_solve_failures` climbing | Non-convergent solves (probably degenerate topology — disconnected components or zero-weight edges) | Check `/api/peers` for connectivity; bump CG max_iter if topology is large + weakly-connected |
  66: | `field_snapshot_age_ms > 30000` | Background loop stuck or thread died | Look for "field snapshot tick failed" in daemon logs; restart daemon |
  67: | `field_snapshot_residual > 1e-3` | Operator badly conditioned (D ≫ Γ or both → 0) | Verify calibration constants match expected One Link defaults (D=100, Γ=0.01) |
  68: 
  69: ## "Routing decisions look weird"
  70: 
  71: Phase E's BE-RAR scorer can pick paths that look counter-intuitive vs.
  72: the heuristic `1/(1−loss)²`. Specifically:
  73: 
  74: - BE-RAR's penalty is **softer at moderate loss** (10–40%): it ranks
  75:   near-tie relays by RTT rather than over-weighting loss.
  76: - BE-RAR's penalty **diverges at extreme loss** (>80%): pathological
  77:   relays still get rejected.
  78: - **BE-RAR can pick a low-RTT, moderately-lossy relay over a high-RTT,
  79:   low-loss one.** This is the correct math, not a bug. If you want the
  80:   heuristic back, set `ONE_LINK_DISABLE_BE_RAR=1`.
  81: 
  82: To compare picks:
  83: 1. Capture `/api/metrics` + `per_peer_field_advisories` while the
  84:    weird pick happens.
  85: 2. Note the peer's `field_score` (0..1) and `cadence_bytes`.
  86: 3. Cross-reference with `_relay_metrics` (RTT + loss for each
  87:    relay) — see daemon logs at DEBUG.
  88: 
  89: ## "Daemon CPU is spiking"
  90: 
  91: The field solve at 100 peers takes ~17µs through the pyo3 surface.
  92: At 10k peers it takes ~33µs (warm-start) or ~1.5ms (cold). A solve
  93: every 5s means **steady-state field CPU is < 0.1%**.
  94: 
  95: If you see CPU spikes correlated with field solves:
  96: 1. Check `field_snapshot_peer_count` — anything > 10k is outside the
  97:    benchmarked range.
  98: 2. Bump `update_interval_s` in `FieldConfig` (default 5s).
  99: 3. If still bad, set `update_interval_s = 60.0` and report a perf bug.
 100: 
 101: ## "Convergent-encryption chunks aren't deduping"
 102: 
 103: Files now flow through `convergent` or `raw` BLAKE3 addressing based on
 104: extension (see `NativeTransferSession._resolve_address_kind`). To check
 105: which scheme a file used:
 106: 
 107: - `.mp4/.mov/.h264/.wav/.flac/.jpg/.png/...` → `convergent` →
 108:   cross-sender dedup works.
 109: - `.docx/.pdf/.zip/.rs/.py/...` → `raw` → per-recipient keys, no
 110:   cross-sender dedup (intentional, privacy-preserving default).
 111: 
 112: If a file you expect to dedup isn't, verify:
 113: 1. Both senders have the same extension (case-insensitive).
 114: 2. Plaintext is byte-identical (any metadata embedded in the file
 115:    header — Premiere project IDs, exif timestamps — breaks dedup
 116:    even at convergent).
 117: 3. `/api/metrics` shows `coherence_field.available: true` on both
 118:    senders (the dispatch helper is gated on Phase E in spirit; the
 119:    address kind itself ships standalone).
 120: 
 121: ## "Ratchet keys feel like they're rotating too often"
 122: 
 123: The field-driven cadence advisory shrinks the chunk size sent to
 124: peers in low-coherence wells, which (via the per-chunk ratchet)
 125: makes rotation faster per byte. Floor is 64 KiB so framing
 126: overhead never dominates.
 127: 
 128: The advisory is **actively wired** into `Daemon.send_file`: after
 129: `_fast_fixed_chunk_size_for_peer` picks the baseline, the daemon
 130: queries `Daemon.cadence_for_peer(peer_short_id)` and clamps down
 131: when the field reports a smaller cadence.
 132: 
 133: To investigate or force baseline:
 134: 
 135: 1. `/api/metrics` — check `per_peer_field_advisories[peer].cadence_bytes`.
 136: 2. Compare with baseline 1,000,000 bytes (1 MiB).
 137: 3. To bypass entirely set `ONE_LINK_FIELD_CADENCE_DISABLE=1` —
 138:    `cadence_for_peer` will return `None` and `send_file` keeps the
 139:    peer-version-derived baseline.
 140: 
 141: ## Field-snapshot manager doesn't seem to be updating
 142: 
 143: The manager runs on a Python `threading.Thread`. To prove it's alive:
 144: 
 145: ```python
 146: # In a daemon REPL (or via an admin endpoint if exposed):
 147: mgr = daemon._field_snapshot
 148: print(mgr is not None)        # True if started
 149: print(mgr._thread.is_alive()) # True if loop is running
 150: print(mgr.metrics())          # Should show non-stale numbers
 151: ```
 152: 
 153: If `_thread.is_alive() == False`, the loop crashed. Daemon logs at
 154: DEBUG level should show the traceback. The manager is engineered to
 155: swallow per-tick errors and continue, so a hard thread death is rare.
 156: 
 157: ## Calibration mismatch across daemons
 158: 
 159: The Helmholtz calibration `(D, Γ)` is compile-time-frozen in
 160: `ol_coherence_field::calibration::one_link`. Two daemons running
 161: **the same build** must report identical calibration. The subprocess
 162: smoke test enforces this:
 163: 
 164: ```bash
 165: pytest tests/test_phase_e_subprocess_smoke.py::test_daemon_pair_field_calibration_matches_across_daemons
 166: ```
 167: 
 168: If two daemons in production disagree, one of them is on a stale
 169: build. Check `/api/status` → `app_version` + `native_status` →
 170: `coherence_field.calibration` on each.
 171: 
 172: ## Tests + benches that gate Phase E health
 173: 
 174: | What | Where | Threshold |
 175: |---|---|---|
 176: | Native unit + integration | `cargo test -p ol_coherence_field --release` | 91 pass / 0 fail |
 177: | Property invariants | `cargo test --release --test pde_invariants_proptest` | 8 properties × 48 cases |
 178: | Dense-linalg cross-check | `cargo test --release --test dense_reference_cross_check` | 5 regimes, ≤1e-6 abs error |
 179: | Fragile-swarm gate | `scripts/phase_e_live_demo.py` | ≥ 80% chunk-loss reduction |
 180: | Cross-domain demo | `scripts/phase_e_cross_domain_demo.py` | All 3 domains converge |
 181: | Adversarial fuzz | `scripts/adversarial_field_fuzz.py --quick` | 8/8 regimes pass |
 182: | Per-PR perf gate | `scripts/coherence_field_perf_snapshot.py` + `bench_gate.py` | ≤ 5% regression vs baseline |
 183: | Bandit-field consistency | `pytest tests/unit/test_phase_e_demos.py` | both demos green |
 184: | Subprocess smoke | `pytest tests/test_phase_e_subprocess_smoke.py` | daemon pair reports field |
 185: 
 186: Run the lot before any release that touches `ol_coherence_field`,
 187: `field_snapshot.py`, or the BE-RAR daemon wiring.
 188: 
 189: ## Emergency: disable Phase E entirely
 190: 
 191: If the field is misbehaving and you need to drop to Phase D
 192: heuristics immediately:
 193: 
 194: 1. Stop the daemon.
 195: 2. Run `pip uninstall one_link_native` (the wheel that ships
 196:    `ol_coherence_field`).
 197: 3. Restart the daemon. It auto-detects the missing crate and falls
 198:    back to Phase D paths everywhere (relay scoring uses the
 199:    `1/(1-loss)²` heuristic, no field-driven cadences, no bandit
 200:    priors).
 201: 
 202: The daemon stays fully functional; you lose only the Phase E
 203: performance + alignment gains.
 204: 
 205: ## Per-feature operator escape hatches (env kill-switches)
 206: 
 207: Each Phase E coupling has its own env-var disable so a misbehaving
 208: coupling can be flipped off without rebuilding the crate or
 209: restarting users. All read at the call site, so toggling takes
 210: effect on the next solve / consumer call.
 211: 
 212: | Env var | Effect when set to `1` / `true` / `yes` / `on` |
 213: |---|---|
 214: | `ONE_LINK_FIELD_DISABLE` | Pauses the whole solve loop. Manager stays running so consumers still query without crashing (they get safe-default fallbacks). Flipping back off resumes solving on the next tick. |
 215: | `ONE_LINK_DISABLE_BE_RAR` | Relay scoring falls back to the heuristic `1 / (1 − loss)²` penalty. |
 216: | `ONE_LINK_FIELD_CADENCE_DISABLE` | `cadence_for_peer` returns `None`; `send_file` keeps the peer-version-derived baseline chunk size. |
 217: | `ONE_LINK_FIELD_HOMOLOGY_DISABLE` | Homology feeder tick still fires but skips the fragility computation. No fragility events get injected. |
 218: | `ONE_LINK_FIELD_PREFETCH_DISABLE` | `field_rank_holders` returns the input order unchanged (any future multi-holder fetch path gets bandit-only ranking). |
 219: 
 220: ## Snapshot persistence across daemon restart
 221: 
 222: The manager now writes its latest snapshot to
 223: `data_dir() / "field-snapshot.json"` after every successful solve
 224: (atomic tempfile + `os.replace`). On boot, the constructor reads
 225: that file and seeds `_current` so consumers get field guidance
 226: **before** the first post-restart solve completes — no 5-second
 227: post-restart gap.
 228: 
 229: A malformed or absent file is silently ignored; the daemon falls
 230: back to "no snapshot until the first tick."
 231: 
 232: ## Upstream feature wirings (now also complete)
 233: 
 234: The two upstream features the field couplings depend on are also
 235: wired into production code paths:
 236: 
 237: - **Multi-holder swarm fetch** — `Daemon.pull_swarm_missing_chunks`
 238:   (the production swarm-fetch path that fans a query out to peers,
 239:   collects claims, plans assignments via `plan_swarm_sources`, and
 240:   pulls in parallel) now passes `coherence_score=field_score_for_peer(fp[:8])`
 241:   into each `ChunkSource`. The planner's `route_score` already had
 242:   a coherence slot ranked above bandwidth/latency, so a high-τ_c
 243:   peer is automatically promoted over a low-τ_c one when trust
 244:   ties. Honors `ONE_LINK_FIELD_PREFETCH_DISABLE=1`.
 245: - **Chunk-holder gossip (for the homology feeder)** — every swarm
 246:   query response (`_collect_swarm_chunk_claims`) now folds the
 247:   returned claims into `_chunk_holders`. The homology feeder's
 248:   cohold-graph view is no longer limited to locally-observed
 249:   FILE_DONE events — every swarm query brightens the picture.
 250: 
 251: ## Things that DON'T exist yet (and why)
 252: 
 253: These are on the production roadmap but NOT shipped:
 254: 
 255: - **Prometheus / OpenMetrics text format** — `/api/metrics` returns
 256:   JSON only. Wrap externally with a Prometheus exporter if you need
 257:   scraping.
 258: 
 259: See [FILE_ENGINE_V2_PLAN.md](FILE_ENGINE_V2_PLAN.md) for the full
 260: remaining-work picture.

   1: # Phone Tier — implementation guide
   2: 
   3: Status: living document. Detailed enough to pick up cold and execute.
   4: Last updated: 2026-05-08.
   5: 
   6: **Owner principle:** [`PRINCIPLES.md`](./PRINCIPLES.md), specifically
   7: principle #2 (Hide the engine) applied at maximum aggression for the
   8: phone form-factor.
   9: 
  10: **One-line claim:**
  11: > A phone user who can't locate a feature isn't missing the feature;
  12: > the feature is failing them by being there.
  13: 
  14: This document is the canonical specification for what changes about
  15: One Link's UI when it runs on a phone. It's deliberately exhaustive
  16: so the work can be picked up after a long pause without re-thinking
  17: every call from scratch.
  18: 
  19: ---
  20: 
  21: ## Why a phone tier exists
  22: 
  23: The desktop UI currently surfaces ~40 settings, 4 pane tabs, a multi-
  24: section device drawer, an Activity feed with filter chips, a
  25: Diagnostics modal, and several power-user controls. On a phone, that
  26: density is hostile:
  27: 
  28: - A 360px viewport can't render filter chips and a search bar and a
  29:   pane tab bar without overflow.
  30: - Touch targets at desktop sizes (28-32px) miss frequently on
  31:   thumbs.
  32: - Most phone users don't read help text; they tap, see, repeat.
  33: - Nobody on a phone debugs wire frames.
  34: - Nobody on a phone configures a rendezvous URL.
  35: 
  36: The phone tier is **value subtraction work**: deciding what *not* to
  37: show. It's harder than feature addition because every cut is an
  38: argument with whoever first added the surface.
  39: 
  40: ---
  41: 
  42: ## The mechanism (two layers)
  43: 
  44: ### Layer 1 — `data-form-factor` on `<html>`
  45: 
  46: Set at boot by a small JS function. Values: `"phone"` | `"tablet"` |
  47: `"desktop"`. Decision rule:
  48: 
  49: ```
  50: const w = Math.min(window.innerWidth, window.innerHeight);
  51: const touch = ("ontouchstart" in window) || navigator.maxTouchPoints > 0;
  52: const ua = navigator.userAgent.toLowerCase();
  53: const ua_mobile = /iphone|ipod|android.+mobile|windows phone/.test(ua);
  54: 
  55: if (w <= 480 || ua_mobile) factor = "phone";
  56: else if (w <= 900 && touch) factor = "tablet";
  57: else factor = "desktop";
  58: ```
  59: 
  60: CSS reads via attribute selectors:
  61: 
  62: ```css
  63: html[data-form-factor="phone"] .desktop-only { display: none !important; }
  64: html[data-form-factor="phone"] [data-tier="advanced"] { display: none; }
  65: html.show-advanced [data-tier="advanced"] { display: revert !important; }
  66: ```
  67: 
  68: Re-evaluated on `resize` events with a 250ms debounce, so a phone
  69: rotated to landscape doesn't immediately flicker into desktop mode
  70: (stays phone unless the user genuinely resizes a browser window past
  71: the threshold).
  72: 
  73: ### Layer 2 — `state.tier` setting
  74: 
  75: Persisted in `chat-prefs` (server-synced via the existing endpoint).
  76: Values: `"default"` | `"advanced"`.
  77: 
  78: - **Phone:** defaults to `"default"`. Toggle in Profile pane: "Show
  79:   advanced controls" reveals everything `data-tier="advanced"`.
  80:   Resets on tab close (per-session, not per-device-persisted) so
  81:   users can't get stuck in advanced mode they don't remember
  82:   enabling.
  83: - **Tablet:** defaults to `"default"`. Same toggle.
  84: - **Desktop:** defaults to `"advanced"` (current full-fat experience).
  85:   Toggle still exists for users who want a leaner surface.
  86: 
  87: Toggling adds/removes class `show-advanced` on `<html>`.
  88: 
  89: ### Tagging convention
  90: 
  91: Every UI element being hidden gets one of two attributes / classes:
  92: 
  93: - `class="desktop-only"` — **truly absent on phone**. Even the
  94:   "Show advanced" toggle does NOT reveal it. Use for things that
  95:   literally don't apply (folder sync, log verbosity dropdown).
  96: - `data-tier="advanced"` — **hidden by default, reveal-able**. Use
  97:   for power-user surfaces that exist but aren't first-class.
  98: 
  99: A few elements get BOTH on different platforms (e.g., the
 100: Diagnostics modal entry point: `desktop-only` for the keyboard
 101: shortcut hint, `data-tier="advanced"` for the Settings → Advanced
 102: button — kbd-shortcut hint is gone on phone, button is reveal-able).
 103:

 302:

 304: |---|---|---|---|

 315: 
 316: ## "Show advanced" reveal UX
 317: 
 318: A single toggle at the bottom of the **Profile** pane:
 319: 
 320: ```
 321: ┌──────────────────────────────────────┐
 322: │ Show advanced controls         [ ○ ] │
 323: │ Reveals power-user surfaces across   │
 324: │ all settings panes + drawers. Off    │
 325: │ by default; resets when you close    │
 326: │ the app.                             │
 327: └──────────────────────────────────────┘
 328: ```
 329: 
 330: Toggle behavior:
 331: - Adds `show-advanced` class to `<html>` (CSS reveals all
 332:   `[data-tier="advanced"]` items).
 333: - NOT persisted across tab close (per-session) so phone users don't
 334:   end up with a sprawl they didn't actively choose.
 335: - On desktop, the toggle defaults to ON and persists. Same toggle,
 336:   different default + persistence, configured in init() based on
 337:   form-factor.
 338: 
 339: Each pane that has hidden items gets a subtle hint at the bottom in
 340: the default tier:
 341: 
 342: ```
 343: 3 advanced controls hidden. [Show]
 344: ```
 345: 
 346: Tapping the hint flips the toggle. Single-source-of-truth: there's
 347: ONE toggle; the per-pane hints are just shortcuts to it.
 348: 
 349: ---
 350: 
 351: ## Pair flow — phone-specific simplification
 352: 
 353: The current pair flow shows 6 SAS digits prominently. On phone, the
 354: visual SAS art (already shipped) becomes the primary; digits sit
 355: under it as accessibility fallback.
 356: 
 357: The "Verify in person" step:
 358: 
 359: **Desktop today:**
 360: > Compare the SAS above with the same value on the other device.
 361: > Face-to-face, on a call, or by reading it aloud.
 362: 
 363: **Phone phrasing:**
 364: > Both screens should show the same row of icons. Match? [Yes] [No]
 365: 
 366: The icon row is the existing SAS art. Yes → mark verified + close.
 367: No → "Try again later. Don't pair until you can confirm in person."
 368: 
 369: This implements the "Hide the engine" principle: the user verifies
 370: *the same thing*, expressed in human-readable form. Hexadecimal
 371: digits are still there for accessibility / power-user / phone-call
 372: audio confirmation.
 373: 
 374: ---
 375: 
 376: ## Adaptive typography + spacing
 377: 
 378: Beyond visibility, on phone:
 379: 
 380: - Base font-size 16px (prevents iOS zoom-on-focus on inputs).
 381: - Line-height 1.5 minimum for body copy.
 382: - Touch target minimum 44x44px on every actionable element.
 383: - Composer sticky-bottom, never above the keyboard (use
 384:   `env(safe-area-inset-bottom)` for notched phones).
 385: - Scroll-restore on pane-switch (when a phone user re-opens the
 386:   app, the conversation is at its last scroll position, not at
 387:   the bottom).
 388: 
 389: ---
 390:

 433: 
 434: ## Ship sequence
 435: 
 436: The phone tier work is not a single ship; it's a progression. The
 437: order matters because earlier ships add the mechanism, later ships
 438: populate it.
 439: 
 440: ### v0.14.2 — Phone tier foundation (immediate next ship)
 441: 
 442: **Mechanism only.** Adds the layer-1 + layer-2 plumbing without
 443: touching the visibility of any specific element yet.
 444:

 446:   on `<html>` set at boot, re-evaluated on debounced resize.

 450:   - `html.show-advanced [data-tier="advanced"] { display: revert !important; }`

 452:   pane that flips it.

 455:   Profile toggle, the per-session reset behavior.
 456: 
 457: After this ship, the phone form-factor is detectable + the reveal

 459: experience is unchanged.** Phone users see the same surface as

 479: - Storage pane: log-level dropdown wasn't there but the
 480:   download-folder input goes desktop-only, the granular
 481:   bandwidth dropdown becomes "Save data on cellular" toggle,
 482:   auto-accept extensions input goes desktop-only.

 484: - Notifications pane: notification-preview toggle + notify-on-

 521: ---
 522: 
 523: ## Edge cases + open questions
 524: 
 525: These are deferred, documented here so they don't get re-raised.
 526: 
 527: 1. **Tablet form factor.** Currently treats tablet as `default`
 528:    tier (same as phone). iPad-in-landscape with a hardware
 529:    keyboard might want desktop tier. Open question: do we offer a
 530:    form-factor override, or detect keyboard presence? Defer until
 531:    we have actual tablet user reports.
 532: 
 533: 2. **Multi-window phone (foldables).** Unknown. Probably treats
 534:    the smaller half as phone. The CSS doesn't break; the question
 535:    is whether we want different behavior. Defer.
 536: 
 537: 3. **The Activity tab disposition.** I marked it ADVANCED. An
 538:    argument exists that it should be REMOVE entirely on phone
 539:    (most phone users will never want a chronological timeline of
 540:    trust events + transfers + key changes). Compromise: ADVANCED
 541:    for v0.14.3, but if no user opens it via Show Advanced after
 542:    3 months in production telemetry... wait, we don't do telemetry.
 543:    So we'll just ask in user interviews.
 544: 
 545: 4. **The hamburger button on phone.** When no peer is selected,
 546:    it's in the top header. When a peer IS selected, it's in the
 547:    convo header. On a folded phone (very narrow), is one of them
 548:    redundant? Defer.
 549: 
 550: 5. **Per-tier defaults that conflict.** A user on desktop with
 551:    advanced ON, who opens the same identity on a phone (after
 552:    v1.0.0 multi-device-per-identity), inherits the chat-prefs.
 553:    Should the phone start in default tier despite the persisted
 554:    `tier="advanced"` from desktop? **Yes.** Form-factor wins over
 555:    persisted preference. The toggle on phone reflects current
 556:    session state, not the synced state. On desktop, the toggle
 557:    reflects synced state. Document this in code; pin in tests.
 558: 
 559: 6. **The "Show advanced" toggle's discoverability.** On phone, it
 560:    lives at the bottom of Profile. Users who don't scroll Profile
 561:    will never see it. The per-pane "N advanced controls hidden.
 562:    [Show]" hints are the discoverability path. Verify in
 563:    first-run usability that users actually find them.
 564: 
 565: 7. **Accessibility regression risk.** Hiding an element at the
 566:    visual layer (`display: none`) also hides it from screen
 567:    readers. This is correct for our use case (a screen-reader
 568:    user on phone shouldn't have to skip past 40 controls they
 569:    can't reach), but document so we don't make a different
 570:    accessibility choice later.
 571: 
 572: 8. **The CSS `!important` on `.desktop-only`.** Necessary because
 573:    inline `style=""` overrides without it. The whole project
 574:    minimizes `!important` usage; this one is justified.
 575: 
 576: ---
 577: 
 578: ## Definition of "done" for the phone tier
 579: 
 580: The phone tier is complete (v0.14.8 ships) when:
 581: 
 582: 1. Every UI element above is dispositioned + tagged.
 583: 2. Every disposition has a regression test in
 584:    `tests/test_phone_tier_v01_*.py`.
 585: 3. A phone user (~360px wide, touch-only) can complete the
 586:    following journey without seeing a single piece of jargon or
 587:    advanced control:
 588:    - Install (PWA add-to-home from v0.15.0+; until then, browse
 589:      the URL).
 590:    - Pair with another device (visual SAS confirmation).
 591:    - Send + receive messages.
 592:    - Send + receive a file.
 593:    - Set a disappearing-msg TTL on a conversation.
 594:    - Mute a conversation.
 595:    - Set a profile name + avatar color.
 596:    - Block a peer.
 597:    - Leave a group.
 598:    - Verify a peer in person.
 599: 4. The same user, after toggling "Show advanced controls,"
 600:    can reach every feature available on desktop.
 601: 5. On rotation / browser resize, the form-factor re-detects
 602:    without UI flicker beyond a single 250ms debounce window.
 603: 
 604: ---
 605: 
 606: ## Audit reminder
 607: 
 608: Per `PRINCIPLES.md`, every quarter:
 609: 
 610: 1. Re-read this document. Anything that drifted?
 611: 2. Pick one element marked ADVANCED. Has anyone needed it on
 612:    phone? If yes, promote to default. If no, consider promoting
 613:    to REMOVE.
 614: 3. Look for new desktop features added since last audit. Are
 615:    they tagged correctly? File a debt ticket if not.

 617: The phone tier is a contract with phone users that the surface
 618: they see is the surface they need. That contract erodes silently
 619: unless someone actively maintains it.

   1: # One Link Operating Principles
   2: 
   3: Living document. Every ship is gated on these. If a ship-spec
   4: fails the checklist, it doesn't merge. No exceptions.
   5: 
   6: ---
   7: 
   8: ## North stars
   9: 
  10: One Link's name is the project's spec. It is not "another P2P chat
  11: app." It is the most direct expression in software of:
  12: 
  13: - **One** — nothing standing between two humans who want to talk.
  14: - **We Are One** — anyone who wants in can get in. Not just
  15:   technologists.
  16: - **Everything is connected** — your message reaches its
  17:   destination whether the recipient is online, offline, on a
  18:   plane, or asleep.
  19: - **It just works for the people** — the protocol's complexity
  20:   is hidden from the user without lying about safety. The
  21:   five-year-old can pair and chat.
  22: 
  23: These are not aspirations to feel good about. They are the
  24: acceptance tests for every line of code we ship.
  25: 
  26: ---
  27: 
  28: ## The four principles
  29: 
  30: ### 1. Reach over polish
  31: 
  32: > Who can use One Link this week who couldn't last week?
  33: 
  34: Polish that doesn't expand reach is allowed but is never the
  35: priority. A new feature that only existing users notice is worth
  36: less than a refactor that lets a new class of user (mobile,
  37: non-technical, offline, low-power) join the network.
  38: 
  39: Every ship spec writes one sentence: **"This ship lets X use One
  40: Link who couldn't before."** If the sentence is hard to write,
  41: the ship is wrong.
  42: 
  43: ### 2. Hide the engine
  44: 
  45: > What protocol detail can this ship stop showing the user
  46: > without lying about safety?
  47: 
  48: Jargon, knobs, and "advanced" settings are technical debt. Pay
  49: them down on every ship. The user shouldn't need to know what a
  50: fingerprint, rendezvous URL, SAS, capability, ratchet, or chunk
  51: hash is to use the product. They will need to know about *some*
  52: of it to make trust decisions — that's where we don't lie. But
  53: zero knobs the user can't make a sane choice about.
  54: 
  55: Every ship spec answers: **"What word, button, or knob disappears
  56: because of this ship?"** If the answer is "none," the surface is
  57: wrong.
  58: 
  59: ### 3. Async by default
  60: 
  61: > Does this feature work when one side is offline, asleep, on a
  62: > plane, or on the move?
  63: 
  64: The model is email/SMS, not phone calls. If the only path through
  65: the feature requires both sides reachable, it is not done. Outbox
  66: is the default; the synchronous path is the optimization. We
  67: build for the assumption that the recipient is asleep right now.
  68: 
  69: Every ship spec answers: **"Where does this feature buffer when
  70: the recipient is gone?"** "It just doesn't" is not an answer.
  71: 
  72: ### 4. Frontier behind the surface
  73: 
  74: > Smart enough to be invisible.
  75: 
  76: Every feature carries at least one component that measurably
  77: pushes a limit. Mediocre internals don't ship even when the
  78: surface looks identical to a "normal" version. We're not
  79: competing on the surface; we're competing on what runs behind it.
  80: 
  81: Frontier means measurable: an SLA, a regression test, a learned
  82: model with a calibrated metric, a proof, a benchmark on a tier
  83: of hardware nobody else targets. "Smart" without a number is
  84: marketing.
  85: 
  86: Every ship spec answers: **"What is the measurable frontier this
  87: ship pushes, and how do we regression-test it?"** If the answer
  88: is "the surface is nicer," the engine isn't done.
  89: 
  90: ### 5. Defang every corporate floor
  91: 
  92: > "For the people" means free of corporations, by default.
  93: 
  94: Every layer of corporate substrate (browser engine, DNS, CDN,
  95: OS keychain, push services, certificate authorities, hardware
  96: RNG, NTP, app stores) is a place a corporation could insert
  97: itself between us and the user. We can't always eliminate the
  98: substrate — Apple still made the phone — but we can eliminate
  99: the influence.
 100: 
 101: For each layer, we ship at least one engineering mitigation that
 102: makes using that substrate against our users prohibitively
 103: expensive: multi-vendor diversity, signed updates, encrypted
 104: payloads, IPFS distribution, optional-not-default opt-ins for
 105: anything that calls home. The default tier is convenient. The
 106: hardened tier is real and tested. The air-gap tier exists.
 107: 
 108: Every ship spec answers: **"What corporate substrate does this
 109: feature touch, and what mitigation are we shipping to neutralize
 110: it?"** If a feature's only path goes through a corporate layer
 111: without an alternative, the spec is incomplete.
 112: 
 113: The full mapping lives in [`SOVEREIGNTY.md`](./SOVEREIGNTY.md);
 114: this principle is the gating rule.
 115: 
 116: ---
 117: 
 118: ## The discipline that pairs with the principles
 119: 
 120: > Smallest surface, deepest internals.
 121: 
 122: The four principles together create a strong gravitational pull
 123: toward sprawl ("we should also do X, and Y, and Z..."). The
 124: discipline that prevents this:
 125: 
 126: **Don't add ten features. Add one feature whose engine is ten
 127: times the depth of the obvious version.**
 128: 
 129: Concrete examples of how this changes ship-specs:
 130: 
 131: - **Mobile UI.** Obvious: CSS breakpoints. Deep: sub-100ms input
 132:   latency as a tested SLA on a 5-year-old phone, predictive
 133:   prefetch of the next likely conversation, frame-budget
 134:   regression tests in CI.
 135: - **Multi-device-per-identity.** Obvious: "messages sync between
 136:   your devices." Deep: your phone has the next message
 137:   pre-decoded before you open the app, paths chosen from a
 138:   learned reachability model, CRDT proofs of commutativity under
 139:   partition + clock skew + edit storms.
 140: - **Auto-accept rules.** Obvious: "this extension allowed." Deep:
 141:   a learned per-user calibrated model of what THIS user has
 142:   accepted historically, prompting only when uncertainty crosses
 143:   a threshold.
 144: 
 145: The user sees the obvious version. The engine delivers the deep
 146: version. They never know why their phone is "just" up to date
 147: instantly.
 148: 
 149: ---
 150: 
 151: ## Ship-gate checklist
 152: 
 153: Every ship-spec answers all five before the first line of code:
 154: 
 155: ```
 156: [ ] Reach:    ________________________________________
 157:     (one sentence: who can use One Link who couldn't before)
 158: [ ] Hide:     ________________________________________
 159:     (what word/button/knob disappears)
 160: [ ] Async:    ________________________________________
 161:     (where this buffers when the recipient is gone)
 162: [ ] Depth:    ________________________________________
 163:     (the measurable frontier + the regression test that pins it)
 164: [ ] Defang:   ________________________________________
 165:     (what corporate substrate this touches + the mitigation
 166:      shipped alongside; cross-reference SOVEREIGNTY.md)
 167: ```
 168: 
 169: If any answer is "n/a" or hand-wavy, the ship-spec needs more
 170: work, not less. The principles are the floor, not aspirations.
 171: 
 172: ---
 173: 
 174: ## What the principles deliberately exclude
 175: 
 176: These things are NOT north stars and ship-specs that prioritize
 177: them get challenged:
 178: 
 179: - "Modern aesthetic." Looking like 2026 is fine; designing for it
 180:   is not.
 181: - "Feature parity with X." We do not ship to match a competitor.
 182:   We ship if it serves the four principles.
 183: - "Power-user productivity." Power users are welcome but they
 184:   are not the customer being optimized for. The grandparent in
 185:   Tulsa is.
 186: - "Faster shipping cadence." Cadence is a side effect. Pushing
 187:   the frontier sometimes takes longer than a quick ship would
 188:   imply; that's correct.
 189: 
 190: ---
 191: 
 192: ## How the principles get audited
 193: 
 194: These principles fail if nobody ever pulls a ship back over them.
 195: Every quarter:
 196: 
 197: 1. Re-read the four principles in light of what shipped.
 198: 2. Pick one ship that BARELY passed the checklist and ask
 199:    honestly whether it should have shipped.
 200: 3. Pick one user-visible surface and ask: would a non-technical
 201:    first-time user understand what this is and why it's there?
 202:    If not, file a hide-the-engine debt ticket.
 203: 4. Pick one feature and ask: where is its frontier? If you can't
 204:    point at a number, file a depth debt ticket.
 205: 
 206: Documents that don't get audited become decoration. Audit these.

   1: # Prior Knowledge Transfer
   2: 
   3: One Link's large-file path should make prior knowledge useful automatically:
   4: if the receiver, another trusted device, or a future model already knows most
   5: of the object, the sender should transmit only the novelty.
   6: 
   7: ## Sources Pulled From OneField Mesh
   8: 
   9: - `tools/onefield_transport/cdc_dedup.py`
  10:   - Sender streams a content-defined chunk manifest.
  11:   - Receiver answers with the chunks it is missing.
  12:   - Sender transmits only missing chunks.
  13: - `tools/calibration/codec_temporal_delta.py`
  14:   - Video-like streams can send keyframes plus prediction residuals.
  15:   - Both sides maintain deterministic predictor state.
  16:   - Drift-sync packets detect state divergence and force re-keying.
  17: - `tools/calibration/test_temporal_delta_drift_sync.py`
  18:   - A lossy-channel simulation proves predictor drift can be bounded by
  19:     periodic state hashes and forced keyframes.
  20: 
  21: ## Implemented In One Link
  22: 
  23: One Link already has CDC file manifests, verified BLAKE3 chunk hashes, durable
  24: transfer intents, retry/resume, and swarm chunk assist.
  25: 
  26: This pass adds local prior assist:
  27: 
  28: 1. The daemon keeps a bounded background index of chunks already present in
  29:    the One Link inbox and configured sync folders.
  30: 2. The index is lazy: it stores path + byte range + mtime metadata, not a
  31:    duplicate copy of every chunk.
  32: 3. When a trusted peer offers a CDC file, the receiver hydrates only matching
  33:    chunks that are actually needed, verifies each by BLAKE3, and then answers
  34:    `FILE_WANTS`.
  35: 4. The receiver asks the sender only for chunks not found locally or through
  36:    trusted swarm assist.
  37: 5. When a trusted peer asks `CHUNK_QUERY`, the daemon can hydrate from the
  38:    lazy prior index before answering.
  39: 
  40: This means a huge video, VM image, dataset, or edited archive can transfer at a
  41: fraction of the bandwidth when the receiver already has a related version.
  42: 
  43: This pass also upgrades trusted swarm assist from "ask another device if it has
  44: a chunk" into a deterministic transfer scheduler:
  45: 
  46: 1. Rarest chunks are pulled first, so chunks that only one trusted device has
  47:    are secured before common chunks.
  48: 2. Sources are scored by trust, reliability, bandwidth, latency, and energy
  49:    cost. Integrity is still enforced by BLAKE3 for every chunk.
  50: 3. Equal sources are byte-balanced, so multiple trusted devices act as one
  51:    parallel fabric instead of one source being overloaded.
  52: 4. The daemon now records the planned schedule, assigned bytes, missing bytes,
  53:    and per-source byte counts for future UI and retry decisions.
  54: 
  55: ## Safety Boundaries
  56: 
  57: - Scans are rooted only in the One Link inbox and configured sync folders.
  58: - Scans are bounded by file count and bytes per offer/query.
  59: - Lazy source reads are accepted only if the source file's size and mtime
  60:   still match the indexed metadata.
  61: - A chunk is usable only if its BLAKE3 hash exactly matches the peer manifest.
  62: - No private local filenames or directory listings are sent as part of prior
  63:   assist.
  64: - If no prior chunks are found, the normal CDC transfer path continues.
  65: 
  66: ## Next Upgrade
  67: 
  68: The next major leap is a true predictive stream mode for video and very large
  69: related media:
  70: 
  71: 1. Negotiate `file_video_delta_v1` only when both peers advertise it.
  72: 2. Send a codec/session descriptor and model hash.
  73: 3. Send periodic keyframes plus residual chunks.
  74: 4. Exchange predictor state hashes.
  75: 5. On drift, force a keyframe or fall back to normal CDC.
  76: 
  77: That mode should be optional and integrity-gated. The default arbitrary-file
  78: path remains exact byte delivery through CDC chunks.
<<<CONTENT_END>>>

   1: # Operating a One Link Rendezvous
   2: 
   3: A One Link rendezvous is a small server that lets paired devices on
   4: different networks find each other. It carries no plaintext payload —
   5: only signed presence beacons — and it can be run by anyone, anywhere.
   6: 
   7: > **TL;DR for impatient operators:**
   8: > ```
   9: > docker run -d --name one-link-rendezvous --restart unless-stopped \
  10: >     -p 7118:7118 onelink/rendezvous:latest
  11: > ```
  12: > Then put `https://your-host` (after fronting it with TLS) into the
  13: > "Connect across networks" field in One Link's Settings. Done.
  14: 
  15: ---
  16: 
  17: ## What it does, what it doesn't
  18: 
  19: **Does:**
  20: - Holds, in memory, a small signed record per pubkey:
  21:   `(pubkey, observed_public_IP, advertised_endpoints[], capabilities)`.
  22: - Replies to lookups: "where is `pubkey X`?"
  23: - Bounded resources: hard cap on registrations (default 200k),
  24:   per-IP rate limit, per-pubkey register rate limit.
  25: - Periodically evicts expired entries.
  26: - All registers and revokes are Ed25519-signed by the device. The
  27:   rendezvous can't impersonate anyone because it doesn't hold private
  28:   keys.
  29: 
  30: **Does NOT:**
  31: - See chat messages, file contents, or any payload bytes. End-to-end
  32:   encryption stays between the paired devices.
  33: - Persist anything to disk. A restart loses all current presence
  34:   registrations — devices re-register within a few minutes.
  35: - Authenticate operators or users. The protocol is symmetric. Trust
  36:   comes from the cryptographic signatures, not the operator.
  37: 
  38: **Threat model summary:**
  39: - A malicious or compromised rendezvous can:
  40:   - Drop or refuse to forward presence (DoS — users notice immediately)
  41:   - Lie about who is registered (clients verify nothing about lookup
  42:     responses except shape; bad data just causes failed dial attempts)
  43:   - Observe public-IP-of-pubkey metadata — *who is online when, from
  44:     where*. v0.5.3 sealed-sender will hide this.
  45: - A malicious or compromised rendezvous **cannot**:
  46:   - Read plaintext (impossible — it doesn't carry payload)
  47:   - Impersonate a device (no private keys)
  48:   - Forge registrations under someone else's pubkey (signature check)
  49:   - Replay old registrations to confuse clients (60s replay window)
  50: 
  51: ---
  52: 
  53: ## Hardware requirements
  54: 
  55: The rendezvous is intentionally small. For up to about 200,000
  56: simultaneous registrations:
  57: 
  58: | Resource | Minimum | Recommended |
  59: |---|---|---|
  60: | RAM | 256 MB | 512 MB |
  61: | CPU | 1 vCPU | 1 vCPU |
  62: | Disk | 100 MB (binaries + logs) | 1 GB |
  63: | Bandwidth | tens of KB/s | 1 Mbps burst |
  64: 
  65: A `$5/month` VPS handles this without strain. If you outgrow one
  66: instance, run more — devices can register with multiple in parallel
  67: and lookups race them.
  68: 
  69: ---
  70: 
  71: ## Deployment
  72: 
  73: ### Option 1 — Docker (recommended)
  74: 
  75: `docker-compose.yml` ships in the repo at `deploy/rendezvous/`:
  76: 
  77: ```yaml
  78: services:
  79:   rendezvous:
  80:     image: onelink/rendezvous:0.5.3
  81:     restart: unless-stopped
  82:     ports:
  83:       - "7118:7118"
  84:     environment:
  85:       ONE_LINK_RDZ_HOST: "0.0.0.0"
  86:       ONE_LINK_RDZ_PORT: "7118"
  87:       ONE_LINK_RDZ_LOG_LEVEL: "INFO"
  88: ```
  89: 
  90: Run:
  91: 
  92: ```bash
  93: cd deploy/rendezvous
  94: docker compose up -d
  95: ```
  96: 
  97: Logs:
  98: 
  99: ```bash
 100: docker compose logs -f rendezvous
 101: ```
 102: 
 103: ### Option 2 — systemd
 104: 
 105: ```ini
 106: # /etc/systemd/system/one-link-rendezvous.service
 107: [Unit]
 108: Description=One Link rendezvous
 109: After=network.target
 110:

 114: Group=onelink

 116:     --host 0.0.0.0 --port 7118

 121: PrivateTmp=yes
 122: ProtectSystem=strict
 123: ProtectHome=yes
 124: ReadWritePaths=

 126: ProtectKernelModules=yes

 128: ProtectControlGroups=yes

 140:

 143: sudo pip3 install one_link

 145: sudo systemctl enable --now one-link-rendezvous
 146: ```

 148: ### Option 3 — bare metal
 149: 
 150: ```bash
 151: pip install one_link
 152: python -m one_link.rendezvous_server --host 0.0.0.0 --port 7118
 153: ```
 154: 
 155: Use a process manager (supervisord, runit, pm2, …) to keep it up.
 156: 
 157: ---
 158: 
 159: ## TLS
 160: 
 161: **Always front the rendezvous with HTTPS.** The protocol is
 162: end-to-end signed, so a compromised TLS hop can't read or forge
 163: content — but TLS prevents passive observers on the LAN from learning
 164: which pubkeys are looking up which.
 165: 
 166: ### nginx + Let's Encrypt
 167: 
 168: ```nginx
 169: # /etc/nginx/sites-available/rendezvous.example.com
 170: server {
 171:     listen 443 ssl http2;
 172:     server_name rendezvous.example.com;
 173: 
 174:     ssl_certificate     /etc/letsencrypt/live/rendezvous.example.com/fullchain.pem;
 175:     ssl_certificate_key /etc/letsencrypt/live/rendezvous.example.com/privkey.pem;
 176: 
 177:     # Reasonable defaults, drop legacy.
 178:     ssl_protocols TLSv1.2 TLSv1.3;
 179:     ssl_prefer_server_ciphers off;
 180:     ssl_session_cache shared:SSL:10m;
 181: 
 182:     # Don't buffer — payloads are tiny.
 183:     proxy_buffering off;
 184:     client_max_body_size 16k;
 185: 
 186:     location / {
 187:         proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:7118;
 188:         proxy_set_header Host $host;
 189:         proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $remote_addr;
 190:         proxy_read_timeout 30s;
 191:     }
 192: 
 193:     # Optional: ban path-traversal nonsense at the edge.
 194:     location ~ \.\. { return 400; }
 195: }
 196: 
 197: server {
 198:     listen 80;
 199:     server_name rendezvous.example.com;
 200:     return 301 https://$host$request_uri;
 201: }
 202: ```
 203: 
 204: ```bash
 205: sudo certbot --nginx -d rendezvous.example.com
 206: ```
 207: 
 208: ### Cloudflare (alternative)
 209: 
 210: Point a DNS A record at your VPS, enable "Proxy" (orange cloud).
 211: Cloudflare terminates TLS on its edge, hits your origin on port 80
 212: or 7118 directly. Set the SSL/TLS mode to **Full (strict)** if you
 213: also have a cert on the origin (recommended).
 214: 
 215: The rendezvous reads `X-Forwarded-For` so client IP is preserved
 216: through the proxy chain.
 217:

 244: relabeling is trivial.

 246: ### From a One Link client
 247: 
 248: In the One Link UI: **Settings → Connect across networks**, paste:
 249: 
 250: ```
 251: https://rendezvous.example.com
 252: ```
 253: 
 254: The status dot turns green and the panel shows your observed public
 255: IP. If you're behind NAT, this is the IP your devices announce to
 256: each other.
 257: 
 258: ---
 259: 
 260: ## Tuning for scale
 261: 
 262: Defaults handle ~200,000 simultaneous registrations on commodity
 263: hardware. To go higher:
 264: 
 265: ```bash
 266: python -m one_link.rendezvous_server \
 267:     --host 0.0.0.0 \
 268:     --port 7118 \
 269:     --max-registrations 1000000 \
 270:     --rate-per-ip-per-min 600 \
 271:     --rate-register-per-pubkey-per-min 60
 272: ```
 273: 
 274: Each registration is roughly 1 KB of process memory. 1M = ~1 GB.
 275: 
 276: For higher throughput than one process can handle, run multiple
 277: behind a load-balancer with `ip_hash` or `consistent_hash` so the
 278: same client IP lands on the same instance (rate-limiter is per-IP
 279: per-instance — sticky routing keeps it accurate).
 280: 
 281: ---
 282: 
 283: ## Federation
 284: 
 285: Devices can register with multiple rendezvous in parallel, and
 286: lookups race all configured rendezvous, returning the first hit. To
 287: provide redundancy:
 288: 
 289: 1. Run two or more rendezvous instances at independent operators.
 290: 2. Have your users add both URLs to **Settings → Connect across
 291:    networks** (one per line).
 292: 3. Both will receive registrations; either can satisfy lookups.
 293: 
 294: There is no protocol-level sync between instances — by design.
 295: Eventual consistency happens through clients re-registering on
 296: their refresh schedule (every TTL/2, default 150 s).
 297: 
 298: ---
 299: 
 300: ## Privacy posture
 301: 
 302: The rendezvous learns:
 303: - Which pubkeys are online and their public IPs (the metadata that
 304:   TLS hides from network observers but the rendezvous itself sees).
 305: - Which pubkeys looked up which other pubkeys (only IF the looking
 306:   pubkey was identifiable; v0.5.0 lookups are anonymous — no auth).
 307: - Approximate device geo from IP (whatever IP geolocation lookup
 308:   reveals).
 309: 
 310: The rendezvous does NOT learn:
 311: - Anything about message content
 312: - Anything about file content
 313: - Group membership (groups are an end-to-end primitive on top of the
 314:   rendezvous, not a rendezvous-side feature)
 315: 
 316: To minimize what the rendezvous sees:
 317: - Put it behind Tor (run an onion service in front of it; the One
 318:   Link client supports `https?://` URLs only in v0.5.3, but a SOCKS
 319:   proxy in front of `aiohttp` is a small client patch).
 320: - Self-host. Operating your own rendezvous means you trust nobody
 321:   outside your house with this metadata.
 322: 
 323: ---
 324: 
 325: ## Incident response
 326: 
 327: If your rendezvous gets compromised:
 328: 
 329: 1. **Rotate the host.** Bring up a new one at a different IP / domain.
 330: 2. **Tell your users to update their rendezvous URL.** They need a
 331:    trusted out-of-band channel for this — exactly the same channel
 332:    they use to bootstrap pairing.
 333: 3. **Don't worry about message confidentiality.** A compromised
 334:    rendezvous can't decrypt anything. The cost of compromise is
 335:    metadata + uptime.
 336: 
 337: A compromised rendezvous can't impersonate any client because it
 338: doesn't hold private keys. The damage is bounded to: knowing who's
 339: online, and (if the rendezvous lies on lookup) directing dials at
 340: the wrong public IP — which fail closed because the One Link channel
 341: verifies the peer's pubkey at handshake.
 342: 
 343: ---
 344: 
 345: ## Why does this exist?
 346: 
 347: Most modern messaging apps need a centralized rendezvous service
 348: operated by the app vendor — Signal, WhatsApp, iMessage — and you
 349: have to trust that vendor's metadata posture. One Link's rendezvous
 350: is the same architectural primitive but the operator can be:
 351: 
 352: - The user's home server.
 353: - A friend's machine.
 354: - A community-run instance.
 355: - A commercial provider you choose.
 356: - Any combination of the above.
 357: 
 358: There is no "official" rendezvous you must use. The protocol is
 359: public, the binary is small, the operating cost is rounding-error
 360: small, and the trust surface is metadata-only. We expect a healthy
 361: ecosystem of small operators rather than one giant.

  71:   hardware inventory, adapter contracts, route scoring,
  72:   activation safety policy, multi-source pull, store-carry-forward,
  73:   safety budgets, and phased ship gates. Phase 1 now has code:
  74:   inventory, route scoring, activation governor, daemon/API fabric
  75:   truth, transfer metadata, and Activity-panel truth surfacing.
  76: 
  77: Read order for someone joining cold:
  78: 1. `PRINCIPLES.md` — what gates ships.
  79: 2. `ROADMAP.md` (this file) — what ships in what order.
  80: 3. `ARCHITECTURE.md` — how the PWA pivot is built.
  81: 4. `SOVEREIGNTY.md` + `SECURITY.md` — the defenses, paired.
  82: 5. `GOVERNANCE.md` — the structural commitments.
  83: 6. `UNIVERSAL_COMMS_FABRIC.md` - how One Link reaches people
  84:    when ordinary networks are missing, weak, or fragmented.
  85: 7. `PHONE_TIER.md` — the phone-specific surface contract.
  86: 
  87: The reorganization from earlier roadmaps groups remaining work
  88: under three tracks instead of tiers. Tiers were "what the protocol
  89: needs"; tracks are "what the user gets." North stars steer the
  90: tracks; the four principles gate every ship.
  91:

 275: ### Track B — Connection
 276: 
 277: > Principle 3 (Async by default): does this work when one side is
 278: > offline, asleep, on a plane, or on the move?
 279: 
 280: The track that turns "Everything is connected" from "if both
 281: sides are online" into "always." Every ship in this track
 282: removes a presence-required precondition.
 283: 
 284: Ordered by leverage:
 285: 
 286: 1. **Multi-device-per-identity (the v1.0.0 target).** Your phone,
 287:    laptop, and desktop are ONE identity to your friends, not
 288:    three contacts. Frontier: predictive cache so your phone has
 289:    tomorrow's reply pre-decoded before you wake up; learned
 290:    model of which device you'll open next; CRDT merge with
 291:    proofs of commutativity under partition + clock skew + edit
 292:    storms. Surface: peers see one of you. Your devices feel
 293:    instantly synchronized.
 294: 
 295: 2. **Async-first delivery enhancements.** Outbox stops being a
 296:    fallback and becomes the default path; the synchronous path
 297:    is the optimization. Frontier: a learned reachability model
 298:    per peer (when do they typically come online?) so messages
 299:    prefer paths that are about to be available. Surface: send a
 300:    message, it's delivered when it's possible to deliver. The
 301:    user never sees "still trying."
 302: 
 303: 3. **Multi-path send** (the orphaned Tier-3 v0.8.3). Send chunks
 304:    over LAN + internet + relay in parallel; fastest path wins
 305:    per chunk. Frontier: the path-allocator is a learned
 306:    bandit, not a heuristic; CDC dedup makes mistakes nearly free
 307:    so the bandit can be aggressive. Surface: large files
 308:    transfer faster than physics says they should.
 309: 
 310: 4. **Large file streaming** (the orphaned Tier-3 v0.8.6). Don't
 311:    materialize the full file before playback; stream chunks to a
 312:    media element as they arrive. Frontier: predictive chunk
 313:    prefetch driven by playback position + recent throughput;
 314:    adaptive bitrate when bandwidth degrades. Surface: voice
 315:    messages and forwarded video play instantly even on a slow
 316:    peer.
 317: 
 318: 5. **Rendezvous default-on, not advanced setting.** Currently
 319:    rendezvous is a "for power users" knob in Network settings.
 320:    Move it to default-configured-on-install (with a curated
 321:    public rendezvous list shipped in `paths.py`). Frontier: a
 322:    pluggable rendezvous discovery that uses DNS, LAN multicast,
 323:    and a fallback DHT in priority order; the user sees nothing.
 324: 
 325: ### Track C — Engine-hiding
 326: 
 327: > Principle 2 (Hide the engine): what word, button, or knob
 328: > disappears with this ship?
 329: 
 330: The track that turns "It just works" from "if you understand
 331: P2P" into "for everyone." Every ship in this track removes a
 332: technical concept from the user's surface.
 333: 
 334: Ordered by leverage:
 335: 
 336: 1. **Channel-level Double Ratchet activation.** The primitive
 337:    shipped in v0.7.2 and has been sitting unused since. Detect
 338:    mutual `double_ratchet_v1` capability and switch the channel.
 339:    Frontier: forward secrecy + post-compromise security, in
 340:    bytes per message <2× the existing X25519+ChaCha20-Poly1305
 341:    path; auditable transcript binding. Surface: zero. Invisible
 342:    safety upgrade.
 343: 
 344: 2. **Pair flow simplification.** Hide the SAS by default for
 345:    casual pairings (auto-accept on LAN with a deny-by-default
 346:    capability set + a "verify in person?" pill that the user
 347:    can engage when they want). Frontier: a calibrated risk model
 348:    that decides whether to surface the SAS based on context
 349:    (LAN vs. internet, hostname-pubkey history, prior pairings
 350:    from the same network). Surface: most pairings just work; the
 351:    SAS appears only when it actually changes the trust decision.
 352: 
 353: 3. **Progressive disclosure for advanced settings.** Mark settings
 354:    as "everyone / power user / engineer" tiers in the settings
 355:    table; default to "everyone." A long-press / shortcut reveals
 356:    the rest. Frontier: settings that auto-tier based on the
 357:    user's interaction history (we know which ones they touch).
 358:    Surface: 80% of users never see 80% of the settings.
 359: 
 360: 4. **Group sender-key rotation cadence.** Currently never rotates;
 361:    add periodic rotation tied to group event log advancement.
 362:    Frontier: rotation is automatic + driven by entropy/usage
 363:    thresholds; the user never knows. Surface: zero new buttons.
 364: 
 365: 5. **Tighter supply-chain gates.** pip-audit / bandit currently
 366:    report-only; promote to fail-the-build after triage. Frontier:
 367:    reproducible builds verified in CI; SBOM auto-published.
 368:    Surface: zero. The kind of safety the user shouldn't think
 369:    about.
 370: 
 371: ---
 372: 
 373: ### Track D — Coherence Mesh (sovereign network + multi-device identity)
 374: 
 375: > Principle: all five. This track is the apex of the engine work —
 376: > turns One Link from "best-in-class file + chat engine" into
 377: > "a global communications layer that no company, government, ISP,
 378: > or attacker can lock out, surveil, censor, or destroy — and that
 379: > any person can use without understanding any of that."
 380: 
 381: Canonical plan: [`COHERENCE_MESH_PLAN.md`](./COHERENCE_MESH_PLAN.md)
 382: 
 383: **The load-bearing insight:** three trust tiers, three default
 384: privacy modes. Self-traffic (your own devices talking to each
 385: other) is direct + fast because there's no metadata to hide.
 386: Friend-traffic is 1-hop-onion + sealed-sender by default.
 387: Paranoid mode is 3-hop-onion + Loopix-class cover traffic for
 388: users in hostile environments. The user never picks; pair-by-QR
 389: puts your devices in self-mesh, friends in pinned-contact, and
 390: paranoid is an explicit opt-in.
 391: 
 392: Phase F ships in 8 sub-phases (F1–F8); see the plan for
 393: acceptance gates per phase. Ordered by leverage:
 394: 
 395: 1. **F1 — Harvest the easy wins.** Port `OneField/onefield/privacy/sharding.cl`
 396:    (Shamir threshold recovery, Tier 15 production) and
 397:    `OneField/onefield/bridge/discovery.cl` (peer-cache TTL/announce
 398:    logic) and `OneField/onefield/mesh/bootstrap.cl` (channel-
 399:    reciprocity pair-trust). All three are pre-built in OneField
 400:    Mesh and harvest directly into Rust crates.
 401: 
 402: 2. **F2 — Pair-by-QR.** Ed25519 + Dilithium handshake + optional
 403:    channel-reciprocity Factor-2. Replaces the `--lan` token URL
 404:    entirely. Eliminates remote-pair vulnerabilities.
 405: 
 406: 3. **F3 — Onion circuits.** 1-hop default for pinned-contact friend
 407:    traffic; 3-hop for paranoid mode. Path selection via Phase E
 408:    coherence-field routing (already shipped).
 409: 
 410: 4. **F4 — Sealed sender + cover traffic.** Loopix-style constant-
 411:    rate background between pinned contacts. Defeats timing analysis.
 412: 
 413: 5. **F5 — Personal Device Mesh.** Master identity + per-device
 414:    subkeys + device-presence CRDT + remote-instruct command channel.
 415:    Your phone, laptop, tablet, desktop are ONE identity to friends
 416:    AND separately addressable to you. Phone in TX grabs file from
 417:    laptop in CA at full network speed (self-traffic skips onion).
 418: 
 419: 6. **F6 — DPI-evading transport.** Cloak/Obfs4-style pluggable
 420:    transport. Bytes on the wire look like generic HTTPS;
 421:    censorship-resistant by default.
 422: 
 423: 7. **F7 — PQ signatures.** Ed25519 + Dilithium hybrid. Survives
 424:    quantum computers. Defense-in-depth: either scheme alone
 425:    authenticates.
 426: 
 427: 8. **F8 — Confidential-compute daemon.** Per-platform: Apple Secure
 428:    Memory / Intel SGX / AMD SEV-SNP / Windows TPM. Local malware
 429:    with root cannot extract identity keys.
 430: 
 431: **End state**: capabilities no other consumer messenger ships
 432: (see comparison table in [`COHERENCE_MESH_PLAN.md`](./COHERENCE_MESH_PLAN.md)).
 433: The "everyone on any device, super easily" promise becomes
 434: literally what the architecture delivers.
 435:
