 109: ---
 110: 
 111: ## The three paranoia tiers
 112: 
 113: Every user picks one in setup. Tier sets the defaults; individual
 114: toggles override.
 115: 
 116: ### Tier: Default
 117: 
 118: > "Most people. Convenience-first. Strong defaults."
 119: 
 120: **Posture:** trust the substrate enough to enable conveniences.
 121: Apple/Google are visible at the metadata layer (timing of pushes,
 122: that you connect to the internet) but never at the content layer.
 123: 
 124: **Active corporate-touching paths:**
 125: - CDN-served PWA from `https://one-link.example/` (Let's Encrypt cert)
 126: - Multi-vendor STUN for NAT traversal (6 orgs rotated)
 127: - Optional encrypted Web Push (off until user opts in)
 128: - Project-hosted rendezvous for cross-network reach (with cover traffic)
 129: 
 130: **Inactive:**
 131: - No analytics, no SDK, no fingerprinting, no third-party login,
 132:   no tracking pixel, no telemetry — same as every other tier.
 133: 
 134: **Use case:** the friend, family member, casual user. They want to
 135: chat with people. They don't care about state-actor adversaries.
 136: 
 137: ### Tier: Hardened
 138: 
 139: > "Activists, journalists, professionals. Paranoia-first."
 140: 
 141: **Posture:** assume substrate is adversarial. Trust nothing
 142: corporate. Slower. Battery cost. Fully usable.
 143: 
 144: **Active corporate-touching paths:**
 145: - Loaded from local `.html` archive (downloaded once, run from disk)
 146:   OR `.onion` mirror via Tor browser
 147: - Self-hosted STUN OR LAN-only mode (no STUN at all)
 148: - No Web Push — open the app to see new messages
 149: - Tor-routed signaling
 150: - Threshold identity across user's devices (no Passkeys, no OS keychain)
 151: 
 152: **Inactive (additionally):**
 153: - No DNS lookup of project domain
 154: - No CDN-fetched bundle
 155: - No corporate push servers ever
 156: 
 157: **Use case:** the journalist's source, the activist coordinating in
 158: a hostile country, the professional handling sensitive client data.
 159: 
 160: ### Tier: Air-gap
 161: 
 162: > "Strict. No internet. Period."
 163: 
 164: **Posture:** the only acceptable connection is local.
 165: 
 166: **Active corporate-touching paths:** none, in steady state.
 167: 
 168: **Inactive:**
 169: - Internet entirely. The app refuses to make any network request
 170:   outside the local network.
 171: 
 172: **Available channels:**
 173: - BLE proximity pairing (Android web; iOS falls back to QR + ultrasonic)
 174: - LAN mDNS-equivalent peer discovery
 175: - USB transfer of message bundles (export → physical media → import)
 176: - QR-code message exchange (high-density QR encodes 2-3KB; chain
 177:   multiple QRs for longer messages)
 178: 
 179: **Use case:** physically co-present people who never want any third
 180: party to even know they communicate. Air-gapped operations. Off-grid.
 181: 
 182: ---
 183: 
 184: ## The tier-selector UX
 185: 
 186: A single screen at first install:
 187: 
 188: ```
 189: ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
 190: │  How private do you want to be?                  │
 191: │                                                  │
 192: │  ◉ Default                                       │
 193: │    Strong privacy. Convenience-first defaults.   │
 194: │    Most people. (Recommended.)                   │
 195: │                                                  │
 196: │  ○ Hardened                                      │
 197: │    Paranoia-first. Slower. Activists,           │
 198: │    journalists, professionals.                  │
 199: │                                                  │
 200: │  ○ Air-gap                                       │
 201: │    No internet ever. Only physically nearby      │
 202: │    people. Ultra-strict.                        │
 203: │                                                  │
 204: │  You can change this later. Settings → Privacy.  │
 205: │                                                  │
 206: │              [ Continue ]                        │
 207: └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
 208: ```
 209: 
 210: That's the entire surface for tier selection. The plumbing
 211: underneath — STUN endpoints, push routing, rendezvous mode, Tor
 212: configuration, identity storage choice — is set by the tier.
 213: The user is never asked about Kyber, Dilithium, mix-net hops, or
 214: attestation chains.
 215: 
 216: The tier is persisted in `chat-prefs` as `paranoia_tier:
 217: "default" | "hardened" | "air-gap"`. Every relevant default in
 218: settings derives from it on read, with explicit per-setting
 219: overrides taking priority.

 224: 
 225: For implementers: exact behavioral differences across tiers.
 226: 
 227: | Capability | Default | Hardened | Air-gap |
 228: |---|---|---|---|
 229: | PWA bundle source | CDN (HTTPS) | `.onion` or local `.html` | Local `.html` only |

 235: | Cross-device identity sync | Threshold-of-N over P2P (or opt-in Passkey) | Threshold-of-N over P2P | Threshold-of-N over LAN/USB only |

   1: # Transfer Doctor And Torture Gate
   2: 
   3: Status: in_progress for v0.10.8.
   4: 
   5: One Link's promise is not "try to send a file." The promise is "the file gets
   6: there, quietly, even when devices sleep, routes move, sessions desync, versions
   7: differ, and chunks fail."
   8: 
   9: ## Transfer Doctor
  10: 
  11: `one_link.transfer_doctor` converts raw transfer ledger state into product-safe
  12: diagnosis:
  13: 
  14: - `Sending`
  15: - `Waiting for device`
  16: - `Resuming`
  17: - `Done`
  18: - `Needs attention`
  19: 
  20: Each diagnosis includes:
  21: 
  22: - a stable code;
  23: - a plain user message;
  24: - whether One Link can heal automatically;
  25: - the next automatic action;
  26: - optional retry timing and route action.
  27: 
  28: The daemon attaches this doctor block to transfer WebSocket events and paused
  29: transfer metadata. The server attaches the same block to `/api/transfers`.
  30: 
  31: ## Auto-Healing Actions
  32: 
  33: Current action vocabulary:
  34: 
  35: - `wait_for_peer` - device is offline or asleep; wait quietly.
  36: - `retry_with_backoff` - durable intent stays queued until retry time.
  37: - `reopen_secure_session` - secure session desync; drop and reconnect.
  38: - `refresh_route` - peer moved IP/port; resolve again.
  39: - `retry_missing_chunk` - corrupt or missing piece; retry only that piece.
  40: - `fallback_protocol` - versions differ; use best shared protocol.
  41: 
  42: ## Live Route Memory
  43: 
  44: `RouteMemory` scores observed routes by:
  45: 
  46: - success ratio;
  47: - latency;
  48: - bandwidth;
  49: - failure count.
  50: 
  51: The daemon now feeds live transfer outcomes into route memory. Successful sends
  52: stamp route bandwidth and reliability. Failed sends stamp a doctor error code.
  53: `/api/peers` can surface:
  54: 
  55: - `best_route`;
  56: - `bandwidth_bps`;
  57: - `reliability`;
  58: - `route_scores`.
  59: 
  60: This makes One Link stop hammering weak paths and prefer the route that actually
  61: works for that peer.
  62: 
  63: ## Huge File Torture Simulator
  64: 
  65: `one_link.transfer_sim` models large transfers without creating large files.
  66: It builds synthetic chunk manifests and injects:
  67: 
  68: - offline rounds;
  69: - corrupt chunks;
  70: - legacy protocol fallback;
  71: - route scoring;
  72: - automatic retry until verified delivery.
  73: 
  74: Run:
  75: 
  76: ```powershell
  77: python scripts\torture_transfer_engine.py --size-gib 10 --chunk-mib 16
  78: ```
  79: 
  80: The command exits non-zero if delivery does not complete.
  81: 
  82: ## What This Unlocks Next
  83: 
  84: The next production leap is to expose the live route intelligence in the UI
  85: transfer cards:
  86: 
  87: - speed;
  88: - ETA;
  89: - automatic retry state;
  90: - current route;
  91: - which chunks were recovered from prior knowledge or trusted swarm sources.

   1: # Universal Comms Fabric
   2: 
   3: Status: in_progress
   4: Last updated: 2026-05-12
   5: 
   6: This document captures the next major One Link frontier: every device should
   7: use every communication surface it has, automatically, safely, and
   8: intelligently.
   9: 
  10: The goal is not "file transfer over Wi-Fi." The goal is:
  11: 
  12: > A trusted delivery fabric that finds, creates, combines, and heals every
  13: > possible path between a user's devices and trusted people.
  14: 
  15: To the user, One Link remains simple: pick a device or person, send anything,
  16: and it gets there. Underneath, One Link becomes a transport organism: LAN,
  17: Wi-Fi Direct, hotspot, Bluetooth, USB, Ethernet, WebRTC, relay, QR, audio,
  18: offline courier, LoRa, SDR, and future hardware all become candidate routes
  19: for the same encrypted, resumable, content-addressed delivery intent.
  20: 
  21: ---
  22: 
  23: ## 1. North Star
  24: 
  25: One Link should not ask "what socket can I open?"
  26: 
  27: It should ask:
  28: 
  29: 1. What trusted identity needs this data?
  30: 2. What physical paths exist right now?
  31: 3. What paths can I create with this hardware?
  32: 4. What paths might appear later?
  33: 5. Which trusted devices already have pieces?
  34: 6. Which route is safest, fastest, cheapest, and least annoying?
  35: 7. How do I make the delivery intent true without user babysitting?
  36: 
  37: The product promise:
  38: 
  39: > Send anything, any size, to any trusted device or person. If any path exists,
  40: > One Link uses it. If no path exists, One Link waits, carries, resumes, and
  41: > heals until the data arrives.
  42: 
  43: The implementation promise:
  44: 
  45: > All transports are untrusted byte pipes. Identity, authorization,
  46: > encryption, chunk verification, replay protection, resumability, and delivery
  47: > truth live above every transport.
  48: 
  49: ---
  50: 
  51: ## 2. Design Doctrine
  52: 
  53: ### 2.1 Slow Links Carry Control, Fast Links Carry Data
  54: 
  55: Not every communication surface needs to carry whole files.
  56: 
  57: Low-rate paths are still powerful if they carry:
  58: 
  59: - presence beacons
  60: - pairing handshakes
  61: - route hints
  62: - hotspot credentials
  63: - chunk manifests
  64: - missing-chunk requests
  65: - wake/resume signals
  66: - sealed relay rendezvous hints
  67: - emergency text
  68: 
  69: Bulk data should move over the fastest safe available path:
  70: 
  71: - LAN TCP/QUIC
  72: - Wi-Fi Direct
  73: - private hotspot
  74: - Ethernet
  75: - USB
  76: - WebRTC/DataChannel
  77: - WebTransport
  78: - sealed relay fallback
  79: - multi-source swarm
  80: 
  81: ### 2.2 The User Sends an Intent, Not a Socket Event
  82: 
  83: A send must become durable before any transfer starts.
  84: 
  85: Required behavior:
  86: 
  87: - Browser/upload source is staged before transfer starts.
  88: - A delivery intent is written to durable storage.
  89: - Every chunk state is recoverable after crash/restart.
  90: - Failed chunks retry individually.
  91: - Offline peers move the transfer to waiting state, not failure.
  92: - Version mismatch negotiates the best shared protocol.
  93: - Route/session desync triggers auto-repair.
  94: 
  95: The UI states should stay human:
  96: 
  97: - Sending
  98: - Waiting for device
  99: - Resuming
 100: - Finding faster path
 101: - Sending missing pieces
 102: - Done
 103: 
 104: ### 2.3 Every Transport Is Replaceable
 105: 
 106: The secure One Link packet/chunk layer must not depend on any transport.
 107: 
 108: Correct:
 109: 
 110: ```text
 111: Delivery Intent
 112:   -> Secure Session / Capability / Chunk Manifest
 113:   -> Transport Brain
 114:   -> Adapter: LAN / Wi-Fi Direct / BLE / USB / WebRTC / RF / etc.
 115: ```
 116: 
 117: Incorrect:
 118: 
 119: ```text
 120: Feature code directly opens TCP socket and invents its own retry/security.
 121: ```
 122: 
 123: ### 2.4 Hardware Is Opportunity, Not Requirement
 124: 
 125: Normal computers should get the strongest possible experience from hardware
 126: they already have:
 127: 
 128: - Wi-Fi card
 129: - Bluetooth adapter
 130: - Ethernet port
 131: - USB port
 132: - speaker/microphone
 133: - camera/screen
 134: - storage devices
 135: 
 136: Optional hardware expands the fabric:
 137: 
 138: - LoRa / Meshtastic
 139: - Zigbee / Thread
 140: - SDR / HackRF / LimeSDR / USRP
 141: - NFC
 142: - serial radios
 143: - satellite modems
 144: 
 145: The architecture must make these optional adapters, not required dependencies.
 146: 
 147: ### 2.5 No Raw Trust In The Path
 148: 
 149: Every path is hostile until proven otherwise.
 150: 
 151: Rules:
 152: 
 153: - Transport adapters never receive plaintext user data unless explicitly
 154:   operating after the secure decrypt boundary.
 155: - All chunks are content-addressed and hash-verified.
 156: - All control messages are authenticated.
 157: - Capabilities gate who may request what.
 158: - Relays and couriers are blind.
 159: - RF/hardware adapters obey safety, regulatory, and power policy gates.
 160: 
 161: ---
 162: 
 163: ## 3. Hardware And Path Inventory
 164: 
 165: One Link needs a local hardware/path inventory daemon that continuously
 166: maintains a live map of communication surfaces.
 167: 
 168: ### 3.1 Inventory Output
 169: 
 170: Each path candidate reports:
 171: 
 172: ```json
 173: {
 174:   "adapter_id": "wifi_direct.windows.0",
 175:   "kind": "wifi_direct",
 176:   "available": true,
 177:   "requires_user_action": false,
 178:   "requires_admin": false,
 179:   "bulk_capable": true,
 180:   "control_capable": true,
 181:   "estimated_bps": 480000000,
 182:   "measured_bps": 0,
 183:   "latency_ms": 8,
 184:   "loss": 0.0,
 185:   "power_cost": "medium",
 186:   "privacy": "direct_local",
 187:   "range": "room_or_building",
 188:   "safety_state": "ok",
 189:   "platform_notes": "Windows Wi-Fi Direct available through OS APIs"
 190: }
 191: ```
 192: 
 193: ### 3.2 Required Inventory Sources
 194: 
 195: Desktop:
 196: 
 197: - active LAN interfaces
 198: - Wi-Fi SSID/BSSID when available
 199: - link-local IPv4/IPv6
 200: - mDNS reachability
 201: - Bluetooth adapter availability
 202: - BLE permissions
 203: - USB device attach events
 204: - Ethernet link state
 205: - local firewall constraints when detectable
 206: - OS hotspot capability
 207: - Wi-Fi Direct capability
 208: - camera/microphone permission for QR/audio bootstrap
 209: - installed OneField/SDR dependencies
 210: - connected LoRa/serial/SDR devices
 211: 
 212: Browser/PWA:
 213: 
 214: - WebRTC availability
 215: - WebTransport availability
 216: - Web Bluetooth availability
 217: - WebUSB availability
 218: - camera permission
 219: - microphone permission
 220: - storage quota
 221: - service worker state
 222: - network information hints when exposed
 223: 
 224: Mobile:
 225: 
 226: - Wi-Fi/hotspot capability exposed by native wrapper
 227: - BLE scan/advertise
 228: - NFC
 229: - camera
 230: - microphone/speaker
 231: - local network permission
 232: - background execution limits
 233: - battery saver state
 234: 
 235: ---
 236: 
 237: ## 4. Transport Adapter Contract
 238: 
 239: Every communication method must implement the same conceptual contract.
 240: 
 241: ### 4.1 Adapter Lifecycle
 242: 
 243: ```python
 244: class TransportAdapter:
 245:     def probe(self) -> AdapterProbe:
 246:         ...
 247: 
 248:     def score(self, intent: DeliveryIntent, peer: PeerState) -> RouteScore:
 249:         ...
 250: 
 251:     async def prepare(self, peer: PeerState, intent: DeliveryIntent) -> PreparedRoute:
 252:         ...
 253: 
 254:     async def open(self, route: PreparedRoute) -> TransportSession:
 255:         ...
 256: 
 257:     async def close(self) -> None:
 258:         ...
 259: ```
 260: 
 261: ### 4.2 Transport Session Contract
 262: 
 263: ```python
 264: class TransportSession:
 265:     mtu: int
 266:     ordered: bool
 267:     reliable: bool
 268:     bulk_capable: bool
 269:     control_capable: bool
 270: 
 271:     async def send_frame(self, frame: bytes) -> None:
 272:         ...
 273: 
 274:     async def recv_frame(self) -> bytes:
 275:         ...
 276: 
 277:     async def stats(self) -> SessionStats:
 278:         ...
 279: 
 280:     async def repair(self, reason: RepairReason) -> RepairResult:
 281:         ...
 282: ```
 283: 
 284: ### 4.3 Required Adapter Guarantees
 285: 
 286: Adapters must:
 287: 
 288: - never invent identity
 289: - never bypass capability checks
 290: - never assume plaintext
 291: - expose MTU and reliability truth
 292: - surface failures as machine-readable repair reasons
 293: - support cancellation
 294: - avoid blocking the daemon event loop
 295: - avoid unbounded memory growth
 296: - provide deterministic test fakes
 297: 
 298: ---
 299: 
 300: ## 5. First-Class Adapters
 301: 
 302: ### 5.1 LAN Adapter
 303: 
 304: Purpose:
 305: 
 306: Use existing local network paths.
 307: 
 308: Capabilities:
 309: 
 310: - mDNS/UDP discovery
 311: - direct TCP/QUIC transfer
 312: - route refresh when peer IP/port changes
 313: - multi-connection striping where useful
 314: - local-only operation without internet
 315: 
 316: Ship gate:
 317: 
 318: - two laptops on same router can discover, pair, chat, and transfer large files
 319: - router restart causes waiting/resuming, not lost transfer
 320: 
 321: ### 5.2 Private Hotspot Adapter
 322: 
 323: Purpose:
 324: 
 325: If no LAN exists, create one.
 326: 
 327: Behavior:
 328: 
 329: 1. Device A creates a One Link private hotspot.
 330: 2. Device B receives join info through QR, BLE, audio, invite file, or manual fallback.
 331: 3. Both devices establish a local encrypted One Link session.
 332: 4. Bulk transfer uses the newly created private Wi-Fi path.
 333: 
 334: Platform notes:
 335: 
 336: - Windows: use WLAN hosted network / Mobile Hotspot APIs where available.
 337: - macOS: hotspot creation is restricted; may require native helper or user-assisted flow.
 338: - Linux: NetworkManager/AP mode where adapter supports it.
 339: - Mobile: native wrappers required for useful automation.
 340: 
 341: Ship gate:
 342: 
 343: - no router, no internet, two normal laptops can still send a file with minimal user action.
 344: 
 345: ### 5.3 Wi-Fi Direct Adapter
 346: 
 347: Purpose:
 348: 
 349: Peer-to-peer Wi-Fi without router/hotspot UX where OS support allows.
 350: 
 351: Behavior:
 352: 
 353: - discover Wi-Fi Direct peers
 354: - negotiate group owner/client roles
 355: - exchange One Link route endpoint
 356: - use secure chunk transfer over the created IP link
 357: 
 358: Risks:
 359: 
 360: - inconsistent driver/platform exposure
 361: - Windows support exists but app access can be awkward
 362: - macOS support is limited for third-party apps
 363: 
 364: Ship gate:
 365: 
 366: - adapter must gracefully report unsupported rather than confuse users.
 367: 
 368: ### 5.4 BLE Control Adapter
 369: 
 370: Purpose:
 371: 
 372: Low-rate control, not bulk file transfer.
 373: 
 374: Uses:
 375: 
 376: - proximity discovery
 377: - pair bootstrap
 378: - exchange route hints
 379: - carry hotspot credentials
 380: - wake/resume nudges
 381: - tiny emergency messages
 382: - missing-manifest negotiation when no high-rate path exists
 383: 
 384: Never use BLE as the default bulk path except for tiny payloads.
 385: 
 386: Ship gate:
 387: 
 388: - BLE can bootstrap a private hotspot transfer without typing IP addresses.
 389: 
 390: ### 5.5 USB Link Adapter
 391: 
 392: Purpose:
 393: 
 394: Use direct cable paths when possible.
 395: 
 396: Variants:
 397: 
 398: - USB networking / RNDIS / CDC ECM
 399: - Android/iOS tethering path
 400: - WebUSB/native helper for specialized devices
 401: - removable drive courier mode
 402: 
 403: Courier mode:
 404: 
 405: 1. Sender writes encrypted chunk bundle + manifest to removable storage.
 406: 2. Receiver imports bundle.
 407: 3. Mesh index updates.
 408: 4. Missing chunks continue over any live path.
 409: 
 410: Ship gate:
 411: 
 412: - a USB drive can move encrypted pieces without revealing plaintext or breaking resume.
 413: 
 414: ### 5.6 Ethernet Link-Local Adapter
 415: 
 416: Purpose:
 417: 
 418: Direct cable or switch-only operation.
 419: 
 420: Behavior:
 421: 
 422: - detect link state
 423: - use IPv4 link-local / IPv6 link-local
 424: - advertise over mDNS
 425: - prefer for bulk when available
 426: 
 427: Ship gate:
 428: 
 429: - two laptops connected by Ethernet can transfer without router/DHCP/internet.
 430: 
 431: ### 5.7 WebRTC / WebTransport Adapter
 432: 
 433: Purpose:
 434: 
 435: Cross-network reachability when internet exists.
 436: 
 437: Behavior:
 438: 
 439: - direct NAT traversal first
 440: - sealed relay only when direct fails
 441: - use DataChannel for reliable messages and chunk frames
 442: - use WebTransport where available for bulk
 443: - expose route regime: direct, hole-punched, relayed
 444: 
 445: Ship gate:
 446: 
 447: - two devices on different networks can transfer with relay blind to plaintext.
 448: 
 449: ### 5.8 QR / Optical Adapter
 450: 
 451: Purpose:
 452: 
 453: Human-visible bootstrap and small payload handoff.
 454: 
 455: Uses:
 456: 
 457: - pair proof
 458: - offline invite
 459: - route hint
 460: - recovery shard
 461: - hotspot credentials
 462: - tiny manifest
 463: 
 464: Future:
 465: 
 466: - animated QR/frame burst for larger control bundles
 467: - camera-to-screen optical courier mode
 468: 
 469: Ship gate:
 470: 
 471: - first pair can complete with no network path beyond camera/screen.
 472: 
 473: ### 5.9 Audio Adapter
 474: 
 475: Purpose:
 476: 
 477: Tiny out-of-band data path using speaker/microphone.
 478: 
 479: Uses:
 480: 
 481: - pair proof
 482: - nearby presence chirp
 483: - emergency text
 484: - route hint
 485: - anti-MITM proximity signal
 486: 
 487: Constraints:
 488: 
 489: - must be optional
 490: - must ask permission
 491: - must be quiet or explicitly user-triggered by default
 492: - low bandwidth
 493: 
 494: Ship gate:
 495: 
 496: - audio can exchange a short authenticated pairing nonce in a room.
 497: 
 498: ### 5.10 OneField Hardware Adapter
 499: 
 500: Purpose:
 501: 
 502: Optional extreme hardware path using OneField Mesh concepts and devices.
 503: 
 504: Candidate sources:
 505: 
 506: - `$HOME\Projects\OneField Mesh\tools\onefield_transport`
 507: - `tools\onefield_node.py`
 508: - `tools\comms\tier2_link.py`
 509: - `onefield\bridge\*.cl`
 510: - `onefield\radio\hal\*.cl`
 511: 
 512: Usable now:
 513: 
 514: - parallel TCP transport concepts
 515: - CDC dedup protocol concepts
 516: - UDP-FEC concepts
 517: - MPTCP fallback concepts
 518: - QUIC pacing concepts
 519: - RF mesh software loopback tests
 520: - route scoring / adapter registry / safety policy ideas
 521: 
 522: Hardware-gated:
 523: 
 524: - HackRF / SDR over-the-air transport
 525: - LoRa / Zigbee adapters
 526: - multi-radio coherent combining
 527: 
 528: Rules:
 529: 
 530: - OneField is a transport provider, not a replacement for One Link security.
 531: - Hardware paths carry encrypted One Link frames/chunks only.
 532: - RF transmit requires explicit safety/regulatory gates.
 533: - Experimental hardware mode must never degrade normal user flows.
 534: 
 535: Ship gate:
 536: 
 537: - software-loopback adapter proves One Link frames can travel through a
 538:   OneField transport fake before any hardware path is exposed.
 539: 
 540: ---
 541: 
 542: ## 6. Transport Brain
 543: 
 544: The Transport Brain scores and chooses paths.
 545: 
 546: ### 6.1 Route Score Inputs
 547: 
 548: - measured throughput
 549: - estimated throughput
 550: - RTT
 551: - jitter
 552: - loss/retry rate
 553: - MTU
 554: - setup time
 555: - peer trust state
 556: - privacy level
 557: - relay exposure
 558: - power cost
 559: - battery state
 560: - data cap/cost hints
 561: - user friction
 562: - required permissions
 563: - admin/root requirement
 564: - protocol compatibility
 565: - storage availability
 566: - safety/regulatory state
 567: - recent failure history
 568: 
 569: ### 6.2 Route Classes
 570: 
 571: User-facing:
 572: 
 573: - Wi-Fi direct
 574: - Local network
 575: - Private hotspot
 576: - Ethernet
 577: - USB
 578: - Internet direct
 579: - Relay fallback
 580: - Bluetooth control
 581: - Offline courier
 582: - OneField radio
 583: - Waiting for device
 584: 
 585: Internal:
 586: 
 587: - `DIRECT_LAN`
 588: - `WIFI_DIRECT`
 589: - `PRIVATE_AP`
 590: - `ETH_LINK_LOCAL`
 591: - `USB_NET`
 592: - `WEBRTC_DIRECT`
 593: - `WEBRTC_RELAYED`
 594: - `BLE_CONTROL`
 595: - `QR_CONTROL`
 596: - `AUDIO_CONTROL`
 597: - `STORAGE_COURIER`
 598: - `ONEFIELD_RF`
 599: - `OFFLINE`
 600: 
 601: ### 6.3 Route Selection
 602: 
 603: The brain should prefer:
 604: 
 605: 1. already-open high-quality direct routes
 606: 2. fast local bulk paths
 607: 3. low-friction generated paths
 608: 4. internet direct paths
 609: 5. sealed relays
 610: 6. offline/courier paths
 611: 7. experimental hardware paths only when enabled and safe
 612: 
 613: But the route choice must be adaptive:
 614: 
 615: - If Wi-Fi slows, add another source/path.
 616: - If a route fails, repair or switch.
 617: - If a peer changes IP/port, refresh route.
 618: - If a faster route appears mid-transfer, migrate.
 619: - If the peer already has most chunks, minimize sent bytes rather than maximize link speed.
 620: 
 621: ---
 622: 
 623: ## 7. Swarm Memory And Multi-Source Pull
 624: 
 625: This is the "everything acts as One" layer.
 626: 
 627: ### 7.1 Chunk Availability Index
 628: 
 629: Every trusted device can advertise, privately and selectively:
 630: 
 631: - file manifest IDs it is allowed to discuss
 632: - chunk hashes it has
 633: - freshness/version
 634: - storage pressure
 635: - willingness to serve
 636: - route quality
 637: 
 638: The advertisement must avoid leaking a user's whole library to every peer.
 639: 
 640: Privacy-preserving options:
 641: 
 642: - pair-specific Bloom filters
 643: - capability-scoped manifests
 644: - salted chunk-set sketches
 645: - request-by-manifest only after authorization
 646: 
 647: ### 7.2 Receiver-Led Pull
 648: 
 649: The receiver should own the final assembly.
 650: 
 651: Flow:
 652: 
 653: 1. Receiver obtains signed manifest.
 654: 2. Receiver checks local chunk store.
 655: 3. Receiver asks authorized trusted devices for missing chunks.
 656: 4. Transport Brain assigns chunks to fastest/safest sources.
 657: 5. Chunks are verified by hash and AEAD before commit.
 658: 6. Failed chunks are retried from another source.
 659: 7. Final manifest root verifies the whole object.
 660: 
 661: ### 7.3 Prior-Knowledge Transfer
 662: 
 663: If receiver already has most content:
 664: 
 665: - detect common chunks through CDC and manifest sketches
 666: - send only missing chunks
 667: - show user the truth: "98% already known"
 668: - avoid recompression/transcoding unless explicitly needed
 669: 
 670: This creates the "impossible" moment: huge files complete fast because the
 671: mesh recognized what was already there.
 672: 
 673: ---
 674: 
 675: ## 8. Delay-Tolerant Operation
 676: 
 677: Devices do not need to be online together.
 678: 
 679: ### 8.1 Store-Carry-Forward
 680: 
 681: Trusted devices may carry encrypted chunks for later delivery.
 682: 
 683: Examples:
 684: 
 685: - laptop carries chunks from home to office
 686: - phone bridges two networks over time
 687: - USB drive carries sealed bundle
 688: - friend device temporarily stores authorized pieces
 689: - office NAS acts as local blind cache
 690: 
 691: ### 8.2 Courier Bundle Format
 692: 
 693: Each bundle should contain:
 694: 
 695: - bundle header
 696: - sender identity
 697: - intended recipient identity or group
 698: - capability proof
 699: - manifest reference
 700: - encrypted chunks
 701: - chunk hashes
 702: - expiration policy
 703: - replay protection
 704: - optional route hints
 705: 
 706: Couriers must not learn plaintext or unauthorized metadata.
 707: 
 708: ### 8.3 Expiration And Abuse Limits
 709: 
 710: To avoid storage abuse:
 711: 
 712: - per-peer storage caps
 713: - per-group storage caps
 714: - expiration policies
 715: - backpressure
 716: - recipient opt-in for large deliveries
 717: - proof-of-authorization before accepting bulk
 718: - quarantine suspicious bundles
 719: 
 720: ---
 721: 
 722: ## 9. Safety And Security
 723: 
 724: ### 9.1 Threats
 725: 
 726: The fabric must defend against:
 727: 
 728: - malicious peer flooding huge fake sends
 729: - malicious courier storing malware-labeled files
 730: - replayed manifests
 731: - chunk poisoning
 732: - relay metadata observation
 733: - path downgrade attacks
 734: - fake route advertisements
 735: - hotspot impersonation
 736: - BLE/QR/audio MITM
 737: - malicious USB devices
 738: - RF regulatory violations
 739: - battery drain attacks
 740: - storage exhaustion attacks
 741: 
 742: ### 9.2 Required Defenses
 743: 
 744: - Every transfer starts with a signed intent and capability.
 745: - Receiver budget checks happen before accepting bulk.
 746: - Large sends require receiver policy approval or trusted auto-accept policy.
 747: - Chunk hashes are verified before commit.
 748: - Manifests are signed and versioned.
 749: - Transport claims are authenticated when they affect trust.
 750: - Path downgrade detection records when a secure/fast route was available but not used.
 751: - Local API remains loopback-bound unless explicitly authorized.
 752: - USB adapter treats attached devices as hostile.
 753: - RF adapter defaults receive-only until operator enables transmit.
 754: - Safety policy gates RF band/power/duty cycle.
 755: - UI shows human action only when automatic recovery is not safe.
 756: 
 757: ### 9.3 Resource Budgets
 758: 
 759: Each peer has budgets:
 760: 
 761: - max active sends
 762: - max active receives
 763: - max bytes accepted without prompt
 764: - max disk reserved
 765: - max memory
 766: - max CPU
 767: - max radio duty cycle
 768: - max relay bytes
 769: - max courier storage
 770: 
 771: Budgets are dynamic:
 772: 
 773: - battery low reduces background work
 774: - metered network reduces bulk
 775: - storage pressure refuses large inbound chunks
 776: - trusted local devices get higher limits
 777: - blocked/quarantined peers get zero
 778: 
 779: ---
 780: 
 781: ## 10. User Experience
 782: 
 783: The UI must show the magic without exposing machinery.
 784: 
 785: ### 10.1 Transfer Truth
 786: 
 787: Examples:
 788: 
 789: - Sending at 640 Mbps
 790: - 98% already known
 791: - Only sending missing pieces
 792: - Using Wi-Fi Direct
 793: - Route: local network
 794: - Resuming automatically
 795: - Waiting for Computer 2
 796: - Pulled from Laptop + Phone + Desktop
 797: - Bluetooth is keeping the connection alive
 798: - Private hotspot created
 799: - USB courier bundle ready
 800: 
 801: ### 10.2 No Scary Raw Errors
 802: 
 803: Bad:
 804: 
 805: ```text
 806: ECONNRESET 10054
 807: ```
 808: 
 809: Good:
 810: 
 811: ```text
 812: Computer 2 changed networks. One Link is reconnecting.
 813: ```
 814: 
 815: Bad:
 816: 
 817: ```text
 818: Protocol mismatch 0.8.0.1 vs 0.7.3
 819: ```
 820: 
 821: Good:
 822: 
 823: ```text
 824: Computer 2 is older. One Link is using the compatible transfer path.
 825: ```
 826: 
 827: ### 10.3 Simple Controls
 828: 
 829: Default:
 830: 
 831: - Send file
 832: - Send folder
 833: - Pair device
 834: - Devices
 835: - Activity
 836: 
 837: Advanced:
 838: 
 839: - route details
 840: - transport preferences
 841: - hardware adapters
 842: - RF mode
 843: - courier bundles
 844: - diagnostics
 845: 
 846: Advanced controls must never be required for normal success.
 847: 
 848: ---
 849: 
 850: ## 11. Implementation Roadmap
 851: 
 852: ### Phase 1: Fabric Core
 853: 
 854: Deliverables:
 855: 
 856: - `hardware_inventory.py` - side-effect-light path inventory
 857: - `transport_adapters/base.py` - adapter/session/probe contract
 858: - `transport_adapters/static.py` - deterministic inventory adapter
 859: - `transport_activation.py` - activation governor and safety policy
 860: - `transport_path_creation.py` - safety-gated platform path creation plans
 861: - `transport_fabric.py` - route score + transfer-brain bridge
 862: - daemon `/api/fabric` snapshot
 863: - daemon `/api/fabric/no-router` readiness kit
 864: - daemon `/api/fabric/path-create` read-only creation plan
 865: - daemon `/api/fabric/path-create/launch` user-visible OS ceremony launcher
 866: - daemon `/api/fabric/path-create/native` opt-in native execution helper
 867: - `/api/status.performance.fabric` and `/api/metrics.fabric`
 868: - Activity-panel fabric truth card
 869: - file-send metadata field `fabric_plan`
 870: - deterministic route, activation, and UI tests
 871: 
 872: Gate:
 873: 
 874: - unit tests prove route selection is deterministic and explainable
 875: - activation tests prove low-risk trusted paths can auto-open while
 876:   admin/user-ceremony/control-only paths cannot be silently abused
 877: - `/api/fabric` is token-guarded like every other API surface
 878: - no existing LAN transfer regression
 879: 
 880: Current implementation status:
 881: 
 882: - `complete` for read-only inventory, route scoring, activation policy,
 883:   daemon/API exposure, file-send metadata, and UI truth surfacing.
 884: - `complete` for active opening of verified durable TCP route candidates
 885:   through the common adapter/session contract. This covers already-proven
 886:   LAN, Ethernet/link-local, and signed-bootstrap endpoints after normal
 887:   key-confirmed promotion.
 888: - `complete` for safety-gated active path creation contracts: the fabric can
 889:   open verified durable TCP paths automatically, guide OS-visible hotspot,
 890:   Wi-Fi Direct, and BLE ceremonies, execute the Windows hostednetwork helper
 891:   only with explicit opt-in, and delegate future platform helpers through a
 892:   redacted native bridge. RF/experimental hardware remains blocked from
 893:   silent transmit until its safety gate is proven.
 894: 
 895: Activation rules now in force:
 896: 
 897: - unavailable paths are visible but cannot be selected
 898: - control-only paths cannot carry bulk file payloads
 899: - admin-required paths never auto-start
 900: - user-ceremony paths require explicit local action
 901: - untrusted peers cannot receive automatic route activation
 902: - cross-internet routes remain end-to-end encrypted and relay-blind
 903: - every active path is still below identity, capability, session crypto,
 904:   chunk verification, durable intent, and retry/reopen logic
 905: 
 906: ### Phase 2: Generated Local Paths
 907: 
 908: Deliverables:
 909: 
 910: - hotspot capability detector
 911: - Wi-Fi Direct capability detector
 912: - Ethernet link-local detector
 913: - verified durable TCP route opener for promoted local endpoints
 914: - BLE control proof-of-concept
 915: - QR route bootstrap payload
 916: 
 917: Gate:
 918: 
 919: - no-router two-device path documented and tested where platform allows
 920: 
 921: Current implementation status:
 922: 
 923: - `complete` for Ethernet/link-local inventory detection and for opening
 924:   verified TCP route candidates through the fabric adapter contract.
 925: - `complete` for signed QR route bootstrap payloads, QR SVG rendering,
 926:   import, replay rejection, paired-issuer checks, and queued endpoint
 927:   verification/promotion. Local bootstrap now opts into Ethernet/link-local
 928:   endpoint hints while normal internet rendezvous publication keeps those
 929:   hints private by default.
 930: - `complete` for a token-gated no-router readiness kit that reports local
 931:   link state, QR/token readiness, trusted local paths, the next safe action,
 932:   structured progress steps, and the safeguards that keep route hints from
 933:   becoming trust bypasses. The Activity panel renders this as a compact local
 934:   path kit so the normal user sees readiness, not endpoint machinery.
 935: - `complete` for live no-router probe progress states: imported route hints
 936:   move through `checking_path`, `trusted_path_ready`, or `route_check_failed`
 937:   based on durable endpoint verification state.
 938: - `complete` for the guided no-router operator flow: the token-gated
 939:   readiness API now returns ranked path options, sender/receiver step guides,
 940:   route-token status, probe status, and clear recovery actions for cable,
 941:   same-LAN, private-hotspot, Wi-Fi Direct, and verified local paths. The
 942:   Activity panel renders those states directly so people see what to do next
 943:   instead of endpoint machinery.
 944: - `complete` for safety-gated local path creation planning:
 945:   `transport_path_creation.py` and `/api/fabric/path-create` describe exactly
 946:   how Ethernet, private hotspot, Wi-Fi Direct, and BLE control paths may be
 947:   created or guided on this platform. The endpoint is read-only, labels
 948:   automatic/user/admin requirements, includes OS settings/command affordances
 949:   where safe, and repeats the non-negotiable safeguards: no pairing bypass,
 950:   route tokens carry endpoint hints only, and every promoted endpoint still
 951:   needs a key-confirmed session.
 952: - `complete` for safe creation-ceremony launch: `/api/fabric/path-create/launch`
 953:   can open only the OS-visible settings/ceremony named by an approved plan
 954:   such as Windows Mobile Hotspot, Wi-Fi settings, or Bluetooth settings. It
 955:   never toggles radios silently, never publishes hotspot credentials, rejects
 956:   unsupported/blocked plans, supports dry-run verification, and honors
 957:   `ONE_LINK_DISABLE_PATH_CREATE_LAUNCH=1` for CI and managed environments.
 958: - `complete` for the first native execution helper:
 959:   `/api/fabric/path-create/native` supports dry-run and explicit opt-in
 960:   Windows legacy hostednetwork command execution for private hotspot setup.
 961:   It validates SSID/passphrase constraints before building commands, redacts
 962:   hotspot keys from every API response, requires
 963:   `ONE_LINK_ALLOW_NATIVE_PATH_CREATE=1` for real execution, honors
 964:   `ONE_LINK_DISABLE_NATIVE_PATH_CREATE=1`, and returns structured unsupported
 965:   evidence for Wi-Fi Direct and BLE where the OS does not expose a safe silent
 966:   public creation API.
 967: - `complete` for the native helper bridge: `ONE_LINK_NATIVE_PATH_HELPERS`
 968:   can register explicit platform helper binaries for paths such as
 969:   `wifi_direct` or `ble_control`. Helpers must be declared by absolute path,
 970:   are dry-run capable, are still blocked unless native execution is explicitly
 971:   enabled, receive a small deterministic command contract, and have command
 972:   secrets redacted from API evidence. This is the production plug-in point for
 973:   future signed/native Wi-Fi Direct and BLE helpers without weakening the
 974:   default safety posture.
 975: - `complete` for route-brain performance telemetry. Fabric plans report
 976:   adapter count, per-stage timings, total planning time, and a `fast` /
 977:   `warm` / `slow` health grade; regression tests keep 512 remembered
 978:   candidate routes comfortably below the interactive budget.
 979: - `complete` for probe reuse in route scoring. Adapters that can score from
 980:   an existing probe do so, preventing the route brain from touching hardware
 981:   or route-memory adapters twice during one plan.
 982: - `complete` for bounded, fast endpoint verification: route-token endpoint
 983:   probes are concurrency-limited and use short connect/handshake deadlines so
 984:   dead local hints surface quickly instead of making people wait.
 985: - `complete` for fast transfer-path planning: live file sends skip slow OS
 986:   hardware probes and use only cheap inventory plus durable route candidates;
 987:   richer hardware discovery remains in cached dashboard snapshots.
 988: - `complete` for the in-repo automatic no-router creation boundary: direct
 989:   Ethernet can be represented, guided, verified, and opened after promotion;
 990:   hotspot, Wi-Fi Direct, and BLE have a safety-gated creation contract plus
 991:   user-visible OS ceremony launch; Windows private hotspot has an opt-in
 992:   legacy hostednetwork executor where available; and Wi-Fi Direct/BLE use the
 993:   explicit native-helper bridge. Platform-specific helper binaries are treated
 994:   as signed external providers to this bridge, not as a reason for the core
 995:   fabric to silently mutate radios.
 996: 
 997: ### Phase 3: Multi-Source Swarm Pull
 998: 
 999: Deliverables:
1000: 
1001: - chunk availability index
1002: - capability-scoped chunk offers
1003: - receiver-led source assignment
1004: - per-source speed scoring
1005: - source failover
1006: - UI: "pulled from N devices"
1007: 
1008: Gate:
1009: 
1010: - test with three local daemons: receiver reconstructs object from two partial sources
1011: 
1012: Current implementation status:
1013: 
1014: - `complete` for receiver-led swarm chunk discovery and pull over trusted
1015:   peers: receivers ask only for missing content-addressed chunks, pull data
1016:   through the secure session layer, verify each chunk by BLAKE3 before cache
1017:   commit, and expose per-source assignment telemetry.
1018: - `complete` for health-aware source planning: candidate sources are indexed
1019:   by chunk hash, ranked by trust, reliability, latency, bandwidth, and field
1020:   coherence, then scheduled rarest-first so scarce chunks are assigned before
1021:   abundant chunks.
1022: - `complete` for adaptive swarm execution: pull concurrency expands with the
1023:   number of live sources up to a bounded cap, each source receives a
1024:   health-derived transfer deadline, and hung or corrupt primary sources are
1025:   retried from alternate holders without blocking the whole object.
1026: - `complete` for regression coverage proving large sparse source claims plan
1027:   quickly, three independent sources reconstruct a file, corrupt primary data
1028:   heals from backup, and a source that answers discovery but hangs during
1029:   transfer is bypassed by deadline failover.
1030: 
1031: ### Phase 4: Store-Carry-Forward
1032: 
1033: Deliverables:
1034: 
1035: - courier bundle format
1036: - import/export bundle UI
1037: - USB/removable storage watcher
1038: - expiration and budget policy
1039: - replay-safe bundle import
1040: 
1041: Gate:
1042: 
1043: - offline sender -> USB bundle -> offline receiver completes transfer without plaintext exposure
1044: 
1045: Current implementation status:
1046: 
1047: - `complete` for the encrypted courier bundle core format in
1048:   `src/one_link/courier_bundle.py`: AES-GCM sealed payload, random unlock
1049:   token with `OLC1.` prefix, expiry, sender/recipient fingerprints, BLAKE3
1050:   per-chunk verification, duplicate detection, strict size/count limits, and
1051:   replay rejection when the importer supplies a seen-bundle set.
1052: - `complete` for daemon UI APIs: `/api/courier/status`,
1053:   `/api/courier/export`, `/api/courier/import`, and
1054:   `/api/courier/assemble` are token-gated and wire directly into the existing
1055:   CDC chunk cache. `/api/courier/files`, `/api/courier/import-file`,
1056:   `/api/courier/outbox`, and `/api/courier/export-file` add safe local
1057:   removable-media folders: dropped files are listed by opaque IDs under
1058:   `data/courier/drop`, staged exports are written atomically under
1059:   `data/courier/outbox`, and no API accepts arbitrary filesystem paths.
1060:   Export refuses missing cached chunks; import stores only chunks that decrypt
1061:   and re-hash correctly; assemble reconstructs a fully cached courier blob
1062:   into the inbox only when the final BLAKE3 file hash matches.
1063: - `complete` for durable courier replay and audit metadata:
1064:   `courier_ledger.json` persists imported bundle IDs across daemon restarts
1065:   and records bounded export/import events with only public manifest facts
1066:   (bundle id, fingerprints, chunk count, byte counts, expiry), never chunk
1067:   plaintext.
1068: - `complete` for adversarial tests covering round-trip import/export,
1069:   ciphertext tamper, wrong key, expiry, wrong recipient, duplicate chunks,
1070:   bad hashes, invalid base64, replay, missing cached chunks, auth-gated
1071:   readiness, restart-persistent replay, malformed ledger recovery, and real
1072:   server-to-cache import/export.
1073: - `complete` for the first people-facing removable-media browser surface:
1074:   Activity now has a courier kit with transfer selection, optional chunk-hash
1075:   input, unlock-token handling, file download/upload, and direct "Courier"
1076:   actions on cached transfer rows. The user path is "export encrypted file,
1077:   carry it, paste token, import file" instead of internal cache machinery.
1078:   The kit also surfaces recent courier activity and replay-guard memory, and
1079:   auto-assembles imported file bundles when the encrypted manifest contains
1080:   the whole-file blob hash. It can also import files dropped into the local
1081:   courier folder and stage export files into the local outbox, which maps
1082:   directly onto USB/removable-drive workflows.
1083: - `complete` for a cross-platform courier folder monitor: the server watches
1084:   drop/outbox signatures on a bounded interval, broadcasts `courier_files`
1085:   changes to connected UIs, exposes monitor evidence in `/api/courier/status`,
1086:   and shuts the monitor down cleanly with the UI server.
1087: - `complete` for the first guided two-role courier wizard: the Activity
1088:   courier kit has Sender/Receiver modes with readiness steps for choosing a
1089:   cached transfer, staging/downloading the bundle, copying the separate OLC1
1090:   key, dropping a received bundle, selecting it, and importing/assembling only
1091:   after verification.
1092: - `complete` for removable-target discovery and safe copy-out:
1093:   `/api/courier/removable` discovers Windows removable drives and POSIX
1094:   media roots, and `/api/courier/copy-to-removable` copies a staged outbox
1095:   bundle into a `One Link Courier` folder on the selected target. The API
1096:   uses opaque target/file IDs and never accepts arbitrary destination paths.
1097: - `complete` for safe copy-in from removable media:
1098:   `/api/courier/removable-files` lists courier bundles under a selected
1099:   target's `One Link Courier` folder, and
1100:   `/api/courier/copy-from-removable` pulls a selected bundle into
1101:   `data/courier/drop` by opaque file ID. Stale IDs and path tricks fail
1102:   closed before import/decrypt.
1103: - `complete` for removable-media event integration: the server now turns the
1104:   cross-platform removable inventory into a deterministic
1105:   `native_compatible_inventory_events` stream with attached, removed, and
1106:   changed events. The courier monitor primes this source, broadcasts
1107:   `removable_media` events to connected UIs, and exposes event-source evidence
1108:   plus counters through `/api/courier/status` and `/api/courier/removable`.
1109:   Platform-specific watcher backends can plug into the same contract, while
1110:   the portable polling source keeps USB workflows working everywhere.
1111: - `complete` for an offline two-home courier proof: tests exercise sender
1112:   cache -> encrypted bundle -> receiver cache, preserve blob context, and
1113:   verify the receiver can reassemble the original file hash from imported
1114:   chunks.

1180: ## 12. Integration With Existing One Link Work
1181: 
1182: Existing One Link systems this must reuse:
1183: 
1184: - durable transfer intent queue
1185: - staged upload/source material
1186: - native chunk store
1187: - CDC/prior-knowledge transfer
1188: - transfer brain/adaptive selector
1189: - peer capabilities
1190: - identity and trust graph
1191: - secure sessions
1192: - per-peer permissions
1193: - relay/rendezvous paths
1194: - activity feed
1195: - production readiness gates
1196: 
1197: Do not duplicate these. The Universal Comms Fabric expands the route layer
1198: under them.
1199: 
1200: ---
1201: 
1202: ## 13. Engineering Rules
1203: 
1204: 1. Add one adapter at a time behind the common contract.
1205: 2. Every adapter gets deterministic fake tests.
1206: 3. Every adapter reports truth to the route brain.
1207: 4. Every route is optional and replaceable.
1208: 5. No transport gets plaintext by default.
1209: 6. No experimental hardware path can break normal sends.
1210: 7. No user-facing feature ships without a recovery story.
1211: 8. No "works on my machine" path ships without platform disposition.
1212: 9. Prefer automatic recovery over user instructions.
1213: 10. Prefer creating a path over failing, when safe.
1214: 
1215: ---
1216: 
1217: ## 14. What Makes This Different
1218: 
1219: Individual pieces exist in other systems:
1220: 
1221: - AirDrop uses local discovery and Wi-Fi handoff.
1222: - Syncthing syncs files P2P.
1223: - BitTorrent pulls from multiple sources.
1224: - Tailscale builds virtual networks.
1225: - Meshtastic sends off-grid LoRa messages.
1226: - Delay-tolerant networking exists in specialized domains.
1227: 
1228: One Link's uncommon goal is to combine them into one open, cross-platform,
1229: user-owned system:
1230: 
1231: > identity + encrypted chunks + content-addressed storage + prior knowledge +
1232: > multi-source pull + local/offline discovery + generated paths + store-carry-
1233: > forward + optional RF hardware + a simple UX.
1234: 
1235: That is the "for the people" version: not a walled garden, not a cloud
1236: subscription, not a single protocol, but a sovereign communications fabric.

  25: **What this changes about the recommended ordering:**
  26: 
  27: * **Phase 2 (First-run experience) shrinks dramatically.** The wizard already exists. Remaining items: first-action chips on the post-pair empty chat, first-send celebration, "What's new" modal on update, in-app diagnostics export, in-app bug-report flow, Settings modal search, per-feature first-use tooltips, recovery phrase verification challenge. Drop the welcome wizard re-build.
  28: * **Phase 3 keeps Forward but reframes** — the action exists; the audit work is to confirm coverage (forward attachments, forward with attribution chip, forward multi-select to multiple targets at once).
  29: * **Phase 5 Privacy adds a UI for the existing peer-version wire data** rather than building the data plumbing.
  30: * **Phase 6 keeps "more accent colors" etc. but the audible-incoming sound is shipped** — the gap is call-specific ringback/ringtone, not message sounds.
  31: 
  32: The remaining items in Sections 4–31 are still gaps. Where this audit got the ship state wrong, that section's "Current state" subsection has been updated below.

  76: 
  77: ## 1. Executive summary
  78: 
  79: One Link ships a serious peer-to-peer chat, file transfer, and call platform. The underlying primitives (Noise sessions, Double Ratchet, ML-DSA hybrid signatures, Sphinx onion routing, threshold recovery, attestation, native Rust hot paths) put it ahead of nearly every messenger in the privacy axis. The UI is more polished than most P2P apps. But it is **not yet at parity with consumer chat apps on the surfaces that drive daily-use feel**.
  80: 
  81: The audit identifies gaps in seven categories, ordered by user-impact:
  82: 
  83: 1. **Acute reliability gaps** that surface as silent failures (send hangs forever, chat doesn't live-render on receiver, calls don't propagate to the second computer). Many were fixed in the May 17 batch. The rest are about getting the rebuilt exe into the field and making peer-version mismatches visible.
  84: 2. **First-run experience.** No welcome wizard, no permission preflight, no tutorial. A new user opens One Link to a blank chat pane and a single "Pair a device" button. They learn by trial.
  85: 3. **Composer parity.** No emoji picker. No GIF/sticker support. No mentions. No `/me`. No schedule send. No voicemail / async-voice surface even though the doctrine names it.
  86: 4. **Photo and file experience.** Now clickable as of today. Still missing image gallery swipe, image markup before send, camera capture, file rename before send, EXIF stripping, video player polish.
  87: 5. **Call experience.** Audible ringback and ringtone are missing. Missed calls don't appear in chat. Reconnect on network drop ends the call. No screen share, PIP, or background blur. No call history view.
  88: 6. **Trust visibility.** Capabilities, SAS state, and verification level exist in the data model but are not consistently visible. Users can't easily tell "is this peer fully verified or just blindly trusted".
  89: 7. **Polish.** No sound effects. No haptic feedback. No system tray badge. No "what's new" modal. No in-app bug report. Microcopy is mostly excellent but inconsistent in tone across surfaces.
  90: 
  91: The recommended approach is to ship **Phase 1 (current-build feels finished) before anything else**, because the value of every later phase compounds on having a non-flaky baseline. Phases 2 through 7 are sequenced by user-impact / cost ratio. None of these are speculative — every item has a concrete implementation sketch in Appendix E.
  92: 
  93: This audit deliberately does not include calendar timelines. Acceptance gates ship work; calendar dates don't.
  94: 
  95: ---
  96: 
  97: ## 2. Methodology and frame of reference
  98: 
  99: ### Source of truth
 100: 
 101: This audit reads the shipped code, not the design docs. When a doctrine doc and the running code disagree, the running code wins (the user never sees the doctrine). All findings include file path and line references that can be verified independently.
 102: 
 103: ### Frame of reference
 104: 
 105: Comparison apps and what they're notable for:
 106: 
 107: | App | Notable for |
 108: |---|---|
 109: | Signal | Privacy-first defaults, sealed sender, safety numbers, disappearing messages |
 110: | iMessage | Polish, Tapback reactions, message effects, SharePlay, Apple ecosystem continuity |
 111: | WhatsApp | Mass-market simplicity, view-once media, last-seen privacy, voice messages |
 112: | Telegram | Sticker / GIF marketplace, channels, polls, themes, custom emojis, schedule send |
 113: | Discord | Voice channels, screen share + audio, slash commands, custom emojis, threads |
 114: | AirDrop | One-step file transfer, auto-discover nearby, multi-file drop, cross-Apple |
 115: | Quick Share | AirDrop equivalent across Android + Windows, drag-drop simplicity |
 116: 
 117: Each section identifies what the comparison apps do, what One Link does today, what the gap is, and what the concrete fix looks like.
 118: 
 119: ### What "exhaustive" means here
 120: 
 121: A real audit names every surface, not just the headline ones. This document is long on purpose: each surface includes the buttons, modals, toggles, edge cases, error paths, and empty states associated with it. Sections that look short have shorter shipped surface to cover.
 122: 
 123: ### What this audit does not cover
 124: 
 125: * Backend architecture, cryptography choices, or threat model. Those are covered in `docs/ARCHITECTURE.md`, `docs/SECURITY.md`, and the per-phase plan docs.
 126: * Build systems, CI, release engineering.
 127: * The Coherence Language platform underneath. That's a separate audit subject.
 128: * Marketing copy or website copy. The `One_link_Website` project is tracked separately.
 129: 
 130: ---
 131: 
 132: ## 3. Right-now pain that needs to clear before anything else
 133: 
 134: These are not feature requests. They are blockers: the things a user just hit and that make every other future improvement irrelevant until they're resolved.
 135: 
 136: ### 3.1. The bundled exe is the OLD code
 137: 
 138: The daemon listening on this machine right now is `$HOME\Projects\Coherence\One_link\dist\one-link\one-link.exe` (a PyInstaller bundle). The source tree contains the May 17 batch (`_broadcast_tail` regression fix, bulletproof send, collapsible long messages, click-to-open files, queued-with-real-reason, Retry-now button). **None of these reach the user until the exe is rebuilt.**
 139: 
 140: **Fix:**
 141: 
 142: ```powershell
 143: # From repo root
 144: $env:PYTHONIOENCODING="utf-8"
 145: python scripts/build_binary.py --gui
 146: ```
 147: 
 148: Then copy the contents of `dist/one-link/` to Computer 2.
 149: 
 150: ### 3.2. The peer card says "Verified · on Wi-Fi · 69 ms" but messages queue
 151: 
 152: The presence indicator (mDNS-level) is decoupled from the wire-path health (Noise channel state). Today the UI exposes only the presence indicator. Users see "online" and don't understand why their messages queue.
 153: 
 154: **Partial fix (shipped May 17):** queued bubbles now surface the daemon's actual reason ("Could not establish a secure connection with the other device.") and a `Retry now` link.
 155: 
 156: **Remaining fix:** the peer card should *also* expose the wire-path health. Concrete proposal:
 157: 
 158: * Small colored dot inside the peer's avatar circle: green (channel active), yellow (channel idle but reachable), red (channel can't establish or peer is older).
 159: * On hover, a tooltip: "Channel established 4m ago · Last bytes 12s ago · Same version as you".
 160: * The current ✓ Verified pill stays, but it's distinct from the channel-health dot.
 161: 
 162: ### 3.3. Peer version mismatch is invisible
 163: 
 164: Two daemons on different builds will sometimes work, sometimes fail. The user has no way to know which build the other side is on.
 165: 
 166: **Fix:**
 167: 
 168: * Every wire handshake exchanges `daemon_version` and `wire_capability_set` ([`src/one_link/capabilities.py`](src/one_link/capabilities.py) already has the capability registry; add `daemon_build` as a top-level field on the handshake).
 169: * The peer card row shows "On v0.21.x · matches you" (gray) or "On v0.20.6 · older than you (your build is v0.21.x)" (yellow).
 170: * When peer is older, expose an "Update this device" affordance that sends them the bundled exe over the file channel.
 171: 
 172: ### 3.4. Send button briefly returned "Queued · Will send when the path is healthy" with no reason
 173: 
 174: **Partial fix (shipped May 17):** the bubble now surfaces the daemon's translated user-facing copy.
 175: 
 176: **Remaining fix:** when the daemon's reason is `handshake_failed` AND the peer's version is older, the bubble should say so explicitly: "Queued · The other device is on an older build. Click *Update them* in the peer card."
 177: 
 178: ### 3.5. Computer 2 doesn't render incoming calls
 179: 
 180: Confirmed root cause: Computer 2 is on the OLD bundled exe, which has the pre-`_broadcast_tail`-wrap fix. After Computer 2 is updated, this clears. Add a section to the diagnostics overlay that confirms peer-side WS event delivery (already partially built into `live_ws_monitor.py` — surface it as a UI option).
 181: 
 182: ### 3.6. Long pasted messages don't visibly send
 183: 
 184: **Fixed May 17.** Optimistic bubble + 25s client timeout + 20s server `wait_for` + retry chain.
 185: 
 186: ### 3.7. Files in the chat aren't clickable
 187: 
 188: **Fixed May 17.** Click-to-open with lightbox for images, new-tab for non-images, sender-side File cache so outbound bubbles also open, hover lift, keyboard-accessible.
 189: 
 190: ### 3.8. Acceptance gates for Phase 1
 191: 
 192: Before any new feature work:
 193: 
 194: | Gate | Pass criterion |
 195: |---|---|
 196: | Rebuild | `dist/one-link/one-link.exe` is the May 17 source build |
 197: | Peer version surface | Peer card shows "matches you / older / newer" |
 198: | Channel-health dot | Distinct from presence dot, accurate within 30s |
 199: | Send + receive | Round-trip TEXT to Computer 2 lands live, no refresh |
 200: | Call originate | Call from Computer 2 raises ring overlay on Computer 1 within 2s |
 201: | Call accept | Both sides flip to active surface within 1s of accept |
 202: | Photo round-trip | Sender clicks own outbound thumbnail and opens lightbox |
 203: | Photo round-trip 2 | Receiver clicks inbound thumbnail and opens lightbox |
 204: | Long-message collapse | >600-char message renders with Show more, click to expand |
 205: | Queued reason | Queued bubble shows daemon's user-facing reason text |
 206: | Retry now | Queued bubble's Retry now link fires a fresh send |
 207: 
 208: When all of these pass on both machines, Phase 1 is done.
 209:

 212: ## 4. First-run and onboarding
 213: 
 214: ### 4.1. Current state
 215: 
 216: **[Corrected]** One Link ships a real first-run experience, not a placeholder.
 217: 
 218: * **6-step welcome wizard** (`#onboarding-backdrop`) at [`index.html:7486-7592`](../src/one_link/web/index.html#L7486):
 219:   * **Step 1 — You are One.** Welcome screen with glyph, tagline, proof chips ("No account", "Encrypted", "Works nearby"), Set up / Skip.
 220:   * **Step 2 — Name this device.** Text input with placeholder ("Alex's laptop"), shows device card preview.
 221:   * **Step 3 — Create your One identity.** Identity creation with "I already have one" branch to step 4.
 222:   * **Step 4 — Add your phone or laptop.** QR rendering, copy-code, SAS confirmation ("Codes match" / "Codes do not match"), Pair later branch.
 223:   * **Step 5 — Send something to yourself.** First-action prompt with Send test message / Send a file / Do this later.
 224:   * **Step 6 — One Link is ready.** Completion checklist, Review safety button, Start using One Link.
 225: * Auto-launches via `maybeShowOnboarding()` at [`index.html:17762`](../src/one_link/web/index.html#L17762). Honors `ONBOARDING_STORAGE_KEY` in localStorage, `state.me.onboarding_completed` from the daemon, and `setup.completed` / `setup.skipped` from the One Setup API. Resumes at the right step if a previous session was interrupted.
 226: * `_markOnboardingComplete()` persists completion to both localStorage and `/api/settings`.
 227: * `skipOneSetup()` posts to `/api/setup` with `action: "skip"` and shows the toast "Setup is waiting in Activity whenever you want it."
 228: * Design spec at [`docs/ONE_SETUP_FIRST_RUN_EXPERIENCE.md`](./ONE_SETUP_FIRST_RUN_EXPERIENCE.md).
 229: * The Settings > Setup pane at [`index.html:6416-6470`](../src/one_link/web/index.html#L6416) gives the user a re-entry point + receipt list + technical-verification disclosure.
 230: * Empty chat pane state at [`index.html:11617-11630`](../src/one_link/web/index.html#L11617) is the fallback for "wizard skipped, nothing paired yet."
 231: 
 232: **Genuinely missing:**
 233: 
 234: * No permission preflight before `getUserMedia` calls on first call. The cold browser prompt fires with no context. Failure surface today is just `"Mic access failed: ${e?.message}"` at [`index.html:18446`](../src/one_link/web/index.html#L18446).
 235: * No first-action chips on the *post-pair empty chat* (Section 4.3.3 below). Wizard step 5 nudges the user once, but if they skip that step the chat pane is silent.
 236: * No first-send celebration moment.
 237: * No "What's new" modal after a daemon-version update.
 238: * No replay-the-wizard affordance in About (other than "skipped" → next launch will reshow).
 239: 
 240: ### 4.2. Gap analysis vs. competitors
 241: 
 242: | Surface | Signal | iMessage | WhatsApp | Telegram | Discord | One Link |
 243: |---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
 244: | Welcome wizard | Yes (3-step) | OS-level | Yes (5-step) | Yes (4-step) | Yes (multi-screen) | No |
 245: | Display name prompt | Forced on first run | Apple ID | Forced | Forced | Forced (later) | Buried in Settings |
 246: | Avatar choice | Photo + initials | Photo + Memoji | Photo + initials | Photo + initials | Photo + color | Color only |
 247: | Permission preflight | Yes | OS-level | Yes | Yes | Yes | No (cold prompt) |
 248: | Pair-a-device demo | Animated | OS handles | QR | QR + animation | OS install | Static modal |
 249: | First-action prompts | Yes ("try sending") | No | No | No | Yes ("Add server") | No |
 250: | Empty chat copy | "Tap a contact" | "Pick a conversation" | "Select chat" | "Select chat" | "Pick a channel" | "Pick someone on the left" |
 251: 
 252: ### 4.3. Concrete recommendations
 253: 
 254: #### 4.3.1. Welcome wizard
 255: 
 256: A 3-step modal that runs on first launch (gated by `state.first_run_complete` flag in localStorage + sqlite):
 257: 
 258: * **Step 1 — Identity.** Show the auto-generated display name (defaults to hostname) and let the user edit. Show the avatar color swatch (8 choices) and let them pick.
 259: * **Step 2 — How others will find you.** Three options as radio buttons with descriptions:
 260:   * *On the same Wi-Fi.* "Other One Link devices on your network can see you."
 261:   * *Across networks.* "Use the rendezvous service to reach devices that aren't on your network."
 262:   * *Strictly QR-only.* "Devices have to scan your QR to find you. Most private."
 263: * **Step 3 — Add your first device.** Render a big QR code immediately, with text: "Open One Link on another device. Tap *Pair a new device*, then scan this." Below: a small "Skip for now" link that closes the wizard.
 264: 
 265: After this, drop the user into the main chat surface with a one-time tooltip on the sidebar pointing at the just-paired device: "This is your other device. Tap to chat with it."
 266: 
 267: #### 4.3.2. Permission preflight
 268: 
 269: Intercept the first click on 📞 voice and 📹 video. Show a small modal:
 270: 
 271: ```
 272: One Link needs your microphone [and camera] for this call.
 273: Your browser will ask next.
 274: 
 275: Nothing is recorded or sent anywhere except to this call.
 276: You can revoke access any time from your browser settings.
 277: 
 278: [ Continue ]   [ Not now ]
 279: ```
 280: 
 281: Only then call `getUserMedia`. This converts the cold browser prompt from "I clicked something and weird UI popped up" into "I asked for a call, the app explained, then asked permission."
 282: 
 283: #### 4.3.3. First-action prompts in empty chat
 284: 
 285: When a user pairs their first device but has zero messages, show three example actions as clickable chips below the empty state:
 286: 
 287: ```
 288: Try:
 289: [ Drag a photo here ] [ Press 🎤 to record voice ] [ Press 📞 to call ]
 290: ```
 291: 
 292: Each chip, when clicked, runs the corresponding flow. Chip cluster auto-dismisses after the first send/call.
 293: 
 294: #### 4.3.4. First-send celebration
 295: 
 296: The first time a user sends a message to a freshly-paired device, render a brief one-time effect on the bubble: a subtle ✨ glow that fades over 1 second. This is the kind of detail iMessage uses to make moments feel rewarded.
 297: 
 298: #### 4.3.5. First-launch-after-update modal
 299: 
 300: Cheap: when daemon version changes, the next opened browser sees a small bottom-sheet: "Updated to v0.21.x. **What's new** · Bulletproof send · Click-to-open photos · Long-message collapse." With a "See full changelog" link.
 301: 
 302: #### 4.3.6. Tutorial replay
 303: 
 304: A "Show me around" button in the About pane that replays the welcome wizard for users who skipped it.
 305: 
 306: ### 4.4. Onboarding edge cases
 307: 
 308: | Scenario | Current behavior | Recommended |
 309: |---|---|---|
 310: | First launch, no network | Empty state forever | Empty state with "Offline · waiting for network" banner |
 311: | First launch, daemon not started | Loading spinner forever | After 5s, show "Can't reach One Link daemon. Restart the app." |
 312: | Pair via QR fails (camera denied) | Generic error | "Camera access denied. Type the device code manually instead." |
 313: | Pair scan succeeded but SAS doesn't match | Modal stuck | "Codes don't match. This might mean someone's intercepting. Cancel and try again." |
 314: | Identity already exists from earlier install | Silent reuse | First-launch wizard offers "This is me again" vs. "Start fresh" |
 315: | Migrating from another chat app | No path | "Import contacts" stub — even just an info modal explaining there's no import yet |
 316: | Restoring from backup | Hidden in Settings | First-launch wizard step 0: "New here? Or restoring a backup?" |
 317:
