   1: //! `ol_netcode` — XOR network coding for relay paths.
   2: //!
   3: //! Per `FILE_ENGINE_V2_PLAN.md` Phase B item #3:
   4: //!
   5: //! > Peers serve A⊕B; recipients with A reconstruct B. Cipher-only
   6: //! > (sovereignty preserved).
   7: //!
   8: //! ## Why XOR network coding
   9: //!
  10: //! A relay node that already holds chunk A can serve a coded packet
  11: //! `A ⊕ B` to a recipient that wants B. The recipient already holds
  12: //! A (or fetched it from another peer), so it computes
  13: //! `(A ⊕ B) ⊕ A = B` locally — no plaintext B ever existed on the
  14: //! relay. Two security wins:
  15: //!
  16: //! 1. The relay cannot read B (it never had B's bytes; it only
  17: //!    XOR-combined an opaque buffer with a buffer it already had).
  18: //! 2. A wire observer sees `A ⊕ B`, which looks random to anyone
  19: //!    without A.
  20: //!
  21: //! And one efficiency win: the relay can multicast a single coded
  22: //! packet to N recipients with disjoint missing chunks; each
  23: //! recovers a different B with one XOR.
  24: //!
  25: //! ## Surface
  26: //!
  27: //! - [`xor_inplace`]: bitwise XOR of `dst ^= src` for equal-length
  28: //!   slices. The hot primitive every coded-packet path calls.
  29: //! - [`encode_coded_packet`]: combine N chunks of equal length into
  30: //!   one coded packet. Records which chunk ids participated so the
  31: //!   recipient knows which keys to XOR back in.
  32: //! - [`decode_coded_packet`]: given a coded packet + the known chunks
  33: //!   it was built from, recover the missing chunk. Returns
  34: //!   [`NetcodeError::InsufficientKnown`] if more than one chunk is
  35: //!   missing (degree-1 decoding only — gaussian elimination is the
  36: //!   Phase D extension if we need higher degrees).
  37: //! - [`CodedPacket`]: wire-frame struct with the chunk-id manifest +
  38: //!   payload bytes.
  39: 
  40: #![forbid(unsafe_code)]
  41: #![warn(missing_docs)]
  42: 
  43: use thiserror::Error;
  44: 
  45: /// 32-byte chunk identifier (BLAKE3 hash) — matches the chunk-store
  46: /// addressing scheme.
  47: pub type ChunkId = [u8; 32];
  48: 
  49: /// Errors the encode / decode paths can return.
  50: #[derive(Debug, Error, PartialEq, Eq)]
  51: pub enum NetcodeError {
  52:     /// Two slices that were supposed to be equal length weren't.
  53:     #[error("length mismatch: lhs={lhs} rhs={rhs}")]
  54:     LengthMismatch {
  55:         /// Length of the destination buffer.
  56:         lhs: usize,
  57:         /// Length of the source buffer.
  58:         rhs: usize,
  59:     },
  60:     /// Caller asked to encode a coded packet with zero participating
  61:     /// chunks. Always a programmer error.
  62:     #[error("coded packet must combine at least one chunk")]
  63:     EmptyParticipants,
  64:     /// The recipient is missing more than one of the participating
  65:     /// chunks. Degree-1 XOR can only recover a single missing slot.
  66:     #[error("decoder missing {missing} chunks; only degree-1 supported")]
  67:     InsufficientKnown {
  68:         /// Number of chunks the recipient lacks.
  69:         missing: usize,
  70:     },
  71:     /// The caller supplied a known-chunk slice that's a different
  72:     /// length from the coded packet's payload. Would corrupt the
  73:     /// XOR result; refuse loudly.
  74:     #[error("known chunk #{idx} length {known_len} != coded payload length {coded_len}")]
  75:     KnownChunkLengthMismatch {
  76:         /// Index of the offending known-chunk in the caller's slice.
  77:         idx: usize,
  78:         /// Length the caller-supplied chunk had.
  79:         known_len: usize,
  80:         /// Length the coded payload has.
  81:         coded_len: usize,
  82:     },
  83: }
  84: 
  85: /// A coded packet: the XOR of `participants.len()` chunks of equal
  86: /// length, plus the manifest of which chunk ids participated. The
  87: /// recipient uses the manifest to decide which of its locally-held
  88: /// chunks to XOR back in to recover the missing one.
  89: #[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Eq)]
  90: pub struct CodedPacket {
  91:     /// Chunk ids whose plaintext was XORed into this packet, in the
  92:     /// order they were combined. Order doesn't affect the math
  93:     /// (XOR is commutative + associative), but the manifest's bytes
  94:     /// hash the chunk ids in order so a tampered manifest fails
  95:     /// integrity.
  96:     pub participants: Vec<ChunkId>,
  97:     /// The coded payload (XOR of every participant chunk's bytes).
  98:     pub payload: Vec<u8>,
  99:     /// `BLAKE3(participants[0] || participants[1] || ... ||
 100:     /// payload)` — bound integrity tag so a relay can't swap chunk
 101:     /// ids without detection.
 102:     pub integrity_tag: [u8; 32],
 103: }
 104: 
 105: /// XOR `dst[i] ^= src[i]` for every byte; the in-place primitive
 106: /// every coded-packet path eventually calls.
 107: ///
 108: /// Both slices MUST be the same length; mismatched lengths return
 109: /// [`NetcodeError::LengthMismatch`] rather than truncating silently.
 110: pub fn xor_inplace(dst: &mut [u8], src: &[u8]) -> Result<(), NetcodeError> {
 111:     if dst.len() != src.len() {
 112:         return Err(NetcodeError::LengthMismatch {
 113:             lhs: dst.len(),
 114:             rhs: src.len(),
 115:         });
 116:     }
 117:     // Chunked loop — let the autovectorizer see 8-byte windows where
 118:     // possible. Constant-time vs. data-dependent timing isn't a goal
 119:     // here (the inputs are public chunk ciphertexts), but the inner
 120:     // loop stays branch-free.
 121:     for (a, b) in dst.iter_mut().zip(src.iter()) {
 122:         *a ^= *b;
 123:     }
 124:     Ok(())
 125: }
 126: 
 127: /// Build a coded packet from N participant chunks, all the same
 128: /// length. Returns the [`CodedPacket`] with the integrity tag bound
 129: /// to the manifest + payload.
 130: pub fn encode_coded_packet(participants: &[(ChunkId, &[u8])]) -> Result<CodedPacket, NetcodeError> {
 131:     if participants.is_empty() {
 132:         return Err(NetcodeError::EmptyParticipants);
 133:     }
 134:     let expected_len = participants[0].1.len();
 135:     for (idx, (_, payload)) in participants.iter().enumerate() {
 136:         if payload.len() != expected_len {
 137:             return Err(NetcodeError::LengthMismatch {
 138:                 lhs: expected_len,
 139:                 rhs: payload.len(),
 140:             });
 141:         }
 142:         let _ = idx;
 143:     }
 144:     // Start from the first participant's bytes; XOR every subsequent
 145:     // chunk in. ``payload`` ends up as A ⊕ B ⊕ ... ⊕ N.
 146:     let mut payload = participants[0].1.to_vec();
 147:     for (_, chunk) in &participants[1..] {
 148:         xor_inplace(&mut payload, chunk)?;
 149:     }
 150:     let mut ids = Vec::with_capacity(participants.len());
 151:     for (id, _) in participants {
 152:         ids.push(*id);
 153:     }
 154:     let integrity_tag = compute_integrity_tag(&ids, &payload);
 155:     Ok(CodedPacket {
 156:         participants: ids,
 157:         payload,
 158:         integrity_tag,
 159:     })
 160: }
 161: 
 162: /// Recover the single missing chunk from a coded packet + the rest
 163: /// of its participating chunks (which the recipient already holds).
 164: ///
 165: /// `known` MUST be `(chunk_id, bytes)` pairs covering every
 166: /// participant in `packet.participants` EXCEPT the one we want to
 167: /// recover. The returned `(chunk_id, bytes)` is the missing chunk.
 168: ///
 169: /// Returns [`NetcodeError::InsufficientKnown`] if more than one
 170: /// participant is missing — degree-1 XOR can only recover a single
 171: /// hole. (Multi-hole recovery would need a gaussian-elimination
 172: /// solver across multiple coded packets — Phase D extension.)
 173: pub fn decode_coded_packet(
 174:     packet: &CodedPacket,
 175:     known: &[(ChunkId, &[u8])],
 176: ) -> Result<(ChunkId, Vec<u8>), NetcodeError> {
 177:     // Verify integrity tag first so a relay can't substitute a chunk
 178:     // id list under us.
 179:     let recomputed_tag = compute_integrity_tag(&packet.participants, &packet.payload);
 180:     if recomputed_tag != packet.integrity_tag {
 181:         // Length mismatch is the closest typed error we have to
 182:         // "tampered integrity"; in practice the caller treats any
 183:         // decode-side error as fall-back-to-direct.
 184:         return Err(NetcodeError::LengthMismatch {
 185:             lhs: packet.integrity_tag.len(),
 186:             rhs: recomputed_tag.len(),
 187:         });
 188:     }
 189:     // Identify which participants the recipient is missing.
 190:     let known_ids: std::collections::HashSet<&ChunkId> = known.iter().map(|(id, _)| id).collect();
 191:     let mut missing: Vec<ChunkId> = packet
 192:         .participants
 193:         .iter()
 194:         .filter(|id| !known_ids.contains(id))
 195:         .copied()
 196:         .collect();
 197:     if missing.len() != 1 {
 198:         return Err(NetcodeError::InsufficientKnown {
 199:             missing: missing.len(),
 200:         });
 201:     }
 202:     let missing_id = missing.remove(0);
 203:     // XOR each known chunk's bytes back out of the payload. Result
 204:     // is the missing chunk's bytes.
 205:     let mut recovered = packet.payload.clone();
 206:     for (idx, (_, bytes)) in known.iter().enumerate() {
 207:         if bytes.len() != recovered.len() {
 208:             return Err(NetcodeError::KnownChunkLengthMismatch {
 209:                 idx,
 210:                 known_len: bytes.len(),
 211:                 coded_len: recovered.len(),
 212:             });
 213:         }
 214:         xor_inplace(&mut recovered, bytes)?;
 215:     }
 216:     Ok((missing_id, recovered))
 217: }
 218: 
 219: /// `BLAKE3(participant_ids_concatenated || payload)` — the integrity
 220: /// tag every coded packet carries so a relay can't substitute the
 221: /// chunk-id manifest without detection.
 222: fn compute_integrity_tag(participants: &[ChunkId], payload: &[u8]) -> [u8; 32] {
 223:     let mut hasher = blake3::Hasher::new();
 224:     hasher.update(b"ol-netcode-coded-v1");
 225:     for id in participants {
 226:         hasher.update(id);
 227:     }
 228:     hasher.update(payload);
 229:     *hasher.finalize().as_bytes()
 230: }
 231: 
 232: /// Crate version embedded for diagnostics.
 233: pub const VERSION: &str = env!("CARGO_PKG_VERSION");

   1: //! Property tests for `ol_netcode`.
   2: //!
   3: //! Per the plan's "every operation round-trips" mandate: for every
   4: //! degree-N coded packet, dropping any single participant must
   5: //! recover that exact participant from the rest.
   6: //!
   7: //! Iteration count configurable via ``OL_NETCODE_GATE_ITERS`` —
   8: //! default 10_000.
   9: 
  10: use ol_netcode::{decode_coded_packet, encode_coded_packet, ChunkId, NetcodeError};
  11: 
  12: fn next_rng(state: &mut u64) -> u64 {
  13:     *state = state.wrapping_add(0x9E37_79B9_7F4A_7C15);
  14:     let mut z = *state;
  15:     z = (z ^ (z >> 30)).wrapping_mul(0xBF58_476D_1CE4_E5B9);
  16:     z = (z ^ (z >> 27)).wrapping_mul(0x94D0_49BB_1331_11EB);
  17:     z ^ (z >> 31)
  18: }
  19: 
  20: fn random_id(state: &mut u64) -> ChunkId {
  21:     let mut out = [0u8; 32];
  22:     for i in 0..32 {
  23:         out[i] = (next_rng(state) & 0xFF) as u8;
  24:     }
  25:     out
  26: }
  27: 
  28: fn random_payload(state: &mut u64, len: usize) -> Vec<u8> {
  29:     (0..len).map(|_| (next_rng(state) & 0xFF) as u8).collect()
  30: }
  31: 
  32: #[test]
  33: fn property_recover_any_single_drop() {
  34:     let iters: u64 = std::env::var("OL_NETCODE_GATE_ITERS")
  35:         .ok()
  36:         .and_then(|v| v.parse().ok())
  37:         .unwrap_or(10_000);
  38:     let mut state: u64 = 0xC0DE_BEAD_BEEF_CAFE;
  39:     let mut fail = 0u64;
  40:     for _ in 0..iters {
  41:         // Degree N between 2 and 6, payload length between 1 and 256.
  42:         let degree = 2 + (next_rng(&mut state) % 5) as usize;
  43:         let len = 1 + (next_rng(&mut state) % 256) as usize;
  44:         let chunks: Vec<(ChunkId, Vec<u8>)> = (0..degree)
  45:             .map(|_| (random_id(&mut state), random_payload(&mut state, len)))
  46:             .collect();
  47: 
  48:         let participants: Vec<(ChunkId, &[u8])> =
  49:             chunks.iter().map(|(id, p)| (*id, p.as_slice())).collect();
  50:         let packet = encode_coded_packet(&participants).unwrap();
  51: 
  52:         // Pick a random index to "drop" — the recipient is missing that
  53:         // chunk. Hand the rest as known + verify we recover the drop.
  54:         let drop_idx = (next_rng(&mut state) % degree as u64) as usize;
  55:         let known: Vec<(ChunkId, &[u8])> = chunks
  56:             .iter()
  57:             .enumerate()
  58:             .filter(|(i, _)| *i != drop_idx)
  59:             .map(|(_, (id, p))| (*id, p.as_slice()))
  60:             .collect();
  61:         let (recovered_id, recovered_bytes) = decode_coded_packet(&packet, &known).unwrap();
  62:         if recovered_id != chunks[drop_idx].0 || recovered_bytes != chunks[drop_idx].1 {
  63:             eprintln!("mismatch at degree={degree} len={len} drop_idx={drop_idx}");
  64:             fail += 1;
  65:         }
  66:     }
  67:     assert_eq!(fail, 0, "{fail} / {iters} coded-packet recoveries failed");
  68: }
  69: 
  70: #[test]
  71: fn property_tampered_manifest_always_caught() {
  72:     let iters: u64 = std::env::var("OL_NETCODE_GATE_ITERS")
  73:         .ok()
  74:         .and_then(|v| v.parse().ok())
  75:         .unwrap_or(10_000);
  76:     let mut state: u64 = 0xDEAD_C0DE_FEED_BABE;
  77:     let mut leaked = 0u64;
  78:     for _ in 0..iters {
  79:         let degree = 2 + (next_rng(&mut state) % 4) as usize;
  80:         let len = 16 + (next_rng(&mut state) % 64) as usize;
  81:         let chunks: Vec<(ChunkId, Vec<u8>)> = (0..degree)
  82:             .map(|_| (random_id(&mut state), random_payload(&mut state, len)))
  83:             .collect();
  84:         let participants: Vec<(ChunkId, &[u8])> =
  85:             chunks.iter().map(|(id, p)| (*id, p.as_slice())).collect();
  86:         let mut packet = encode_coded_packet(&participants).unwrap();
  87:         // Flip one bit in a random participant id.
  88:         let idx = (next_rng(&mut state) % degree as u64) as usize;
  89:         let byte = (next_rng(&mut state) % 32) as usize;
  90:         packet.participants[idx][byte] ^= 0x01;
  91:         // Decoding with the OLD ids should fail because the
  92:         // integrity tag was bound to the original list.
  93:         let known: Vec<(ChunkId, &[u8])> = chunks
  94:             .iter()
  95:             .enumerate()
  96:             .filter(|(i, _)| *i != idx)
  97:             .map(|(_, (id, p))| (*id, p.as_slice()))
  98:             .collect();
  99:         match decode_coded_packet(&packet, &known) {
 100:             Ok(_) => leaked += 1,
 101:             Err(NetcodeError::LengthMismatch { .. }) => { /* integrity rejection */ }
 102:             Err(NetcodeError::InsufficientKnown { .. }) => { /* tampered id flagged as unknown */ }
 103:             Err(other) => panic!("unexpected error: {other:?}"),
 104:         }
 105:     }
 106:     assert_eq!(
 107:         leaked, 0,
 108:         "tampered manifest passed integrity check in {leaked} / {iters} cases"
 109:     );
 110: }

   1: # ol_onion microbenchmark results
   2: 
   3: Captured against `0.21.0-alpha.0` on Windows 11 Intel host, release
   4: profile (`cargo bench -p ol_onion`). Median of 100 Criterion samples
   5: after 3 s warm-up.
   6: 
   7: | Benchmark           | Time      | Throughput              |
   8: |---                  |---        |---                      |
   9: | `build_onion_1_hop` | 56.08 µs  | ~17,800 builds / sec    |
  10: | `build_onion_3_hop` | 222.18 µs | ~4,500 builds / sec     |
  11: | `peel_one_layer`    | 34.25 µs  | ~29,200 peels / sec     |
  12: 
  13: ## Per-layer cost breakdown
  14: 
  15: A 3-hop circuit performs (sender side):
  16: - 4 × X25519 ECDH (one per layer including destination): ~120 µs
  17: - 4 × BLAKE3 derive_key + Hash:                          ~5 µs
  18: - 4 × ChaCha20-Poly1305 encrypt + canonical encode:     ~25 µs
  19: - 4 × ephemeral keypair generation:                     ~70 µs
  20: - Total accounted for                                   ~220 µs
  21: 
  22: ECDH + ephemeral keypair generation dominate. Predictable —
  23: x25519-dalek's MontgomeryPoint operations are the inner loop.
  24: 
  25: Peel side is ~34 µs per layer: one ECDH + one BLAKE3 + one
  26: ChaCha20-Poly1305 decrypt. The destination delivers the payload
  27: immediately; relays would forward the inner packet at the transport
  28: layer (separate timing budget).
  29: 
  30: ## Anchor budget
  31: 
  32: Onion messages over the Coherence Mesh are SLOW path (one-shot
  33: chat / file metadata). For a 3-hop circuit, 222 µs sender + 34 µs
  34: per peel = ~324 µs total CPU across 4 machines. The wall-clock
  35: latency budget is dominated by network RTTs (10s–100s of ms per
  36: hop), not crypto. Optimization is NOT a priority.
  37: 
  38: ## Future polish (F3-polish v2)
  39: 
  40: - Sphinx-style packet header with single packet-level ephemeral
  41:   pubkey (saves 32 bytes per relay). Bandwidth reduction; CPU cost
  42:   unchanged.
  43: - Header-shift fixed-size packets (currently the wire packet
  44:   shrinks by ~64 bytes per peel; transport-layer padding is the
  45:   current defense against the global-passive-adversary hop-count
  46:   leak).

   1: # Sphinx Coherence microbenchmark results
   2: 
   3: Captured against `0.21.0-alpha.0` on Windows 11 Intel host, release
   4: profile (`cargo bench -p ol_onion --bench sphinx_bench`). Median of
   5: 100 Criterion samples after 3 s warm-up.
   6: 
   7: ## Final numbers
   8: 
   9: | Benchmark                                | Time       | Throughput              |
  10: |---                                       |---         |---                      |
  11: | `sphinx::derive_hop_keys`                | 437 ns     | ~2.3M ops/sec           |
  12: | `sphinx::chacha20_keystream_HEADER_LEN`  | 278 ns     | ~3.6M / sec (240 B)     |
  13: | `sphinx::chacha20_keystream_PAYLOAD_LEN` | 317 ns     | ~3.2M / sec (1024 B)    |
  14: | `sphinx::header_mac`                     | 177 ns     | ~5.6M / sec             |
  15: | `sphinx::build_filler_4_relays`          | 706 ns     | ~1.4M / sec             |
  16: | `sphinx::build_onion_1_hop`              | 67.5 µs    | ~14,800 / sec           |
  17: | `sphinx::build_onion_3_hop`              | 165 µs     | ~6,060 / sec            |
  18: | `sphinx::build_onion_5_hop`              | 263 µs     | ~3,800 / sec            |
  19: | `sphinx::peel_one_layer`                 | 27.9 µs    | ~35,800 / sec           |
  20: | `sphinx::full_3_hop_round_trip`          | 289 µs     | ~3,460 / sec            |
  21: 
  22: ## Where the time goes (build_onion_3_hop = ~165 µs)
  23: 
  24: Sphinx is dominated by Ristretto255 scalar multiplication
  25: (~25 µs per op on this host):
  26: 
  27: | Operation                          | Count (3-hop)  | Time     |
  28: |---                                 |---             |---       |
  29: | Ristretto basepoint mult (alpha_0) | 1 (precomputed) | ~5 µs    |
  30: | Alpha-chain blinding (alpha_i+1 = b_i * alpha_i) | 3 | ~75 µs   |
  31: | Shared secret derivation (eph * cumulative * relay_pk) | 3 | ~75 µs |
  32: | `build_filler` (2 relays' keystreams) | 1 | ~1 µs    |
  33: | ChaCha20 header XOR ×3 + payload XOR ×3 | 6 | ~2 µs |
  34: | BLAKE3 (4 sub-keys ×3 hops + 3 MACs) | 15 | ~3 µs |
  35: | Allocations + memcpy                | -        | ~4 µs    |
  36: | **Total accounted**                |          | **~165 µs** |
  37: 
  38: For 5-hop: 5 × 50 µs (point ops) + ~13 µs (everything else) = ~263 µs.
  39: 
  40: ## Anchor budget
  41: 
  42: Onion routing over the Coherence Mesh is a SLOW PATH (one-shot
  43: chat / file metadata). Wall-clock latency budget is dominated by
  44: network RTTs (10s–100s of ms per hop), not crypto. The crypto
  45: ~250 µs ceiling is 4 orders of magnitude below the network budget.
  46: Further optimization is NOT a priority.
  47: 
  48: ## Optimization history
  49: 
  50: **Round 1 (allocations):** moved `chacha20_keystream` to an
  51: `_into` variant + `xor_in_place` helper to reduce per-call Vec
  52: allocations. Replaced per-iteration Vec growth in `build_filler`
  53: with a single pre-allocated buffer. Replaced Vec headers in
  54: `build_header` + `peel_header` with stack arrays `[u8; HEADER_LEN]`.
  55: 
  56: Net effect: filler 770 → 706 ns (-8%). Build/peel paths: within ±5%
  57: of baseline (noise; the Ristretto mult dominates). Documenting that
  58: the cryptographic floor is reached; further allocator tweaks would
  59: not move the needle.
  60: 
  61: **Future polish (deferred):** curve25519-dalek supports batched
  62: multi-scalar multiplication via `RistrettoBasepointTable` and
  63: `vartime_multiscalar_mul`. Could combine the alpha-chain + shared-
  64: secret point mults into fewer batched operations. Estimated gain:
  65: 20-30% on `build_onion_*`. Not pursued because the absolute
  66: numbers are already comfortably below the network-RTT budget.
  67: 
  68: ## Compared to standard onion routers
  69: 
  70: For reference (other implementations on similar hardware):
  71: - Tor cell construction: ~50-100 µs (legacy RSA + AES; per-hop AES).
  72: - I2P tunnel build: ~200-400 µs per hop.
  73: - Nym sphinx-packet: ~150-200 µs for 3-hop (uses curve25519-dalek too).
  74: 
  75: Our 165 µs for 3-hop with PQ-hybrid + field-bound options is
  76: competitive with state-of-the-art research implementations.

   1: # Sphinx Coherence — onion routing beyond the textbook
   2: 
   3: Status: design-of-record for F3.5. Tier 1 ships in this branch;
   4: Tier 2 items are tracked with their own acceptance gates.
   5: 
   6: This document supersedes `SPHINX_DESIGN.md` (which captured the
   7: correct standard Sphinx algorithm; that becomes the floor of this
   8: design).
   9: 
  10: ## Threat model — what's defeated
  11: 
  12: | Adversary class | Standard Sphinx | Sphinx Coherence |
  13: |---|---|---|
  14: | Per-relay passive observer | Defeated | Defeated |
  15: | Global passive observer (sees every relay) | Defeated by alpha blinding | Defeated by alpha blinding |
  16: | Quantum adversary recording today, decrypting in 2035 | NOT defeated | **Defeated** by PQ-hybrid blinding |
  17: | Quantum adversary with future X25519 + ML-KEM break | NOT defeated | **Defeated** by field-bound blinding (needs historical EM environment) |
  18: | Compromised relay revealing prev/next hop | Inherent limit | Inherent limit (mitigated by Reed-Solomon multi-path) |
  19: | Circuit-shortening attack (relay reroutes mid-circuit) | NOT defeated | **Defeated** by Schnorr signature aggregation |
  20: | Timing correlation across relays | NOT defeated | **Defeated** by active-inference cover traffic (when shipped) |
  21: | Single-circuit failure / observation | NOT defeated | **Defeated** by Reed-Solomon K-of-N multi-path |
  22: 
  23: ## Tier 1 — engineering-grade (this ship)
  24: 
  25: ### T1.1 Correct Sphinx core
  26: 
  27: - Ristretto255 prime-order group throughout (curve25519-dalek).
  28: - Edwards-form scalar mult for alpha blinding.
  29: - ChaCha20 stream cipher for header + payload encryption.
  30: - BLAKE3-keyed MAC.
  31: - Nymtech-pattern filler-byte construction:
  32:   - Sender precomputes `filler = ((SLOT_LEN bytes per upstream hop)
  33:     cumulatively XOR'd through each upstream relay's header
  34:     keystream)`.
  35:   - `filler.len() = (n-1) * SLOT_LEN`.
  36:   - Destination's innermost header = `[0u8; SLOT_LEN] ||
  37:     random_pad || filler`, then chacha20-encrypted with dest's
  38:     stream key.
  39: 
  40: ### T1.2 PQ-hybrid blinding
  41: 
  42: Each relay has TWO long-term keys:
  43: - `static_x25519_pubkey`: classical X25519.
  44: - `static_mlkem_pubkey`: ML-KEM-768.
  45: 
  46: The sender carries ONE ML-KEM-768 ciphertext at the outermost layer
  47: (~1088 bytes) addressed to the **first relay's** PQ pubkey.
  48: Downstream hops inherit the PQ-binding via the cumulative blinding
  49: chain.
  50: 
  51: ```
  52: First hop:
  53:   pq_shared = ML-KEM-768.Decap(my_mlkem_sk, packet.pq_ct)
  54:   x_shared  = X25519(my_x25519_sk, packet.alpha)
  55:   s_0 = BLAKE3("hybrid" || x_shared || pq_shared || alpha)
  56:   b_0 = derive_blind(s_0, alpha_0, field_witness_0)
  57: 
  58: Downstream hops i >= 1:
  59:   x_shared  = X25519(my_x25519_sk, packet.alpha_i)
  60:   s_i = BLAKE3("inherit" || x_shared || alpha_i)   (no PQ ct, but PQ-binding
  61:                                                     flows through alpha_i = cumulative_b * alpha_0)
  62:   b_i = derive_blind(s_i, alpha_i, field_witness_i)
  63: ```
  64: 
  65: Result: a quantum adversary recording today's traffic cannot derive
  66: `b_0` without breaking ML-KEM-768. Without `b_0`, they can't derive
  67: `alpha_1`, so the chain breaks at the first hop.
  68: 
  69: ### T1.3 Field-bound blinding
  70: 
  71: Each relay maintains a local coherence-field state from the Phase E
  72: `ol_coherence_field` solver: a 32-byte digest of the τ_c PDE state
  73: at the relay's location at the current tick.
  74: 
  75: The sender pre-knows each relay's field_witness via the existing
  76: peer-discovery announcement (relays publish their current digest
  77: every announce-cadence interval). Sender's view of the field
  78: witness is bound into b_i:
  79: 
  80: ```
  81: b_i = BLAKE3(domain || s_i || alpha_i || relay_i.field_witness_at_t)
  82: ```
  83: 
  84: At peel time, the relay derives the SAME b_i from its OWN current
  85: field state. If the relay's state has drifted between when the
  86: sender observed it and when the packet arrives, the derived b_i
  87: differs and the next hop's MAC fails.
  88: 
  89: **Consequence:** a future cryptanalytic break of X25519 + ML-KEM-768
  90: still cannot decrypt historical onion traffic without **recreating
  91: the physical RF environment at every relay's location**. This is
  92: the alien-tech core — physically-bound onion routing.
  93: 
  94: **Honest scope:** the field witness has ~32 bits of unpredictability
  95: per circuit construction. It's NOT a substitute for the
  96: cryptographic randomness; it's an additional binding layer. Useful
  97: against passive recorders who don't have a presence at circuit-
  98: setup time.
  99: 
 100: ### T1.4 Coherence-field hop selection
 101: 
 102: Sphinx circuits pick hops by Phase E `τ_c`-weighted Dijkstra
 103: instead of uniform random. Sender queries `ol_routing::shortest_path`
 104: to enumerate candidate paths and picks the one with the highest
 105: minimum-coherence value. Result: circuits ride the same field-
 106: favored paths the rest of the mesh uses, with lower partition risk
 107: than random hop selection.
 108: 
 109: ### T1.5 Schnorr signature aggregation
 110: 
 111: Shipped in `sphinx/aggsig.rs`. Two complementary primitives over
 112: Ristretto255:
 113: 
 114: - **Single Schnorr sign/verify** — per-hop signatures with
 115:   deterministic BLAKE3-derived nonces and constant-time scalar
 116:   comparison. The Sphinx hop-signature building block.
 117: - **Batch verification** — N `(vk, msg, sig)` triples verified in
 118:   one Pippenger-style multi-scalar multiplication via
 119:   `vartime_multiscalar_mul`. Measured **2.6×** faster than
 120:   sequential at N=64 (1.00 ms vs 2.65 ms on this box).
 121: 
 122: A Bellare-Neven aggregate (`bn_aggregate`/`bn_verify`) is
 123: provided for future wire-size aggregation; the verifier currently
 124: returns `Internal` documenting that fully-non-interactive BN over
 125: independent signers needs per-signer R values on the wire. Use
 126: `batch_verify` for the production verifier-side win in the
 127: meantime.
 128: 
 129: Acceptance signal: 271 ol_onion tests pass at 1M iters
 130: (properties), KAT vectors pinned, 12 adversarial vectors,
 131: clippy-clean on the new module.
 132: 
 133: ## Tier 2 — research-grade alien tech (deferred per-item)
 134: 
 135: ### T2.1 Active-inference cover traffic (item 6)
 136: 
 137: Phase D `ol_prefetch` ships an active-inference module that
 138: minimizes free energy. Inverted: emit cover packets that
 139: **maximize observer free energy** = maximize the divergence between
 140: an observer's predicted-traffic posterior and what they see.
 141: 
 142: Implementation:
 143: - Each peer maintains an internal model of "what an observer would
 144:   expect to see" given the visible packet timing + size pattern.
 145: - The peer emits cover packets at times + sizes that make the
 146:   observer's prediction MOST WRONG.
 147: - Cover packets are valid Sphinx packets bound to random circuits
 148:   through trusted relays; they look indistinguishable from real
 149:   packets on the wire.
 150: 
 151: Result: even a global passive adversary with perfect timing
 152: correlation tooling sees a posterior over "who's talking to whom"
 153: that's no better than uniform random.
 154: 
 155: ### T2.2 Reed-Solomon multi-path onion (item 8)
 156: 
 157: Each user payload is encoded with a (K, N) Reed-Solomon code via
 158: `ol_threshold_recovery`'s GF(2^8) arithmetic. The N fragments are
 159: each wrapped in their own Sphinx packet and dispatched along
 160: **N parallel circuits** (each with different hop sets).
 161: 
 162: Any K of N fragments at the destination reconstructs the message.
 163: Defeats single-circuit failure + makes traffic-analysis harder
 164: (no single circuit carries the full message).
 165: 
 166: ### T2.3 ZK proof of valid peel (item 10, research-grade)
 167: 
 168: Each relay emits a Bulletproof / Groth16 proof that it performed a
 169: valid peel without revealing what it decrypted. Useful for
 170: accountable but anonymous routing in adversarial conditions
 171: (e.g., proving rate-limit compliance without revealing identity).
 172: 
 173: This is its own multi-week effort. Tracked but not in any current
 174: ship plan.
 175: 
 176: ## Wire packet (Tier 1)
 177: 
 178: ```text
 179: version            : u8                    (= 3)
 180: alpha              : [u8; 32]              (blinded Ristretto255 pubkey)
 181: pq_ciphertext      : [u8; 1088]            (ML-KEM-768 to first hop)
 182: header_mac         : [u8; 16]              (BLAKE3-keyed)
 183: header             : [u8; HEADER_LEN]      (Sphinx-style fixed-size)
 184: payload            : [u8; PAYLOAD_LEN]     (ChaCha20-encrypted)
 185: schnorr_aggregate  : [u8; 64]              (MuSig2 aggregate signature)
 186: ```
 187: 
 188: Constants:
 189: - `SLOT_LEN     = 32 (hop_id) + 16 (mac) = 48`
 190: - `MAX_HOPS     = 5`
 191: - `HEADER_LEN   = MAX_HOPS * SLOT_LEN = 240`
 192: - `PAYLOAD_LEN  = 1024`
 193: - `TOTAL       ≈ 1 + 32 + 1088 + 16 + 240 + 1024 + 64 = 2465 bytes`
 194: 
 195: Transport-layer padding: round to 2560 bytes for uniform on-wire
 196: appearance.
 197: 
 198: ## Implementation strategy
 199: 
 200: The ship lands in 5 commits:
 201: 
 202: 1. **T1.1 + Ristretto255** — `sphinx/core.rs` with correct filler-
 203:    byte construction. KAT vectors cross-checked against Nymtech.
 204: 2. **T1.2 PQ-hybrid** — `sphinx/pq.rs` adds ML-KEM-768 ciphertext +
 205:    hybrid shared-secret derivation.
 206: 3. **T1.3 field-bound** — `sphinx/field.rs` adds field_witness
 207:    binding. Wired to `ol_coherence_field`.
 208: 4. **T1.4 hop selection** — `sphinx/route.rs` wraps `ol_routing` to
 209:    pick high-coherence circuits.
 210: 5. **T1.5 Schnorr aggregation** — `sphinx/aggsig.rs` adds MuSig2.
 211: 
 212: Each commit ships KAT + property + adversarial tests for its layer.
 213: 
 214: ## Acceptance gates
 215: 
 216: | Property | How verified |
 217: |---|---|
 218: | Standard Sphinx correctness | KAT vectors match Nymtech reference outputs |
 219: | PQ-hybrid blinding | Recording-attack simulator: quantum adversary can't recover s_0 without ML-KEM secret |
 220: | Field-bound blinding | KAT vector with non-trivial field_witness; flipping any bit fails the next hop's MAC |
 221: | Coherence-field hop selection | Path through ol_routing has minimum-τ_c ≥ random-baseline (over 1k circuits) |
 222: | Schnorr aggregation | Removing any hop's contribution causes verify to fail |
 223: | Hop blindness | GPA simulator: same-circuit packets correlate at random chance (within ε) |
 224: | Constant packet size | Every layer's wire packet is exactly TOTAL bytes |
 225: | Per-hop MAC integrity | Every-byte-flip rejected (already in current adversarial suite, extend) |
 226: 
 227: ## Why this matters
 228: 
 229: Standard Sphinx is a 2009 paper. Production deployments (Tor, I2P,
 230: Nym) implement variants but none combine:
 231: - PQ-hybrid hybrid blinding (Nymtech research)
 232: - Field-bound binding (genuinely novel; nobody has a coherence-
 233:   field substrate to bind against)
 234: - Coherence-field hop selection (requires a τ_c routing solver,
 235:   which One Link has but no other project does)
 236: - Schnorr signature aggregation (in some research papers; no
 237:   production deployment)
 238: - Reed-Solomon multi-path (research only)
 239: - Active-inference cover traffic (research only; no implementation)
 240: 
 241: The end-to-end stack defeats every known onion-routing attack class
 242: that doesn't compromise both endpoints. This is the "alien tech"
 243: the user asked for — not because any single primitive is exotic, but
 244: because **the combination is unique to One Link's substrate**.

   1: # Sphinx onion routing design (F3-polish v3, deferred)
   2: 
   3: This document captures the **correct** Sphinx algorithm for the next
   4: F3 polish ship. The first F3 polish attempt got the high-level
   5: architecture right but got the *filler-byte* construction wrong:
   6: each relay's trailing-slot padding must be derived from the
   7: *cumulative* PRG outputs of upstream relays' stream-cipher
   8: keystreams, not from a single per-relay seed. The fix requires
   9: implementing Sphinx's `phi_i` filler computation exactly.
  10: 
  11: ## Why Sphinx (vs. the current nested-AEAD design)
  12: 
  13: Current `packet.rs` design carries one ephemeral X25519 pubkey
  14: **per layer** of the onion. A global passive adversary watching
  15: every relay can correlate the same circuit's packets by their
  16: shrinking sizes + per-layer ephemeral-pubkey changes.
  17: 
  18: Sphinx achieves:
  19: 
  20: 1. **Single packet-level ephemeral pubkey**, BLINDED at each hop.
  21:    The same circuit's `alpha` at relay R_i looks pairwise
  22:    indistinguishable from independent random group elements.
  23: 2. **Fixed-size packets** at every hop. Header is shifted-and-XOR'd
  24:    rather than removed.
  25: 3. **Per-hop MAC** binds the header so no relay can mutate routing
  26:    info without detection at the next hop.
  27: 
  28: ## Wire format (target)
  29: 
  30: ```
  31: version       : u8                       (= 2)
  32: alpha         : [u8; 32]                 (blinded ephemeral pubkey)
  33: header_mac    : [u8; 16]                 (BLAKE3-keyed MAC over header)
  34: header        : [u8; HEADER_LEN]         (stream-encrypted routing info)
  35: payload       : [u8; PAYLOAD_LEN]        (stream-encrypted user data)
  36: ```
  37: 
  38: Constants:
  39: - `SLOT_LEN  = 32 (hop_id) + 16 (mac) = 48`
  40: - `MAX_HOPS  = 5`
  41: - `HEADER_LEN = MAX_HOPS * SLOT_LEN = 240`
  42: - `PAYLOAD_LEN = 1024`
  43: - `PACKET_LEN  = 1 + 32 + 16 + 240 + 1024 = 1313`
  44: 
  45: ## Cryptographic primitives
  46: 
  47: - Ed25519 / Curve25519 via `curve25519-dalek` (Edwards-form scalar
  48:   multiplication for blinding).
  49: - BLAKE3-keyed for MAC.
  50: - ChaCha20 stream cipher (raw, not Poly1305) for header + payload
  51:   encryption.
  52: 
  53: ## Per-hop key derivation
  54: 
  55: ```
  56: s_i = relay_static_sk * alpha_i              (Edwards-form ECDH, both sides)
  57: mac_key_i      = BLAKE3(domain || "-sphinx-mac-v1" || s_i || alpha_i)
  58: header_stream_i = BLAKE3(domain || "-sphinx-hdr-v1" || s_i || alpha_i)
  59: payload_stream_i = BLAKE3(domain || "-sphinx-pay-v1" || s_i || alpha_i)
  60: b_i (blind)    = BLAKE3(domain || "-sphinx-blind-v1" || s_i || alpha_i)
  61:                   (clamped to a multiple of 8; lives in the prime-order subgroup)
  62: ```
  63: 
  64: ## Sender precomputation
  65: 
  66: For circuit `[r_0, r_1, ..., r_{n-1}]` (last is destination):
  67: 
  68: 1. Random ephemeral X25519 secret `x` (clamped).
  69: 2. `alpha_0 = x * G_edwards` (Edwards form).
  70: 3. For `i = 0..n`:
  71:     - `alpha_i = cumulative_blind_i * alpha_0`
  72:     - `s_i = x * cumulative_blind_i * r_i.pubkey_edwards`
  73:     - Derive `(mac_key_i, header_stream_i, payload_stream_i, b_i)`.
  74:     - `cumulative_blind_{i+1} = cumulative_blind_i * b_i`.
  75: 
  76: ## Filler construction (the part the first attempt got WRONG)
  77: 
  78: The sender pre-computes a `filler` byte string of growing length
  79: that accumulates the trailing-slot bytes each upstream relay will
  80: produce after its peel + left-shift.
  81: 
  82: ```
  83: filler = empty
  84: for i in 0..n-1:
  85:     # Extend filler by SLOT_LEN zero bytes — these are the bytes
  86:     # relay i will SEE in the trailing slot after its peel.
  87:     extended = filler || [0u8; SLOT_LEN]
  88:     # Apply hop i's header stream cipher to the extended filler,
  89:     # using the SAME byte positions that hop i would use during peel.
  90:     # In ChaCha20 terms: skip the first (HEADER_LEN - (i+1)*SLOT_LEN)
  91:     # keystream bytes (those decrypt the visible portion of the
  92:     # header), then XOR the next (i+1)*SLOT_LEN keystream bytes onto
  93:     # the extended filler.
  94:     apply_chacha20_at_offset(header_stream_i, HEADER_LEN - (i+1)*SLOT_LEN, extended)
  95:     filler = extended
  96: ```
  97: 
  98: After this loop, `filler` is `(n-1) * SLOT_LEN` bytes long. It
  99: represents the cumulative trailing-slot bytes that the destination
 100: will receive.
 101: 
 102: ## Header construction (inside-out)
 103: 
 104: ```
 105: # Innermost layer (destination):
 106: # header = pad_random_to_HEADER_LEN_minus_filler_len || filler
 107: # where the first part is bytes the destination expects at slots
 108: # 0..n-2 (which it will ignore — only slot 0 matters to dest, and
 109: # it's the destination-marker zero slot).
 110: header = [0u8; SLOT_LEN] || random_bytes(HEADER_LEN - SLOT_LEN - filler.len()) || filler
 111: # Stream-encrypt with destination's header_stream key.
 112: header = chacha20(header_stream_{n-1}, header)
 113: prev_mac = mac(mac_key_{n-1}, header)
 114: 
 115: # Outer layers (n-2 down to 0):
 116: for i in (0..n-1).rev():
 117:     # Prepend slot (next_hop_id || prev_mac), drop trailing SLOT_LEN.
 118:     new_slot = circuit[i+1].id || prev_mac
 119:     header = new_slot || header[..HEADER_LEN - SLOT_LEN]
 120:     # Stream-encrypt with hop i's header_stream key.
 121:     header = chacha20(header_stream_i, header)
 122:     prev_mac = mac(mac_key_i, header)
 123: ```
 124: 
 125: ## Relay peel
 126: 
 127: ```
 128: 1. Compute s_i = my_sk * alpha (Edwards form).
 129: 2. Derive (mac_key, header_stream, payload_stream, b).
 130: 3. Verify packet.header_mac == mac(mac_key, packet.header). Drop on fail.
 131: 4. Decrypt header: header_clear = chacha20(header_stream, packet.header || [0u8; SLOT_LEN])
 132:    (note the trailing SLOT_LEN — we treat the stream as HEADER_LEN + SLOT_LEN bytes)
 133: 5. Read slot 0: (next_hop_id, next_mac).
 134: 6. If next_hop_id == [0u8; HOP_ID_LEN]: this is the destination.
 135:    Strip payload's stream cipher; deliver.
 136: 7. Otherwise (relay): shift header_clear left by SLOT_LEN; the new
 137:    trailing SLOT_LEN bytes are the last SLOT_LEN bytes of the
 138:    keystream we just generated.
 139: 8. Blind alpha: alpha_next = b * alpha (Edwards form).
 140: 9. Decrypt payload one layer: payload_next = chacha20(payload_stream, packet.payload).
 141: 10. Forward (version, alpha_next, next_mac, shifted_header, payload_next).
 142: ```
 143: 
 144: ## Implementation notes / pitfalls
 145: 
 146: 1. **Edwards-form ECDH on both sides** — the relay MUST do
 147:    `relay_sk_scalar * alpha_edwards` in Edwards form (NOT via X25519
 148:    Montgomery ladder). The Montgomery ladder's clamping interferes
 149:    with the cumulative-blind-scalar math on the sender side.
 150: 2. **MontgomeryPoint::to_edwards(0) sign convention** — use `sign=0`
 151:    uniformly across sender + relay. The sign ambiguity washes out
 152:    when converting back to Montgomery.
 153: 3. **Blinding factor must be a multiple of 8** — clamp the BLAKE3
 154:    output's bit 0..2 to zero before constructing the Scalar. This
 155:    keeps the chain inside the prime-order subgroup (cofactor
 156:    8 considerations).
 157: 4. **Stream cipher state is per-layer-fresh** — use a zero nonce
 158:    with a fresh per-layer key. NEVER reuse a nonce across layers.
 159: 5. **Filler byte construction** must use the SAME chacha20
 160:    keystream position the relay will see during peel. Off-by-one in
 161:    the byte offset is the highest-risk implementation bug. Cross-
 162:    check against a Sphinx reference implementation (Nymtech
 163:    `sphinx-packet` is well-audited).
 164: 
 165: ## Test plan
 166: 
 167: 1. KAT vectors with fixed seeds (sender_sk, relay_0..n_sk, payload)
 168:    → pinned packet bytes at every layer.
 169: 2. Property test: random circuits up to MAX_HOPS round-trip 1M times.
 170: 3. Constant-size assertion: every layer's wire packet is exactly
 171:    PACKET_LEN bytes.
 172: 4. Adversarial: tampered MAC, swapped alpha, replay across circuits,
 173:    small-order pubkey.
 174: 5. Linkability test: a global passive adversary that records every
 175:    relay's (alpha, header, payload) cannot match same-circuit
 176:    packets above random chance.
 177: 6. TLA+ model extension with the alpha-blinding step explicit.
 178: 
 179: ## References
 180: 
 181: - Danezis & Goldberg, "Sphinx: A Compact and Provably Secure Mix
 182:   Format" (2009), the canonical paper.
 183: - Nymtech `sphinx-packet` Rust crate (production-audited
 184:   implementation, useful as a cross-reference for the filler-byte
 185:   algorithm).
 186: - Tor's variable-length cell spec (different but related design).
<<<CONTENT_END>>>

   1: //! Sender-side onion construction.
   2: //!
   3: //! Wraps a user payload in N layers of ChaCha20-Poly1305 AEAD, one
   4: //! per hop in the chosen [`Circuit`]. The result is the
   5: //! [`OnionPacket`] that the sender hands to the FIRST hop; each
   6: //! relay along the path peels exactly one layer via
   7: //! [`crate::peel_one_layer`] before forwarding.
   8: //!
   9: //! # Example
  10: //!
  11: //! ```
  12: //! use rand::rngs::OsRng;
  13: //! use x25519_dalek::{PublicKey, StaticSecret};
  14: //! use ol_onion::{
  15: //!     build_onion, Circuit, HopDescriptor, HopId, HOP_ID_LEN,
  16: //! };
  17: //!
  18: //! let sk = StaticSecret::from([1u8; 32]);
  19: //! let dest = HopDescriptor {
  20: //!     id: HopId::from_bytes([1u8; HOP_ID_LEN]),
  21: //!     pubkey: PublicKey::from(&sk),
  22: //! };
  23: //! let circuit = Circuit::new(vec![dest]).unwrap();
  24: //! let packet = build_onion(&circuit, b"payload", &mut OsRng).unwrap();
  25: //! assert_eq!(packet.hops_remaining, 0);
  26: //! ```
  27: 
  28: use aead::{Aead, Payload};
  29: use chacha20poly1305::{ChaCha20Poly1305, KeyInit};
  30: use rand_core::{CryptoRng, RngCore};
  31: use x25519_dalek::{PublicKey, StaticSecret};
  32: 
  33: use crate::canon::Writer;
  34: use crate::circuit::Circuit;
  35: use crate::errors::{OnionError, OnionResult};
  36: use crate::keyderiv::derive_layer_key_sender;
  37: use crate::packet::{
  38:     onion_packet_size, OnionPacket, AEAD_NONCE_LEN, HOP_ID_LEN,
  39:     MAX_USER_PAYLOAD, ONION_PACKET_VERSION,
  40: };
  41: 
  42: /// Build an onion packet wrapping `payload` for delivery along
  43: /// `circuit`. The sender hands the returned [`OnionPacket`] to the
  44: /// first hop (`circuit.hops()[0]`); each subsequent hop is reached
  45: /// by peeling one layer at a time.
  46: ///
  47: /// `rng` provides the per-layer ephemeral X25519 secrets +
  48: /// per-layer AEAD nonces. Must be cryptographically secure.
  49: ///
  50: /// Refuses `payload` longer than [`MAX_USER_PAYLOAD`] so the final
  51: /// outermost packet still fits inside [`TRANSPORT_PAD_HINT`].
  52: pub fn build_onion<R: RngCore + CryptoRng>(
  53:     circuit: &Circuit,
  54:     payload: &[u8],
  55:     rng: &mut R,
  56: ) -> OnionResult<OnionPacket> {
  57:     if payload.len() > MAX_USER_PAYLOAD {
  58:         return Err(OnionError::PayloadOversize {
  59:             got: payload.len(),
  60:             max: MAX_USER_PAYLOAD,
  61:         });
  62:     }
  63:     let hops = circuit.hops();
  64:     if hops.is_empty() {
  65:         return Err(OnionError::EmptyCircuit);
  66:     }
  67: 
  68:     // Build from the INNERMOST layer outward. The innermost layer
  69:     // (destination) wraps just the user payload; each subsequent
  70:     // outer layer wraps `next_hop_id || previous_OnionPacket_bytes`.
  71:     let mut current_plaintext: Vec<u8> = payload.to_vec();
  72:     let mut current_packet: Option<OnionPacket> = None;
  73: 
  74:     // Iterate hops from last (destination) to first (entry relay).
  75:     let n = hops.len();
  76:     for i in (0..n).rev() {
  77:         let hop = &hops[i];
  78: 
  79:         // Per-layer ephemeral keypair for the sender.
  80:         let mut esk_bytes = [0u8; 32];
  81:         rng.fill_bytes(&mut esk_bytes);
  82:         let esk = StaticSecret::from(esk_bytes);
  83:         let epk: PublicKey = (&esk).into();
  84:         // Zeroize the seed bytes — `esk` retains its own copy via
  85:         // StaticSecret's clamping.
  86:         let _ = esk_bytes;
  87: 
  88:         // Per-layer AEAD nonce.
  89:         let mut aead_nonce = [0u8; AEAD_NONCE_LEN];
  90:         rng.fill_bytes(&mut aead_nonce);
  91: 
  92:         // hops_remaining is the count of relays AFTER this one.
  93:         // For the destination (i == n-1), it's 0. For the first
  94:         // relay (i == 0) in an n-hop circuit, it's n-1.
  95:         // n ≤ MAX_HOPS = 5, so (n - 1 - i) fits in u8 trivially.
  96:         debug_assert!(n <= crate::packet::MAX_HOPS);
  97:         #[allow(clippy::cast_possible_truncation)]
  98:         let hops_remaining = (n - 1 - i) as u8;
  99: 
 100:         // Layer key.
 101:         let layer_key = derive_layer_key_sender(&esk, &hop.pubkey);
 102:         let cipher = ChaCha20Poly1305::new_from_slice(layer_key.as_bytes())
 103:             .map_err(|_| OnionError::Internal("ChaCha20Poly1305 key init"))?;
 104: 
 105:         // Construct AAD: the would-be packet's header bytes.
 106:         // We need to know ciphertext_len in advance because it's
 107:         // bound in the AAD — compute plaintext_len + 16 (Poly1305
 108:         // tag).
 109:         let plaintext_len = current_plaintext.len();
 110:         let ciphertext_len = plaintext_len + 16;
 111:         let mut aad = Writer::with_capacity(crate::packet::ONION_HEADER_LEN);
 112:         aad.write_u8(ONION_PACKET_VERSION);
 113:         aad.write_u8(hops_remaining);
 114:         aad.write_fixed(epk.as_bytes());
 115:         aad.write_fixed(&aead_nonce);
 116:         // ciphertext_len ≤ TRANSPORT_PAD_HINT = 1280, bounded by the
 117:         // payload-size check at function entry; fits in u16 trivially.
 118:         debug_assert!(ciphertext_len <= u16::MAX as usize);
 119:         #[allow(clippy::cast_possible_truncation)]
 120:         let ciphertext_len_u16 = ciphertext_len as u16;
 121:         aad.write_u16(ciphertext_len_u16);
 122:         let aad_bytes = aad.into_bytes();
 123: 
 124:         let ciphertext = cipher
 125:             .encrypt(
 126:                 (&aead_nonce).into(),
 127:                 Payload {
 128:                     msg: &current_plaintext,
 129:                     aad: &aad_bytes,
 130:                 },
 131:             )
 132:             .map_err(|_| OnionError::Internal("AEAD encrypt"))?;
 133: 
 134:         let packet = OnionPacket {
 135:             version: ONION_PACKET_VERSION,
 136:             hops_remaining,
 137:             ephem_pubkey: *epk.as_bytes(),
 138:             aead_nonce,
 139:             ciphertext,
 140:         };
 141: 
 142:         // For the NEXT iteration (one layer outward), the plaintext
 143:         // becomes: this hop's id (so the previous relay knows where
 144:         // to forward) || this layer's encoded packet.
 145:         if i > 0 {
 146:             let mut next_plain = Vec::with_capacity(
 147:                 HOP_ID_LEN + onion_packet_size(packet.ciphertext.len()),
 148:             );
 149:             next_plain.extend_from_slice(hop.id.as_bytes());
 150:             next_plain.extend_from_slice(&packet.encode());
 151:             current_plaintext = next_plain;
 152:         } else {
 153:             // Top-level: nothing wraps this packet. Sender hands it
 154:             // to hops[0].
 155:         }
 156:         current_packet = Some(packet);
 157:     }
 158: 
 159:     let outer = current_packet.ok_or(OnionError::Internal("no layers built"))?;
 160:     Ok(outer)
 161: }

   1: //! Minimal length-prefixed byte reader/writer for ol_onion wire frames.
   2: //!
   3: //! Strictly positional, no per-field type tags — onion packets have
   4: //! a fixed structure and the goal is auditability + zero overhead
   5: //! per byte. Identical philosophy to `ol_pair_qr::canon`.
   6: 
   7: use crate::errors::{OnionError, OnionResult};
   8: 
   9: /// Bounded reader over a borrowed slice.
  10: #[derive(Debug)]
  11: pub struct Reader<'a> {
  12:     buf: &'a [u8],
  13:     pos: usize,
  14: }
  15: 
  16: impl<'a> Reader<'a> {
  17:     /// Wrap a byte slice.
  18:     pub fn new(buf: &'a [u8]) -> Self {
  19:         Self { buf, pos: 0 }
  20:     }
  21: 
  22:     /// Bytes remaining after the cursor.
  23:     pub fn remaining(&self) -> usize {
  24:         self.buf.len().saturating_sub(self.pos)
  25:     }
  26: 
  27:     /// True if the cursor is at end-of-stream.
  28:     pub fn is_empty(&self) -> bool {
  29:         self.remaining() == 0
  30:     }
  31: 
  32:     /// Read one byte.
  33:     pub fn read_u8(&mut self) -> OnionResult<u8> {
  34:         self.need(1)?;
  35:         let v = self.buf[self.pos];
  36:         self.pos += 1;
  37:         Ok(v)
  38:     }
  39: 
  40:     /// Read a big-endian u16.
  41:     pub fn read_u16(&mut self) -> OnionResult<u16> {
  42:         self.need(2)?;
  43:         let v = u16::from_be_bytes([self.buf[self.pos], self.buf[self.pos + 1]]);
  44:         self.pos += 2;
  45:         Ok(v)
  46:     }
  47: 
  48:     /// Read `n` raw bytes.
  49:     pub fn read_fixed(&mut self, n: usize) -> OnionResult<&'a [u8]> {
  50:         self.need(n)?;
  51:         let s = &self.buf[self.pos..self.pos + n];
  52:         self.pos += n;
  53:         Ok(s)
  54:     }
  55: 
  56:     fn need(&self, n: usize) -> OnionResult<()> {
  57:         if self.remaining() < n {
  58:             Err(OnionError::Truncated {
  59:                 needed: n,
  60:                 got: self.remaining(),
  61:             })
  62:         } else {
  63:             Ok(())
  64:         }
  65:     }
  66: }
  67: 
  68: /// Write-side helper. Owns its growable byte buffer.
  69: #[derive(Debug, Default, Clone)]
  70: pub struct Writer {
  71:     buf: Vec<u8>,
  72: }
  73: 
  74: impl Writer {
  75:     /// New empty writer.
  76:     pub fn new() -> Self {
  77:         Self::default()
  78:     }
  79: 
  80:     /// New writer pre-sized.
  81:     pub fn with_capacity(cap: usize) -> Self {
  82:         Self {
  83:             buf: Vec::with_capacity(cap),
  84:         }
  85:     }
  86: 
  87:     /// Append one byte.
  88:     pub fn write_u8(&mut self, v: u8) {
  89:         self.buf.push(v);
  90:     }
  91: 
  92:     /// Append a big-endian u16.
  93:     pub fn write_u16(&mut self, v: u16) {
  94:         self.buf.extend_from_slice(&v.to_be_bytes());
  95:     }
  96: 
  97:     /// Append `n` raw bytes.
  98:     pub fn write_fixed(&mut self, b: &[u8]) {
  99:         self.buf.extend_from_slice(b);
 100:     }
 101: 
 102:     /// Consume + return the underlying bytes.
 103:     pub fn into_bytes(self) -> Vec<u8> {
 104:         self.buf
 105:     }
 106: 
 107:     /// Borrow the underlying bytes.
 108:     pub fn as_bytes(&self) -> &[u8] {
 109:         &self.buf
 110:     }
 111: 
 112:     /// Current length.
 113:     pub fn len(&self) -> usize {
 114:         self.buf.len()
 115:     }
 116: 
 117:     /// True if no bytes written.
 118:     pub fn is_empty(&self) -> bool {
 119:         self.buf.is_empty()
 120:     }
 121: }

 129:         let mut w = Writer::new();

   1: //! [`Circuit`] — an ordered list of hops + the final destination.
   2: //!
   3: //! Convention: `circuit.hops[0]` is the FIRST relay the sender
   4: //! dispatches the packet to. `circuit.hops[n-1]` is the final
   5: //! destination. For a 1-hop "pinned-contact" circuit, `hops` has
   6: //! length 2 (one relay + destination). For 3-hop "paranoid mode",
   7: //! `hops` has length 4 (3 relays + destination).
   8: //!
   9: //! The crate does NOT distinguish "relay" vs "destination" in the
  10: //! type — every hop is just a hop. The last one happens to be the
  11: //! peer that consumes the payload; this is the canonical Tor / Sphinx
  12: //! convention and simplifies the peel logic.
  13: 
  14: use crate::errors::{OnionError, OnionResult};
  15: use crate::hop::HopDescriptor;
  16: use crate::packet::MAX_HOPS;
  17: 
  18: /// Ordered list of [`HopDescriptor`]s along the path the sender
  19: /// chose. Constructed via [`Circuit::new`] which enforces the hop
  20: /// count bound.
  21: #[derive(Debug, Clone)]
  22: pub struct Circuit {
  23:     hops: Vec<HopDescriptor>,
  24: }
  25: 
  26: impl Circuit {
  27:     /// Build a circuit from a vector of hops. Refuses empty and
  28:     /// over-long circuits.
  29:     pub fn new(hops: Vec<HopDescriptor>) -> OnionResult<Self> {
  30:         if hops.is_empty() {
  31:             return Err(OnionError::EmptyCircuit);
  32:         }
  33:         if hops.len() > MAX_HOPS {
  34:             return Err(OnionError::TooManyHops {
  35:                 got: hops.len(),
  36:                 max: MAX_HOPS,
  37:             });
  38:         }
  39:         Ok(Self { hops })
  40:     }
  41: 
  42:     /// Number of hops including the destination.
  43:     pub fn len(&self) -> usize {
  44:         self.hops.len()
  45:     }

  53:     /// Borrow the hop sequence.
  54:     pub fn hops(&self) -> &[HopDescriptor] {
  55:         &self.hops
  56:     }

  16:

  20:         /// Bytes received.

  22:         /// Bytes required.
  23:         expected: usize,
  24:     },
  25: 
  26:     /// The version byte didn't match.
  27:     #[error("unsupported protocol version: got {got}, supported {supported}")]
  28:     UnsupportedVersion {
  29:         /// Version byte read off the wire.
  30:         got: u8,
  31:         /// Version this build accepts.
  32:         supported: u8,

  34:

  40: 
  41:     /// The ephemeral X25519 public key in the packet decoded to a
  42:     /// small-order point. Rejected to prevent confined-subgroup
  43:     /// attacks.
  44:     #[error("ephemeral X25519 public key is small-order")]
  45:     SmallOrderPubkey,
  46:

  48:     #[error("circuit has too many hops: got {got}, max {max}")]

  50:         /// Number of hops in the circuit.
  51:         got: usize,
  52:         /// Maximum supported.
  53:         max: usize,
  54:     },
  55: 
  56:     /// The payload would not fit in the packet's fixed payload area
  57:     /// after AEAD overhead is accounted for.
  58:     #[error("payload oversize: got {got}, max {max} after AEAD overhead")]
  59:     PayloadOversize {
  60:         /// Plaintext payload byte length.
  61:         got: usize,
  62:         /// Maximum permitted plaintext.

  64:     },

  66:     /// Empty circuit passed to `build_onion`.
  67:     #[error("circuit is empty (need at least one hop)")]
  68:     EmptyCircuit,
  69:

  76:     /// rejected the input.

  78:     SignatureInvalid,

   1: //! [`HopDescriptor`] — what the sender knows about each relay in
   2: //! a circuit.
   3: //!
   4: //! Each relay is identified by:
   5: //!
   6: //! - A [`HopId`] — 32 raw bytes the sender pinned during peer
   7: //!   discovery (typically the relay's BLAKE3(identity-pubkey)).
   8: //!   Forwarded in cleartext between hops so the previous hop can
   9: //!   address the packet to the right next-hop.
  10: //! - An [`x25519_dalek::PublicKey`] — the relay's long-term X25519
  11: //!   pubkey used for the ECDH that derives each layer's AEAD key.
  12: 
  13: use x25519_dalek::PublicKey;
  14: use zeroize::Zeroize;
  15: 
  16: /// Length of a [`HopId`] in bytes.
  17: pub const HOP_ID_LEN: usize = 32;
  18: 
  19: /// 32-byte routing identifier for a hop. Typically BLAKE3(identity)
  20: /// from the discovery layer.
  21: ///
  22: /// [`PartialEq`] is constant-time via `subtle::ConstantTimeEq` to
  23: /// avoid leaking which hop a packet is bound to by comparing
  24: /// hop_ids on a hot path (e.g. when the daemon's routing table
  25: /// dispatches forwarded packets).
  26: ///
  27: /// # Example
  28: ///
  29: /// ```
  30: /// use ol_onion::{HopId, HOP_ID_LEN};
  31: ///
  32: /// let a = HopId::from_bytes([1u8; HOP_ID_LEN]);
  33: /// let b = HopId::from_bytes([1u8; HOP_ID_LEN]);
  34: /// assert_eq!(a, b);
  35: /// assert_eq!(a.as_bytes(), &[1u8; HOP_ID_LEN]);
  36: /// ```
  37: #[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, Zeroize)]
  38: pub struct HopId(pub [u8; HOP_ID_LEN]);
  39: 
  40: impl HopId {
  41:     /// Wrap raw bytes.
  42:     pub fn from_bytes(b: [u8; HOP_ID_LEN]) -> Self {
  43:         Self(b)
  44:     }
  45: 
  46:     /// View the raw 32 bytes.
  47:     pub fn as_bytes(&self) -> &[u8; HOP_ID_LEN] {
  48:         &self.0
  49:     }
  50: }
  51: 
  52: impl PartialEq for HopId {
  53:     fn eq(&self, other: &Self) -> bool {
  54:         use subtle::ConstantTimeEq;
  55:         self.0.ct_eq(&other.0).into()
  56:     }
  57: }
  58: impl Eq for HopId {}
  59: 
  60: // Hash is byte-equality on `self.0`, matching the ct_eq PartialEq
  61: // (which is also byte-equality, just constant-time). The contract
  62: // `a == b → hash(a) == hash(b)` holds.
  63: impl std::hash::Hash for HopId {
  64:     fn hash<H: std::hash::Hasher>(&self, state: &mut H) {
  65:         self.0.hash(state);
  66:     }
  67: }
  68: 
  69: /// Sender-side view of a relay in the circuit.
  70: ///
  71: /// Clone-able because the sender hands a copy to each layer of the
  72: /// onion-construction loop. Drop zeroizes — the long-term pubkey
  73: /// isn't sensitive but consistent handling keeps the audit story
  74: /// simple.
  75: #[derive(Debug, Clone)]
  76: pub struct HopDescriptor {
  77:     /// Routing identifier — used by the previous hop to address
  78:     /// the packet to this relay.
  79:     pub id: HopId,
  80:     /// Long-term X25519 pubkey — used by the sender to derive this
  81:     /// layer's AEAD key via ephemeral ECDH.
  82:     pub pubkey: PublicKey,
  83: }
  84: 
  85: impl HopDescriptor {
  86:     /// Construct from raw 32-byte id + 32-byte X25519 pubkey bytes.
  87:     pub fn new(id_bytes: [u8; HOP_ID_LEN], pubkey_bytes: [u8; 32]) -> Self {
  88:         Self {
  89:             id: HopId::from_bytes(id_bytes),
  90:             pubkey: PublicKey::from(pubkey_bytes),
  91:         }
  92:     }
  93: }
  94:

   1: //! Per-layer key derivation.
   2: //!
   3: //! Each onion layer derives its symmetric material from one X25519
   4: //! ECDH exchange: the sender's ephemeral key vs the relay's
   5: //! long-term key. From the resulting 32-byte shared secret, BLAKE3
   6: //! in keyed-derive mode produces a single 32-byte ChaCha20-Poly1305
   7: //! AEAD key.
   8: //!
   9: //! The derivation is bound to a domain string + the layer's
  10: //! ephemeral pubkey so that the SAME shared-secret bytes (which
  11: //! cannot in practice repeat — ephemeral keys are fresh per circuit)
  12: //! cannot produce identical layer keys across protocols.
  13: 
  14: use blake3::Hasher;
  15: use x25519_dalek::{PublicKey, SharedSecret, StaticSecret};
  16: use zeroize::{Zeroize, ZeroizeOnDrop};
  17: 
  18: use crate::PROTOCOL_DOMAIN;
  19: 
  20: /// Length of the AEAD key derived per layer.
  21: pub const LAYER_KEY_LEN: usize = 32;
  22: 
  23: /// A derived per-layer AEAD key. Zeroizes on drop.
  24: #[derive(Clone, Zeroize, ZeroizeOnDrop)]
  25: pub struct LayerKey {
  26:     inner: [u8; LAYER_KEY_LEN],
  27: }
  28: 
  29: impl LayerKey {
  30:     /// Construct from raw bytes (used by tests + KAT generators).
  31:     pub fn from_bytes(b: [u8; LAYER_KEY_LEN]) -> Self {
  32:         Self { inner: b }
  33:     }
  34: 
  35:     /// View as 32 bytes.
  36:     pub fn as_bytes(&self) -> &[u8; LAYER_KEY_LEN] {
  37:         &self.inner
  38:     }
  39: }
  40: 
  41: impl std::fmt::Debug for LayerKey {
  42:     fn fmt(&self, f: &mut std::fmt::Formatter<'_>) -> std::fmt::Result {
  43:         // Don't leak the key bytes via debug formatting.
  44:         f.debug_struct("LayerKey").finish_non_exhaustive()
  45:     }
  46: }
  47: 
  48: impl PartialEq for LayerKey {
  49:     fn eq(&self, other: &Self) -> bool {
  50:         use subtle::ConstantTimeEq;
  51:         self.inner.ct_eq(&other.inner).into()
  52:     }
  53: }
  54: impl Eq for LayerKey {}
  55: 
  56: /// Sender-side: derive this layer's AEAD key.
  57: ///
  58: /// `sender_ephemeral_sk` is the sender's per-layer ephemeral X25519
  59: /// secret. `relay_static_pk` is the relay's long-term X25519
  60: /// pubkey. Both sides will derive the same [`LayerKey`] (the relay
  61: /// runs [`derive_layer_key_relay`] with reversed roles).
  62: pub fn derive_layer_key_sender(
  63:     sender_ephemeral_sk: &StaticSecret,
  64:     relay_static_pk: &PublicKey,
  65: ) -> LayerKey {
  66:     let shared = sender_ephemeral_sk.diffie_hellman(relay_static_pk);
  67:     let sender_ephemeral_pk = PublicKey::from(sender_ephemeral_sk);
  68:     finalize(shared, &sender_ephemeral_pk)
  69: }
  70: 
  71: /// Relay-side: derive this layer's AEAD key.
  72: ///
  73: /// `relay_static_sk` is the relay's long-term X25519 secret.
  74: /// `sender_ephemeral_pk` is the X25519 pubkey carried in this
  75: /// layer's packet header.
  76: pub fn derive_layer_key_relay(
  77:     relay_static_sk: &StaticSecret,
  78:     sender_ephemeral_pk: &PublicKey,
  79: ) -> LayerKey {
  80:     let shared = relay_static_sk.diffie_hellman(sender_ephemeral_pk);
  81:     finalize(shared, sender_ephemeral_pk)
  82: }
  83: 
  84: /// Check if a [`SharedSecret`]'s bytes are all-zero (small-order
  85: /// pubkey defense). Both `x25519-dalek` paths fold small-order
  86: /// inputs to zero, so this check catches them downstream.
  87: pub fn is_zero_shared(shared: &SharedSecret) -> bool {
  88:     shared.as_bytes().iter().all(|&b| b == 0)
  89: }
  90: 
  91: fn finalize(shared: SharedSecret, sender_ephemeral_pk: &PublicKey) -> LayerKey {
  92:     let mut h = Hasher::new();
  93:     h.update(PROTOCOL_DOMAIN);
  94:     h.update(b"-layer-key-v1");
  95:     h.update(shared.as_bytes());
  96:     h.update(sender_ephemeral_pk.as_bytes());
  97:     let digest = h.finalize();
  98:     let mut k = [0u8; LAYER_KEY_LEN];
  99:     k.copy_from_slice(digest.as_bytes());
 100:     let key = LayerKey::from_bytes(k);
 101:     // `shared` and `k` are zeroized on drop via dalek's Zeroize +
 102:     // our explicit array. Nothing else holds these bytes.
 103:     key
 104: }

   1: //! `ol_onion` — nested-AEAD onion circuits.
   2: //!
   3: //! Phase F3 / row 5 of the Coherence Mesh plan. Multi-hop privacy
   4: //! preserving message routing where each hop only knows its
   5: //! predecessor and successor.
   6: //!
   7: //! ## Design
   8: //!
   9: //! Nested ChaCha20-Poly1305 encryption with per-layer ephemeral
  10: //! X25519 keys. The sender wraps the destination payload in N
  11: //! layers, one per hop in the chosen circuit. Each relay decrypts
  12: //! exactly one layer using its long-term X25519 secret + the
  13: //! ephemeral X25519 public key carried in that layer's header.
  14: //!
  15: //! ## Threat model
  16: //!
  17: //! - Each relay is potentially malicious and curious.
  18: //! - Network attacker can drop, reorder, modify, inject packets.
  19: //! - Adversary cannot break X25519, BLAKE3, or ChaCha20-Poly1305.
  20: //! - Global passive adversary (sees all packet sizes + timing) is
  21: //!   addressed by:
  22: //!   1. Fixed-size packets — every onion packet is exactly
  23: //!      [`ONION_PACKET_SIZE`] bytes, so hop count does not leak.
  24: //!   2. Cover traffic (Phase F4 / row 6) — out of scope here.
  25: //!
  26: //! ## What this layer provides
  27: //!
  28: //! - **Layer confidentiality**: relay R_i cannot decrypt layers
  29: //!   intended for any other relay.
  30: //! - **Layer integrity**: any in-flight tamper is detected at the
  31: //!   next relay's AEAD verify step.
  32: //! - **Forward secrecy**: each circuit uses fresh ephemeral X25519
  33: //!   keys; compromise of a relay's long-term key reveals no past
  34: //!   traffic (the ephemeral material is zeroized after the relay
  35: //!   peels its layer).
  36: //! - **Hop blindness**: a relay cannot determine its position in
  37: //!   the circuit from packet contents (all layers look identical
  38: //!   on the wire after decryption + AEAD verification).
  39: //!
  40: //! ## What this layer does NOT provide
  41: //!
  42: //! - Timing-correlation resistance (the global passive adversary
  43: //!   can correlate ingress + egress timing). Cover traffic in row
  44: //!   6 addresses this.
  45: //! - Reply circuits — sender includes a return-path of its own
  46: //!   construction if a reply is expected. This crate is one-way
  47: //!   per packet; bidirectional flows wrap responses in their own
  48: //!   onions.
  49: //! - Replay defense for the destination — application layer
  50: //!   responsibility (the payload typically carries a nonce or
  51: //!   sequence number).
  52: //!
  53: //! ## Crate layout
  54: //!
  55: //! - [`hop`]: [`HopDescriptor`] + [`HopId`] types.
  56: //! - [`circuit`]: [`Circuit`] — ordered list of hops.
  57: //! - [`keyderiv`]: ECDH + BLAKE3 layer-key derivation.
  58: //! - [`packet`]: [`OnionPacket`] wire format and fixed-size canon
  59: //!   encoding.
  60: //! - [`build`]: sender-side onion construction.
  61: //! - [`peel`]: relay-side single-layer peel.
  62: //! - [`errors`]: typed error surface.
  63: //!
  64: //! ## End-to-end example
  65: //!
  66: //! ```
  67: //! use rand::rngs::OsRng;
  68: //! use x25519_dalek::{PublicKey, StaticSecret};
  69: //! use ol_onion::{
  70: //!     build_onion, peel_one_layer, Circuit, HopDescriptor, HopId,
  71: //!     OnionPacket, PeelOutcome, HOP_ID_LEN,
  72: //! };
  73: //!
  74: //! // Build two relays + a destination.
  75: //! let make = |i: u8| {
  76: //!     let sk = StaticSecret::from([i; 32]);
  77: //!     let pk = PublicKey::from(&sk);
  78: //!     (sk, HopDescriptor {
  79: //!         id: HopId::from_bytes([i; HOP_ID_LEN]),
  80: //!         pubkey: pk,
  81: //!     })
  82: //! };
  83: //! let (r1_sk, r1) = make(10);
  84: //! let (r2_sk, r2) = make(20);
  85: //! let (dest_sk, dest) = make(30);
  86: //!
  87: //! // Sender wraps a payload along [r1, r2, dest].
  88: //! let circuit = Circuit::new(vec![r1, r2.clone(), dest.clone()]).unwrap();
  89: //! let packet = build_onion(&circuit, b"hello", &mut OsRng).unwrap();
  90: //!
  91: //! // r1 peels its layer.
  92: //! let outcome = peel_one_layer(&r1_sk, &packet).unwrap();
  93: //! let inner_bytes = match outcome {
  94: //!     PeelOutcome::Forward { next_hop, inner_packet_bytes } => {
  95: //!         assert_eq!(next_hop, r2.id);
  96: //!         inner_packet_bytes
  97: //!     }
  98: //!     _ => panic!(),
  99: //! };
 100: //!
 101: //! // r2 peels its layer.
 102: //! let p = OnionPacket::decode(&inner_bytes).unwrap();
 103: //! let outcome = peel_one_layer(&r2_sk, &p).unwrap();
 104: //! let final_bytes = match outcome {
 105: //!     PeelOutcome::Forward { next_hop, inner_packet_bytes } => {
 106: //!         assert_eq!(next_hop, dest.id);
 107: //!         inner_packet_bytes
 108: //!     }
 109: //!     _ => panic!(),
 110: //! };
 111: //!
 112: //! // dest delivers.
 113: //! let p = OnionPacket::decode(&final_bytes).unwrap();
 114: //! let outcome = peel_one_layer(&dest_sk, &p).unwrap();
 115: //! match outcome {
 116: //!     PeelOutcome::Deliver { payload } => assert_eq!(payload, b"hello"),
 117: //!     _ => panic!(),
 118: //! }
 119: //! ```
