   1: """v0.12.0 — bandwidth pacing primitive (token bucket).
   2: 
   3: The Settings → Storage → Bandwidth limit dropdown stores a single
   4: integer (bandwidth_cap_kbps). The transfer engine's chunk send path
   5: calls `await pacer.pace(len(data))` BEFORE each send. When the cap
   6: is 0 (Unlimited) the call is a fast no-op; when the cap is > 0 the
   7: caller awaits until enough budget has refilled to cover the bytes.
   8: 
   9: Why a token bucket vs. a sleep-after-send: bucket smooths bursts.
  10: A 100ms-window cap that fires sleep(remaining_window) after each
  11: send produces sawtooth throughput; a token bucket produces a
  12: plateau. Same average rate, much friendlier to the receiver's
  13: write-side flow control.
  14: 
  15: The bucket is global (combined send + receive) so the cap describes
  16: *One Link's footprint on this machine's link*, not per-direction.
  17: A future refinement could split into separate up/down buckets but
  18: the headline UX promise is "this app uses at most X MB/s" — single
  19: bucket matches that.
  20: 
  21: The pacer is process-local — no IPC or shared memory across
  22: daemons. Multiple daemons on the same box will each get their own
  23: budget. That's fine: the cap is per-instance.
  24: 
  25: Thread/async note: the bucket uses an asyncio.Lock so concurrent
  26: .pace() calls serialize through the budget calculation. Each call
  27: holds the lock for ~µs (just arithmetic + maybe one sleep
  28: schedule); under heavy parallelism the lock is not a hot point.
  29: """
  30: 
  31: from __future__ import annotations
  32: 
  33: import asyncio
  34: import time
  35: from dataclasses import dataclass
  36: from typing import Optional
  37: 
  38: 
  39: @dataclass
  40: class _State:
  41:     """Token-bucket internals. Capacity = burst tolerance =
  42:     cap_bytes_per_second × BURST_SECONDS. Tokens refill linearly."""
  43:     cap_bytes_per_second: float
  44:     capacity_bytes: float
  45:     tokens: float
  46:     last_refill_ts: float
  47: 
  48: 
  49: # 0.5s of burst headroom. Big enough that small chunks pass without
  50: # scheduling overhead; small enough that the average rate stays
  51: # close to the cap on long sustained transfers.
  52: BURST_SECONDS = 0.5
  53: 
  54: # Minimum sleep to avoid burning CPU on tiny waits. asyncio
  55: # scheduling itself costs ~0.1ms; sleeping less than that gains
  56: # nothing.
  57: MIN_SLEEP_SECONDS = 0.001
  58: 
  59: 
  60: class BandwidthPacer:
  61:     """Awaitable token bucket for global bandwidth pacing.
  62: 
  63:     Pace before every chunk send::
  64: 
  65:         await pacer.pace(len(payload))
  66:         await channel.send(encode_msg(chunk_msg))
  67: 
  68:     The pacer auto-no-ops when set_cap(0) is in effect, so call
  69:     sites don't need to branch on whether the user has a cap set.
  70:     """
  71: 
  72:     def __init__(self, *, cap_kbps: int = 0) -> None:
  73:         self._lock = asyncio.Lock()
  74:         self._state: Optional[_State] = None
  75:         self.set_cap(cap_kbps)
  76: 
  77:     @property
  78:     def cap_kbps(self) -> int:
  79:         s = self._state
  80:         if s is None:
  81:             return 0
  82:         return int(s.cap_bytes_per_second * 8 / 1024)
  83: 
  84:     @property
  85:     def is_unlimited(self) -> bool:
  86:         return self._state is None
  87: 
  88:     def set_cap(self, cap_kbps: int) -> None:
  89:         """Update the cap live. Pass 0 / negative to disable.
  90: 
  91:         Existing in-flight sends drain through whatever budget is
  92:         still in the bucket; new sends pace against the new cap.
  93:         Cheap, idempotent."""
  94:         if cap_kbps is None or cap_kbps <= 0:
  95:             self._state = None
  96:             return
  97:         bytes_per_sec = float(cap_kbps) * 1024 / 8
  98:         capacity = bytes_per_sec * BURST_SECONDS
  99:         prev = self._state
 100:         if prev is None:
 101:             tokens = capacity
 102:         else:
 103:             # Carry over remaining tokens but never exceed the new
 104:             # capacity (a downsize shouldn't grant a free burst).
 105:             tokens = min(prev.tokens, capacity)
 106:         self._state = _State(
 107:             cap_bytes_per_second=bytes_per_sec,
 108:             capacity_bytes=capacity,
 109:             tokens=tokens,
 110:             last_refill_ts=time.monotonic(),
 111:         )
 112: 
 113:     async def pace(self, n_bytes: int) -> None:
 114:         """Reserve n_bytes of budget; await if not yet available.
 115: 
 116:         Idempotent on n_bytes <= 0 (returns immediately). When the
 117:         pacer is unlimited, returns immediately without acquiring
 118:         the lock — the hot path stays cheap."""
 119:         if self.is_unlimited or n_bytes <= 0:
 120:             return
 121:         async with self._lock:
 122:             s = self._state
 123:             if s is None:
 124:                 return
 125:             await self._reserve_locked(s, n_bytes)
 126: 
 127:     async def _reserve_locked(self, s: _State, n_bytes: int) -> None:
 128:         # Refill based on elapsed wall time.
 129:         now = time.monotonic()
 130:         elapsed = max(0.0, now - s.last_refill_ts)
 131:         s.tokens = min(s.capacity_bytes, s.tokens + elapsed * s.cap_bytes_per_second)
 132:         s.last_refill_ts = now
 133:         if n_bytes <= s.tokens:
 134:             s.tokens -= n_bytes
 135:             return
 136:         # Need to wait. If n_bytes exceeds capacity (a single chunk
 137:         # bigger than the bucket), drain to zero then sleep enough
 138:         # to cover the overflow at the cap rate.
 139:         deficit = n_bytes - s.tokens
 140:         wait = deficit / s.cap_bytes_per_second
 141:         if wait < MIN_SLEEP_SECONDS:
 142:             wait = MIN_SLEEP_SECONDS
 143:         # Optimistically debit the full request now and sleep; this
 144:         # keeps the bucket math identity-preserving across awaits.
 145:         s.tokens = 0.0
 146:         # Release the lock during sleep so other paces can queue
 147:         # (they'll see tokens=0 and add to the wait line correctly).
 148:         # asyncio.Lock is reentrant via async-with, so we drop it
 149:         # explicitly.
 150:         # NOTE: we DO want serialization on the math; only the
 151:         # sleep itself runs unlocked.
 152:         await self._sleep_outside_lock(wait, s)
 153: 
 154:     async def _sleep_outside_lock(self, wait: float, s: _State) -> None:
 155:         # Subtle: we're already inside `async with self._lock`. To
 156:         # release for the sleep, we have to exit the context. Easier
 157:         # pattern: schedule the sleep then re-enter to update
 158:         # last_refill_ts. We approximate by NOT actually releasing
 159:         # the lock — the next caller will queue on the lock and
 160:         # then refill against the post-sleep clock, which yields
 161:         # correct serialized behavior.
 162:         await asyncio.sleep(wait)
 163:         s.last_refill_ts = time.monotonic()
<<<CONTENT_END>>>

   4: Per COHERENCE_MESH_PLAN.md Phase F2 — in-person pair-by-QR trust

   6: chain key by exchanging an Ed25519-signed QR code + a network
   7: response, then comparing a short authentication string (SAS) out
   8: of band. No third-party server is trusted at any point.
   9:

 259: def render_invite_qr_svg(

 266:     """Render an Invite payload as a scannable QR code SVG.
 267: 
 268:     Uses QR binary (byte) mode for compactness — INVITE_MAX_BYTES

 270:     level M, leaving headroom for the rendered SVG to remain
 271:     phone-camera-readable at typical screen sizes.

 280:                         "Q" (~25%), "H" (~30%).

 282:     Returns: SVG document as UTF-8 bytes ready to write to disk or
 283:     serve directly from an HTTP response.

 288:         import qrcode.image.svg  # type: ignore[import-untyped]

 309:             f"INVITE_MAX_BYTES={INVITE_MAX_BYTES}"
 310:         )

 313:         border=border,
 314:         box_size=box_size,

   1: """Pairing: 8-digit SAS (Short Authentication String) for trust-on-first-use.
   2: 
   3: The user-facing flow:
   4:   1. User clicks Pair on a discovered peer.
   5:   2. Both daemons display the same 8-digit code, derived from BOTH peers'
   6:      long-term Ed25519 public keys AND the encrypted-channel handshake
   7:      transcript hash (a fresh per-session value bound to both sides'
   8:      ephemerals + signatures).
   9:   3. User on each side compares the codes verbally / visually and clicks
  10:      "Match" or "Mismatch."
  11:   4. When both sides confirm Match, both peers auto-pin each other.
  12:      A code mismatch means a man-in-the-middle is intercepting the LAN —
  13:      the user rejects.
  14: 
  15: After successful pairing, the peer is `pinned` permanently. Subsequent
  16: launches reconnect silently with no UI prompts (the magic feel).
  17: 
  18: The SAS is derived as (v2, v0.20.7+):
  19:     h = BLAKE3(transcript_hash || sorted_concat(pubkey_a, pubkey_b) || "OL-SAS-v2")
  20:     sas = (first 5 bytes of h, big-endian) mod 100_000_000
  21: 
  22: Why the bump (security audit H11):
  23: 
  24:   v1 was a static function of the long-term pubkeys only — exactly
  25:   20 bits of entropy (`% 1_000_000`). A LAN-active MITM grinding
  26:   ~1M Ed25519 keypairs (under a minute on commodity hardware) could
  27:   find a key whose v1 SAS-with-Alice matched a chosen target value;
  28:   with offline grinding both sides of a two-sided substitution
  29:   became feasible.
  30: 
  31:   v2 folds in the encrypted channel's transcript_hash — fresh per
  32:   session, bound to both peers' ephemerals + signatures — so an
  33:   attacker can no longer pre-compute a colliding key. They have to
  34:   grind during the live pair window, against a code that's also
  35:   longer (8 digits ≈ 26.6 bits, so ~100M Ed25519 ops per single
  36:   collision instead of ~1M). 5-minute pairing TTL caps the live
  37:   grind window. Birthday bound on 8 digits is comfortable for the
  38:   trust ceremony.
  39: 
  40: Sorting the inputs ensures both sides compute the same value
  41: regardless of who initiated. Both sides have the SAME transcript_hash
  42: because the channel-handshake transcript is mirror-identical on
  43: either end of the same TCP connection (audit fix #10 verified).
  44: 
  45: Backward compatibility (v1 fallback):
  46: 
  47:   If a caller invokes compute_sas without a transcript_hash (e.g. a
  48:   pre-v0.20.7 peer that doesn't carry one through), the function
  49:   falls back to the legacy 6-digit v1 SAS so the existing pair-flow
  50:   doesn't break in the upgrade window. New users always get v2.
  51: """
  52: 
  53: from __future__ import annotations
  54: 
  55: import time
  56: from collections import OrderedDict
  57: from dataclasses import dataclass, field
  58: from enum import Enum
  59: from typing import Optional
  60: 
  61: import blake3
  62: 
  63: 
  64: _SAS_INFO_V1 = b"OL-SAS-v1"
  65: _SAS_INFO_V2 = b"OL-SAS-v2"
  66: 
  67: # v0.20.7 (security audit H12): pair contexts auto-expire after 5
  68: # minutes. Without this, a stale "Match" prompt that the user
  69: # ignored at 10:00 stays armed forever; an attacker positioned
  70: # later can ride the still-armed ctx into a confirm. The TTL is
  71: # enforced at the daemon layer where the user-facing PAIR_REQUEST
  72: # / PAIR_CONFIRM handlers live; the helper here exposes is_expired().
  73: PAIR_CONTEXT_TTL_MS = 5 * 60 * 1000
  74: 
  75: # v0.20.7 (security audit M19): PairingTracker hard-cap. A LAN
  76: # attacker who hops MAC / short_ids can otherwise grow the in-memory
  77: # tracker without bound. 256 is generous (typical user has < 10
  78: # devices); on overflow we evict the oldest insertion.
  79: MAX_PAIR_CONTEXTS = 256
  80: 
  81: 
  82: def compute_sas(
  83:     my_pubkey: bytes,
  84:     peer_pubkey: bytes,
  85:     *,
  86:     transcript_hash: Optional[bytes] = None,
  87: ) -> str:
  88:     """Same code on both sides for the same channel handshake.
  89: 
  90:     With transcript_hash (v2): 8-digit code bound to the encrypted
  91:     channel transcript so offline grinding cannot pre-compute a
  92:     colliding key. With transcript_hash=None (v1 legacy): 6-digit
  93:     code from pubkeys only, kept solely for compatibility with
  94:     pre-v0.20.7 peers that did not carry the transcript through to
  95:     the SAS-display call site.
  96:     """
  97:     if len(my_pubkey) != 32 or len(peer_pubkey) != 32:
  98:         raise ValueError("pubkeys must be 32 bytes (Ed25519 raw)")
  99:     pair = sorted([my_pubkey, peer_pubkey])
 100:     if transcript_hash:
 101:         h = blake3.blake3(
 102:             bytes(transcript_hash) + pair[0] + pair[1] + _SAS_INFO_V2
 103:         ).digest()
 104:         n = int.from_bytes(h[:5], "big") % 100_000_000
 105:         return f"{n:08d}"
 106:     # Legacy fallback.
 107:     h = blake3.blake3(pair[0] + pair[1] + _SAS_INFO_V1).digest()
 108:     n = int.from_bytes(h[:4], "big") % 1_000_000
 109:     return f"{n:06d}"
 110: 
 111: 
 112: def format_sas(sas: str) -> str:
 113:     """Display form: '12 345 678' for v2 (8 digits) or '123 456' for v1.
 114:     Picking 3-digit groups for v2 keeps it easy to read aloud."""
 115:     if len(sas) == 8:
 116:         return f"{sas[:2]} {sas[2:5]} {sas[5:]}"
 117:     s = sas.zfill(6)
 118:     return f"{s[:3]} {s[3:]}"

 120: 
 121: class PairState(str, Enum):
 122:     NONE = "none"            # never tried
 123:     REQUESTED = "requested"  # we sent PAIR_REQUEST, awaiting peer's confirm
 124:     INCOMING = "incoming"    # peer sent us PAIR_REQUEST, we haven't decided
 125:     CONFIRMED = "confirmed"  # we said yes; awaiting peer's yes
 126:     PAIRED = "paired"        # both sides confirmed → trust='pinned' set
 127:     REJECTED = "rejected"    # user rejected the SAS — possible MITM

 130: @dataclass
 131: class PairContext:
 132:     peer_fp: str
 133:     sas: str
 134:     state: PairState = PairState.NONE
 135:     started_ms: int = field(default_factory=lambda: int(time.time() * 1000))
 136:     we_confirmed: bool = False
 137:     they_confirmed: bool = False
 138:     # v0.20.7 (security audit M20): set when the per-peer trust state
 139:     # at the moment we begin a fresh pair attempt was already
 140:     # `rejected`. The daemon surfaces this in the WS pair_request
 141:     # event so the UI can show a "previously blocked" warning before
 142:     # the user clicks Match — closes the social-engineering re-pair
 143:     # path where an attacker who was previously blocked simply asks
 144:     # the user to re-add them and the trust=rejected → pinned flip
 145:     # was silent.

 147:     # v0.20.7 (security audit H12): explicit TTL on the context so
 148:     # the daemon can reject stale "Match" prompts.
 149:     ttl_ms: int = field(default=PAIR_CONTEXT_TTL_MS)
 150: 
 151:     @property
 152:     def both_confirmed(self) -> bool:
 153:         return self.we_confirmed and self.they_confirmed
 154: 
 155:     def is_expired(self, *, now_ms: Optional[int] = None) -> bool:
 156:         cutoff = (now_ms if now_ms is not None else int(time.time() * 1000))
 157:         return cutoff - self.started_ms > self.ttl_ms
 158: 
 159: 
 160: class PairingTracker:
 161:     """In-memory pairing-attempt tracker. Persists nothing; trust state is
 162:     persisted via state.set_peer_trust('pinned') once both sides confirm.
 163: 
 164:     v0.20.7 (security audit M19): bounded at MAX_PAIR_CONTEXTS via
 165:     insertion-order LRU. Backed by OrderedDict so an oldest-first
 166:     eviction is O(1). Expired contexts are evicted lazily on read
 167:     (get / we_confirm / they_confirm) to keep an attacker who hops
 168:     short_ids from indefinitely growing the dict."""
 169: 
 170:     def __init__(self) -> None:
 171:         self._by_peer: "OrderedDict[str, PairContext]" = OrderedDict()
 172: 
 173:     def _maybe_evict_expired(self, peer_fp: str) -> None:
 174:         ctx = self._by_peer.get(peer_fp)
 175:         if ctx is not None and ctx.is_expired():
 176:             self._by_peer.pop(peer_fp, None)
 177: 
 178:     def get(self, peer_fp: str) -> Optional[PairContext]:
 179:         self._maybe_evict_expired(peer_fp)
 180:         return self._by_peer.get(peer_fp)
 181: 
 182:     def begin(
 183:         self,
 184:         *,
 185:         peer_fp: str,
 186:         sas: str,
 187:         incoming: bool,
 188:         previously_rejected: bool = False,
 189:     ) -> PairContext:
 190:         ctx = PairContext(
 191:             peer_fp=peer_fp,
 192:             sas=sas,
 193:             state=PairState.INCOMING if incoming else PairState.REQUESTED,
 194:             previously_rejected=previously_rejected,
 195:         )
 196:         # Replace any stale ctx for this peer in-place; touch insertion
 197:         # order so the new entry is youngest.
 198:         self._by_peer.pop(peer_fp, None)
 199:         self._by_peer[peer_fp] = ctx
 200:         # v0.20.7 (security audit M19): hard cap. On overflow drop the
 201:         # oldest entry. begin() being the only insertion point means
 202:         # we can enforce here without scanning.
 203:         while len(self._by_peer) > MAX_PAIR_CONTEXTS:
 204:             self._by_peer.popitem(last=False)
 205:         return ctx
 206: 
 207:     def we_confirm(self, peer_fp: str) -> Optional[PairContext]:
 208:         self._maybe_evict_expired(peer_fp)
 209:         ctx = self._by_peer.get(peer_fp)
 210:         if not ctx:
 211:             return None
 212:         ctx.we_confirmed = True
 213:         if ctx.both_confirmed:
 214:             ctx.state = PairState.PAIRED
 215:         else:
 216:             ctx.state = PairState.CONFIRMED
 217:         return ctx
 218: 
 219:     def they_confirm(self, peer_fp: str) -> Optional[PairContext]:
 220:         self._maybe_evict_expired(peer_fp)
 221:         ctx = self._by_peer.get(peer_fp)
 222:         if not ctx:
 223:             return None
 224:         ctx.they_confirmed = True
 225:         if ctx.both_confirmed:
 226:             ctx.state = PairState.PAIRED
 227:         return ctx
 228: 
 229:     def reject(self, peer_fp: str) -> Optional[PairContext]:
 230:         ctx = self._by_peer.get(peer_fp)
 231:         if ctx:
 232:             ctx.state = PairState.REJECTED
 233:         return ctx
 234: 
 235:     def clear(self, peer_fp: str) -> None:
 236:         self._by_peer.pop(peer_fp, None)
 237: 
 238:     def all(self) -> list[PairContext]:
 239:         return list(self._by_peer.values())

   1: """Path-PII protection for the daemon's at-rest indexes.
   2: 
   3: Audit M30 (2026-05-09): the desktop daemon stores fully-qualified
   4: filesystem paths in two indexed columns:
   5: 
   6:   - ``chunk_sources.path`` — used to hydrate cache misses by reading
   7:     bytes from a known location on disk
   8:   - ``file_index_cache.path`` — used to look up a previously-computed
   9:     chunk manifest for the same source file
  10: 
  11: These paths reveal the user's home-dir layout (e.g.
  12: ``/Users/Alex/Documents/Confidential/...``) to a T4 (lost device)
  13: attacker who has unlocked at-rest access. The audit's recommended
  14: fix was to hash the path or store basename + folder-root reference.
  15: 
  16: The trouble with both naïve fixes:
  17: 
  18:   - **Hash-only**: kills the path → bytes lookup. We need to actually
  19:     open the file at that path to serve a chunk; an opaque hash
  20:     can't do that.
  21: 
  22:   - **Basename + root reference**: requires schema redesign, restricts
  23:     every path to be under a known synced folder, breaks the
  24:     ad-hoc-send case where any file on disk can be a chunk source.
  25: 
  26: Outside-the-box fix: **deterministic authenticated encryption** with
  27: AES-SIV (RFC 5297). Same plaintext path → same ciphertext (so
  28: indexes work + lookup is fast), but the ciphertext is opaque to
  29: anyone without the seed-derived key. Authenticated, so a flipped
  30: byte invalidates the tag.
  31: 
  32: Why AES-SIV and not AES-GCM?
  33: 
  34: AES-GCM with a fixed nonce is broken (catastrophic key recovery
  35: after two collisions). AES-GCM with a random nonce is non-
  36: deterministic, which kills our index. AES-SIV is purpose-built for
  37: deterministic AEAD: it derives a synthetic IV from the plaintext +
  38: AAD via a CMAC-like construction, so the same input deterministically
  39: produces the same output, but the IV remains effectively random for
  40: distinct inputs. RFC 5297 + Hoang et al. 2017 prove the security
  41: bound: the only structural attack is "same plaintext under same key
  42: produces same ciphertext" — which is exactly what we want for
  43: indexing.
  44: 
  45: Wire format
  46: -----------
  47: 
  48: Encrypted paths are written as ASCII strings prefixed with
  49: ``~OL1~`` (tilde-bracketed marker that real filesystem paths never
  50: start with, on either Windows or POSIX). The body is the urlsafe-
  51: base64 of the AES-SIV synthetic-IV-prefixed ciphertext.
  52: 
  53: Reads detect the marker and decrypt; absent the marker, they treat
  54: the value as legacy cleartext so old rows remain accessible. New
  55: writes always go through encryption when a key is available.
  56: 
  57: Backward compat — what happens without a master seed?
  58: -----------------------------------------------------
  59: 
  60: The encryptor is only constructed when the daemon has a seed (the
  61: v0.20.7 master-seed flow). Daemons without a seed (legacy installs
  62: that never ran ``backup init`` or ``backup restore``) keep storing
  63: cleartext paths. The audit threat is T4 + at-rest unlock; for a
  64: seed-less install there's no recoverable secret to derive a key
  65: from anyway, so cleartext is no worse than the prior posture.
  66: """
  67: from __future__ import annotations
  68: 
  69: import base64
  70: from typing import Optional
  71: 
  72: from cryptography.hazmat.primitives import hashes
  73: from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.ciphers.aead import AESSIV
  74: from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.kdf.hkdf import HKDF
  75: 
  76: 
  77: PATH_PII_MARKER = "~OL1~"
  78: # AES-SIV with a 64-byte key (two 32-byte AES halves internally).
  79: PATH_PII_KEY_LEN = 64
  80: # HKDF info string for the path-PII key. Distinct from every other
  81: # subkey derived from the master seed so a leak of the path-PII key
  82: # doesn't compromise the DRK / identity / backup keys.
  83: _INFO_PATH_PII = b"OL/master/path-pii-aes-siv|v1"
  84: 
  85: 
  86: def derive_path_pii_key(seed: bytes) -> bytes:
  87:     """Derive a 64-byte AES-SIV key from the 32-byte master seed.
  88: 
  89:     The path-PII key is a separate domain from every other derived
  90:     key. If it's ever compromised, the worst case is "attacker can
  91:     decrypt path columns for this install." It cannot be used to
  92:     decrypt chat content, identity-sign, or unwrap the backup key."""
  93:     if len(seed) != 32:
  94:         raise ValueError("master seed must be 32 bytes")
  95:     return HKDF(
  96:         algorithm=hashes.SHA256(),
  97:         length=PATH_PII_KEY_LEN,
  98:         salt=None,
  99:         info=_INFO_PATH_PII,
 100:     ).derive(bytes(seed))
 101: 
 102: 
 103: class PathPIIEncryptor:
 104:     """Deterministic AEAD wrapper for filesystem-path columns.
 105: 
 106:     Construct once at daemon startup with the master seed. Pass to
 107:     ``State.set_path_pii_encryptor`` so chunk_sources / file_index_cache
 108:     reads + writes go through ``wrap`` / ``unwrap``.
 109: 
 110:     Same plaintext + AAD → same ciphertext (the property we need so
 111:     SQLite's PRIMARY KEY + UNIQUE indexes still de-duplicate on the
 112:     canonical path). Different plaintext or different AAD → different
 113:     ciphertext. RFC 5297 Sec 6 proves the security bound.
 114:     """
 115: 
 116:     def __init__(self, seed: bytes):
 117:         self._key = derive_path_pii_key(seed)
 118:         self._aead = AESSIV(self._key)
 119: 
 120:     def wrap(self, path: str, *, aad: bytes = b"") -> str:
 121:         """Encrypt a path string; return the marker-prefixed
 122:         urlsafe-base64 ciphertext. Empty input yields empty output
 123:         (callers that want NULL semantics keep storing NULL)."""
 124:         if not path:
 125:             return ""
 126:         plaintext = path.encode("utf-8", errors="strict")
 127:         # AESSIV.encrypt takes a list of associated-data items.
 128:         # We use one: a domain-separation tag bound to the column
 129:         # (caller-supplied) so the same path encrypted under a
 130:         # different AAD produces different ciphertext — keeps
 131:         # chunk_sources rows from accidentally matching
 132:         # file_index_cache rows on the same path string.
 133:         ct = self._aead.encrypt(plaintext, [aad])
 134:         body = base64.urlsafe_b64encode(ct).rstrip(b"=").decode("ascii")
 135:         return PATH_PII_MARKER + body
 136: 
 137:     def unwrap(self, value: str, *, aad: bytes = b"") -> Optional[str]:
 138:         """Decrypt a wrapped path. Legacy cleartext (no marker) is
 139:         returned unchanged. Returns None if the value is wrapped but
 140:         decryption fails (tamper / wrong key / different install).
 141: 
 142:         The legacy-cleartext passthrough is the rolling-upgrade hatch:
 143:         rows written before this module was wired in stay readable
 144:         until they're rewritten via the normal write path."""
 145:         if not value:
 146:             return value
 147:         if not value.startswith(PATH_PII_MARKER):
 148:             # Legacy cleartext path — return as-is.
 149:             return value
 150:         body = value[len(PATH_PII_MARKER):]
 151:         try:
 152:             pad = "=" * ((4 - len(body) % 4) % 4)
 153:             ct = base64.urlsafe_b64decode((body + pad).encode("ascii"))
 154:             plaintext = self._aead.decrypt(ct, [aad])
 155:             return plaintext.decode("utf-8", errors="strict")
 156:         except Exception:
 157:             return None
 158: 
 159: 
 160: def is_wrapped(value: str) -> bool:
 161:     """True iff ``value`` is a wrapped (marker-prefixed) path."""
 162:     return isinstance(value, str) and value.startswith(PATH_PII_MARKER)
<<<CONTENT_END>>>

   1: from __future__ import annotations

   3: import os
   4: from pathlib import Path
   5: 
   6: from platformdirs import user_config_dir, user_data_dir
   7: 
   8: APP = "One_link"
   9: AUTHOR = "Coherence"
  10: 
  11: # ONE_LINK_HOME overrides both config and data dirs. Useful for running
  12: # multiple daemons on one machine (smoke testing) and for portable installs.
  13: HOME_ENV = "ONE_LINK_HOME"
  14: 
  15: 
  16: def _home_override() -> Path | None:
  17:     """Resolve ONE_LINK_HOME if set, after sanitization.
  18: 
  19:     v0.20.7 (security audit M28): the previous implementation did
  20:     Path(env_value).expanduser() with no validation, which let an
  21:     attacker (or a stale setup script) point One Link at any path
  22:     they liked — including ``/etc``, ``$HOME/../other-user``, or a
  23:     UNC share on Windows. A daemon running with elevated
  24:     privileges (sudo, installer, CI runner) would then mkdir
  25:     config / data subdirs at the attacker's chosen location.
  26: 
  27:     The hardening:
  28:       - Reject empty / whitespace-only values.
  29:       - Reject any path component equal to ".." (no traversal).
  30:       - Reject UNC paths on Windows (``\\\\server\\share``) — those
  31:         route storage onto a network share, which is generally not
  32:         what a multi-daemon-on-one-machine override is for.
  33:       - Require absolute paths after expanduser/resolve to fail
  34:         loudly on relative-path env injection.
  35:       - Refuse to write under a parent directory that the current
  36:         process does NOT own (POSIX only — the typical attack is
  37:         ``sudo one-link daemon`` with ONE_LINK_HOME=/etc/something,
  38:         where the operator's intent was a user-scoped install but
  39:         the elevated daemon now writes config under root-owned
  40:         directories where they'll be unrecoverable without sudo).
  41:     On rejection we log a clear warning and fall through to the
  42:     default platform dirs.
  43:     """
  44:     v = os.environ.get(HOME_ENV)
  45:     if v is None:
  46:         return None
  47:     raw = v.strip()
  48:     if not raw:
  49:         return None
  50:     # No traversal segments — even after expanduser/resolve, ".."
  51:     # in the original env value signals an attempt to break out of
  52:     # whatever the operator thought the override would be.
  53:     if ".." in raw.replace("\\", "/").split("/"):
  54:         import logging
  55:         logging.getLogger("one_link.paths").warning(
  56:             "ONE_LINK_HOME contains '..' (rejected): %r — falling "
  57:             "back to platform default",
  58:             v,
  59:         )
  60:         return None
  61:     # UNC on Windows: //server/share or \\server\share. Reject.
  62:     if os.name == "nt":
  63:         normalized = raw.replace("\\", "/")
  64:         if normalized.startswith("//"):
  65:             import logging
  66:             logging.getLogger("one_link.paths").warning(
  67:                 "ONE_LINK_HOME is a UNC path (rejected): %r — "
  68:                 "falling back to platform default",
  69:                 v,
  70:             )
  71:             return None
  72:     try:
  73:         p = Path(raw).expanduser()
  74:         # Resolve to an absolute path; fail if the value still
  75:         # comes out relative (which can happen on a tmp-cwd layout
  76:         # we don't control).
  77:         if not p.is_absolute():
  78:             try:
  79:                 p = p.resolve()
  80:             except OSError:
  81:                 pass
  82:         if not p.is_absolute():
  83:             import logging
  84:             logging.getLogger("one_link.paths").warning(
  85:                 "ONE_LINK_HOME is not an absolute path (rejected): "
  86:                 "%r — falling back to platform default",
  87:                 v,
  88:             )
  89:             return None
  90:         # Parent-ownership check (POSIX). Walk upward to the deepest
  91:         # existing ancestor and confirm it belongs to our euid. On
  92:         # Windows, the analogous primitive is much messier (SID
  93:         # comparison via win32security) and the typical sudo-attack
  94:         # vector doesn't exist there; we skip the check and rely on
  95:         # ACLs at the per-file write paths instead.
  96:         if os.name != "nt":
  97:             ancestor = p
  98:             while not ancestor.exists() and ancestor != ancestor.parent:
  99:                 ancestor = ancestor.parent
 100:             try:
 101:                 st = ancestor.stat()
 102:                 euid = os.geteuid()  # type: ignore[attr-defined]
 103:                 if st.st_uid != euid:
 104:                     import logging
 105:                     logging.getLogger("one_link.paths").warning(
 106:                         "ONE_LINK_HOME parent %s is owned by uid=%d "
 107:                         "(daemon euid=%d) — rejected to avoid clobbering "
 108:                         "another user's data; fix the path or rerun "
 109:                         "without sudo",
 110:                         ancestor, st.st_uid, euid,
 111:                     )
 112:                     return None
 113:             except OSError:
 114:                 # Stat failed — likely a permission issue under elevated
 115:                 # contexts. Be conservative: refuse rather than write
 116:                 # into something we can't even introspect.
 117:                 import logging
 118:                 logging.getLogger("one_link.paths").warning(
 119:                     "ONE_LINK_HOME ancestor %s could not be stat'd — "
 120:                     "falling back to platform default",
 121:                     ancestor,
 122:                 )
 123:                 return None
 124:         return p
 125:     except (ValueError, OSError) as e:
 126:         import logging
 127:         logging.getLogger("one_link.paths").warning(
 128:             "ONE_LINK_HOME unparseable (%s): %r — falling back to "
 129:             "platform default",
 130:             e, v,
 131:         )
 132:         return None
 133:

   1: """v0.20.4 — Self-signed HTTPS for the daemon.
   2: 
   3: Why this ship exists
   4: ====================
   5: 
   6: iOS Safari (and most modern browsers) gate Web Crypto Subtle to
   7: "secure contexts" — HTTPS or `localhost`. A phone connecting to
   8: the desktop daemon over `http://192.168.1.42:7117` fails to do
   9: ANY Web Crypto operation: `crypto.subtle.generateKey({name:
  10: "Ed25519"})` either rejects, throws, or returns undefined.
  11: 
  12: The browser-as-peer architecture (v0.16-v0.20.3) needs Web Crypto
  13: on the phone for: identity generation, signature verification,
  14: SAS pairing, all of it. Without HTTPS, the entire arc is unusable
  15: on iOS Safari over LAN.
  16: 
  17: This module solves it by minting a self-signed certificate on the
  18: daemon, persisting it to data_dir, and serving an HTTPS listener
  19: on a parallel port. The phone gets a "Not Private" warning the
  20: first time it scans the pair QR; the user taps "Continue" once
  21: per device, and from then on Web Crypto works and the pair flow
  22: actually completes.
  23: 
  24: Cert design
  25: ===========
  26: 
  27: - Algorithm: ECDSA P-256. RSA-2048 also works but produces
  28:   larger certs; Ed25519 is rejected by some browsers (Safari) for
  29:   TLS server certs as of 2026. P-256 is the universal sweet spot.
  30: - Validity: 365 days, auto-rotated when within 30 days of expiry.
  31: - Common Name: "One Link Self-Signed"
  32: - Subject Alternative Names: covers every interface the daemon
  33:   might reach the phone on:
  34:       DNS: localhost, *.local, onelink.local
  35:       IP:  127.0.0.1, ::1, plus any LAN IPv4/IPv6 we can detect
  36: - Persisted to:
  37:       <data_dir>/peer_https/cert.pem
  38:       <data_dir>/peer_https/key.pem
  39:   Both 0o600. Regenerated if missing or expired.
  40: 
  41: What this ship does NOT yet do
  42: ==============================
  43: 
  44: - Cert pinning on the phone side. v0.20.4 just relies on the
  45:   user accepting the "Not Private" warning once. A future ship
  46:   could pin the SHA-256 of the cert in the QR (so the phone can
  47:   verify "this is the SAME cert my laptop minted") — that closes
  48:   the residual MITM window during the cert-trust ceremony.
  49: - mDNS broadcasting of `onelink.local`. We include `onelink.local`
  50:   in the SAN so a future mDNS-enabled daemon can use it without
  51:   cert regen, but we don't actually broadcast it yet.
  52: """

  95: def _detect_lan_addresses() -> list[str]:
  96:     """Best-effort enumeration of every IPv4 + IPv6 address the
  97:     daemon might be reached on. Used to populate SAN entries on
  98:     the cert so the phone doesn't trip a hostname-mismatch."""
  99:     out: set[str] = set()
 100:     out.add("127.0.0.1")
 101:     out.add("::1")
 102:     # Egress-interface IPv4 — the LAN address other devices on the
 103:     # same Wi-Fi will reach us on.
 104:     s = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_DGRAM)
 105:     try:
 106:         s.connect(("8.8.8.8", 80))
 107:         out.add(s.getsockname()[0])
 108:     except Exception:
 109:         pass
 110:     finally:
 111:         s.close()
 112:     # All IPv4 addresses bound to this host.
 113:     try:
 114:         hostname = socket.gethostname()
 115:         _, _, addrs = socket.gethostbyname_ex(hostname)
 116:         for a in addrs:
 117:             out.add(a)
 118:     except Exception:
 119:         pass
 120:     return sorted(out)

 122: 
 123: def _build_subject_alt_names(
 124:     extra_dns: list[str] | None = None,
 125:     *,
 126:     short_id: str = "",
 127: ) -> x509.SubjectAlternativeName:
 128:     """Build the SAN extension. We include every IP we can detect +
 129:     a fixed set of useful DNS names so the cert is valid against
 130:     common access paths.
 131: 
 132:     v0.20.7 (security audit M12): also include a per-daemon
 133:     DNSName ``<short_id>.onelink.local`` so a phone with two
 134:     different One Link daemons in its trust store (e.g. laptop
 135:     + work-machine) can disambiguate which one it's connecting
 136:     to without relying purely on TOFU."""
 137:     names: list[x509.GeneralName] = []
 138:     base_dns = ["localhost", "onelink.local"]
 139:     if short_id:
 140:         base_dns.append(f"{short_id}.onelink.local")
 141:     for dn in base_dns + (extra_dns or []):
 142:         names.append(x509.DNSName(dn))
 143:     for ip_str in _detect_lan_addresses():
 144:         try:
 145:             ip = ipaddress.ip_address(ip_str)
 146:             names.append(x509.IPAddress(ip))
 147:         except ValueError:
 148:             continue
 149:     return x509.SubjectAlternativeName(names)

 152: def generate_self_signed(
 153:     base: Path,
 154:     *,
 155:     valid_days: int = CERT_VALID_DAYS,
 156:     short_id: str = "",
 157: ) -> tuple[Path, Path]:
 158:     """Mint a fresh ECDSA-P256 self-signed cert + key. Persists both
 159:     to <base>/peer_https/{cert.pem,key.pem} with 0o600 perms.
 160: 
 161:     Returns (cert_path, key_path). Idempotent — call as many times
 162:     as you want; each call writes a fresh cert.
 163: 
 164:     v0.20.7 (security audit M12): the cert subject now includes
 165:     a per-daemon Common Name (``One Link Self-Signed (<short_id>)``)
 166:     so a phone trust store containing certs from multiple daemons
 167:     can identify which is which without inspecting fingerprints.
 168:     The Ed25519 short_id is the identity hint (8 hex chars).
 169:     """
 170:     d = https_dir(base)
 171:     d.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
 172:     cp = cert_path(base)
 173:     kp = key_path(base)
 174: 
 175:     # ECDSA P-256 keypair.
 176:     key = ec.generate_private_key(ec.SECP256R1())
 177:     cn_text = (
 178:         f"One Link Self-Signed ({short_id})"
 179:         if short_id else
 180:         "One Link Self-Signed"
 181:     )
 182:     subject = issuer = x509.Name([
 183:         x509.NameAttribute(NameOID.COMMON_NAME, cn_text),
 184:         x509.NameAttribute(NameOID.ORGANIZATION_NAME, "One Link"),
 185:     ])
 186:     now = datetime.datetime.now(datetime.timezone.utc)
 187:     cert = (
 188:         x509.CertificateBuilder()
 189:         .subject_name(subject)
 190:         .issuer_name(issuer)
 191:         .public_key(key.public_key())
 192:         .serial_number(x509.random_serial_number())
 193:         .not_valid_before(now - datetime.timedelta(minutes=5))
 194:         .not_valid_after(now + datetime.timedelta(days=valid_days))
 195:         .add_extension(
 196:             _build_subject_alt_names(short_id=short_id),
 197:             critical=False,
 198:         )
 199:         .add_extension(
 200:             x509.BasicConstraints(ca=False, path_length=None),
 201:             critical=True,
 202:         )
 203:         .add_extension(
 204:             x509.KeyUsage(
 205:                 digital_signature=True,
 206:                 content_commitment=False,
 207:                 key_encipherment=False,
 208:                 data_encipherment=False,
 209:                 # v0.20.7 (security audit M11): drop key_agreement.
 210:                 # ECDHE cipher suites use the ephemeral key for
 211:                 # agreement; the cert's static key only signs the
 212:                 # handshake, so the key_agreement bit is unused.
 213:                 # Removing it shrinks the attestation surface and
 214:                 # matches the modern TLS 1.3-only profile.
 215:                 key_agreement=False,
 216:                 key_cert_sign=False,
 217:                 crl_sign=False,
 218:                 encipher_only=False,
 219:                 decipher_only=False,
 220:             ),
 221:             critical=True,
 222:         )
 223:         .add_extension(
 224:             x509.ExtendedKeyUsage([x509.ExtendedKeyUsageOID.SERVER_AUTH]),
 225:             critical=False,
 226:         )
 227:         .sign(key, hashes.SHA256())
 228:     )
 229: 
 230:     cert_pem = cert.public_bytes(serialization.Encoding.PEM)
 231:     key_pem = key.private_bytes(
 232:         encoding=serialization.Encoding.PEM,
 233:         format=serialization.PrivateFormat.PKCS8,
 234:         encryption_algorithm=serialization.NoEncryption(),
 235:     )
 236:     cp.write_bytes(cert_pem)
 237:     kp.write_bytes(key_pem)
 238:     # 0o600 — only the daemon-running user can read the private key.
 239:     # Best-effort; non-POSIX filesystems may ignore the chmod.
 240:     try:
 241:         os.chmod(cp, 0o600)
 242:         os.chmod(kp, 0o600)
 243:     except Exception:
 244:         pass
 245:     log.info(
 246:         "peer-https: minted self-signed cert (valid_days=%d, sha256=%s)",
 247:         valid_days,
 248:         cert.fingerprint(hashes.SHA256()).hex()[:32],
 249:     )
 250:     return cp, kp

 252: 
 253: def needs_rotation(
 254:     cert_path_to_check: Path,
 255:     *,
 256:     rotate_within_days: int = CERT_ROTATE_WITHIN_DAYS,
 257: ) -> bool:
 258:     """Return True if the cert is missing, unparseable, or expires
 259:     within `rotate_within_days`. Don't ship a cert that's about to
 260:     expire — phones cache trust decisions and a sudden invalid cert
 261:     produces an aggressively-bad UX."""
 262:     if not cert_path_to_check.is_file():
 263:         return True
 264:     try:
 265:         data = cert_path_to_check.read_bytes()
 266:         cert = x509.load_pem_x509_certificate(data)
 267:     except Exception as e:
 268:         log.warning("peer-https: cert unparseable, will rotate: %s", e)
 269:         return True
 270:     now = datetime.datetime.now(datetime.timezone.utc)
 271:     # not_valid_after_utc is the modern attr; fallback for older
 272:     # cryptography versions.
 273:     expiry = getattr(cert, "not_valid_after_utc", None)
 274:     if expiry is None:
 275:         expiry = cert.not_valid_after.replace(tzinfo=datetime.timezone.utc)
 276:     return expiry - now < datetime.timedelta(days=rotate_within_days)
 277: 
 278: 
 279: def ensure_cert(base: Path, *, short_id: str = "") -> tuple[Path, Path]:
 280:     """Return (cert_path, key_path), generating fresh material if
 281:     the existing cert is missing, unparseable, or near expiry."""
 282:     cp = cert_path(base)
 283:     kp = key_path(base)
 284:     if needs_rotation(cp) or not kp.is_file():
 285:         return generate_self_signed(base, short_id=short_id)
 286:     return cp, kp

 289: def build_ssl_context(
 290:     base: Path, *, short_id: str = "",
 291: ) -> Optional[ssl.SSLContext]:
 292:     """Build an ssl.SSLContext loaded with the daemon's self-signed
 293:     cert. Returns None if the cert can't be created (e.g. the data
 294:     dir is read-only) — callers fall back to HTTP-only.
 295: 
 296:     v0.20.7 (security audit M11): TLS 1.3 only by default. The
 297:     previous profile permitted TLS 1.2 + 1.3 with no cipher
 298:     restriction, which kept whole classes of historical attacks
 299:     in scope (BEAST, CRIME, ROBOT, Lucky13, etc.). The browsers
 300:     we target (Chrome 113+, Safari 17+, Firefox 121+) all speak
 301:     TLS 1.3 unconditionally; pinning to 1.3-only loses no
 302:     practical clients and removes those attack classes. We also
 303:     disable compression + session tickets for forward-secrecy
 304:     hygiene (TLS 1.3 already negotiates fresh keys per session,
 305:     but OP_NO_TICKET keeps the in-memory session-state surface
 306:     smaller).
 307:     """
 308:     try:
 309:         cp, kp = ensure_cert(base, short_id=short_id)
 310:     except Exception as e:
 311:         log.warning("peer-https: couldn't ensure cert: %s", e)
 312:         return None
 313:     ctx = ssl.SSLContext(ssl.PROTOCOL_TLS_SERVER)
 314:     # v0.20.7 (M11): TLS 1.3 only.
 315:     ctx.minimum_version = ssl.TLSVersion.TLSv1_3
 316:     ctx.maximum_version = ssl.TLSVersion.TLSv1_3
 317:     # Defense-in-depth flags. NO_COMPRESSION defeats CRIME-class
 318:     # leaks; NO_TICKET shrinks the long-lived state surface.
 319:     with contextlib.suppress(AttributeError):
 320:         ctx.options |= ssl.OP_NO_COMPRESSION
 321:     with contextlib.suppress(AttributeError):
 322:         ctx.options |= ssl.OP_NO_TICKET
 323:     try:
 324:         ctx.set_alpn_protocols(["h2", "http/1.1"])
 325:     except (NotImplementedError, ssl.SSLError):
 326:         # Some platforms don't support ALPN on the server side
 327:         # (rare); HTTP/1.1 fallback is still fine.
 328:         pass
 329:     try:
 330:         ctx.load_cert_chain(certfile=str(cp), keyfile=str(kp))
 331:     except Exception as e:
 332:         log.warning("peer-https: load_cert_chain failed: %s", e)
 333:         return None
 334:     return ctx
 335:

 337: def cert_fingerprint_sha256(cert_path_to_read: Path) -> Optional[str]:
 338:     """SHA-256 fingerprint of the cert in lowercase hex with no
 339:     separators. The pair QR can embed this so the phone-peer can
 340:     verify "this is the same cert my laptop minted" before
 341:     accepting the TLS connection — closing the residual MITM
 342:     window during the trust-on-first-use ceremony.
 343: 
 344:     Returns None if the cert can't be read."""
 345:     try:
 346:         data = cert_path_to_read.read_bytes()
 347:         cert = x509.load_pem_x509_certificate(data)
 348:     except Exception:
 349:         return None
 350:     return cert.fingerprint(hashes.SHA256()).hex()

 416:         "PayloadUUID": str(uuid.uuid4()).upper(),
 417:         "PayloadDisplayName": profile_display_name,
 418:         "PayloadDescription": (

 420:             "so your phone can pair with it over HTTPS without seeing "

 422:             "Settings → General → VPN & Device Management."

 426:         # the profile any time they want, no admin intervention.

   1: """QUIC transport adapter — Phase A2 cutover.
   2: 
   3: Wraps ``one_link_native.quic`` (the ``ol_quic`` crate built on
   4: ``quinn``) with the same outbound/inbound shape as ``peer_rtc.py``,
   5: so the daemon's transport-selection layer can route via either
   6: WebRTC or QUIC without the call sites caring which.
   7: 
   8: Per [PHASE_A2_QUIC_CUTOVER_PLAN.md](../../docs/PHASE_A2_QUIC_CUTOVER_PLAN.md),
   9: the cutover is **dual-stack**:
  10: 
  11: - WebRTC stays the always-working default.
  12: - QUIC activates per-peer when both peers advertise ``QUIC_TRANSPORT_V1``.
  13: - Browser-as-peer paths stay on WebRTC (browsers don't speak QUIC
  14:   datagrams without WebTransport).
  15: - v0.20.x daemons (no cap advertised) keep using WebRTC.
  16: 
  17: This module ships the **adapter** that the daemon's send/recv paths
  18: will call when a peer is on the QUIC track. The transport-selection
  19: logic itself lives in `daemon.py`'s `_choose_transport_for_peer`.
  20: 
  21: Threading model:
  22: - Endpoint lives on the asyncio loop; the underlying ``quinn``
  23:   runtime is wrapped via blocking calls (`*_blocking` suffix) that
  24:   release the GIL during I/O.
  25: - Per-peer ``Connection`` objects are owned by the daemon's peer
  26:   table; the adapter does not retain global state.
  27: 
  28: Sovereignty: ``quinn`` is MIT/Apache, pure-Rust, no Microsoft. See
  29: the sovereignty table in `FILE_ENGINE_V2_PLAN.md`.
  30: """
  31: 
  32: from __future__ import annotations
  33: 
  34: import logging
  35: from dataclasses import dataclass
  36: from typing import Optional, Protocol
  37:

  72: class PeerTransport(Protocol):
  73:     """Common shape that both WebRTC and QUIC transport adapters
  74:     implement. The daemon's send/recv paths target this protocol so
  75:     they don't care which underlying transport carries a peer."""
  76: 
  77:     def is_connected(self) -> bool: ...
  78: 
  79:     def rtt_ms(self) -> Optional[float]: ...

  86: @dataclass
  87: class QuicEndpointConfig:
  88:     """Local QUIC endpoint configuration. Mirrors the subset of
  89:     ``ol_quic::EndpointConfig`` the daemon actually drives at runtime."""
  90: 
  91:     bind_addr: str = "0.0.0.0:0"
  92:     """Bind address. ``0.0.0.0:0`` picks an OS-assigned port; the
  93:     daemon publishes the resulting port via mDNS / rendezvous."""
  94: 
  95:     keep_alive_interval_ms: int = 5_000
  96:     """How often the endpoint sends a PING to detect dead peers.
  97:     5s matches the field-snapshot tick so the per-peer state stays
  98:     fresh."""
  99: 
 100:     max_idle_timeout_ms: int = 30_000
 101:     """How long without traffic before the connection is considered
 102:     dead. 30s is conservative enough to survive a cellular handoff."""

 104: 
 105: def make_endpoint(
 106:     config: Optional[QuicEndpointConfig] = None,
 107: ) -> Optional[object]:
 108:     """Build a local QUIC endpoint. Returns ``None`` when the native
 109:     crate isn't installed — callers fall back to WebRTC for all
 110:     transports.
 111: 
 112:     The returned object exposes:
 113:     - ``connect_blocking(addr) -> Connection`` for outbound
 114:     - ``accept_blocking() -> (Connection, addr)`` for inbound
 115:     - ``local_addr() -> (host, port)`` for advertising
 116:     - ``close()`` for shutdown
 117: 
 118:     The daemon owns one endpoint per running instance.
 119:     """
 120:     if not HAS_NATIVE:
 121:         return None
 122:     cfg = config or QuicEndpointConfig()
 123:     # `Endpoint.server(identity, is_paired_callback, config)` requires
 124:     # a native ``Identity`` object + a Python callback + a native
 125:     # ``EndpointConfig`` — the full plumbing to derive the Identity
 126:     # from the daemon's existing Ed25519 keypair and build the
 127:     # paired-peer callback is Phase A2 datapath work that hasn't
 128:     # landed yet. Per PHASE_A2_QUIC_CUTOVER_PLAN.md the capability is
 129:     # advertised so peer negotiation works, but the endpoint stays
 130:     # unbuilt at startup until the Identity bridge ships.
 131:     #
 132:     # Returning None here means transport_choice_for_peer falls back
 133:     # to WebRTC for every peer. No log spam, no warning — this is
 134:     # the documented Phase A2 wiring state, not a failure.
 135:     _ = cfg
 136:     return None
 137: 
 138: 
 139: class QuicPeerSession:
 140:     """Per-peer QUIC transport state.
 141: 
 142:     Holds a single ``Connection`` (one QUIC stream multiplexes all
 143:     frames per peer; multiplexing across multiple streams is a
 144:     follow-up). Mirrors the API surface that the daemon's
 145:     `_outbound_sessions` table expects.
 146: 
 147:     Thread-safe in the same sense as the underlying Connection:
 148:     `send_frame` is single-writer; `recv_frame` is single-reader.
 149:     The daemon's existing per-peer locking is sufficient.
 150:     """
 151: 
 152:     def __init__(self, connection) -> None:
 153:         self._conn = connection
 154:         self._closed = False
 155: 
 156:     def is_connected(self) -> bool:
 157:         return not self._closed and self._conn is not None
 158: 
 159:     def rtt_ms(self) -> Optional[float]:
 160:         if not self.is_connected():
 161:             return None
 162:         try:
 163:             return float(self._conn.rtt_ms())
 164:         except Exception:
 165:             return None
 166: 
 167:     def remote_address(self) -> Optional[str]:
 168:         if not self.is_connected():
 169:             return None
 170:         try:
 171:             return str(self._conn.remote_address())
 172:         except Exception:
 173:             return None
 174: 
 175:     def send_frame(self, frame_type: int, payload: bytes) -> bytes:
 176:         """Send a frame + read the response. The QUIC stream is
 177:         request/response per the existing ``ol_quic`` wire spec; for
 178:         fire-and-forget frames (PING, CLOSE) the response is the
 179:         canonical ACK.
 180: 
 181:         Returns the response payload. Raises if the connection is
 182:         closed or the peer rejects the frame.
 183:         """
 184:         if not self.is_connected():
 185:             raise RuntimeError("QuicPeerSession is closed")
 186:         return bytes(self._conn.send_frame_round_trip(frame_type, payload))
 187: 
 188:     def recv_frame(self, timeout_ms: int = 5_000) -> tuple[int, bytes]:
 189:         """Read one incoming frame from the peer-initiated direction.
 190:         Returns ``(frame_type, payload)``.
 191: 
 192:         Raises ``one_link_native.OlQuicError`` on timeout / peer close.
 193:         """
 194:         if not self.is_connected():
 195:             raise RuntimeError("QuicPeerSession is closed")
 196:         # The native API returns a (frame_type: int, payload: bytes) tuple.
 197:         return self._conn.recv_frame_blocking(timeout_ms)
 198: 
 199:     def close(self) -> None:
 200:         if self._closed:
 201:             return
 202:         self._closed = True
 203:         try:
 204:             self._conn.close()
 205:         except Exception:
 206:             pass
 207: 
 208: 
 209: def open_outbound(endpoint, remote_addr: str) -> Optional[QuicPeerSession]:
 210:     """Dial a remote peer over QUIC. Returns ``None`` when the
 211:     endpoint isn't initialised (no native crate) or the connection
 212:     attempt fails — callers fall back to WebRTC."""
 213:     if endpoint is None:
 214:         return None
 215:     try:
 216:         conn = endpoint.connect_blocking(remote_addr)
 217:         return QuicPeerSession(conn)
 218:     except Exception as e:
 219:         log.info("QUIC dial to %s failed (%s); caller should fall back", remote_addr, e)
 220:         return None
 221: 
 222: 
 223: def should_prefer_quic_for_peer(local_caps: tuple[str, ...], peer_caps: tuple[str, ...]) -> bool:
 224:     """Transport-selection predicate. Both peers must advertise
 225:     ``QUIC_TRANSPORT_V1`` for the daemon to choose QUIC over WebRTC.
 226: 
 227:     This is the single decision point — every other path that asks
 228:     "which transport for peer P?" goes through here so the policy
 229:     stays consistent.
 230:     """
 231:     from one_link.capabilities import QUIC_TRANSPORT_V1
 232: 
 233:     return QUIC_TRANSPORT_V1 in local_caps and QUIC_TRANSPORT_V1 in peer_caps
 234: 
 235: 
 236: def _require_native() -> None:
 237:     if not HAS_NATIVE:
 238:         raise RuntimeError(
 239:             "QUIC transport requires one_link_native.quic; not installed"
 240:         )

   1: """v0.20.0 — Browser-as-peer ↔ daemon WebRTC transport.
   2: 
   3: Lets a browser running /peer (the v0.16-v0.19.2 architecture)
   4: connect directly to the desktop daemon over a WebRTC DataChannel.
   5: DTLS-SRTP at the transport layer + DataChannel framing at the
   6: app layer. Same wire kinds the daemon already speaks ride this
   7: new transport unchanged once `v0.20.2` bridges the two layers.
   8: 
   9: Design principles
  10: =================
  11: 
  12: - **Hidden by default.** Users never see SDP, ICE candidates,
  13:   or signaling URLs. Browser scans a QR (v0.20.1) or
  14:   rendezvous-discovers; signaling is over a WebSocket the
  15:   daemon already serves. No manual paste.
  16: 
  17: - **Trust via pairing token, not manual SAS.** The user
  18:   ceremony is "scan the QR I'm showing on my laptop." Possessing
  19:   a fresh, signed, single-use, short-TTL token that came directly
  20:   off the laptop's screen IS the trust ceremony. We do NOT
  21:   re-prompt the user for SAS confirmation — that would be
  22:   asking them to verify what they just verified by scanning.
  23: 
  24: - **Pubkey-bound returning peers.** Once paired, the browser's
  25:   Ed25519 pubkey is stored as a peer record. Subsequent
  26:   reconnects from the same pubkey skip pairing entirely; the
  27:   signature on the SDP offer envelope authenticates them.
  28: 
  29: - **Single-process state.** All browser-peer connections live
  30:   in `BrowserPeerManager` on the daemon. This module is the
  31:   single source of truth for what's connected, what's pending,
  32:   and which pairing tokens are active.
  33: 
  34: Wire format
  35: ===========
  36: 
  37: Signaling (WebSocket text frames):
  38: 
  39:   Browser → daemon:
  40:     {"v":"OL-PEER-RTC-1", "t":"offer",
  41:      "sdp":"<full SDP offer>",
  42:      "pubkey_b64u":"<browser Ed25519 pubkey>",
  43:      "pair_token":"<optional pairing token>",
  44:      "fingerprint":"<algo>:<hex>",
  45:      "ts":<ms>,
  46:      "signature":"<Ed25519 over canonical(envelope minus signature)>"}
  47: 
  48:   Daemon → browser:
  49:     {"v":"OL-PEER-RTC-1", "t":"answer",
  50:      "sdp":"<full SDP answer>",
  51:      "daemon_pubkey_b64u":"<daemon's Ed25519 pubkey>",
  52:      "ts":<ms>}
  53: 
  54:   Either direction (during ICE):
  55:     {"v":"OL-PEER-RTC-1", "t":"ice",
  56:      "candidate":{"candidate":..., "sdpMid":..., "sdpMLineIndex":...}}
  57: 
  58:   Either direction (errors):
  59:     {"v":"OL-PEER-RTC-1", "t":"error",
  60:      "code":"<short>", "message":"<human>"}
  61: 
  62: DataChannel (post-connection, JSON text frames):
  63: 
  64:   {"v":"OL-PEER-1", "t":"ping", "ts":<ms>}
  65:   {"v":"OL-PEER-1", "t":"pong", "ts":<ms>}
  66: 
  67:   v0.20.2 layers chat / file / peer-roster wire kinds on top.
  68: 
  69: Pairing-token contract
  70: ======================
  71: 
  72:   Daemon mints a 32-byte base64url token via api_mint_pairing.
  73:   Token is stored in `BrowserPeerManager._pending_pairings` keyed
  74:   by token → {created_ms, ttl_ms, fp_hint}. TTL default 5
  75:   minutes. Token is consumed (deleted) when redeemed; only one
  76:   redemption per token. After redemption, the browser's pubkey
  77:   is marked as a paired peer and any future reconnect with the
  78:   same pubkey skips pairing.
  79: 
  80:   The QR encoded for the user has a deep-link to /peer with the
  81:   token embedded as `?pair=<token>` (v0.20.1 wires this).
  82: 
  83: Security model
  84: ==============
  85: 
  86:   - Pair token leaked → an attacker who scans the same QR (or
  87:     intercepts it) can pair. Mitigation: 5min TTL, single-use,
  88:     QR is on-screen for the user only.
  89:   - DTLS-SRTP fingerprint pinning (browser ↔ daemon) handled
  90:     by aiortc + browser WebRTC stacks.
  91:   - Ed25519 signature on the offer envelope binds the SDP
  92:     to the browser's claimed pubkey. A malicious signaling
  93:     relay cannot forge an offer for a different pubkey because
  94:     they'd have to break Ed25519.
  95:   - Daemon's signaling endpoint is unauthenticated by HTTP
  96:     standards (no Bearer token) because the browser is signing
  97:     its own claim. Auth happens at the WebRTC peer-pubkey layer,
  98:     not at the WS-route layer.
  99: """

 125: # v0.18.0's /peer page defines WEBRTC_CONTROL_LABEL = "one-link-control-v1"

 132: # Pairing-token TTL. 5 minutes is enough for the user to physically

 135: # without a clear cause.

 137: PAIRING_TOKEN_BYTES = 32
 138: 
 139: # Signature freshness window — accept offer envelopes with a
 140: # timestamp within this many ms of "now". Prevents trivial replay
 141: # of a stale captured offer. WebRTC SDP itself isn't sensitive
 142: # (it's network-routing info), but we still bind freshness so a
 143: # stolen signed offer can't be re-played weeks later.

 146: MAX_SDP_BYTES = 128 * 1024

 149: _B64URL_ALPHABET = frozenset("ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZabcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz0123456789-_")

 151: # Audit H8/H9 May 2026 — per-peer rate-limit caps for the two

 162: # ── helpers (b64url no padding, canonical JSON) ──────────────────────
 163: 
 164: def _b64u(data: bytes) -> str:
 165:     return base64.urlsafe_b64encode(data).rstrip(b"=").decode("ascii")
 166: 
 167: 
 168: def _b64ud(s: str) -> bytes:
 169:     if not isinstance(s, str) or any(c not in _B64URL_ALPHABET for c in s):
 170:         raise ValueError("invalid base64url")
 171:     pad = "=" * ((4 - len(s) % 4) % 4)
 172:     try:
 173:         return base64.urlsafe_b64decode((s + pad).encode("ascii"))
 174:     except (binascii.Error, UnicodeEncodeError, ValueError) as e:
 175:         raise ValueError("invalid base64url") from e
 176: 
 177: 
 178: def _extract_dtls_fingerprint(sdp: str) -> str:
 179:     """v0.20.7 (security audit C1): extract the DTLS-SRTP fingerprint
 180:     from an SDP blob. The fingerprint line is per-RFC 8122:
 181:         a=fingerprint:<algo> <colon-separated hex bytes>
 182:     Returns "<algo>:<UPPERCASE-HEX>" (e.g. "sha-256:AB:CD:..."), or
 183:     "" if no a=fingerprint line is present. Both endpoints can call
 184:     this on their local + remote SDPs to verify the cryptographic
 185:     identity bound into the DataChannel transport.
 186: 
 187:     Used in the signed answer envelope so the browser can cross-
 188:     check the SDP it received against the value the daemon
 189:     cryptographically committed to. A MITM rewriting the SDP
 190:     a=fingerprint to point at the attacker's DTLS cert would
 191:     invalidate the cross-check and the browser would refuse the
 192:     DataChannel.
 193:     """
 194:     if not isinstance(sdp, str):
 195:         return ""
 196:     import re
 197:     m = re.search(
 198:         r"^a=fingerprint:(\S+)\s+([0-9A-Fa-f:]+)",
 199:         sdp,
 200:         re.MULTILINE,
 201:     )
 202:     if not m:
 203:         return ""
 204:     algo = m.group(1).strip().lower()
 205:     fp = m.group(2).strip().upper()
 206:     return f"{algo}:{fp}"
 207: 
 208: 
 209: def _canonical(payload: dict) -> bytes:
 210:     """JSON canonicalization matching the browser's _canonicalJson:
 211:     sorted keys, no whitespace, ASCII-only (\\uXXXX escapes for
 212:     non-ASCII), exclude the 'signature' field."""
 213:     body = {k: v for k, v in payload.items() if k != "signature"}
 214:     return json.dumps(
 215:         body, sort_keys=True, separators=(",", ":"), ensure_ascii=True,
 216:     ).encode("ascii")
 217: 
 218: 
 219: def _now_ms() -> int:
 220:     return int(time.time() * 1000)

 237: # ── connected browser-peer record ────────────────────────────────────
